I had a brief scare when my + button wasn't working, but it turned out that I had simply over-tightened an internal screw--something I had no difficulty correcting.

I will say that I hadn't noticed from the pictures that the replacement shell does not include the front panel of the console housing, nor the cartridge slot cover. While the switch looks awesome from behind, I'm really disappointed that I can't tell from the front that any case-modding has even taken place. Aesthetically, it means that the console doesn't match the fully-clear joycons, as it's half-clear and half-black.

Nevertheless, I had to give this product all five stars because of its superior quality.

I wrote this review of my own volition and bought this product with my own damn money.

title: Feels like the real thing... almost.
text:
HORI did an excellent job reproducing the look and feel of the original GameCube controller. Compared to the first-generation "bar of soap" classic controller, this is a major step up in comfortability and functionality. To my knowledge, this is also one of the first Wii classic controllers with a turbo feature, so if you play any button mashers, this will definitely give you an edge.
PROS:
- The ZL, ZR, A, B, X, and Y buttons and the D-pad all depress with a satisfyingly loud, uh, button-pressing sound, and they have a strong, quick return.
- The analog sticks feel just like the originals and recenter perfectly.
- The turbo feature works for the L, ZL, R, ZR, A, B, X, and Y buttons and the D-pad, and any number of them can be set to turbo simultaneously.
- The turbo speed switch is easy to move without being too loose.
- The Pikachu artwork on the front is applied with the same quality as the GameCube logo was applied to the original. It doesn't stand above the surface visibly or tactilely and it feels like it's going to last. It's not some cheap decal or stencil-job.
- The case screws are regular Phillips-head screws, not Nintendo's proprietary tri-wing screws, making the controller somewhat easier to repair.
CONS:
- The C-stick was cast with a slight misalignment. It left an obvious, though structurally-sound, seam on one side.
- As there is no analog trigger support in Nintendo systems following the GameCube, the L and R buttons now hinge from the top (like the B button on a Wii remote) and have about the same amount of travel as the other buttons, leaving me to miss the plunger-action and satisfying *click* of the original L and R buttons. They also have a shallower curvature, making it easier for your finger to slip off.
- The turbo, start/+, select/-, and home buttons are all rubber like TV remote buttons instead of hard plastic like the GameCube controller's start button was. There's nothing inherently wrong with this, but they feel less satisfying to press and will likely wear out sooner than plastic.

title: Conquer the world...or at least try
text:
This is the most recent incarnation of the popular CIVILIZATION game. For those not familiar with it's predessors the object is to either conquer the world by either military force, cultural superiority, diplomataic means or winning the space race. The player can either play as an individual against the computer or against other human players or as part of a team. The player dons the persona of one of several world leaders (Washington, Bismark, Victoria, Montezuma etc) and beginning the game from several different eras ranging from ancient through modern. There are various degrees of difficulty ranging from the chieftain, (the easiest) to diety, (nearly impossible). The player has the option of customizing the game, choosing various starting conditions for land masses, sea level and climate and other factors as well as a choice of several preset scenarios taken from historical situations.

The numerous options give the player almost limitless playing options making this a game that can literally keep a player occupied for years. A game can range from a few minutes to hours depending on the options selected. The challenges can progress as the players skill level increases.

I have played this game, in a couple of different versions for years and for many more hours than I would care to admit and still have not come even close to exhausting it's full potential, or becoming bored. When it ceases to be challenging I alter a parameater or two and it is a whole different set of challenges.

There are a few problems though. Although I am playing on a new Mac laptop, with plenty of memory the game slows and hangs up fairly often, requiring a 'save' exiting the game and re-entering - a process that takes 5 to 10 minutes. Each time the game is entered the entire opening sequence is played and while it is an interesting, well animated piece after a few dozen viewings it becomes a bit annoying. Also some of the charactitures of the non Eurpean/American make this WASP a bit uncomfortable.

Overall this is one of the best computer games I have played. The flexibility allows those into shoot'em up games to wage war to their hearts' content as well as those who do not to permanently declare peace and focus on other challenges.

title: Join the CSI team
text:
This game is based on the popular original CSI show, the actors from the cast provide the voices. The premise is to solve a series of crimes along with the CSI team. Clues are located by sliding over the crime scene then using the appropriate method to interpret the evidence. Witnesses and suspects are questioned using prompts provided, the answers are added to the physical evidence and used to obtain warrents and ultimately solve the crimes.

The graphics are well done, the plot lines are interesting and the game runs quite well, without the hangups or crashes I have experienced with some other Mac platform games. So why only 4 stars? It is possible to locate clues simply by rolling over the scene until the clue reveals itself, wrong choices of tools are met with only a prompt as are other wrong guesses, which 'dumbs down' the experience. The game can be solved by persistence, intelligence only makes the process smoother and quicker. The biggest problem, however, is that once the game is solved it is done a problem with all games of this puzzle genre. Unlike the more complicated MYST or Seventh Guest games this one is not sophisticated enough to make going back over solved puzzles to enjoy the experience or challenging enough to make this a long term project.

Still it is a fun game, a good way to spend a few hours. If the more difficult puzzle games have frustrated you or you are new to this type of game, then this one is perfect for you. If you are a fan of the CSI series this is a good way to spend sometimes between episodes but if you are a serious puzzle gamer and looking for a real challenge this one is not for you.

This is a three to four star keyboard, depending on your price range. I love a solid mechanical keyboard for most applications. I let my son try gaming on it, and he liked it better than the k70. However, when I asked which he thought was the better value, he said the k70.

So, bottom line is that if you're a gaming enthusiast whose budget is limited, you may not need to go with this. I don't have experience with the really really expensive keyboards to tell you whether those are worth the money to, like, competitive gamers. But for someone who plays for fun, I think this one is worth the money if you have it. Otherwise, go for the k70.

title: Harder than Just Dance 3 - Mobility Impaired Can Still Do, Though
text:
I'm playing this game with lupus and inflammatory arthritis. I can't do all the moves. I will never be able to do all the moves, but I have a really good time doing what I can. The Just Sweat mode is a lot harder than it was on Just Dance 3. Instead of being able to pick a goal and then pick your way through the songs you like, this one has you commit to an amount of time (up to 45 minutes, give or take) and pick a style (cheerleader, martial arts, salsa, etc.) and then it blasts you through alternating dance sessions and workout sessions (dance - kick box - dance - kick box - like that). It's more like a traditional work out video in that respect.

As for the Just Dance function, I have arthritis in my hips and spine, so, as I stated above, I cannot do all of the moves. But you can get through the Wii U version of this game without being able to do all of the steps as long as you can do a pretty good approximation of the arm stuff. And it's really fun, even for an old geezer like me.

My 12 year old son refuses to play it with me. He's pretty mortified at the very thought that I *dance* *at* *all* - so watching me do it isn't high on his to do list. He's also kind of a little rock snob, and this game does seem to have an even higher concentration of dance-y, disco-y new music than Just Dance 3 had, so I probably wouldn't recommend this as a gift for the little metalhead in your life - stick with Rock Band for that one. I still highly recommend it for anyone who needs to exercise but gets bored easily.

P.S. There's no training mode for this game and no way to back up in the middle of a song. If you want to practice/learn the steps, and you're slow like me, you can go to youtube and search for videos. Watch them and rewind to your heart's content. Then, pop in your game and head to town.

title: Excellent for older and/or mobility impaired adults
text:
I have SLE with mobility issues (inflammatory arthritis) and chronic fatigue, which puts me in a catch 22 situation of needing to exercise to keep from losing ground with both my mobility and my stamina, while having to fight an uphill battle just to get to the point that I CAN exercise. Going to a gym with any kind of regularity is out of the question. I used to be really active before I got sick, and I much prefer doing "something" to jogging on a trampoline or working through a list of exercises from my physical therapist. So I thought I would give this a try.

I love love love it. Unlike the Wii Fit game, your mii doesn't shame you over a one star performance (okay, I think that's funny, but your mother or your grandmother might not). Also, Just Dance makes it extremely easy to start from right where you are, mobility-wise. You can start sitting down, if you need to.

The game is also very flexible in terms of how you structure your sessions. You can use the Just Dance feature to browse through songs and move to what you like to hear or to learn the moves (which actually seems to be helping with my cognitive function) to the dance routines you like the best. If you're just looking to get in, get some cardio, and get out, you can go into the Just Sweat section and do that. You can even set weekly goals for yourself.

My favorite part about the game is that it is so low key and hassle free. You turn it on, and get right to whatever you want to do. When you are finished, it's fast and easy to shut the thing down. The songs are eclectic (some content might not be appropriate for young children), and replay value is high. I like it so much that I got Just Dance 4 for Wii U.

The only thing I don't like about it is that it doesn't always record your movement correctly or save your progress. It's no mean feat for me to hit my daily goal, so when I go back the next day after meeting my daily objective and the last dance I did didn't get its points saved, it's a bit of a disappointment. Not a super big deal, though. I'm not exactly getting graded or paid by the point : )

title: Still Playing This One
text:
UPDATE: Two Years Later My Son and I Both Revisit These Games Frequently ENough to Make This One of the Best Values Ever for a Pokemon Game

Original Review: I have been playing these games with my now-10-year-old son since he was three (I bought used GBCs and color pokemon games and let him figure it out - he also learned to read). Together, we have gone through the Gameboy Color, Gameboy Advance, the Sinnoh games, and Heart Gold/Soul Silver. I almost didn't buy a copy of Pokemon Black, because the games had been getting kind of stale for me. My son still loves them (as do his classmates - if you have a fourth grade boy on your gift list, and he doesn't already have this? You will be making a little boy ecstatic.

Anyway, my son really wanted me to play, and I gave in a bit reluctantly, but, now that I'm playing the game, I love this iteration for the following reasons:

1. I do not want to spoil the storyline, but the antagonists' issues and ethical positions are fairly sophisticated. Team Plasma is actually asking some interesting questions about trainers' relationships with their pokemon. Those questions also apply to our own relationships with other (real) creatures here in our world.

2. The smack-talk from rivals and other trainers is toned way down from generations past.

3. The game helps you along, which makes it much less frustrating (at least for me). For example, before each of the three gym battles I've done so far, you get an opportunity to get a pokemon who has a helpful type and a high enough level to ensure that you don't spend a ton of time fighting and re-fighting the same battles.

4. The graphics are really amazing for a handheld game, and the towns have lots to do besides gym battling, so your kid isn't likely to beat this game in a day and toss it aside. You get your money's worth.

5. There are new battle modes, new pokemon, new ways of interacting with friends in person and over the Wifi Connection. Nintendo also made Black and White just different enough from each other to make it worthwhile to purchase and play both.

I deducted one star because my game cartridge arrived glitchy. In the first battle, my pokemon, a female Oshawott could not execute any attacks. Every time I selected an attack, the game went to a screen describing the attack and showing my trainer statistics. I had to shut down the game and restart several times, all with the same result (except never again did I get a female starter), before I decided to try cleaning the cartridge, which worked (use a q-tip and rubbing alcohol gently to clean the game cartridge and let it dry completely). This is the first time since the Gameboy color games (which I bought used) that I have had a quality control issue with a pokemon game.

I recommend this game for kids who enjoy the anime and the other rpg and for adults who either want to play along with their children or enjoy gentle (mostly) nature/environmental-themed rpgs. It's fun and has good replay value for the money.

Its also a little bulky and is almost too large for the battery terminal bay, and heats up a little bit when charging.

The battery type and the tolerances used scream cheap product, but it does work. it just introduces a number of other issues.

The gameplay has been streamlined so there's practically no lull between encountering a situation and deploying the appropriate power or weapon. This game told a more interesting and compelling story than any I can really remember from any recent game. Half Life 2, Gears 2, Fallout 3, and the first Darkness come to mind as runners up. I also felt myself getting nostalgic for Vampires: Bloodlines as another game that presented an engaging and dark fantasy world very well.

The graphics and art style are meant to resemble the comics, and they might look a bit garishly colorful and cartoony in the still shots. However, I found the mood appropriately dark, serious, and immersive when the game is actually in motion.

To sum it up, yes the game might be a little short. However, I'd rather have that than be force to plow through filler that broke up the plot. I rarely felt the presence of the game designers deliberately setting up different challenging situations to play through, but such situations arose in a natural-feeling succession. To me, this is the sign of a great game. I imagine I'll play it through again sometime soon.

title: Strong, but not perfect, in all areas
text:
This is basically a totally plot-driven game with reasonably good gameplay dynamics (shooting, character motion, car physics, etc.). The game's plot and characters are extremely well-written and well voice-acted. The actual game action alone would be enough to make this and "ok" and unremarkable game, but the plot and characters are what really make it worth noticing.

Note to parents: this game involves plenty of swearing, sex, brutal violence, and even collectible items that are actual photos taken from vintage Playboy magazines. This is a game for adults.

If I had to sum this game plot up in one sentence, I'd simply call it "Goodfellas the game." Of course it borrows heavily from all areas of popular culture gangster lore, but it does so most obviously and best from Goodfellas. The plot is intricate, involving, and woven around very deep and perfectly voice-acted characters. There are several plot events and characters pulled straight from the movie. The most intense moments gain their intensity from the drama and importance of the moment, not the sheer quantity or size of the baddies the game decides to throw at you at any given moment. It even contains perhaps the most clever and mind-bending nod to the previous game in the series that I've ever seen. I really did enjoy watching characters and the country evolve over the course of a few years.

The driving physics, shooter controls and feel, sandbox-style gameplay, melee fight sequences, development of player character abilities, and so on are all done quite well. None are totally perfect or ground-breaking, but they do the job of keeping the player immersed in the story, which is the central driving force in the game. The graphics are up to modern standards.

This is a sandbox / crime game which of course must then invite comparisons to Grand Theft Auto. I'd say that this game is darker, more realistic, and takes itself more seriously than the recent GTA installments, including Red Dead Revolver. The first Mafia was pretty much the same way. The player gets quite a bit less freedom to do side quests and the like. Players who like to horde cash, guns, cars, outfits, and other goodies will be driven nuts by the times their character gets into trouble and loses it all. In a way it's the opposite of the direction Saints Row took the genre, which was one of total freedom with outrageous action and comedy. The added realism here means there are fewer "wow that was awesome" moments, but such moments are that much cooler and more special.

This is a great game for anyone who enjoys classic gangster movie themes and video games with great stories and characters. It is more challenging than other similar games (with the difficulty turned up), and as such makes the plot development that much more rewarding. I would rate the replay value of the game fairly low, so I'd advise people to go to the console versions. I bought the PC version. While it was a great experience, I can't resell it now that I'm done with it. I have high hopes for DLC to be released later, and I do think the as-released content was adequate for a full new title. I think I'll jump for the DLC if it's reasonably priced, and I'll post updates to this review after I do.

title: A great mouse, just not for me
text:
So please take this review with a grain of salt. I really love the idea of this mouse - I LOVE the idea of the ring finger click button, but it the mouse just wasn't comfortable for me.

For the past 14 years I've been using a Razer Naga mouse for gaming (WoW mostly). My Naga broke and I thought I'd get something cheaper that had even more functionality. I'm a woman and think I have average size hands - maybe even slightly bigger than average (I'm 5'10") but this mouse was uncomfortable. It's quite a bit wider than the Naga. Because of the ring finger click key you really are only holding on to the side of the mouse with your pinkie. The mouse is so wide that it was just an uncomfortable grip to move my pinkie finger out that much. That being said, I might have been able to adjust to that except...

I also had a problem with the side mouse buttons. On the Razer Naga the 12 side keys are a bit more spaced out and they aren't angled into two different groups like this mouse. The Naga makes it easy to seamlessly move between the 5 and 8 keys but on this mouse the 8 key is the top middle of the second group and you have to really move your thumb a lot to get it out of the first set of 6 into the 2nd set.

Basically, it was just hard to overcome 14 years of using the same mouse and I felt like it would take too long for me to learn to use this one. It's not the mouse, it's me! It's probably a really fantastic mouse if you're not moving from a Naga.

title: Nice for my first 60% keyboard.
text:
I picked this up because I wanted a small form keyboard to take with me to use with my laptop while traveling. It arrived, it was decently packaged, nothing too fancy, but I didn't buy it for the box. Opening it, I found a clear plastic key cover over the keyboard, a few papers, and under a flap of cardboard was the USB cable, A to micro, and the wire key cap puller.

I removed it from the box and was immediately impressed with the feel and weight of it. The aluminum chassis felt sturdy and had a nice matte finish to it. Then, using the included key cap puller, I pulled a few of the keys off and found Cherry MX Red switches. Replaced the keys and plugged in the keyboard for a test run.

First thing I noticed when I powered it on was that a couple of the keys weren't lit. I immediately thought there was a problem, but then after flipping through the manual, they are supposed to be off, and will come on when activated, (caps lock. num lock, and scroll lock). All of the lighting options are controlled through the keyboard via the FN + another key. Which is nice, at one place I work, I can use this keyboard if I want but they won't let me install any software so it's nice I don't need that to work the lights.

The lights have a few modes, there is always on, a key strike ripple effect, a line by line scrolling mode, and another key press mode that just lights the keys you've recently pressed, which is kinda nice... You are able to dim or turn off the LED lights if you wish.

The Function keys are nested close to the number keys, saving space which is nice, the entire keyboard is very ascetically appealing as well as very functional. It's got a mode that allows you to use a secondary function on the keys to act as a numpad.

I have 3 small cons about the keyboard. one being the elevation legs, they are solid rubber, and definitely hold it secure, but they aren't adjustable, however, they are at a comfortable angle for everyday typing. But the fact they don't fold away makes it hard to stick this in my laptop bag when packing up.

The other being the space bar, seems to ride rough on the right side when pressing it (if pressed in the center it feels nice, but if you hit it off to the side, you can feel a hesitation)

Lastly the keycaps have a ncie font on them, but some of them, the F6, the 6 and F8 and 8 keys to me look slike G's and the 8 just doesn't look right to me, that last thing does not affec the performance of the keyboard, just something worth pointing out, I plan on replacing them at some point anyways, just undecided on what I want to use.

Overall very pleased with this purchase and may even pick up another with some Cherry MX Blues.

I loved the Adams-family type humor, the characters, the voice acting, but the plot-that most attractive of elements in any adventure game- most of all. I would have liked to know what it was for complete happiness.

<--"END SPOILER"
In short, play it, play it soon, and you won't regret it.

LEDs: The LEDs start very bright, but the Number Lock key is hardly visible in daylight anymore because it has faded so much due to being on constantly. Therefore the quality of the LEDs used in the board are low.

All in all, if you are not a fast typer, or if you don't plan to play video games, but still want a sturdy keyboard that feels good, this might be the fit for you.

title: Three attempts, three bad eggs.
text:
Let me start off by saying that this is a nice looking keyboard, and it has all of the features I want in a keyboard; Click keys, fast response times, and designated media keys. I tried this and the Blackwidow Chroma, and learned that this keyboard has better response times, and registers more keys pressed. The Keyboard feels good to type on, when the keys work... I tried THREE times to get a functioning keyboard, and all three times the keys were defective! So much for Cherry MX being the best there is... The first keyboard I got from amazon had working keys, but the buttons seems really loose, and would almost bend when I would push them (especially the tab button, which would also stick). The second and third keyboards I got from a local store and both of them had keys that would not make any click or tactile feedback ( I even checked and they were blues). Maybe I'm just unlucky from a consumer perspective, 3 strikes and you're out for me.

I really wanted to love keyboard, but the quality control seems to be atrocious. If you are a lucky one that gets a working keyboard, congratulations; you'll likely love it.

If you are new to the mechanical keyboard world, you might even want to consider buying a refurbished g710, because they are supposed to test them before shipping them, so you might have better luck, plus they're only $66.

Also, I am going to mention this because no one talks about this, but this keyboard, like most other LED back-lit keyboards has a noticeable flicker when your eyes move in it's presence on any other setting than the brighest (which is bright!). This is why I returned the Blackwidow Chroma; because it had to much flicker for my eyes, even though I had gotten an incredible deal on it. You can argue that flashing is the nature of LEDs, but there are plenty of examples of where the flicker is not noticeable, such as a TV, phone screen (unless you shake it), or even the LEDs in my mouse, desktop fans, and power strip. If you also suffer from the useless super power of being able to see the flicker, and it also bothers you, the Corsair Strafe RGB is the only keyboard that I have not noticed a flicker on. I've only tried the MX Silents, which I did not like, so I can't vouch for any other trait of the keyboard.

Hopefully this helped with your decision. Let me know if you have any questions. Best of luck finding a new keyboard.

Oh, and also you could check out massdrop for keyboard deals. They have a great deal every once in a while.

title: Sweet and well-written
text:
Auggie Pullman loves Star Wars, his family, and his dog. His parents and his big sister Via have always looked out for him, and the folks on his block in upper Manhattan are used to him and care about him too. But now that he's starting fifth grade, his parents decide that it's time for him to venture outside his little world and go to school -- regular school -- where he'll have to deal with a whole lot of new people. That would be a challenge for any kid, but it's especially challenging for Auggie, whose face is not like other kids' faces.

But this isn't a depressing, "kids-with-issues" book. In fact what struck me about it was how much Auggie's struggles are like other kids' struggles. His specific situation gives him difficulties that most other kids don't have to deal with. But he deals with them pretty much the way any kid would -- or maybe a little better. The story is told first from Auggie's point of view, then from his sister's and other characters', so we see the impact of Auggie's facial deformity on others around him as well. The book reminded me of the best of Judy Blume, with its realistic characters of various ages. But it's maybe a tad more optimistic about human nature. Aimed at ages 8 and up, I can see this book being enjoyed by teens and adults as well as younger kids.

title: This is a great little device that streams your Steam games to your ...
text:
This is a great little device that streams your Steam games to your television over your home network. It works flawlessly, and the games are easily started. On my wired gigabit network, the lag between the computer and the television is rarely noticeable.

Since it is in-home streaming though, it consumes both the computer and the television. Therefore if someone wants to use the computer while you are using Steam Link, they cannot unless they boot you from the software by closing Steam locally. Additionally, many games for the PC are designed with a viewer that is ~ 3 feet from the display. This makes written words difficult to see when translated to a living room environment. I look forward to seeing more games in the future have a "Big Screen" option that can scale both the User Interface as well as any subtitles or important text that may appear on the screen.

The next step in advancement for this kind of device would be streaming of a virtual display that both reflects the resolution of the television (should it be higher or lower) and allows routine use of the computer in the background.

title: This is the one: a helpful review
text:
Here's the thing, I wanted a charging dock for my Xbox Series X controllers. So, I did what any person does nowadays, I searched for reviews... and then I searched for more reviews and then more. Spoiler, reviews were shockingly limited unhelpful. So, here is a helpful review.

1. quality - this charger feels solid and is easy to use; the controller fits on the dock easily, doesn't feel unstable or tippy. The led "breathes" to let you know it's charging and turns solid once charged. I've never struggled to connect the controller properly or fumbled with putting them on.

2. charging time - I haven't timed it (sorry?) but it's fast and you can charge both at once or only one at a time.

3. battery life - hours... I can't say more or I'll sound even less like I have a life than I do now, but it's hours.

4. battery covers - it comes with two one for the X and one for the Series X. They fit perfectly and they even look good on the blue controllers. The gap in the cover for the connection to the dock isn't too much. It's not too ugly and it doesn't interfere with use or plugging the controller in by usb-c.

5. usb - here's my biggest complaint, the plug for the dock is not usb, so you must use the cable it comes with, you can't use another cable and have to have a wall plug nearby. It was fine for me, but if you're out of room on your power strip, you have my sympathies.

6. battery - this one has the largest battery that I could find out of all the charging docks, so that's a plus.

7. licensed - it's officially approved by Xbox, so I don't have to worry about it killing my $60 controllers.

8. size - it's not tiny, but it doesn't take up unnecessary space, it isn't too tall or too long, pretty much perfect for storing / charging 2 controllers.

9. color - it only comes in black, which is fine because it matches my Xbox, but if you wanted it in white or to match your controller, it's not going to happen.

This is the charging dock to buy if you want to charge 2 controllers. It's easy to use, has a good battery life, doesn't take up too much space, quick charging, and looks cool. I appreciate the peace of mind of knowing Xbox was ok with it and the fact that I can store my controllers on it and not worry about where they are or if they've been charged lately.

title: A worthy sequel!
text:
I’ve been playing the Dragon Quest series for about 30 years now (the original Dragon Warrior game came free with a Nintendo Power subscription.) In fact, this series is what got me into RPGs, to begin with!

For months now, I’ve been eagerly awaiting the release of Dragon Quest XI. To date, I’ve played and enjoyed every release, except for DQX. A review I saw said that this new installment felt old – it reused the same tropes that the previous games have played. Well, there is a bit of truth to it. Many of the familiar enemies show up, the combat, modes of exploration… Yes, this does feel very much like a Dragon Quest game, and that’s exactly what I was hoping for!

The game is marvelously-rendered, and the scoring is beautiful. I can’t say the story has been all that standard so far (not terribly surprising, but it has started off different than the previous installments.) title: A worthy addition to the series
text:
I was a huge fan of the original Metroid and Super Metroid growing up. The games were challenging, and games that require "skill" tend to be a bit hard for me. This game, for the most part, is true-to-form. I've sank a few hours into the game since receiving it. Overall, the look, sound and feel is very much on par with the original series (with some obvious improvements as the technology has advanced significantly.) The play control is very responsive - maybe slightly too responsive. I really have one gripe - and that's the need for repeated use of the counter-attack. Metroid games have always required fast response times, and the need to recognize patterns during boss fights. Each enemy takes several shots to kill (even when using missiles or charged beam.) Most will wind up and charge you. You can either dodge, and pick them off, or master that counter. If you pull off a successful counter, the enemy is stunned for a period, and can be dispatched readily. Unfortunately, I find myself losing the advantage it gives (due to terrain or another incoming enemy.) The counter could be a great mechanism, but it seems to be a bit overdone. Ultimately, this is a balance issue. I feel that Samus's weapons are underpowered, while the enemies attacks are overpowered, and you NEED to rely on the new counter in order to really make progress.

All that being said, I got used to employing the counter attack, and the game is flowing. It does a nice job scratching that nostalgia itch while feeling current (which makes 2 games in a row on the 3DS... this and The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds.)

Ultimately, I'd highly recommend this game to any RPG fan. For those who've played the game before and enjoyed it, I think this will be a refreshing way to capture some nostalgia, as the visual improvements are definitely worthwhile. Those who couldn't get into the original due to the rather terrible graphics, well... give this a whack!

text:
I picked up Guild Wars 2 when it first came out, and at the time, thought it was only okay. I returned to the game a few months ago, and I have to say it has improved substantially. Many of the old mechanics have been modified/improved (added way points, loyalty bonuses, exploration bonuses) and there have been some great additions, like gliding. I really like how Heart of Thorns got rid of the cut scenes for story progression, as it feels more natural, and thus gives a more immersive experience. The addition of the mastery point system for max level characters is great. Nearly everything important is linked to the account (magic find, masteries, outfits, boon-bearing items, etc.) The lack of a subscription fee is very nice. The gem shop offers some cosmetic/minor game-enhancing items for a dollar amount. None of these are necessary to enjoy the game, but I can see why many folks would choose to spend some bucks on these items (mostly bag/character/bank slot increases, account-wide inventory slots, etc.)

Some of the most attractive features for me are the map events, the fact that you never really "outgrow" a zone, and the sharing of resources and kills. The map events keep things fresh, and provide decent rewards upon completion. If you were to enter say a "starting zone," you'd "level-down" to the appropriate level. Of course, your abilities and improved help out and you will be more powerful than other low-bes, but you'll still earn experience and rewards. Finally, the fact that everyone can mine the same nodes, chop the same trees, and gather the same herbs is wonderful. There are no "tagging of mobs," either. If you land a hit, you get full experience and access to the drops. These features give Guild Wars 2 a more pleasant play experience than some other popular MMO's (WoW, I'm looking at you!)

Ultimately, I'm really enjoying the game.

title: Great Expansion! (Long Review...)
text:
My background: I’ve been playing World of Warcraft since about a month before The Burning Crusade was released. I saw most of the PVE and PVP content while it was current in The Burning Crusade, Wrath of the Lich King, and Mists of Pandaria (I took a 2 year leave during the Cataclysm.) In summary, I feel that Warlords of Draenor has been one of the best expansions that The World of Warcraft has received. If that’s enough for you, then you can stop now. This review might be a bit lengthy!

I pre-ordered this expansion, but did not get time to level my main character to 100 until after the New Year, hence the delay in my review. While leveling my paladin, I made sure to try to enjoy each zone as much as possible before moving on to the next. I will break this review up into sections:

#Questing - Over all, the questing in WoD has been very nice. Blizzard has made it a point to make this as streamlined as possible. The combination of the journal and the interactive maps really help you figure out where you need to go, and what you need to do. The developers really made it a point to ensure that the rewards are class/spec specific, which is wonderful! Each item you receive has the potential of receiving an item level upgrade too, which further enriches the experience.

#Exploration - Those who really like to explore the zones and discover what the game has to offer are in for a treat. Mists of Pandaria had this to some extent but Warlords of Draenor really nailed it. There are “rare spawns” and miscellaneous treasures littered throughout the world here. Sometimes they’re just off the beaten path and relatively easy to find. Other times, you really need to work at it. Like the quest rewards, each item has the chance of automatically being upgraded.

#Garrisons - This is really the biggest change that The World of Warcraft has seen yet. The ability to build your own fortress, and “staff” it with followers has been a lot of fun (though it can be tedious if you try to maintain a garrison for each of your alts!) There is a fair amount of flexibility here with what buildings you can choose, which adds to the appeal. Each building has its own unique advantages/disadvantages, and will have a significant impact on the feel of the garrison (you can change things up too, so if you don’t like one, you can build over it!) Your followers can be sent off on missions, which can offer some pretty nice rewards, either for them, or for your own character. Your garrison will eventually have its own mine and herb garden, which significantly reduces the need for a gathering skill.

#PvP - I’ve only dabbled a little bit with this. Overall, it seems that Blizzard has made some significant improvements with the whole PvP/PvE gear conundrum. The current PvP gear is at ilvl 620, but boosts to 675 when you’re in a PvP situation. The stats are also geared more toward PvP instead of PvE still. This seemed like a thoughtful way to help with the “raiding in PvP gear” problem.

#Dungeons and Raids - The developers really seem to work hard to come up with ways to make the dungeons feel new and exciting. Each expansion adds something new to the dungeon experience. The Dungeon Finder is still far superior to the previous way of finding groups (either being in a good guild, or spamming trade chat.) They also did a nice job with the loot system, as each player gets a personal chance at gear, instead of rolling on whatever drops. I’ve seen each of the raids a few times now, and I do like the fact that they are significantly shorter than the raids in Mists of Pandaria.

#General Improvements - It’s nice that multiple players can beat on the same rare spawn or unique mob, and still receive credit for the kill (Guild Wars 2 had this feature a while ago, and I thought it was great!) I also like the expanded Void Storage and the Reagent Bank, as well as the tools used to search and sort your inventory.

Now here are some annoyances I’ve found with this expansion. None of them are really game-breaking, but I feel they should be addressed (and, according to the patch notes for 6.1, which should land soon, many will be!)

#Crafting - This is where Blizzard seems to have dropped the ball. Crafting was totally reformed. Some of the changes make a lot of sense. Others leave me scratching my head wondering “why?” Regardless of what trade you’re picking up, you learn a bunch of skills all at once. This is nice, as you don’t need to hover near the trainer when leveling your skill. More powerful plans can be learned a bit more slowly, as you make the currency to purchase them, and you can make one per day. Some trades are still fairly useful. Others, like engineering, inscription, and especially alchemy feel a lot less useful now. Even enchanting and jewelcrafting feel a little stripped-down.

#Garrisons - It doesn’t make much sense that the herb garden comes so late in the game. You need to be level 96 before you can open it up, yet the fishery (which is pretty close to useless for my play style) opens up at 94. Then again, alchemy and inscription aren’t nearly as useful as they once were, either. Some of the buildings also have quirks that aren’t obvious. The rank 3 Stables perk doesn’t stack with Death Knights’ or Paladins’ movement speed buffs. Trapping animals for the barn also can be a pain in the ass. Primal Spirits are fairly hard to come by, and if you buy the wrong item, the vendor will only give you silver in return, and not the primals. The animations for the completion of follower missions is fairly boring, especially if you’ve sat through several hundred of them.

#Dialog/Voice Acting - The dialog and voice acting in this expansion, especially in the dungeons and raids, is really bad. I wish you could turn it off.

#Gathering Skills - The introduction of the mine and herb garden made herbalism and mining less useful. Having them will help speed up your other trade skills, but the materials are not worth anything on the auction house (on my server, at least.)

title: Better than Cataclysm
text:
Over all, I would say that World of Warcraft remains to be the best MMO that I have played. There as a three month tryst with Final Fantasy XI before WoW, and another few month fling with Guild Wars 2 during my 2 year hiatus from WoW. But I inevitably came back to this game. I played until the launch of Cataclysm, which in my opinion, was dismal. They ruined my favorite class (ret paladin) and seemed to try to recycle a lot of old content. So I quit. Anyway, after chatting with some friends about our old days, I decided to give Mists of Pandaria a try. They insisted it was better. Well, they were right. It is an improvement upon Cataclysm.

I started playing about 3 weeks ago, and since then, I've managed to level 2 of my higher levels to 90, and see the first 2 sets of raids. I have returned to many changes. Many were for the better. Some, well... not so much. Here is what I've noticed. (Please note that I have been away for a couple years, and I might not know when such changes were implemented.)

The good:

1. On an asthetic level, WoW has seen some substantial improvements. You don't need the best hardware to crank everything up, which seems to be Blizzards MO. The world is still a bit cartoon like, but that is part of its charm (and always has been!)
2. The Raid and Dungeon finder has made things much nicer for casuals. You do run the risk of running with inappropriately skilled/geared players, but over all, it is a nice feature. It seems to have been improved since I quit (and Raid Finder is completely new.) Some folks complain about LFR for a number of reasons - lower gear quality and reduced fight mechanics. I am personally fine with this. I mainly play to see content. Not have the best purples. It would, however, be nice to see a buff given to tanks who meet the minimum gear requirement. Speaking as someone who started tanking heroics with an item level of 440 last week, it can be hard to maintain threat when 2 or 3 of your DPS are pulling 100k plus.
3. Guild Perks! Experience and rep boosts, mass resurrection, faster flying... The list goes on. Very nice for leveling an alt! (Though it could be bad if you're a sucker for the story... you tend to outgrow quest zones and dungeons pretty fast.)
4. Traveling is considerably more convenient. Most classes have at least an optional bonus to movement speed perk to choose from, and they seem to have allowed mounts in more areas.
5. I leveled a Death Knight from 55 as a blacksmith/miner. They rearranged the zones, so gathering had a few hang-ups. But once I got going, things were a lot easier (mainly because I could fly from level 60 on.)

The Bad:

1. The change I like the least is probably the Cross Realm business. Zones are flat out crowded now. I've had to wait in line to kill a unique mob, and folks seem to be fighting over items to be gathered. Depending on the time of day, questing can be nearly as bad as it is during launch week. I get that Cross Realm dungeon finder was necessary. I can even see why they'd want it for regular zones, as well. But they should tone it down a bit. (I was in Loch Modan last night, and the place was CRAWLING with panda.)
2. Scenarios! These are flat out boring. There is one that gives you a 450 weapon of choice. That is worth doing once you hit level 90, and if you didn't get lucky in any of the higher level dungeons on normal mode.
3. The Isle of Thunder. It's a crazy rep grind. I suppose it would be worth it if you're in a hard-core raiding guild. I took my Death Knight there as soon as he hit 90 (in quest greens and blues.) It seems to me that the place was tuned for people who were at least raid-ready. The non-elite mobs have about 500k health, and the elites have way more.
4. The music in this expansion is flat out annoying. This is sad, because music has been one of Blizzard's strongest suits in ALL of their games.
5. I didn't spend much time in Cataclysm dungeons, and I didn't step foot in a single raid from that content. The dungeons in this expansion are pretty lame. I don't care much for the story line in many of them (Stormstout Brewery, for example.) The boss fights and mobs seem pretty annoying. I appreciate that they are trying to add new mechanics into the dungeons. Some things worked. Some didn't. It would be nice if they allowed us to skip some of the NPC dialog once we've seen it once.
6. While the story line here seems a bit more original than what they did with Cataclysm, I still don't care for it as much. The Burning Crusade and Wrath of the Lich King both had outstanding stories.

The Nit-Picks:

1. Pandas! This was just like all the other expansions where they introduced new classes/races. Everyone needs to be the new thing. I rolled a dwarf shaman, and I was the only non-panda in a Shadowfang Keep run!
2. My Death Knight is a blacksmith. I've leveled up through WotLK in the passed. Cataclysm's gear seemed like it was pretty logical. I am not happy with some of the changes they made. All the ghost-forged armor pieces have "random enchants." This would be more annoying if we weren't tripping over ghost iron nodes, but is still slightly annoying none the less. There is no control over what stats you get on a piece of armor, and sometimes you have to make several in order to get the desired result. It is nice that they gave you about a 10% chance to make a level 415 blue, however. I also don't like how they made Living Steel a main component in all epic gear (in relatively large quantities, no less.) Lightning Steel is pretty much useless. The only purpose it serves is to "learn" new plans on a once-daily cool down.
3. A huge focus on daily questing for rep. I liked the dungeon grinds better. Wrath of the Lich King seemed to have the best flexibility with rep grinds! Choice daily quests and tabbards for the desired faction!

title: A much needed RPG for the PS Vita
text:
The PlayStation Vita is a great system, but it really needed a solid RPG. Well, we finally have one! I've played Persona 1 and 3, so the series isn't new to me. Much like the previous entries, you're playing as a group of high school kids who're trying to combat an evil presence in your hometown. As many people say, the game is an RPG with some sort of "Sims" elements. I've never played The Sims, but I think I can see where they're coming from. You need to balance your in-game life. You can do whatever you'd like after school and at night. Whether it be dungeon-crawling in the afternoon and sleep at night, or socializing then work. But if you don't strike some sort of balance, then it's Game Over. Now let's get into some impressions that I have about this game...

Sound and Graphics:
The graphics are cell-shaded anime style, and are quite fluid. The style fits the game perfectly. The music, much like the rest of the titles in the series, is made up of catchy J-pop'ish tunes. I really like what they've done here!

Gameplay:
The controls are pretty standard. I haven't had any real issues with figuring anything out (no manual was needed.) The social-life aspect, as well as the fusion of personae keeps things interesting. There is no "best" way to play the game. You'll likely find a way that suits your tastes, and it'll likely be different from other players. Over all, I really like the mechanics of the game.

Characters and Story:
I find that characters in many JRPG's can be very annoying and over-the-top. Not so much the case here. Each character was well-written, and the voice acting is well-done. (They also have an option to turn off the voices during gameplay. With this feature enabled, you only have to listen to them during the cut-scenes.) The storyline is quite good, in my opinion. They have this whole mysterious murder thing going on, and you are hellbent on figuring out what's going on; quite original, from my experiences.

Ultimately, I couldn't recommend this game more if I wanted to. The awesome story with good characters, great graphics and music, intuitive play controls and an interesting mix between RPG and life-simulation make for a winning combination. Any Vita owner who is looking for a solid RPG should check this game out! Hell, I'm sad that I missed it on the PS2! :(

title: Creepy Dungeon-Crawler
text:
The last Silent Hill game that I played was Homecoming. I thought it was decent - enjoyed the story and the creep factor well enough. When I pre-ordered Book of Memories, I realized that it wouldn't be anything like the series. I was actually grateful for the differences, as I am a fan of dungeon-crawlers in general. For the most part, the graphics and music seem very "Silent Hill'esque." The more "top-down-isometric view" is a complete departure from what we're used to from the series, so you will not get the same feel as you would from the previous titles.

**Combat**
Over all, I found the combat to be very fluid and easy to figure out. I don't care much for the weapons breaking, but thus far, so many are available in each stage, you should be OK (though you might not be able to use your favorite one all the time.)

**Story**
The story has only been OK so far. A little convoluted, but I expected that. The game play is why I'm here.

**Game Play**
Classic dungeon-crawler! Mash buttons when you see enemies. Move out of the way when they swing at ya. Some drop loot and of course you have limited inventory space (which is upgradable.)

**Verdict**
Hardcore fans that want another entry in the Silent Hill series might be disappointed. This is a game that uses themes and characters/monsters from the series, but feels almost nothing like any of it's predecessors. The game is pretty good in it's own right. I definitely recommend this to those who like hack-and-slash games (though this one has less loot) with puzzle-solving components. Actually, this game seems a lot like Zelda without an overworld!

You equip it, and within a handful of mobs, you've unlocked all the possible abilities linked with it (hot-keyed 1-5.) Each type of weapon has it's own style of combat. With a warrior, I prefer a 2-handed sword and either a bow or gun in my secondary slot.

Questing still feels the same, even though I've moved on to the new zone. It's a bit of a grind at times, but frequently "events" will happen nearby. These tend to involve killing an elite or escorting a NPC, and have a significant reward (XP, Karma and of course, money.) I actually look forward to these, as they break up the grind a bit, and encourage teamwork.

(XP, drops, etc.) This actually encourages players to work together, and not compete. The same thing goes for resource nodes. You see a copper or iron ore deposit, you get it. No fighting or stealing!

I chose to make weapons and armor, and I finally figured out that making the components for the weapons or armor pieces of choice, you can combine them with other crafted items and learn new patterns (thanks to YouTube!) Each discovery gives you 1 of the item that you discovered, the ability to continue making them, AND a ton of XP toward your craft. This seems like it cuts the resource grind from ridiculous to just very long. Currently, I'm level a level 46 armorsmith, and have put a significant amount of effort into gathering resources. I need to eventually hit 75 so I can use the materials that I'm gathering in the 15-20+ zone.

You can even participate in the events for more XP, karma and money, and yet you won't have a significant edge over folks that belong in the area (your gear is better, but you're otherwise gimped to their level.)

************** ORIGINAL REVIEW ****************
*************************************************

Currently, I have a level 10 character, which I rolled up after abandoning a level 6 character that I didn't like.

**LOGISTICS & TECHNICAL THINGS**

First off, this game has no monthly fee! Which is great! I've probably dropped a few hundred dollars in subscription fees for the other two MMO's that I used to pay. Not having one is great!

I bought the game from a store, and figured the installation would be faster since I wouldn't have to wait for a download at peak times. I was rather wrong... I still had about 3 hours between inserting the discs and finally playing; about 2 of those hours were from downloads!

My gaming rig has an AMD FX-4100 CPU, 4GB of DDR3 RAM and an EVGA 550 Ti card, and I'm able to run with the graphics set to pretty high (almost peak) levels. My GPU hardly notices, though the CPU is running all 4 cores at 50%+ load most of the time. The RAM is stuck between 3.0 and 3.2GB at any given time. Not once have I had a dip in frame rates or lag (I set the max frames at 60FPS, just because anything more is completely unnecessary.) In short, this game seems fairly CPU-intensive, yet not very dependent on the GPU. (Diablo 3, on the other hand, is the complete opposite.) My system is by no means cutting edge, yet GW2 runs great on it.

The graphics are decent, though I haven't notices much in the way of physics being used. The weather effects look a bit dated (I think WoW's environments were nicer, actually.) Sound-wise, I feel the game lacks. The music is your standard-fare fantasy RPG symphonic music, and the voice acting is OK at best (in fact, I turned voice volume all the way down and just read the subtitles.) I can't complain too much here, as lowering the graphical intensity will allow for more players.

**STORY**
The Norn's starting zone is very reminiscent of what you'd expect in WotLK or Skyrim - a winter wonderland filled with things to kill! The story so far is only OK... Rather typical fantasy, but fine enough to drive the MMO. The intro has alluded to a menacing dragon and a power struggle. Again, things seem fairly routine here.

**GAMEPLAY**
When it comes to combat and exploration, the mechanics are fairly intuitive and things flow pretty freely here. The map has plenty of icons, so once you figure them out, you should be able to find anything you want. Fast Travel is very straight forward and inexpensive. here are several fast travel points through the starting zone, and once you discover them, you can jump to one from anywhere on the map for a nominal charge (5 or 6 coppers, so far.) The Norn's hometown is connected in a similar fashion. One thing I found rather strange were the "Active Events." From time to time, you'll get an onscreen notice saying "An event is happening nearby." Said event is usually a raiding party of baddies, or an NPC needing protection. Anyone is free to join, and participation yields rewards on many levels. Objectively, watching what's going on is a lot like watching little league ball games - it's just a giant cluster-@!#* of players chasing after mobs! Regardless, they only take a few minutes, and the rewards are rather nice.

Since this game was recently launched, the servers are getting hit. Instead of making you wait to log on, they've implemented an Overflow Server. You can jump right into the game, do all your quests, exploration and what-not, and all of that will transfer over to your main server once your queue pops. From what I understand, only World Events won't transfer over, though I haven't had to deal with that quite yet... Ultimately, I'm very appreciative of this Overflow Server idea! It sure beats the 15min+ queue times that I had to deal with when FFXI and WoW were popular.

Crafting so far hasn't been as clear. As a warrior, I picked the very original professions of Armorsmith and Weaponsmith. It seems like you need a tremendous amount of ore in order to make even the most basic item. Then again, I'm used to crafting in WoW, where you can get started very quickly with a minimal amount of materials. In the several hours of play time that I've already invested - a good chunk of that dedicated to gathering ore - I've only been able to make 4 inventory boxes, a sword and 2 pieces of armor. I must've gathered a couple hundred pieces of copper ore. I have yet to use the Discovery Tab, but I haven't found enough materials to do so. Hopefully I can make more sense out of the system before long. After all, I've just started.

Questing is rather silly... Outside of your "personal story" quests, you find a quest giver (empty beige hearts on the map) and do what they say. You never have to return to them. Once you complete the objective, you get a message in the mail, which will also include the award. Speaking of mail, you no longer need to find a mailbox. It's just a tab at the top of your screen! Sure, this may lack "realism," but let's face it. All the realism we had in previous MMO's tended to bog down the game, and just required way more of our time.

**Current Verdict**
As it stands, I'm quite happy with my purchase. Guild Wars 2, for the most part, is a very well thought out MMO. You can tell the people who designed this had the player in mind. If you're here for great sound and graphics, you'll be disappointed. The story is a little lack-luster, but the over-all gameplay makes up for it. The crafting system seems a little complicated at the moment, but hopefully I'll sort those issues out on my own. (I'm wondering of others feel the same way, however.) They have greatly simplified questing, but again, I feel that they did this to reduce the amount of backtracking we need to do (player-focused design!) This isn't a perfect game, but it's a very solid attempt. Considering the fact that they don't require a monthly fee, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who's looking for an MMO!

title: Not bad, but not the best of the series.
text:
I grew up on the Dragon Warrior series. I've played all of the DW/DQ games, from the NES to PS1/PS2 and the DS. When it comes to the DS titles, DQ4 and DQ5 are amazingly good. This one isn't bad, but it felt "weird" do me. The story and game play, for the most part, were good. I really didn't like certain mechanics, however. For example, talking to EVERYTHING in a town before you can advance the story (including the animals) was frustrating and annoying. A tower was dark and filled with pit-falls, yet you had to navigate through them. I don't mind a little challenge, but I hate tedium, and that's what I felt like I had in this game from time to time (more frequent than the normal grind-induced tedium from the other games in the series.)

This game is certainly not bad, and definitely worth investing in for the hard-core Dragon Quest fan. I personally just found it a bit underwhelming, though I have pretty high standards (Dragon Quests 4 and 5 were two of my favorite RPG's of all time.)

title: Wonderfully Done Action RPG
text:
I must say, I'm impressed! I only have several hours into this game, but it has me hooked! Though this game gets great reviews, it didn't seem to make much of a splash when it hit the shelves. I pre-ordered it, and finally got the time to fire it up. If I were to compare it to other games, it seems like it's closer to Fable or Nier, than it is to other RPG's like The Elder Scrolls or Final Fantasy.

***Sound, Graphics and Technical Stuff***
The graphics in this game remind me a bit of WoW - not so much as a direct copy - just in spirit! You'll see lots of vivid colors and a slight cartooniness throughout the game. The voice acting is top notch, though the lip syncing leaves a little to be desired (no real bearing on the over all quality, though!) KoA: Reckoning also feels fairly polished. The frame-rates are largely stable, and I haven't dealt with any crashes or glitches.

Those interested in padding their trophy list will be happy - I think there are 100 or so available in KoA: Reckoning. Many of which are awarded just for playing a game (and might be hidden.)

***Game Play and RPG Elements***
So far, the story has my attention, and I'm eager to see what happens next. The side quests are numerous and for the most part, rather interesting. Right off the bat in games like Skyrim, Oblivion or Fallout, I often feel overwhelmed. This feeling frequently stays for the first several hours of play time. Kingdom of Amalur, on the other hand, feels quite welcoming as soon as you start! Things aren't nearly as forced as they are in say a Final Fantasy game, but not being as open as the more sandboxy titles is actually a welcome change of pace!

Questing feels almost exactly like it did in WoW. They even highlight quest-givers with yellow "!" and "?" when they have a quest to give or receive. If you're not familiar with these, let me sum it up: The world of Amalur, or whatever they call it, is filled with lazy and weak people that make you do their bidding. The quests consist of target hunts, gathering of items/goods, acquiring goods (like make potion X or buy item Y, and bring it back,) and clear dungeon Z. Rewards are given in experience points, and often money/items.

I really like the way you can custom-build your character, and not feel pressure (you can redo your "spec," if you wish!) The crafting system is also nice - simple, yet effective. Combat is also nicely done here. There is enough button-pushing to make you feel engaged the whole time, but not overly done, like they do in some other Action RPG's. Leveling up is easy enough in this game. As I mentioned before, quests grant experience, as does combat and finding various things (stones, hidden treasures, etc) while exploring and opening locked chests.

The crafting system is simplified enough to not be confusing. You can salvage your weapons and armor, which provides you with parts to make new things. Relying on only salvaging, however, is a crap-shoot. After salvaging countless weapons and armors, I still haven't found the right things to make a chest piece for my rogue. Many shops will sell you components (often really high end ones, too) for a price. Alchemy works in very much the same way it does in other big MMO's or sandbox RPG's - find herbs in the wild and combine for potion effects.

Ultimately, I highly recommend this title!

title: A bit pricey, but very fun!
text:
The Vita has a pretty limited selection of games at the moment. This game was one of the most attractive to me, however. I own the PS3 version, and had a lot of fun with it. This one is the same game, with some added tweaks. Don't expect anything more as far as story! The quests and main plot are all the same. They did add several new features when it comes to game play, however. You have more control over the faeries, and they made good use of the touch capabilities of the Vita. It also seems that this version has WAY more trophies. For players that want to pad their trophy catalog, I suppose this'd be a good place to invest your money (in a few hours time, I think I racked up between 10 and 15...)

I noticed that this game has been receiving a lot of poor reviews, and I'm surprised by this. DH:A is a dungeon crawl. You kill lots of things, and get lots of loot. Lather-rinse-repeat. In fact, it does a pretty good job at doing it's job. If you enjoy these sorts of games (Diablo, Torchlight, Dungeon Siege, Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance, etc...) you should be right at home here.

As far as technical aspects, the game fits the bill just fine. Play control is fluid, and sound/graphics, while not cutting edge, are perfectly serviceable. Again, I like how they added in some additional controls with the Vita's touch screen/rear touch panel, and how they added some additional game play features.

The only criticism that I really have is that it has a rather steep price tag, especially considering that the original version was less than half the cost (I think I paid $10 or so when it was on sale with my PlayStation Plus membership.) This game is a lot of fun, and I find that it's worth what I paid. It's very nice to have this one available while on-the-go!

title: Impressive Piece of Hardware
text:
When the Nintendo DS was announced, I didn't think much of the touchscreen. I even waited until the release of the DS Lite before I jumped on that bandwagon. Even now, I never use the touch screen on it. When the PlayStation Vita was announced, I had a different mindset. Touchscreen technology seems to have improved immensely since it was introduced in cellphones and tablets. Sony also had me very curious about the touch-sensitive back panel (and VERY happy that this system had 2 analog control sticks!) I was also rather impressed by the hardware specs... This little machine is a BEAST! Over all, I am really happy with my purchase, and I'll be happy to fill in the details why. There are also a few gripes (nothing worth docking a star, but worth mentioning,) that I have as well.

At any rate, I finally picked one up, and have had a few days to mess with it. The set-up was fairly intuitive, and I had to deal with an update, but that took about 5 minutes to download and install, so no harm there! I avoided buying any games at the store. I decided that I'll stick mainly with the PSN for purchasing my games, and with that in mind, I went with the moderately sized 8GB memory card, in hopes that the prices of those come down by the time it fills up. The first 2 games that I picked up for the PS Vita were Touch My Katamari and Super Stardust. I was a fan of the previous installments of these games, both were relatively cheap, and seemed like they'd make decent use of the new interfaces (which they did!) The graphics and sound pumped out on this thing really are top notch. The controls work perfectly, and having the second analog stick really is necessary for most modern games. Some reviewers mention that the analog sticks are way too sensitive. I had absolutely no issues with them. The buttons are very responsive, and have nice tactile response. The touchscreen is probably the best I've ever used, and I really like the implementation of the rear touch panel, though I'm still getting used to it.

When it comes to some of the more physical features, I'm largely satisfied as well. Some reviewers mention how big it is, as if they're almost disappointed (though I haven't read any that said that it's so big that it detracts from the experience.) For me, the size is fine, as I've never been one to take my portables everywhere I go. In fact, I appreciate the fact that it's larger than the PSP! You get way more screen real estate! (For the record, I mainly keep them at home, or take them with me when I travel. I've never been one to cart these to work/school!) Battery life is sufficiently long, especially considering what's under the hood! I was actually surprised that the PS Vita lasts so long, and is still pretty light weight.

The launch lineup is relatively sparse, but that always seems to be the case with a new console. I looking forward to a few of the titles that'll be hitting this year: Silent Hill will have a PS Vita release, and Final Fantasy X will be revamped in HD, and released for the Vita (as well as PS3.) The system seems to be a hit thus far, so I imagine that developers will be drawn to it, and the list of titles will bulk up soon enough!

As I mentioned before, I do have a few nitpicks. Since I'm used to Sony, I expected these, and I'm willing to deal with them, but these are some issues I'd like to see changed:

*No internal storage, and VERY expensive proprietary (Sony Brand-only) memory card options is a bit on the absurd side. It would make sense that this machine should have enough memory internally to at least handle software updates, game saves and apps that you'd always want access to, like Netflix (this app does have a decent interface, by the way, and while a bit on the small side for long viewing stints, the picture is nice!) Flash-based memory isn't that expensive, and something like 4GB wouldn't cost them much to install, nor would it take up much room inside. I get why Sony is trying to lock their cards, but damn... they're a bit harsh on the wallet! If there was a rating for "Affordability," the system would definitely lose a star. But this doesn't affect the over-all quality, nor does it make the games any less fun, so I will stay at 5 stars.

*While I like the rear touch panel, it does get in my way at times. I tend to hold my handheld systems with my fingers stretched across the back of the unit. I find black holes popping up randomly in Super Stardust, and my Katamari seems to get stretched out randomly. I'm sure that I'll get used to it, but for now, it's a minor annoyance.

*The lack of PlayStation Classics support upon launch is a bummer, but Sony says that they'll add that in once it's ready.

Ultimately, I'm very pleased with my purchase!

title: A wonderful addition to the TES series [UPDATED]
text:
I've been a fan of The Elder Scrolls since Morrowind, and I was quite excited for this release. I must admit, that between the issues I had with finally getting Oblivion to run, and what I heard about Fallout: New Vegas (I fortunately didn't have time to play that one right away,) I was nervous that Bethesda would release yet another title with game-breaking bugs. Well, I haven't had any problems thus far (several hours of play so far.) What I have noticed is how much they improved the system! It looks to me like they borrowed heavily from the recent Fallout titles. My review will be focusing on the mechanical aspects of the game:

*Skills and leveling seem less obtuse. They got rid of the stats, so you have more freedom to decide which skills you level. You no longer have to worry about the age-old TES question "Should I tag that skill? Or will it cripple my character?" They also removed the "you must rest in order to level up" requirement, which is a bit more convenient.

*The crafting system seems to borrow heavily from Fallout: New Vegas (and games like World of Warcraft.) You no longer need to carry repair hammers around. Instead, you find raw materials and instead of maintaining your equipment, you can improve it. Over all, this makes the skills feel more useful, and at the same time, it seems that it reduces the tedium (stopping in the middle of a dungeon to repair my damn boots in Morrowind/Oblivion was always annoying!)

*Questing has improved! The quest log is far easier to follow than it has been in previous titles.

*Combat hasn't changed too much, though they added the ability to equip a weapon in your offhand. Getting the rhythm down to fight this way takes a little time, but it's a welcome change!

*The voice-acting is immensely better than it was in Oblivion! The towns feel more fleshed out this time around.

*Of course the graphics have improved. TES series seems to have always been on par or ahead of the rest when it comes to visuals. And consistently with the previous titles, the music is still great!

*The men in this game are so manly that they don't wear coats! EVEN WHEN STANDING AROUND WAITING TO MUG YOU ON A SNOWY MOUNTAIN!

A word of advice: Leave the giants alone!

Update (1/7/12)

Still adding on hours to the game, and I haven't ran into anything game-breaking. Every now and then the game will threaten to lock up, but I don't think I had to ever reset my console. Also, I haven't had too many problems with quests, which seems to be a common complaint from other users. Again, I've played other Bethesda titles, and I think dodging some of the big glitches is the luck-of-the-draw; I've had attempts at Oblivion and Morrowind that stalled within the first few hours, and I've also had complete play-throughs with very few hang-ups.

Update (4/3/12)

Still playing this game from time to time! And I still haven't run into many serous glitches. A few graphical errors, and that's about it. If I play for a long time, the game seems to get a little fussy (and it may be because of heat issues with the PS3 itself.) There are still many areas to explore, and tons of quests to complete, so I haven't tested everything yet (even after all this time!) Skyrim still has my highest recommendation! In fact, with respect to my experiences, it's probably the most stable game Bethesda has released to date, and every bit as fun as the previous titles!

title: Surprisingly, kind of boring
text:
I've been following the Dragon Quest series since the original was released for the NES (I got mine for free with a Nintendo Power subscription!) Needless to say, I'm a huge fan. When this game got announced for the DS, I was extremely excited. I pre-ordered it, and couldn't wait to get my hands on it. Well, I got it, played it some, and then I let it sit. Over the past several months, I've picked it up here and there. I'll play it in fits-and-starts. Ultimately, I can't bring myself to really play it. Sure, the graphics are very polished and nice, and I love the music (just like any other title from the series!) There are also some bright spots scattered here and there too. The game, however, feels like that the people behind this game wanted to make a game that would last a long time. Well, they succeeded with quantity over quality. The most important feature of any RPG is story, and with DQ9, we're being told a story that's only OK. I can deal with a story that's only OK, if the game has engaging game-play. But we don't even have that here! What we did get was an annoying level-up/jobs system, a mess of tedious side quests and forced grinding. Let me fill in some details here:

Level Up System -- It takes a lot of XP to level up as you move through the game if you stick with one class. Sure, you can switch classes and knock out a few easy levels and get some skill points, but the best skills come at higher levels. Trying to make an uber-character can take too much time and research. When playing a Dragon Quest game, I kind of just want to move through the story.

Side Quests -- You'll run across some NPC's with blue-colored conversation balloons over their heads. These folk have side quests that you can complete. Unfortunately, many of them are of the form "go kill X number of enemy Y using tactic Z." These tactics used seem to be the most annoying way to fight (go kill them with an under-powered skill, or weak weapon, for example.) Some of these side quests are required if you'd like to train a character in a particular job, which is unfortunate. Others have rewards that don't mean nearly as much to the game, and are there for our amusement (or in my case, annoyance.)

Characters -- You recruit a party of generic members in this game, very much like you did in DQ3. It was fine back then, as personality had no role what-so-ever in the first few Dragon Quest titles. But once they hit DQ4, characters with at least a smidgen of personality were introduced. Here, we get customized sprites. They simply follow you around and follow orders.

This game did have some interesting ideas behind it. The combo-system is neat when you can get it to work. I also like how the characters appearance change when you equip different things (even if the new look was sometimes awful!) Running around and NOT having random encounters is a huge plus for me. In fact, random encounters can ruin my taste for a game sometimes. With DQ9, you almost always know when a fight will take place!

So is this game terrible? No. I've certainly played worse. But I do think it might be the worst of the series! I expect some level of grinding with any Dragon Quest (or RPG) title. It's kind of the nature of the beast here. We're kind of forced into a grind here, though, and it really detracts from the game. Especially when the story is rather weak! (The story actually had an interesting start, but became a lather-rinse-repeat throughout.) I'm sure fans of the series will appreciate the game on some level. In the end, I found some appreciation for the parts that I played. But it's not on my "I need to finish this" list. I may get around to it, but not any time soon.

title: An outstanding game with seemingly endless possibilities
text:
I'm not big on FPS games. In fact, Morrowind, Oblivion and the newer Fallout games are about as close as I normally get to FPS. I couldn't resist this game, however. Being from Detroit kinda influenced that; I wanted to see how much of my hometown they incorporated. I have to say, some things are familiar (including bums digging in the trash cans!) They really encouraged exploration here, with shops and hidden passageways scattered about. The streets of Detroit are more accurate than I expected, and they also included some nice landmarks.
