title: All patched up and awesome!
text:
I pre-ordered the collectors edition, but ended up sitting on the game for a while due to numerous complaints of bugs. I've had several issues with bugs from Bethesda's titles in the past. Morrowind and Oblivion, while some of my favorite games, were a nightmare to start up because of some of the bugs. Fallout 3 was notorious for crashing my PS3 (especially the expansion material.)

Well, recently started this game, and I'm several hours into it. So far, I haven't run across a single bug (that couldn't be killed by my machete.) The story is pretty good. Good enough for a sandbox game. I'd say the graphics feel cleaner and smoother than Fallout 3's. The voice acting is at least as good as Fallout 3's, and I love the music - The fine folks at Obsidian did an amazing job with integrating the music! It really feels like "The Wild, Wild West!"

I'd also like to take the time to point out the improvements of the skill system. Having a repair skill doesn't just allow you to fix up your weapons. It allows you to convert ammo you don't use into ammo that you do use! I really like how the speech and barter skills have been beefed up: Instead of your skill level giving you a % chance of succeeding, they put a quota - A dialog option, for example, will say [Speech 25] and if you have a 25 or higher, you automatically succeed! Survival is also a very useful skill now. Having higher ranks of the skill will allow you to cook food and make some equipment.

The perks you can chose from at the start aren't that great (Wild West was the only one that didn't have ridiculous negative effects on you.) Once you start leveling up, the perks that become available are quite nice.

Over all, I really like this game!

title: Engrossing game with a few flaws
text:
I've seen some pretty bad reviews for this title, and I don't think it deserves it. Granted, the game isn't perfect, it is FAR from bad!. In fact, I think it's pretty damn good. Aside from the facial features of the characters during conversations, the graphics are amazing. The music is very nice, though it seems to be a bit off queue at times (not often, but enough to warrant me mentioning it.) Over all, the game play is good. Combat seems pretty smooth, and it can be a challenge at times.

There are some bugs in it, though. For example, when I first came across the Judge in her office, Alex was floating in the air while they were having a conversation (his feet were about the same level as the top of her desk!) The biggest problem I have with the game is the lack of save-points. They are too few and the distance between them is substantial. Unless you're using a guide, or have played through the game before (or fairly lucky/fast at playing,) the exploratory nature of the game makes it so you can expect a good 45 minutes to an hour between saves. The challenge of the game steadily increases, and losing an hour of play can be demoralizing to some. The story is good enough to keep me going back for more though (the nurses in the Grand Hotel ate me alive for a while there!)

Advice for those playing through for their firs time: Save as much as you can, and make multiple save-files. Otherwise you might find yourself starting over because you used up all your ammo or recovery items a few hours in. Coming up with some solid tactics can save you a fair amount of grief later in the game.

Over all, this is a very welcome addition to the Silent Hill series, as well as the Survival Horror genre in general!

title: Wonderful Dungeon Crawl with a Strong RPG Feel.
text:
As a fan of the classic CRPG's Baldur's Gate II, Fallout and Planescape: Torment, I had high hopes for the Neverwinter Nights series. I was hoping for parties of characters that shared colorful banter. This game isn't that, but that's not necessarily a bad thing! Even though this game is rather old, it still holds up, in my opinion! Yeah, the graphics are a bit dated, but they still look nice. The game play is a mix between Baldur's Gate style games, and Diablo. It's a top-down dungeon crawl with a bit more menu to work with. Combat will be a bit slower than Diablo, and you pay more attention to detail in this game than you would in say Baldur's Gate (you only have one character to deal with, not 6.) I've only played through the main campaigns, and here's my summary of them:

NWN: The game is fine enough, as the story line is only fairly interesting. The game-play is where this one shines, though! I found the combat in this game to be very fun. I played through most of the game as a rogue, then all the way through as a paladin. You only get one side character at a time, and each one has a little bit of story. Basically, take one with you and do some adventuring. As time goes on, they'll fill you in on their past and ask you to do a favor for them. Once it's complete, they will reward you with a magical item that'll prove fairly useful. As the game progresses, these trinkets can be upgraded. My personal favorite character was the halfling rogue. His story was the most interesting, and his skills can be very useful. The cleric wastes all her magic on destroying undead, so I found playing through the as a paladin and taking the rogue with me whenever possible was the best for me. This portion of the game gets a solid 4 stars from me.

SoU: This expansion basically serves as an interlude to get you form the previous to the next. The story was only OK, and there wasn't much new added to the game-play (though you lose karma in this title if you use the rogue to pick locks!) If I recall correctly, you get some ability to control your NPC's inventory, which is nice. I mostly took the dwarf rogue with me through this portion. None of the NPC's really had my interest for long. She took care of traps for me, and that was enough. This part only got 3 stars in my book...

HoU: This expansion was AMAZING for me. Going through the Underdark is a lot of fun, and you get a wopping 2 NPC's at a time. YES! THERE IS BANTER! The kobold bard from the previous title (was pretty annoying then) follows you through out. He's pretty much comic relief. I really enjoyed the story and the characters here. I think there might have been a slight graphical upgrade too. Also, there is a way to customize your gear, so you can make your awesome magical gear even more awesome! 5 stars! It's pretty awesome!

One day I'll get to King Maker and some of the other modules. If so, I'll be sure to edit this post with my input!

title: Great Dungeon Crawler!
text:
New Impression:
I've played several hours now. My initial intent on the review was to indicate that the game wasn't as bad as others have made it out to be. Now I'm hooked! The story continues to pick up, and there have been a few times when I find myself very much impressed by the sound and graphics. Over all, SE/Obsidian did a fine job on this one! Everything seems very fluid, and over all, I'm having a blast!

Previous Impression:
I'm seeing some negative reviews on this, and I'm rather surprised. This game pretty much delivers what's advertised. When I saw the initial trailers, I expected a clone of Diablo/Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance, and that's exactly what you get. The graphics and sound are far sharper than it's predecessors, and the play control is solid. I'm about 5 or 6 hours into the single player game as Lucas. The story is fine enough (these types of games never have mind-blowing story lines anyway) and the characters are about what you'd expect. I'd say the voice-actors are about on par with Diablo/BG:DA.

Is this "Game of the Year?" Probably not.
Is this a fun game? Definitely!
Does this game offer anything new to the genre? Not really. It's just prettier and more polished.

If you've enjoyed previous dungeon crawlers, you might want to give this one shot.

Edit: 8/11/2011
I still really enjoy this game, and I'm rather disappointed by its over-all reception; it's a fun dungeon crawl, and I'm not sure why people expected anything else. Granted, it's a bit short, but there is some replay value here (thank the Trophy system for that.) I'd expect the average person to play through it in about 10 hours. Some grinding will be necessary if you want an easier time with the end. Trying to complete the game when you're in your low-mid 20's can be tough for some. If you're short on cash, this is definitely worth a rent. It's certainly easy enough to complete in a weekend.

title: Should have stopped at Wrath...
text:
I started playing World of Warcraft right when The Burning Crusade came out. Granted, I wasn't one of the Vanilla Veterans, I have put quite a bit of time in. I had a blast with BC; raided all the way through The Black Temple. Wrath of the Lich King was extremely fun. They made questing a blast, and the storyline was top notch. I was on the fence when Cataclysm was announced. "Resetting" everything didn't seem like such a good idea. I kind of wish I would have listened to my instincts. The game is boring now. I can't even bring myself to level to 85, and from what I saw, it doesn't take long to do so (a good chunk of my friends had hit it by the time the first week was done.) Some of the changes they made were nice; streamlining the way skills worked and changing some of the classes around. Others weren't as fun (I really didn't like what they did with Ret Paladins.)

I could go on to list what I don't like about the game. It would be a long and nit-picky list. Ultimately, I think Blizzard should have quit while they were ahead and put their efforts into World of Warcraft II, or Diablo III. Killing Arthas should have finished it. title: You did it again Enix
text:
What a game- let me tell you. There are some great parts from the original one they included; unique bosses, awesome new weapons, a great storyline. Though were there are some great parts there must be bad.

Kingdom Hearts II was a blast, I loved battling enemy after enemy, the tiny stars that flash up when you attack something with your keyblade reassured me of that. Let me tell you though the beginning started off very slow and confusing. Let me tell you now if you haven't beaten Kingdom Hearts 1 you'll probably be scratching your head the whole game.

You first start off as Roxas, a boy who is suddenly plunged into the Kingdom Hearts storyline. Similar to Kingdom Heart's first part of the game, I can honestly say(and I'm sure many would agree with me) that is was extremely boring and slow. Agh chore after chore, job after job. I hated collecting all that money, preforming stupid tricks on some skateboard that you couldn't skip! The only thing that really struck my attention in that part were the dreams Roxas had- It got me interested in the mysterious, devolping storyline yet to come. Well you can't blame Enix I suppose, I guess they were only trying to build up to the juicy parts.

Oh yes the juicy parts, chopping and slicing every enemy I see with my trusty keyblade- classic Kingdom Hearts. The "ultima" keyblade has returned, just as hard to make, just as powerful, and just as awesome looking. Saving world after world, it was very entertaining how different and unique each world was.

Although I was not use to the whole new gummi ship system, I grew to like it and now I realize it was a ton better than the first one. The trips where you battle hoards of flying enemies might be a little slow and easy at first, but trust me it really starts heating up when you get to the harder worlds. They now have a new boss system, where a boss might randomly attack you in battle. These guys are toughies if you don't have the right equipment, and I think Enix really tried to encourage that. Not only that, you can now travel to the same trips but on a different difficulty level. Rewards for completion include rare gummi peices. Perfect Enix, perfect.

One of my favorite parts were the drive powers. The game so totally needed this. Sora now has the power to weild TWO keyblades at once. That's right... you heard me, two! There are four drive powers that you can activate with a new drive bar similar the magic bar. Already the first power given to you early in the game allows Sora to weild two keyblades. I won't go over the next two, but the last one is a whopper! The final form, as Enix named it is just awesome. Sora's clothes turn totally silver and black, two keyblades hover(that's right hover!) around his hands, he hovers around in midair, and to top it all off when you attack you do insane damage, along with special moves you couldn't do with regular attacks. I would have to say this was one of the most enjoyable parts of this wonderful game.

I'm sorry to say though that the game was really quite easy. Now if I recall correctly one of the fairy people in the beginning mentioned something like "This adventure is going to be twice as difficult!". Man I was all prepared for this great journey, but at the end when I beat it I felt a sence of dispair. I felt as if I had just pressed the "x" button over and over, as a previous customer mentioned. Bosses that use to take quite a long time to kill can now be killed in less than a minute, and you don't even have to be a high combat level. When I defeated bosses in the first one, I felt a sence of accomplishment, but now I don't when the bosses kneel before me in KH2.

Overall- I like to say congratulations Square Enix for once again creating a great game.

title: Flashy but Boring Game Loop
text:
This game, stylistically similar to the Persona universe, is a grindfest with a thin storyline and average musical score. You basically roam around areas, fighting groups of demons, and try to recruit and fuse them to get more powerful demons to aid you. You can talk to demons to get items and recruit them but they might also ask for things from you or attack outright.

This series, unlike Persona, is centered around grinding more than story. I find it to be quite boring, actually. You need to grind to find collectibles, grind for XP, grind to get items, and grind to fuse and level demons. It's just grinding. The story is forgettable and trite.

I got this game and played it for about 10 hours total. Then set it aside and will probably sell it. It's like the other entries in the series; if you love a boring grindfest, you'll really like this one because the mechanics are set up well. If you want a story or some character development like P5, you are better off skipping this one.

title: Boring but Beautiful but BORING
text:
The graphics are really good on the PS4 and the environments look wonderful but the controls are clunky and you can't really interact with much. Townspeople say generic things and most of the settings look like animatronic rides that cycle animations...all the people look wooden.

The story is kind of OK. I am 10 hours in and just don't care about it. Alphen and Shionne have a ridiculous relationship where they love each other one minute and hate each other the next. The little interstitial dialogues you activate with R1 (when you notice the tiny message in the bottom right corner) paint Shionne as a weirdo...in these, she's goofy, hungry, absent-minded, etc. but in the main game dialogue, she's an icy cold princess who will destroy anything in her path. None of the characters are well developed and it's hard to care about them at all.

The music is garbage. It's the usual symphonic mess that all blends together, sounds exactly the same as every other game, and offers no emotional cues other than annoyance. I turned it down to 10 in the menu, as should you. The voice acting is OK but the characters repeat the same phrases during battle over and over again in either Japanese or English. The Japanese-to-English translation is also pretty liberal and I switched over to the English-only option because my ears were hearing things that the subtitles were not saying.

The battle system is stupid. All enemies, even the low-level trash mobs, have a ton of HP and take an excessive amount of time to clear as you don't do much damage unless you get the ultra-precise combo strings every single time. You can also just run in circles to avoid damage but, since you don't do much damage yourself, it takes way too long to take out even weak enemies. It got to the point where I was trying like hell to avoid battles...but then this game requires you to grind battles to get any kind of levels to face bosses. You also don't get much money to upgrade your gear. Bandai Namco wants you to buy upgrades (+5 levels, 100000 gald, etc.) with real cash and the game reflects that in its core design. It's bullshit that forces you to pay with cash or your own valuable lifespan just to get to the next boring, non-interactive map.

The game is pretty lame; it has main characters with nice modeling and various sexy outfits that keep the incels happy but it's shallow, boring, and trite. A very, very poor showing for a late-generation PS4/early-gen PS5 game that could have been so much more.

title: Mediocre Combat System with Weeaboo Eye Candy
text:
This game has a LOT to offer and is VERY hyper Japanese. If you are a weeaboo or Japanophile who can't speak Japanese, this is really the game you want to get. The area you get to explore is very accurate and looks quite a lot like Kabukicho in Tokyo while the voice acting is really well done. Although it's kind of corny and melodramatic, the story is also kind of fun but the translation is loose in places and some liberties are taken with what the characters say. The graphics are kind of blocky but serviceable and you will see just how much collectible stuff is there to find when you first start up the game. In addition, you get a few free items to start with that can really help you on the mean streets.

What I DO NOT LIKE are the following points: CONTROLS and BATTLE SYSTEM. This is a button mashing third person fighting game and the controls are soft, unresponsive and mushy. Your character moves sluggishly and reacts to your button presses a half second after input. Keeping the enemy in the camera view alone is a pretty big challenge. Although you get several fighting styles and some super moves to use, the fighting system is mostly based on you attacking and the AI just standing there for the most part. In low-level/trash mob battles, you will wipe the floor with them and not really do anything but mash attack over and over. However, when you face a boss, you are in for a good 10 minute fight with repetitive quicktime action events and AI that blocks 99.98% of your attacks. This turns boss battles into an unrewarding grind that becomes annoying very quickly. It wouldn't be so bad if the controls were tight but you are expected to react in a split second with button presses that take ages to translate into character actions.

I'm sure this game is good, but I wish I could press a button and skip the fights. It's seriously the worst part of the game and I am surprised that no one mentions how annoying it is.

title: Repetitive, flat, dull and predictable.  The Hype Machine Strikes Again!
text:
This game has a lot of promise but just seems to come off as a half-finished game where they did EVERYTHING to one half completion and then packaged it up as a full game. I bought it new and and stopped playing about halfway through the second playthrough. I should not have listened to all the paid hype around this game when it was first released and I have learned my lesson.

The Graphics: They are bleak but serviceable. There is at least consistency within the game's backdrops and the user interfaces are also very clean. Sparkles and little visual signals make sure you don't miss dropped items and the details in the settings, when they are there, are very well done. The only reason everyone says this is graphically great is that you can see up the skirt of 2B. Otherwise, the graphics are OK and reflect the current level of PS4 development capability.

The Gameplay: The combat system is only half finished. A game like Bayonetta or Devil May Cry is much better from a standpoint of fluid combat and combat options. You basically have a light or heavy weapon attack (as 2B) or a light weapon/hacking attack (9S). However, while you flip and twirl and kick swords out at people, you can't interrupt your combos once you get them going. I ended up using the third mode of attack, a drone weapon (bullet stream, laser, missiles, etc.) that strikes from a distance about 90% of the time. It doesn't do as much damage but all you have to do is strafe around a target, lock the drone on it and hold the button down until it explodes. This works on bosses, too, and is the only way to beat them without taking any damage at all. Melee attacks are more powerful but since you can't interrupt a combo easily, you'll take a hit more often than not.

The enemy AI: A JOKE. The bad guys all look like Android OS mascots and come in several varieties....but most differences are just cosmetic. There are probably only a handful of enemy types in the game and you will run into them over and over again. Bosses are easy: just strafe-dodge and hammer away with the drone gatling gun or missles, occasionally using the charged drone laser.

The sound: The soundtrack is VERY good but I only ever heard a few songs playing. Sound effects are adequate.

The story: Told from 3 viewpoints, you will have to play through the game 3 times to find out everything. Just like Bravely Default was able to copy and paste the first half of the game into a second half and score a full title with only 50% of the effort, this game copies and pastes TWO times to give a "complete" game with only 33% of the effort! It was OK the first time and got so boring the second time that I just quit playing. If I want to sit through the rest, I'll watch a longplay on YouTube. The story boils down to "we thought robots were bad BUT WE WERE WRONG. OR WERE WE?" and you have to get all the right endings to get the final ending. There are also joke endings (try selling your OS chip) that basically force you to reload the game and those are just irritating. The game is trying to be clever but ends up falling flat. There is no real story to speak of in this game....this bland, vanilla game. The game itself has a bunch of fetchit quests that are neither fun nor entertaining.

The chip modification system is OK, but the seemingly endless variety of configurations are not always useful and only a few setups will allow you to progress through the game. For my playthroughs, I equipped a healing chip or two and then never worried about dying again.

The main characters: 2 stereotypes wander around killing hordes of bland, similar enemies. Neither one has a dynamic personality. One is goth loli bait with white panties and the other is a twink 12 year old with schoolboy shorts.

Overall, this game was frustrating because, like many recent Japanese games, it focuses all the effort on finishing 50% of everything (combat, characters, story) and then just throws in cheap filler at ship time. I did enjoy the first playthrough somewhat (3.5 stars on that) but I can't recommend this game to anyone who wants a deep, engaging action RPG.

title: Couldn't Get Into It
text:
I picked this up with my PS4 and was looking forward to playing it but I was pretty disappointed to see that it's not really any different from the 200 other "third person sword swing run around a lot" games. The story is OK, the options are diverse in combat and dialogue, the animation and movies are top-notch and even the voice acting is good. The game world is also very well done. I just couldn't get into the wonky combat system and the horrible controls.

Geralt moves on a hair trigger, so it is very hard to control in a pinpoint manner. You'll sprint-stop endlessly to try to get to one NPC to talk to. You'll dance and shimmy around enemies you are trying to target. You'll overshoot your marks dozens of times an hour. The fact that enemies tend to gang up on you and you don't have a way of precisely and rapidly retargeting (you'll keep choosing the enemies you don't want) makes combat frustrating, especially since ranged attacks are not so powerful. I made it about 4 hours into the game before I couldn't take it anymore. This one's going back and I'll look somewhere else.

I really think that gaming has gotten into a rut where EVERY GAME has to be third person with the same controls, the same wobbly camera, the same minimap/quests and cliched story with grim/muscular heroes and tons of lore that doesn't mean anything. I really couldn't tell if this was Dragon Age VI: the Swordening or not. It would be nice to get more games with real plots like Planescape:Torment....

title: Boring, Repetitive Assembly Line Game
text:
If you ever thought that working in a Chinese factory was a fun way to pass your time, this game will make you very happy. If you're looking for a deep story, good mechanics and a well-crafted game world, you need to move along to another game.

I could never get into the Atelier series. They seemed custom crafted to appeal to gamers who love chirpy, super cute graphics. Atelier Shallie promised to be the best of the series so I checked it out and was very disappointed.

Graphics:
The graphics are pretty good. The environments can be a little sparse but the character design is bright and colorful with quite a lot of details. You can tell that Gust was working on attracting the neckbearded anime nerds and female Goth/Loli lovers with the designs. The menus are bright and the color palette seems to strike the right blend of gloom (the world maps) and cute (the menu screens).

Sound:
The music is bland and entirely forgettable. The character voices are stereotypically Japanese (if you play with Japanese dialogue turned on). Girls' voices are at the upper end of dog hearing and the guys are about 1 notch below. Enemies don't make much noise, at all.

Gameplay:
The main thrust of the game is doing missions and synthesizing items with alchemy. This is about 80% of the game and if you are into this kind of thing then you will love this game. The areas (just one or two screens each) can be selected and you can run through them and battle enemies and harvest items. The items and monsters respawn each time you go through. The big problem is that battles are either really easy or impossible. You'll blow through normal enemies and then you'll meet a HUGE monster that you cannot even dent. Death means nothing and you just go back to the World Map. The battle mechanics are OK and you can keep a reserve member to help defend or attack. The problem is that the battle animations are rough: enemies fade away, attack animations are choppy and the battles seem like just a waste of time. You get seemingly arbitrary amounts of experience points and there's no real way to judge if a battle will be easy other than to just try and see if you can win.

Plot:
Milquetoast Shallie or Incompetent Shallie has to do a bunch of quests because blahblahblahblah. The plot is almost nonexistent and creates no urgency or wonder or anything but "now do this quest and then after that do this one." It's like running down a checklist. None of the characters have anything but basic, stereotypical personalities.

This game has potential but falls short on an enjoyable experience. It's almost as if a design team said "what if we stopped taking time to write a plot and just made the sidequests into the main quests?"

title: Mediocre.
text:
It's mediocre but a good way to waste 10 or so hours. The game graphics are OK, but there is a lot of character model clipping and it can be difficult to shoot around obstacles. Here are some highlights of why I give a 2 star rating, rather than rehash what has already been said:

1. The game starts pretty well. Heavy story and good usage of cutscenes to draw you in. The aiming system isn't such a stickler for accuracy so shooting isn't bad.
2. LOTS of guns! Each one is useful in some way. You'll never run short on ammo unless you are camping.
3. Lots of different things to do. From a guided drone tank to heli flying, you get to do lots of good stuff.
4. Lots of save points

What I didn't like:
1. Models are kind of clunky, even if they are detailed. Korean soldiers mostly wear yellow and red so you can see them; there's no tactical value in dressing like a paramilitary Ronald McDonald.
2. Over-the-top movie morals where the bad guys are so HORRIBLY bad that you have full license to kill them in any way you can....unless it's part of the plot to feel sorry to kill them.

title: A Great Game For the Money:  Good Value!
text:
This game is pretty good. Although it didn't make the superstar ranking on IGN or the other review sites, it has a surprisingly big fan base and I hope Sega puts out a good sequel.

The plot of the game is kind of like the movie AI, where robots get smart enough to supplant Humanity. The best part of the game is the variety of robots and the smooth animations and tactical decisions they make in firefights. There is a special set of algorithms that the robots use to try to flank you, use cover, alert others and focus fire. Even when you've blown off their legs, they will reboot and crawl towards you to clutch your legs and impede you! Normal bots are pretty dopey, but several different bots have super specializations and you will curse the shinobi and sniper bots towards the end of the game. This game is NOT an unrealistic tactical game; if you charge in with guns blazing, you WILL DIE. You need to use cover and keep your squad focused. You need to manage ammo early on and the need for upgrades versus immediate supplies versus nanomachine augments for your squad. There's a LOT to this little game and you wouldn't know it from reading some of the cursory reviews from the "big name" sites that obviously didn't get into the game's depth.

The game IS a shooter on rails, but it's well done. I lived in Japan for years and the old Tokyo looks like shitamachi areas and the Upper City really has that Japanese technofuturistic feel. There is plenty of Japanese dialogue (which is well done, even if the translations are off a bit) and I really like how the signs and real brand names are incorporated into the backgrounds to really give life to the city.

The controls are OK and take a little getting used to. You will get knocked about, knocked down and staggered when taking damage and that can work against you when you take a shot from a boss, fall down and then he stomps you flat. You'll also have to complete some of the quicktime events more than once....as they are easy to screw up. Your squadmates can be a little obtuse, too, jumping in front of your fire and then griping about it.

The trust system is pretty cool but it doesn't affect your squad very much. What it DOES do, however, is affect the ending you see and you will want to keep high trust through the entire game. Just answer logically when they ask a question, don't shoot them and go for melee kills and headshots to bump that trust up.

The boss fights can be a little cheap. Each major boss has several attacks that will stagger you mid run and the final boss will aggravate you for a half hour with weapons that take you out in one hit. Thankfully, your squadmates can revive you and you can use first aid kits to both revive yourself AND your squadmates...which you want to do before they die! They will also help each other. The shops sell spare first aid kits, nanomachine upgrades, ammo, grenades, bosonic charge for your rifle and a limited selection of weapons.

It's not a long game. I'd estimate 10 to 15 hours total to get through it. But it's a good game with a pretty cool story. If you can pick it up for less than $20, definitely do so.

**Note: I had a mic but never really used the voice commands with that. You can hit a button and do the same thing.

title: All Hype, No Fun
text:
The original Deus Ex was a masterpiece for its time and I was eagerly awaiting this update to see what modern graphics could do...and I was immediately disappointed by the generic gameplay. This game is bargain bin, at best.

Story: You're some tough-looking generic guy with generic tough guy personality (gruff and serious) and you interact with poorly voice acted stereotypes to advance a storyline about augmenting humans with technology. This story rips off Shadowrun/cyberpunk and does a poor job. The story serves only to give the player something to think about while the load screen whisks the character off to the next linear stage. 1 out of 5

Graphics: The backgrounds look good (sharp and crisp) and the textures are VERY hi res and nice...however, in 2011, I expect a game to be in 1080p, not 720p. I also expect non-blocky character models that don't have bratwurst fingers and clipping on the mouths when characters speak. This game's graphics would have been excellent in 2007...in 2011, they are just mediocre. 2 out of 5

Sound: The sounds are good, but the voice acting is terrible...it's wooden, stilted and the characters SOUND like they're reading a script. If there is music, it's not memorable enough to remember or care about. The blips and bloops that the augments and environment make are right on, though. 2 out of 5

Controls: Pretty good. The walking animation is jerky and the hold+cover system is a little wonky, but the controls are pretty good. Aim assist helps when trying to aim with analog nubs. 4 out of 5

Gameplay: This is where Deus Ex: Human Revolution goes from "GAME OF THE YEAR BECAUSE WE GOT PAID TO SAY SO" (IGN) to the worst game that's come out this year. Almost nothing in the game world can be manipulated...in the original, all objects could be manipulated or messed with, somehow. In Deus Ex, the gorgeous environment is static: glass doesn't break unless it's a giant pane of it, microscopes can absorb bullets without moving, the only things to move are vending machines, boxes, crates and so on. Your super augmented avatar must eat and drink to restore energy to do melee attacks and use augmentations...yet, he cannot bust open a 12-pack of soda or open a glass door fridge. You can only get single cans left around. Lockers and drawers in offices contain boxes of bullets or grenades. You can't hop over obstacles while covered. Upgrades are hard to obtain.

(New paragraph!) Another huge problem is that this game offers NOTHING new in the genre. Modern games are ALWAYS: tough guy goes in against bad guys and is gruff and serious (or gruff and funny) and gets a lot of weapons, starting with a pistol and there's a rocket launcher somewhere. You need keys and you can upgrade abilities. THERE IS A COVER SYSTEM...hoo boy! Enemy AI is sad. You can headshot them and pitch a grenade in when their friends come to investigate. There is no point to being stealthy because your health regenerates...I didn't see anything in this game that other games haven't already done better. 0 out of 5

The best part of this game is that the box art is good and there are a LOT of people from Quebec that worked on it. The worst part is the game itself and that I cannot return it for a refund after opening it...

AVOID THIS GAME (or at least rent it, first). It's ALL hype and you know that the developers had to do some serious payday to the big magazines to get everyone convinced that clunky voice acting, mediocre graphics and boring gameplay are what people really want in 2011.

I am old enough to remember when innovation was the key driver for gaming, not graphics and a cover system....

title: Everything Is Great But the Controls!
text:
When I first played Resident Evil for the PSX, I thought it was just a limitation of the controls or PSX hardware that made the characters utterly unable to move while using a weapon...but it's something that's persisted through EVERY SINGLE GAME IN THE SERIES! With this being 2011 and the PS3 having more than enough horsepower to do it, I cannot understand why Capcom won't let you walk and shoot in this game!!! The graphics, sound, secrets and anything else becomes distant to the problem controls that you'll fight more than the onscreen zombies! Let's go through the specifics:

1. Graphics: Appropriately next gen in color and very gritty and realistic. Backgrounds are busy, but not so much that you'll lose your way (there is a good map system to help). The only crappy parts are the low res models of things you interact with (like in the first level where the melons look like billiard balls or the guts and goats look like PS2-era models). This game only runs in 720P, so you're not getting the 100% 1080P experience. The character models are very detailed and you get costumes for them, too, which is nice, but the faces suffer from that blockiness that plagues all games done before LA Noire...

2. Sound: The voices are a little less corny than usual and the music is OK. It's more for mood than anything, so you won't remember any of the tunes. The gun sounds are good and the zombie moans are also good.

3. Gameplay: 100% AWFUL. HORRIBLE. MISERABLE. What the other reviews fail to mention (except for the one star ones!!!) is that the controls are really complex and painful to get used to. You cannot shoot or melee and move at the same time, so you must plant in one place, move the nub to aim (no aim assistance!) and fire. If you melee, you must plant at the perfect distance from an enemy and swing your knife...if you're too far away, you'll miss and get jumped, whacked, stabbed, or axed. The camera is sort of fixed in a "cameraman" view, which means that it's 3rd person, slightly offset so that your character is on the left part of the screen. He/she also fills a good third of the screen, too, meaning that your field of vision is VERY limited. You can't see much on your left and you'll see only from your character's waist up, meaning that it is that much harder to estimate melee distance unless you are always looking downwards. In groups, you'll be jumped from all directions and never know it. Although I am sure none of this is a problem with the Move, it's really aggravating with the regular controller. Your partner gets in the way most of the time and only comes in handy when you're blindsided (which will happen very often) and kicks a zombie off of you or revives you. The controls alone make this game annoying to the point of breaking it, but add the limited field of vision and you're looking at a miserable experience.

4. Story: Standard RE stuff: zombies somewhere, Chris goes there, meets a woman, teams up. I frankly never even cared about the story, I was so dreading the actual gameplay.

I spent 10 minutes on this game and returned it. You'd think that moving and shooting would be standard in ANY action game, but Capcom distinguishes RE by eschewing that in favor of planting in one place. If you're a fan of awkward controls that get in the way of the gameplay (see Uncharted 2 for an awesome control system!) and make you not even CARE about the story, then get this game. If you need smooth controls, avoid this at ALL COSTS.

title: Looks Good, Plays Horribly
text:
The entire Armored Core series of games have always centered around large robots, infinitely customizable, and pilotable in multitudes of environments on various genres of missions. AC:For Answer definitely fits this pedigree and looks amazing. However, there are some serious flaws in this game that ruin the fun and remove this from the Must Play list of the casual gamer.

1. Camera: The camera angle is just a LITTLE too close to the player unit to be useful. You get a very narrow range of forward vision, so you'll constantly be straining to see what's directly ahead of your unit. The WORST part is that the right analog stick, used to look around, becomes extremely hard to use during duels with other ACs. Since those ACs strafe in a circle around your AC constantly and since they often have nicer boosters than you do, you spend 90% of your duel time trying to simply FIND the enemy with the camera spinning around. You spend the other 10% of your time locating the enemy and then waiting for missile lock. You'll spend quite a bit of time getting nailed by energy blasts and gunshots from behind, the side and everywhere you can't see.

2. Difficulty: Some missions are so easy, they're laughable. Others are so difficult, you'll die within seconds and not know why. The best one is where you get a VOB (booster) unit strapped to your back and rocket towards a large target while supporting units fire at you. Since you can't maneuver well, you take 5 hits and the mission's over. Lather, rinse, repeat.

3. Infinitely customizable, but...: There are thousands of combinations to choose from and each part can be further tuned with units of FRS memory, which is awarded for completing missions. However, out of the many combinations of equipment, only a few certain assemblies have any chance of surviving missions. Since there is no advance way to know just how long a mission will be or how many enemies you'll face, it's nearly impossible to plan a weapons loadout that would suit the mission until you play through it. To prevent this, specialty loadouts (i.e., all beam energy or all missle) are best shelved until the replay. I found the most success with a balanced loadout.

4. SLOWDOWN: On a lot of the missions when things get crazy, I saw my framerates drop to nothing. Arms Forts are HUGE and MASSIVE fortresses that spray missles all over the place (99% of them will unerringly home in on you) and when you rush up on one to destroy it, expect your framerates to drop to an almost unplayable level. I am not sure if installing the game to the PS3's hard drive ameliorates this, but it's horrible to see the PC gaming experience come to the PS3...

In all, this game is good for the hardcore fans and for anyone who enjoys spinning the camera around like crazy. For the casual gamer, though, this game is not enough fun and too much annoyance to be worth a purchase.

title: Great All-Around Mouse That Excels At Gaming, Too
text:
Let me just say that I've been playing FPS (first person shooter) games since the old days of Castle Wolfenstein and I've always used regular mice to play. When I was younger, it wasn't a problem to spend hours on a game with no aches and pains, but now I can't use a normal mouse for much longer than an hour without a twinge somewhere or another in my hand. When I was looking into getting a new mouse to replace the little optical one I had been using (quite painfully, might I add), I came across this in a computer store. I tried the demo model and ordered one immediately. I was hooked!

This mouse is BIG and HEAVY when compared to most mice and, when put up against the Logitech gaming lineup, it seems to be at a disadvantage. The mouse seems less graceful and the buttons aren't as hair-trigger responsive as the Logitech lineup...however, once I started seriously using this mouse in everyday situations (net surfing, Photoshop, etc.) it really showed its excellent design. It fits comfortably in the hand and doesn't require that the fingers be constantly poised above the buttons. You can rest your fingers across the buttons and push easily when you want to click. This is CRITICAL in games for me, since holding my fingers over the buttons (as I had been doing before) was what seriously wore my finger tendons out so quickly. Being able to rest my fingers, yet respond quickly to input helped keep my game scores up while not wearing out my hand. The weights seemed gimmicky at first, but I quickly learned that extra weights really helped me keep the mouse stable and it reduced my twitching in FPS games.

The LCD IS a gimmick, no doubt, but the ability to switch 3 DPI settings on the fly is nice. In FPS games, general gameplay is good around 2000 DPI, but precision shooting (like for a sniper class in an FPS) requires MUCH less mouse movement over a broad area and more controlled movement in a smaller area. 1600DPI is perfect for this. I can instantly switch, as needed, with no delays. The side buttons are also perfect for alt fire and are easily pressed with the thumb. I haven't used the macros, so I can't comment on that feature, but even the heavy scroll wheel just feels much nicer on the fingers.

The feet might make a difference if you're not using a nice mousepad.

The best feature by far is the weighted box that stores the spare feet and weights. It holds down the cable very well. Kudos to Microsoft for getting that right!

In conclusion, I would say that if you still have the ability to poise your index and middle finger over sensitive mouse buttons for hours on end, you might find better results with another mouse. However, if you've got scars on your tendons from too much mouse use, trying this mouse out will be wonderful. The weight, button presses and ergonomics are great. The bonuses of the DPI switch, adjustable weights/feet and the cable weight box just turn this mouse into an excellent value.

5 stars. A worthy recipient of the Sidewinder name.

title: FInally, A Game For PSP That Makes SENSE
text:
If you're a PSP owner, then you're no doubt aware that a lot of PSP games are either rush jobs for a quick buck or poorly-done ports of old PS1 games. Developers also want to take a system not designed for handling a lot of polygons and lots of analog action and try to make action games for them...so you'll be pleased to discover that Metal Gear Acid 2 is a game that is made for the limitations of the PSP and works WITH the system to give a sound, fun and solid(us?) gaming experience.

First off, the game eschews long, drawn-out dialogue scenes for long, drawn-out text passages. It seems like bloviating and long-winded proselytizing are trademarks of the MGS line, so adding a fast text skip button gets you into the action quickly. However, there IS some small snippet here or there of dialogue and it breaks things up a bit. I'm glad they chose not to go with full motion polygon movies and speech because they used that saved space very wisely. The game looks..well, gorgeous, with the characters sharp, cel-shaded, loudly-colored and detail all over the place. The art is classic Konami excellence with none of that messy, brush splatter confusion of Ashley Wood anywhere to be seen. You get crisp, cool, cartoony Snake and Friends and it looks marvelous. Anime speed lines, camera cuts and a very decent in-game camera control make this game a treat to play. Also included is a cardboard version of those Magic Eye puzzles where you get a split screen image and the included cardboard box overlay makes it pseudo-3D (you can also use your eyes, if you're good at those Magic Eye things.) This is just a little extra and you don't lose anything by leaving it out. The designers also included a ton of secret cards and the capability to access MGS3 for the PS2 via USB to USB mini cable for photo transfer! The sounds are generic, as is the music, but it fits and doesn't stomp all over the game.

The game itself doesn't rely on quick reflexes so much as it does planning, some strategy and luck (on card draws). The game and manual are no real help for newbies and unless you can find someone else to explain it better, you'll be sort of lost through the first few missions as you learn the game's fine points. I particularly enjoy the turn-based aspect of this game. As I've grown older, I've lost a lot of the ability to play fast reflex games and the PSP, with its small screen, isn't ideally suited for games where a camera angle is the difference between life and death. That's just frustrating (see: MGS:Portable Ops for this problem). This game allows for planning moves and seeing the battlefield; this is something I appreciate. This game seems more fun and relaxing than worrying that the wall you can't see around has 14 guards to ruin your gametime.

This game is interesting, unique and oddball enough with plenty of flair to attract those not really into fast action games. However, it's also a good diversion from the usual PSP fare.

I highly recommend this!

title: A Standard-Setting Game
text:
With a game like this, it's easy to see how much expectation there was for the PSP. Killer graphics (even by today's standards), great sound (if you like the techno beats from the PS version), great, responsive gameplay and strategy all wrapped up in a tiny silver disc! It even has online features and playing with friends is a blast! That most PSP games are pathetic ports of PS1 games and crappy movie adaptations is disappointing in the face of games like this. It's almost like Sony said, "OK guys, HERE'S how you make a PSP game," and then the developers promptly ignored them!!!

First off, the graphics are gorgeous. Futuristic and smooth. The music is appropriate and very techno. The controls are crisp and mastering the airbrake system on each racer is the key to victory...since hamfisted handling WILL result in eating wall and losing races. There is a certain strategy to hitting boost points and picking up weapons for use against others or for a quick energy boost. You can't just mash the button and ride a rail all the way to the finish line; you have to be involved and jink/dodge/boost/draft/ram your way in!

I got this game used for $9.99 and it's more fun than the new crop of PSP games coming out. I highly recommend it; even if you get frustrated racing against others, you can do time trials or free racing as a quick diversion and play against yourself.

Can't go wrong here. AWESOME game. WHERE'S WIPEOUT 2?

title: A Great Game, But Only If You're Hardcore
text:
What made the Metal Gear series so wonderful was the concept of a lone operative sneaking into a base a la James Bond, but doing it realistically (crawling, hiding, sniping) instead of getting invited to a white-tie dinner by the bad guy. In the first PS1 game, you could be a novice player and still make it through the game, each time you play making you better and better. The PS2 games got more and more complex, sort of bloating up the concept with more complex controls and quick reaction scenarios where the average player would get creamed over and over again until the learning curve was passed. These "frustration points," as I call them got more and more numerous until MGS3, where the entire last third of the game was essentially one long frustration point (e.g., oops, stepped wrong, you die, oops, didn't make the shot, you die, oops, didn't lead the girl through 5 screens of bad guys safely, start over, etc.) To a hardcore gamer, these challenges are meat and potatoes, but to a casual gamer that can't play daily, the fourteenth time that 3 Metal Gears blow Snake into atoms is the time that the game gets shelved permanently. This is where MGS:Portable Ops puts itself: it's JUST hard enough to make the hardcore MGS fans want more, but JUST hard enough to frustrate the casual gamer into just shelving it.

First off, the game looks great and the sounds are perfect. How they crammed all of this into a UMD is spectacular and shows how well software developers can compensate for poorly-designed hardware. The controls aren't too bad, but the analog nub can be hard to control at times. The real permanent frustration point in the game comes with the camera, which seems to have a mind of its own. Dragging enemies (a HUGE part of the game) becomes a comedy of errors as the whirling camera causes you to spin around while you get used to the analog nub...you look like you're tangoing with a drunken partner! The camera likes to sit right up against your active man, so you can't pan out and get a wider view of things...this is especially fatal when going through doors, where you can see an all clear and pop out right into a guard's line of fire. For me, the camera is enough to make the game unpleasant...but I suppose it can be gotten used to. The missions are broken up into little ones (UMD format again) and they seem fine. They make sense and you do have some sense of time in the game. Well done!

MGS games are all about sneaking and infiltrating. Well, this MGS takes it one step further by allowing you to recruit soldiers for different teams (this has been explained in other reviews.) This is sort of a tactics-style development where you can outfit the troops, put them in squads and deploy them as a team. However, the developers decided to hamstring this potentially fun feature by making it so killed soldiers never return...so you can get a secret character for a major accomplishment...and he gets an unlucky camera angle on the next mission and ends up getting jumped by 3 guards. Well, your hard-earned man is now gone forever unless you reload. By making the risk too great, this keeps casual gamers from risking hard-earned troops on the battlefield. They should have an option for an easier mode where the soldiers can be brought back. However, the saving grace is that the unique characters (such as Snake) can be brought back and recover slowly.

This game is very complex and mastering it, or even proceeding in it takes a large time investment...unfortunately, it's not one that most casual or older gamers might be able to make. The manual only tells you how things work on a basic level and, like ALL NEW GAMES TODAY, you can't just have fun and play through...you've got to have the FAQ/game guide/cheat sheet with you or you'll never get 100% complete and the best ending. Lame.

With very little to reward the casual gamer, I can't recommend this as a 5-star pick. I'd rate it a 1. However, since it's so appealing by its tough nature to hardcore gamers (5 stars for them!), it DOES merit a 3 on the fun factor (1+5/2). The polish of the game is super and only the whirly camera demon knocks it down to 4 stars.

title: Pretty, But Flawed
text:
This game is lush, rich with color and has graphics that will go down forever as some of the best that Square-Enix has ever produced. The game mechanics are sound and more like the online FFXI (no loading screens for every battle!) but the game, like most Final Fantasies, loses its lustre about halfway through.

The numerous other reviews cover the pros and cons of the game in detail so I won't repeat them here. What I WILL say, though, is that the designers seem to always want the gamers to lose interest in their game 50% of the way through. For example, if you've enjoyed the game up to the 5 mandragora fight, the frustration and irritation will be enough to make you quit. It's one thing if there's a strategy or some tactic to use and discover, but this fight is just a borefest of repetitively hitting one monster, watching your entire party get hit with 5 status effects simultaneously and having them lose 80% of their HP. You barely survive, inflict a scratch or two on one of the 5 monsters...and repeat, repeat, repeat. After 3 hours of this, I had enough. Checking game guides and FAQs reveals that this battle is exactly how I described it. Even though each monster has a weakness, you won't want to win the fight. Also, getting money is so difficult, that boss battles will WRECK your item stores and you have to sit and gather money for hours just to move forward. It gets to the point where I can't stand it anymore and I just use a Gameshark to get 9999999999 gil!

There is also a lot of random wandering and wasted time backtracking if you don't have some sort of game guide map. If you're like me and you have a day job and can only play games for a few hours a week, you want to get the most out of your games and see more of their stories...not slog around the same area for 5 months just to get to level ____ so you can barely beat the area boss! I know that the game has to be made to satisfy a large cross section of gaming styles, but it would be nice to have all the straightforward bosses and areas be critical to the game and put the super-annoying bosses and areas to the side so that casual gamers can play through and see more of the entrancing storyline and visuals and the hardcore gamers can wear themselves ragged on beating some stupid turnip people. This game will make boss fights so hard that you cannot pass them at a reasonable level...or you have to have the foresight to buy some gambit or license or spell or weapon to win...if you didn't, then you have to start over from the last save point and slog back to town and then slog back to the boss.

I wish, I wish, I wish this game could be more story-oriented than "let's make the player hang out for 15 hours of power-leveling and gil-gathering goodness so he can tear his eyeballs out when he gets beaten by the bosses and finds out he needs SIXTEEN hours of leveling!"

Slogging through endless battles and having to go backtrack in resource gathering as well as terrain-wise gets this game a 2 in fun. The visuals, sound, voice acting, plot and the world it creates merits a 4. This game is flashy...but not so much fun.

NOTE: I have played and beat every Final Fantasy from 1-10 (plus X-2) and the mechanics of having to sit and level in some way are similar in all of them...I'm just too busy to enjoy sitting around to do it anymore.

title: Ignore the Subject Matter...This Game Is Just Plain Fun!
text:
OK, just ignore the fact that this game is Pokemon-based for a moment. DS games are fun because the stylus allows for new types of gameplay and games that use this feature in novel ways are fast becoming a trademark for Nintendo, who can sell truckloads of DS units for each PSP that is sold. Why? Well, rather than try to make PS2 games work on a tiny unit that can't process the polygons or duplicate the controls, Nintendo wisely decided to make new, fun games for the DS and leave direct ports to GBA carts that DS owners could also pick up if they want some old-school action. This concept of fun leads into the review of Pokemon Rangers.

The premise is fairly easy, since Pokemon products are targeted at kids. You're a male or female Pokemon Ranger neophyte, fresh in from the sticks and ready for training. Your job is to basically assist people and Pokemon whenever they need it and defend Pokemon from greedy and neglectful individuals. The intro is a bit long, but it's good to get the basics and story down. You have a special Ranger tool called the "Capture Styler" that can, with your effort and goodwill, impart a calming emotion to wild or upset Pokemon and calm them down. This is the entire capturing concept. Once you've captured the Pokemon, its info is registered in the browser on the top screen and you can have the Pokemon follow you around. Captured Pokemon can be used in several ways: certain Pokemon have "field moves" that can break rocks, cut fences, grapple posts to pull you across water and so on. Most Pokemon can also assist you in capturing by enhancing your styler with powers (e.g., grass assist makes your styler trail into grass, which stops Pokemon that touch it) and the electric Pokemon can recharge your styler. This recharge capability becomes critical later on, as there is no real violence, but Pokemon can attack your styler line and damage it (0 styler energy=game over) and having a refill is always handy. The kicker to this entire concept of using Pokemon is that, in the interest of not exploiting the Pokemon unfairly, you can only use their power once. The only exception is your personal Pokemon, which you can charge up and use over and over. Additionally, you may only have a limited number of captured Pokemon at one time and you have to let them free whenever you leave their native area. This makes for some serious strategy, as you have to balance their usefulness in capturing with the necessity to clear obstacles with their field moves. Also, do you carry a bunch of recharge Pokemon and only one field move one or do you balance out your herd with a battle-useful one, a recharge one and maybe a couple of field-useful ones? This element is a welcome change of pace from the usual "your gun can always fire unlimited bullets, just go get this one key and run across the map to unlock the door." In this game, if you choose wisely, you can have a herd assembled and just blaze through obstacles.

This game offers no real violence, as said before. The "battles" are just capture sessions with no real time limit. The Pokemon (one or more) appear in the bottom screen and immediately begin to amble, fly or ooze about. Most of them have attacks that randomly go off and some can respond to seeing the styler capture loop...the trick is to time the capture correctly and avoid damage to the styler. It gets progressively harder, forcing you to not just draw stupid circles all day, but wait and figure out patterns, try new strategies and take risks. I'm sure it can get old after 4 or 5 hours straight, but in short doses, this is a welcome change of pace.

The only real downside to the game is the sound. The music is lame and the Pokemon make generic-sounding shrieks or cries instead of saying their name like they do in the cartoons. The graphics are cartoonish, but fairly sharp and you can interact with a lot of objects. The bottom screen holds all of the interaction and the top is taken up by the Stylus radar screen, so it's good use of the DS real estate.

This game is good for kids because it teaches them resource management, hand-eye coordination and risk taking and does so in a very kid-friendly manner that doesn't involve blood, gore and foul language. For adults, the premise and graphics might seem puerile, but the game IS fun in doses and is great for a breaktime distraction.

This game is worth getting, in my opinion. There's just too much fun and strategy to be had in such a small package.

title: Updated, But Never Overrated or Outdated
text:
I remember buying FF2/4 the day it came out and playing it for 12 straight hours. The combination of the graphics and lush (for that time) scenery was almost too much to handle and the music is STILL stuck in my head to this day. Much like FF3/6, this game is one of the classics that's in the Top 10 RPGs of ALL time. Here is a breakdown of the game according to my rating system, with the original being the perfect standard:

Graphics: The GBA/DS doesn't disappoint with the sharper resolution and what seems to be slightly enhanced colors. The portrait redraws are OK and the sprites all seemed to have at least been retouched with some more saturation. The Mode 7 effects and all the magic effects are still the same. There wasn't much improvement in this area and since GBA games are almost direct copies of SNES games, this isn't a big deal. I was a little disappointed that they didn't add some richer textures and patterns in the games to make it sort of like the eye-popping visuals of FF3/6, but since it copies the original, that's OK. 8 out of 10

Sound: This is where the limitation of the GBA hardware comes into play. The sounds are tinny, with none of that rumbly bass the SNES sound engine had (even with high quality headphones.) The songs haven't been changed, but they're running through a different wavetable and it is obvious to those who remember the old SNES sounds. It's still good, though. This is one of the nicest soundtracks ever made to a game and it holds up well to anything today. 7 out of 10

Translation: I've played the full Japanese and original versions and I have to say that I am both pleasantly and unpleasantly surprised by the new dialogue. While it DOES flow smoothly and articles are in place (i.e., THE Sand Ruby, instead of Sand Ruby), the translation takes minor liberties with the dialogue that can sort of spoil the original feel. For example, fans of the original will be disappointed to learn that the magic spells are changed from FIRE 1, FIRE 2, FIRE 3 to the modern standard of Fire, Fira and Firaga. It's not a huge deal, but I kind of miss the old names. While "spoony bard" is still there, the package from the original is replaced with Bomb Ring. Part of the mystery and sadness of Mysidia's destruction was that Cecil and Kain had no idea what was in the package and were just dupes. Well...if you can't guess what a BOMB RING does, then you are as dull as a...well, Dark Knight's buttplate. The text can be tiny at times...for old folks like me with bad eyesight, this can be troublesome. Overall, the story hasn't changed and is as good as ever. 7 out of 10

Gameplay: This is where the game shines, as nothing has been subtracted from the original. Rather, things have been added: easier gameplay through the first half, additonal dungeons, and bestiary. 10 out of 10.

If you liked the SNES version and need a portable one, then you need this game. However, unlike FFI&II: Dawn of Souls, you're not getting a huge upgrade over the original and, in cases like the music, you're getting a little shortchanged. If you don't need this to take on a trip, I'd recommend just playing the SNES version. I know I still have mine!

Overall, I'd highly recommend this: 32 out of 40. Grade: A

title: quality + great value
text:

title: Great compact, ergonomic mouse
text:
I have MANY mice and am always buying new ones to try and find something better. I was a huge fan of the Roccat Kone XTD. It was a little large for my hand, but the shape was perfect. This is essentially the same mouse but like 15% smaller.

When I first bought the mouse I didn't like it and almost returned it. The case material is pleasant feeling, but slippery and my hand would just slide up the mouse body and off. I put 4 strips of grip tape on the mouse and it's a whole nother animal. The tape make it just a hair larger which I like, but more importantly it sticks to my hand. My thumb and ring finger fit in the grooves perfectly and my other fingers lay on top of the mouse. I've been trying to find another like this but I haven't. The closest is the Mionix Castor, which does have a similar shape.

Ergonomics is the most important factor for me, but it also has a premium scroll wheel and quality buttons (My previous Roccat mice had Omron switches, I haven't opened this one yet). There is an LED logo and to be honest I don't know if it is RBG. I've used the Swarm software really only to change the DPI presets so I have not delved into it too deeply. I know for some the software will make or break their experience, but for me it is not important. You can set them (DPI) and use the buttons on the mouse to scroll up and down through your chosen presets. I am also a fan of the braided cable.

The grip is not for everyone and if you have larger hands , I would imagine the smaller size would cause your hand to cramp. Also, as I said, I found the mouse unusable without sports grip tape. I prefer wired mice, but I do wish this was available in a wireless variant.

text:
I purchased these keycaps to replace the ones on my DROP Alt keyboard.

title: One of the best prebuilt keyboards available.
text:
I just purchased this and have not owned it for long, but I was anxious to type at length. The main reasons I purchased this board were for it's hotswap capabilities as well as the low profile/zero tilt case. For some reason flat enthusiast mechanical keyboards are almost unheard of. I have lower profile board in space gray, with Halo Clear switches.

Keycaps- The keycaps are certainly better than average, and they better be for the cost of this board. I prefer PBT- I like the harder material, the sound, and the rougher texture. However, these are almost too rough- they are gritty like sandpaper. My favorite keycaps are Leopold. Just to compare the keycaps on the Anne Pro II are also PBT, but they are pretty smooth and not ideal. I like the font and the shine through legends. On two sides they measure 1.33mm and the other two 1.01. I'm not sure why they are not even all around. The are OEM profile and have a pleasant sound. I may replace them, but am not rushing to do so.

Switches- This board has Halo Clears, though there are about 1/2 dozen other choices available. These are rated at 63 grams I believe, but they bottom out at 80 grams. They are heavy. The are smooth and have good tactility- and I like the force curve. They all ping like crazy however which annoys the heck out of me. I like these a lot, but I will be swapping the springs out for lighter ones. There is minimal switch wobble, but I think the heavier springs help to mitigate some of that.

Case- the case is flat and low profile which I like. It is aluminum which I'm neutral about. I'm perfectly fine with plastic and the metal adds cost to the whole package. This is a "floating switch" design, meaning the bottom of the switches are exposed. I used to like this, but I actually prefer the more tradition kind where the bezel covers the base of the switch. The case has zero tilt which was my number one requirement. It comes with magnetic feet which are quite sturdy and raise the incline about 4-5 degrees. There are recessed hole the feet go into and the case can even be declined. Don't worry they are not coming off if you slide the board. I actually had a really difficult time getting them off after I attached them.

RGB- These can be adjusted using FN plus various letters and there are controls for brightness, breathing, color, scrolling pattern, etc. I don't know if there is more fine tuning control when you flash the firmware (I just use a dim backlight). There is also RGB going around the base of the case which I turn off.

Stabilizers- I can detect just a slight rattle in the space bar, but I think the heavier springs help to prevent some vibration. I have read that the stabs are not very good so I have already purchased new ones and will be installing them tomorrow.

Software/Programmability- I have not experimented with this yet. There is a process to flash the firmware for the layout you desire. I would remap the Fn to the CapsLock and then the arrows to I,J,K,L.

Overall Value- $200 dollars is a lot of money for a keyboard. At this price point you can just about build the board yourself and choose the components. I would have chosen different switches (though I'm really starting to like these) and a plastic case which would have saved money, and different keycaps. However, I paid $140 for this new on eBay and I feel at this price it is a great value. Ultimately it was the flat case that made me pull the trigger. I have heard of people complaining about the rattling stabilizers which they felt should not happen at this price point.

I should also point out that there may be some issues with the USB-C cable. Some cables are not compatible- I believe they need to be rated for 2.4a, and not just data. I will say that my own USB- Cable would not even fit in the port which was strange- I did not force it. For people who like to use the fancy coiled cables they may not work.

Included in the case is a switch puller, keycap puller, and the feet. The are all wedged in the foam base.

title: Mionix Castor review- shark fin grey
text:
I am not a frequent gamer, but I enjoy using products endorsed by the gaming community. My Roccat Kone XTD was beginning to wear after 2 years, so I thought about replacing it with the same mouse. I decided however to try a different mouse that caters to somebody with a different grip. I don't have much to say, but I will comment on the features that are important to this group:

First_ the box. I like the way the product was presented. The box is of quality, but I would love to have it exist in just a clamshell package and a 1 page sheet with info and a link to downloads and any relevant product manual. Use the money for some other feature, like a second DPI button.

Second_ the software. It's minimalist. There are adjustments for anglesnap and many other features. I like that you can control the number of steps. The Roccat however, the software just blows me away. It tracks every click and turns it into awards when certain milestones are reached. It's fun. You can use this information in your gameplay, and it's kind of fun. Oh, I've said that already, lol.

Third_ the building materials. The surface is kind of a rubberized material. IDK if it contains latex. It is comfortable, but I still prefer the build of the Roccat. This surface retains heat from the user's hand and with use is warm to the touch. The buttons are LOUD. The clicks feel of quality. I prefer the clicks of the Omron switches. I like the braided cord. The mouse however is too light. I am however used to the Roccat which is larger and has added weights.

Fourth_ ergonomics. I have a small hand. The mouse feels a little small, but I'm a palm grip user. I bought this because I thought it was good looking and I wanted something different that would make me want to use other grips. The forward button is a little hard to reach. The scroll feels of quality and the clicks are distinct, but it's a little small. I noticed now that you can't click the mouse wheel right and left. There are grooves that support your last two fingers, however.The Roccat lacks these grooves, but the height prevents your fingers from touching. The Castor is a little slippery, which makes the lift and drop technique possible.

It is quite comfortable, but the biggest flaw (to me) is the lack of height from the heel, but this comes from a person who prefers a palm grip. This is a fingertip style mouse, which the Roccat does quite well. Claw grip work best with tiny notebook style mice. FOUR stars **** . I would not buy again, but I think it's a good buy, especially at the now lower 38 dollar price tag. Enjoy! I hope I was helpful.

title: Roccat Kone XTD
text:
Let me start off by saying, this is a BIG mouse. It is long and wide.

In the realm of "gaming" mouses (I don't game) there are many options, but there are few with a tilting scroll wheel. That severely limited my choices and is what made me pull the trigger on this. I love the texture, the lights, and the responsiveness of this mouse. The mouse is ever so slightly big for my hand, but it is a right handed grip which kind of tells your hand exactly where to go. The scroll wheel feels of quality, but it is quite stiff. The cord is braided and light and you can barely tell it is there.

My previous mice were a Logitech M510 and LX8 cordless mouse. These were smaller and ambidextrous and I found the grip to be perfect. In fact I just came across a mouse called the M500 which is corded and has all the features I like. I may in-fact purchase that one too.

Edit:I have used the mouse for a few additional weeks and it has grown on me. My older mouse makes my hand feel like cramping when I use it. I however keep my old M510 nearby in case I feel like using the claw grip, but compared to this one it seems so inaccurate and unresponsive. I am changing my review from 4 stars to 5 stars.____ This is a "palm grip" mouse, no question about that. But I can move my hand back and still use a claw grip if I so choose, and it feels comfortable.

Choosing a mouse without trying it first is difficult. You can read reviews and they can give you some insight, but it is a subjective experience. This is definitely one of the ones you should try, along with a few other names like the death adder.

Edit: I've had this for 3 1/2 years and it's still the best I've used. The forward and back buttons are in the perfect spot. The DPI buttons are conveniently located. I initially liked the Deathadder, but I now think it's crap. It feels cheap, the button clicks feel cheap, and the forward and back buttons both double and triple click. I haven't owned enough mouses to comment on the sensor as some say there are better ones, but it feels 100% accurate for me. I would say that a corded mouse is infinitely better than a wireless one.

With smaller mouses I tend to rest the heel of my hand on the desk and it causes me wrist and finger pain. This allows me to keep my wrist straight.

title: It's a winner
text:
I had been interested in mechanical keyboards for a long time, but honestly I didn’t really know what to expect. From the moment I pulled this thing out of the box I could instantly tell it was a very high quality piece of hardware. It has a metal frame with very solid keys. I eagerly plugged it in and connected my mouse through the port extension on the back of the keyboard.

There was a solid, deep red glow emanating from the keys. Very impressive. Typing on it is pure joy, despite quite a long learning curve. I don’t mind the adjustment because it's so pleasing to type on something so well made. The reason why it’s taken a while to adjust is because the Rapidfire indicates extreme sensitivity of the keys – if they travel just over a millimeter they will signal a keystroke. This means you have to be accurate and not attack your keyboard like you would with a cheaper brand. The backspace key posed the largest problem when browsing, as just north of it F11 triggers full screen browsing and F12 opens the source examine pane in Chrome. A little adjustment is all it took and now I’m learning to quickly and accurately graze the keys in order to type instead of bottoming out. It truly is a joy to type on the K70 Rapidfire.

It’s very comfortable to type on this keyboard. I usually don’t keep the included wrist rest attached unless I have some heavy word processing to do. It doesn’t seem like it adds much ergonomically, but it makes a huge difference when cranking out detailed reviews for Amazon :D (I’m on it right now).

Regarding the RGB indicated in the name, it’s a nod to the LED Array under the keys, and I’ve only mentioned the ominous red embers. In order to truly make use of these functions you need to get on Corsair’s website and download the Corsair Utility Engine (CUE) software. Be prepared when you do – the rainbow of color explosion that happens when you first fire up the CUE program is dazzling. It gives you a good idea of exactly how much control you have. It took some learning and a bit of video tutorial hunting but I learned to navigate the program and was creating my own custom color combos and animations in an afternoon – This is especially helpful to label hotkeys for your commonly used programs.

Protip: You can download presets for the K70 Rapidfire, but many won’t work by default. Once you download the *.prf files you’ll need to use a program like Notepad++ to open and edit the name of the hardware in the line of code that says modelName>K70 RGB RAPIDFIRE</modelName – Make sure it has this modelname (I know the K70 standard models work, but others may too) This is a new keyboard and it doesn’t have many presets yet, but the ones I use from other models that look great are Poison, Knight Rider, Hologram, and Sonar.

The only problem that I have with this keyboard is that it’s spoiled me rotten. Look how much I typed in this review xD. I’m going to have to replace my keyboards at the office too :P

5 stars. Get one. You won’t regret it.

(Btw, one sexy feature I forgot to mention that I’m crazy about is the knurled metal wheel in the top right hand corner that controls the volume. It looks really cool and feels great to use. It’s the only control that’s not assignable on this keyboard and it doesn’t need to be. It’s absolutely perfect the way it is.)

I like this controller a lot – I’ll definitely be hanging on to it for my PC gaming.
