title: This is the best XBox-style controller ever made - as many top PC reviews have acknowledged
text:
I have own several MS controllers over the years - first the 360 series, then two controllers since, the latest MS controller was the XBox One Wireless for XBox and PC. It was a solid controller. BUT....

Fast forward just a couple years and Razer have delivered truly superior controllers. In my opinion, the best of these is this one, the Razer Wolverine Ultimate. Not only are the extra paddle controllers seriously well-designed and implemented, but the alternative shoulder buttons [two of the six extra controls in all] are, for me, more easily accessible and that translates to better mobility and faster response for me.

I was a bit disappointed to discover that the full setup and sensitivity adjustment is only available from their XBox Controller Setup and Configuration utility (their own website and documentation indicate that this can be done from their Synapse software, but it cannot be. That is wrong [not a misprint really - it blatantly says that Synapse will handle setup]. This is not an issue for most, but since they make the utility ONLY available from Microsoft Store, it is an issue for many like myself.

Fortunately, most game software today will provide at least minimal adjustment of sensitivity [for stick controls, i.e. deadzone and x/y responsiveness]. The MS Store is often a corrupted mechanism on Windows computers - just google a little and you'll find out that many suffer from MS Store AppxBundles not being handled or failing to install due to "unknown error 0x800700005" and similar - which turn out to be registry permissions corruptions (mine were caused by a Windows patch via "Windows Update" of all things). This means no Razer setup utility for me. (I am not going to reinstall the OS and all my software and configuration tweaks just to get this utility working). I don't need MS Store and I will never use it... even though MS cons their direct competitors (yes, MS manufactures an XBox controller too, did you know? lol) in to relying upon them for this Software Distribution.. i.e. fox and henhouse. They make Synapse, along with the Macro module, and the Chroma/RGB software available from Razer's website, but not this one controller setup utility [which is Razer software, after all]. Not sure why.

You can get by FINE without this Razer utility though - the controller is ONBOARD programmable, i.e. the means to override the default settings for the six "M buttons" is built in to the device itself and documented in the user guide. There is even a MACRO capability available via Synapse and an add-on module. This allows complex keyboard sequences to be associated to one or more button presses [i.e. L-Shoulder longpress + A, B, X, Y, etc...].

This controller is the best I've ever used for PC gaming [if I still used XBox that would apply as well]. I love it. I don't really need the RGB light-show, which is admittedly cool I guess, and even rarely use the M buttons. It is just the feel and response that I find unequaled.

title: One of the best out there...well worth the money!!!
text:
I came back to review this, and saw my original review never went through...I had rated it after a day of playing it and only gave it 2 stars!

I picked it back up a couple months ago and have played it nearly nonstop! There is SO MUCH to do in this game! You get to choose your Life, or Lives really. I started out as an Angler (fisherman) and it was really fun. Later, I almost wished I'd started off as a Paladin or Mercenary because I really needed those particular stats to beat higher "monsters". Presently, I'm at Hero rank as Angler, Paladin, Carpenter, Cook, Woodcutter, and a Master at Crafting. Honestly, I'm glad I didn't start out my "main" or first life as a crafter, carpenter, cook, or woodcutter. Maybe it's ok if you switch often into other lives like Paladin for instance. I'm finding Paladin to be probably most important as I've got the add-on content of Origin Island and the enemies are even harder to defeat.

It's charming, I love the scenery and the characters, and the fact you can buy different houses in different lands and decorate them, also there is the quick travel which helps immensely when you're striving to complete certain quests. I have played so many hours on this, and still have several lives to start still. I think sewing will be fun to make new outfits but for now I'm so busy battling I'm usually in my Paladin gear.

There is just so much to do in this game it's unbelievable. You shop, buy, sell, create, decorate, chop down trees, mine, become an alchemist, do witchcraft, craft, make furniture, battle, fish...and going to different lands makes for an amazing experience. The graphics are great and the details are amazing. As the storyline progresses as well you are able to add many different parties (like the Princess, the Dark Lord, and many others) to accompany you on your adventures. When you level up you get points you can add to you or other members in your party (like attack, intelligence, dexterity, etc). There is no shortage on what you can do!

title: My Favorite New Keyboard
text:

There is less key travel, so it feels comparable to a membrane keyboard. The keys have a satisfying sound, making typing fun.

My only gripe is that the battery doesn't last longer. I got about 3 days out of it before it completely died on me. Mind you, they were not 3 full days of work and clocked in much less than the advertised 48 hours. I have turned down the backlight to 50% power, so we'll see if I can get at least another day out of it. Since the keyboard has RGB backlight, I want rainbow vomit, so dimming the backlight kind of bums me out. But TBH, the backlight and the lack of shine through keycaps don't really make the backlight stand out as much as I wish it could.

A want but not a must would be alternative keycaps in a different color palette (i.e. not blue or grey) and the ability to order keycaps with different language layouts. I'm planning on participating in a group buy for pink and mint keycaps, so I guess that'll work. I'm sure that since NuPhy is a smaller company, they don't have the inventory to stock as many choices as a company like Apple does. Oh well! One can hope for the next time I purchase a keyboard from NuPhy!

title: Help, I'm addicted! Only one drawback for me otherwise I love it 🙌🏼
text:
First thing to know and keep in mind is that I'm a newbie to Animal Crossing- about a month into the world of it (so I'm not able to compare to old school versions) and I started out playing Pocket Camp. While I love Pocket Camp and don't want to have to stop playing that version, I just can't do the cost part of it. I was tempted to but thought I'd just put money into buying New Horizons, instead (I'd probably have spent more on Pocket Camp!). We already have a Switch to play on. I'm so glad I got it! It's just as addicting. Purchasing the online code and downloading it to our Switch was a breeze and pretty fast to do.

I’ll try to group different points/subjects, regarding the game, in paragraphs below since it might be long and to hopefully help read or skim through. Even with a lengthy review, there’s a lot more to it...especially since I’m still fairly new to it myself!

***MULTIPLAYERS*** This may be a long-winded paragraph but I feel like this is one of the most important things to know about this game. Normally, I’m that person that does a ton of research before buying pricey items but I guess since I had been so into Pocket Camp and was excited about getting New Horizons, I didn’t spend as much time researching it. I still would have purchased the game but the main issue I have with it--and my reason for giving only 4-stars-- is because you can have only ONE island PER CONSOLE. It’s a bit frustrating in our house and I could see this being even more disappointing for others (especially if they too didn’t know beforehand). Such as families with more than one kid wanting to play (we just have one child). For example, I was the first person to play the game and set up the island. I remembered seeing something about multiplayers so I later started to play with my daughter and looked up how to do so. We soon figured out that she could have a seperate profile and character but her character has to live on my island and share resources for collecting items and all. This means that certain functions, like naming the island and being in charge of certain things, won’t work for her. Also, we can play at the same time but this can potentially get frustrating since you have to take turns to do certain functions and requires switching back-and-forth between players to do the activity. The assigned leader can do things like sell or craft items, and the follower can only “stand” there and wait until they’re done. The follower can collect items at the same time as the leader but it won’t go into their inventory- instead it goes to a bin at a certain part of the island. They can go and get the items to add to their inventory but it requires going to that part of the island and toggling to become the leader to add the items. It all just makes things a little more time consuming, though it is still a bit fun to play together. For some people this may not even be an issue. For us, we have played Minecraft on Playstation together and assumed it would be set up like that-- you can play in one world at the same time but the screen is split which allows each player/character to go to different parts of the world, do different tasks and get different items...or even build something together. I personally would really like it if they would allow that to happen on Animal Crossing! Though, compared to Pocket Camp, it is cool to at least be on the same screen together instead of only being able to visit each other’s camps at seperate times.

TIME SPENT AND CHARACTER SETUP-
Note that this game is very time consuming! It goes by real-life time (at setup you’ll choose your time zone), so if it’s night time for you- it will be night time on your game. Being that it’s so time consuming, It may not be for everyone- understandably! It’s certainly getting me through this time, in real-life, with the pandemic going on and staying at home. You of course can stop playing at any point but to level-up and do different activities, it does take a good bit of time...and patience! While I did purchase this game for me, I occasionally let my 9 year old play and give her a certain amount of time to do so. She gets a bit impatient with it since there’s so many things to do and can take time to do so. Also, as mentioned above, she gets bummed that she can’t do certain functions since she was not the one that set-up the island. The set-up process is probably the longest. You start off with basically nothing and are to build up the island by collecting items and crafting. It can take a while to gather certain items. Also, you’re basically in tutorial mode for a long time (and likely throughout most levels). It takes a good bit of time listening/reading directions from the characters and learning the different buttons, how to move around and the various functions of items.

EXPENSES/EARNING: I'm about 8 days into New Horizons and so far I haven't come across any extra real-life expenses required, as Pocket Camp requires. Instead you earn/buy things by spending time playing the game doing various activities. You can also collect bells by selling items and finding bells in various locations.

NOOK PHONE: You get an in-game smartphone that tracks earnings, information, map, recipes...and allows you to call other characters/friends, etc. You get one right at the beginning/start-up process.

CRAFTING/BUYING ITEMS: There are different ways to obtain various items. There are DIY (do it yourself) recipes that you can earn, buy and receive from characters. They are cards that will list the materials that you will need to gather in order to craft the item. Then you will craft it at the “community” crafting table (or eventually make your own table). Unlike on Pocket Camp where you had to order something to be crafted (and sometimes wait up to days before it is ready), you get the item you craft right away. Though, sometimes when purchasing items you might have to wait for them. There are a few different ways to buy items. One way allows you to purchase, with bells, items like tools and get them instantly. Or you can order rotating items like clothing or furniture and get them in your mailbox the next day (in human real-life time). Also, as you advance in the game, other ways of purchasing become available- like vendors coming to the island to sell.

FORTUNE COOKIES- Unless they end up appearing on New Horizons at a later level than I’m at, so far there have been no signs of fortune cookies like those on Pocket Camp.There are prizes that come wrapped as a gift and floating through the sky on a balloon. You use a slingshot to pop the balloon and open your present. Sometimes it’s a material for crafting or a piece of furniture or clothing item. Those are fun! Plus, until April 12 they have a “Bunny Day” event that allows you to collect about 6 different types of eggs that are used to craft Bunny Day recipes (for furniture, outfits, housing materials,etc)

OVERALL: My only reason for not rating 5-stars is due to what I wrote above regarding issues with multiple players on one console. There are TONS more features to the game that I didn’t even cover. I love all the details of the game. As mentioned, I can only compare New Horizons to Pocket Camp but I personally love this one a lot more (though, I loved Pocket Camp too!). Be prepared to put a lot of time into it (especially to get your $ worth!) but if it’s your thing, it is worth it and a lot of fun.

text:
I am in the middle of a move I don’t want to make. Long story short – I’m being kicked out so the management team can spiffy up my unit to rent for more money.

That said …

One thing I have tried, over the past 30+ years has been to protect my NES and SNES collection – my original devices and games. It hasn’t been easy. I only have ONE box that a game came in. The cases I used for my NES games – long since broke and fell apart.

My SNES games were left to be put in Ziploc bags.

title: Absolutely Worth It!
text:
These games provide hours of fun (and education!) and I’m going to review each game separately so you'll know about them. Each game is easy to learn and doesn't require more than the cards to play.

The United States
Of the three, this one is my favorite. (It’s my 6-y-o nephew’s favorite too.) A great way to practice learning about the States, when they came into the Union, their size, population, number of counties, and their distance from DC. You also get a wonderful picture on each one, and a small map that shows the location of the state in the country. And there is so much more! Postal abbreviation, nickname, state flower, and more. This is probably my very favorite of all the Top Trumps games I’ve played, and I highly recommend it!

U.S. Presidents
If you are studying the presidents, this would be a great game to play. You will find yourself starting to recognize the faces of the presidents, and when they were born or took office. One of the fun facts you can choose from is the number of pets each president had. (Did you know that George Washington had 10 pets?) There is a short bio about each person, and you can see what year he died (if he’s already dead). Highly recommended.

Washington DC
While this was somewhat interesting, I found it a little more confusing and not as much fun. Yes, the pictures of the places were fun, and reading the little bit about each place was great, but I didn’t find myself interested in how much it costs, or the number of visitors and how many minutes each place took. And the Top Trumps Picks were just an opinion and not facts, so it felt a little out of place. My almost 13-y-o niece enjoys this one though. I suppose if you were planning a trip to DC it might be good to play this game and learn more about the city before you went.

Overall, this is a fun pack of three games, and I know many more hours will be spent playing these.

Outside the castle the player controls Nancy from above, meaning that the graphics are quite simplistic, and it's more like an arcade game than a mystery. I much prefer to see the game through Nancy's eyes. In sum, Nancy Drew addicts will definitely want to play this game, and there are certainly things to recommend here, but it's not one of the better Nancy Drew games. Be careful to not disconnect anything and set aside pieces as you get into the insides of the controller. Once you have the casing separated, you need to get under the battery. There is one to three phillips head screws (depending on left or right joycon) holding a plastic piece that holds the battery for the controller. Once you have the plastic piece holding the battery off, you will see the circuit board for the controller. Carefully remove the joystick using the screwdriver and tweezers. You will need to disconnect the cord coming off of it. Once you pop the joystick out, you just need to put the new one in the same was and connect the cord to the controller! After that, you just need to reassemble your controller and test it out!

title: Comfortable headset, subpar performance
text:
This review is for the Logitech G735 Wireless Gaming Headset. The headset is part of the Aurora collection, which combines aesthetics and comfort, especially with “fit for all gamers inclusive of smaller head sizes.”

That IS the biggest plus for me: these headphones are insanely comfortable. The ear cups are well padded and so is the headband. This is a headset I can wear for 7 or 8 hours and not get a headache. I rotate between headsets and earbuds because most headsets give me a headache from pressure and weight after a few hours. Not the G735s.

The comfort is the only reason I keep using them, because nearly everything else is subpar. I expect better from Logitech, and I definitely expect better performance for the high price.

I’ve used the headphones for over a month, so I’ve spent plenty of time with them. One of the biggest annoyances is they seem to amplify ambient sound. Part of the reason I use over ear headphones is to block out the annoying noises in my house. Right now, I have the headphones on and music playing. A family member is on the phone in the next room, I can hear every single word of their conversation and the TV show they’re watching. If I take the headphones off, the ambient volume actually drops. It’s like the headset is a mini echo chamber for outside noise.

They shut off randomly and without warning. That is not ideal, especially when gaming! If I’m playing a console game and using Discord on my phone or computer, I don’t always realize the headphones shut off until I get messages asking why I’m not responding to chat.

The headphones also have volume inconsistencies. This happens when audio pauses, due to buffering or if I pause playblack of music or streaming. After the pause, the audio will jump up in volume. Ear blasting volume. I jump every time it happens.

The firmware is up to date, so I know that’s not contributing to the random shutoffs and volume jumping.

Logitech G HUB is required for all customization. The headset connects via Bluetooth or wireless dongle (LIGHTSPEED USB receiver). G HUB can’t find the headset unless connected via wireless dongle, which is a pain.

Once G HUB finds the headset, you can customize the sound and lighting effects. I was disappointed there weren’t more presets for lighting built into the headphones, it would be fun to change that on the fly, rather than needing G HUB.

Battery life isn’t great. I get about 10-12 hours with lighting, and maybe 20 with the lighting off. Turning off the lighting is supposed to get up to 56 hours, I did not have that experience.

Overall, while the headphones are extremely comfortable, I can’t get past the poor performance.

title: Buttons take force to click
text:
The Uciefy U26 Wireless RGB Gaming Mouse is … okay. Would I consider it a gaming mouse? No. It lights up, but lights do not make a gaming mouse. The right and left buttons take force to press. If I’m rapid clicking in a game, my fingers are going to get tired very quickly. Other than M1 and M2, the mouse only has forward, backward, and DPI adjustment buttons.

Here’s the biggest strike against this mouse: it doesn’t track on dark mousepads. I was using a light blue desk mat and the mouse worked fine. I switched to a black mat, with a dark green and gray design, and the mouse suddenly stopped working. I flipped the mat out of the way, the mouse worked again. Most gamers I know have dark mouse mats or mouse pads, so that’s a big minus.

The mouse connects via wireless dongle, Bluetooth, or wired. The included cable for wired/charging is USB-C, and it’s actually quite nice. The cable is braided, so it lays flat on the desk and isn’t too stiff.

I connected the mouse via Bluetooth to my Mac. Connecting is easy, but the LED indicator for the mode is on the front of the mouse while the button is on the bottom. So if you’re switching modes, you have to hit the button and turn the mouse over quickly. And there’s no label on the front to tell you the different modes, you have to remember the order or check the instructions.

As for lighting, the light mode can be adjusted, but only the light stripe around the bottom half of the mouse is customizable. The other spots light up green when using the mouse. I do like that the mouse doesn’t have any branding on it, the logo on the base of the mouse is a fierce cat.

title: Burst Pro Air
text:
This is a review for the Roccat Burst Pro Air, the new wireless version of the Burst Pro.

“Lightweight” is a bit of a misnomer, the mouse weighs 81 grams. That’s a little heavier than some other wireless gaming mice, but to be honest, once I started using the mouse, I didn’t notice the weight. It’s balanced really well, and the mouse skates are buttery smooth.

The mouse is comfortable in the hand, and this is coming from someone with small hands. I am really picky about mouse feel and shape, this one just feels good. I use a palm grip, so the bump at the base of the mouse gives a lot of space for my palm to rest.

The RBG lighting looks so cool! I have the white version, so the lighting is very obvious. I like how the colors shine through the honeycomb design. Roccat’s software allows you to customize the lighting and other functional things, like remapping buttons, creating macros, DPI switcher, etc. The software is Windows only. The mouse can store five onboard profiles, which is nice. If I use the mouse on a different computer, I don’t have to download Swarm and re-customize everything.

I’m not a big fan of the M1 and M2 buttons. This is my first time using Titan optical switches so maybe that’s why, but the buttons have a bit too much resistance for me. It takes effort to click. Not mushy, but there’s some resistance. I haven’t gotten used to the M1 and M2 buttons after using the mouse for a month. The other buttons feel better, including the scroll wheel.

title: Lightweight, average sound
text:
I was drawn to the Logitech G435’s because of the design for smaller heads and how lightweight they are. Headphones that are too heavy or tight give me a headache, and many of the headsets designed for male gamers are just too big for me.

The G435’s are VERY light, weighing in at 5.8oz. That’s light enough to dangle off my pinky finger. Some comfort is sacrificed to reduce the weight -- the headband has no padding. A tightly woven mesh sleeve covers the top portion of the headphones, I can easily feel the frame. I can see the mesh getting snagged if you put these in a backpack or bag, it’s not super durable. The earcups are also some sort of mesh, which I found comfortable for a few hours, but not a super long gaming session.

The earcups do not “lock” or click into position. So every time you put them on or take them off, the earcups slide up and down, and you have to readjust the fit. The earcups are on the smaller side; these headphones are best for kids, teens, or adults with small heads. The description says, “fits a wide range of people but designed for younger players with memory foam ear cushions and sizing for smaller head sizes.” Definitely younger and smaller head sizes, not a wide range of people.

Sound quality is on the lower end of average. Not quite tin can, but “hollow” is the best way for me to describe it. Quite frankly, I expect better from Logitech. I don’t use a gaming headset for just gaming -- I use a headset for everything, including listening to music and watching tv/movies. When I was trying the G435’s and listening to music or watching a show, I found myself reaching for my usual headphones because the sound was just not great.

The headphones do not have any play controls on the earcups, only power, volume up/down, and a mute button.

The headphones have no noise cancelling, and in fact, I thought they magnified background noise. My mom watches videos in the next room and I could still hear her videos over whatever I had playing when using the G435’s. I have other headphones that don’t have noise cancelling but they still block out the background noise. Not so with the G435’s.

title: Abysmal battery life, high form factor
text:
This is a review for the BlackWidow V3 Mini - Phantom Edition with Yellow Switches (Linear & Silent).

My current daily driver keyboard is a HyperX Alloy Origins Core with HyperX Red Linear Switches. I really like that keyboard and the linear switches, but it takes up a little too much room on my desk. So I like the smaller form factor of the V3 Mini, and the Bluetooth/wireless connectivity options.

The V3 Mini is 65%, which is another plus for me. I tried to go down to a 60% but I can’t live without arrow keys. It does take a few days to get used to the placement of the arrow keys on the V3 Mini, but I use them constantly and like that the keyboard has them.

I’m currently not gaming, so my main use for the V3 Mini has been writing and work. I usually write 1k a day if not more, and I’ve noticed my wrists ache after a long writing session. The keyboard is high profile even at the lowest height setting.

Battery life is abysmal. “Up to 200 hours” is only achievable without using Chroma backlighting and HyperSpeed. The battery indicator is on the back of the keyboard, so I was shocked the first time I ran the battery down. That was after 2-3 days of use. I get about 15-20 hours per charge (and charging takes about 5 hours) with backlighting and connected via Bluetooth.

The switches aren’t silent, but they aren’t as loud as many mechanical keyboards. I think “Silent” is something of a misnomer here. Going on semantics, I expected a silent or nearly silent keyboard. As I said, the switches aren’t as clicky as others, but I can hear myself type with over-ear headphones and music playing. They do feel nice to type with, very responsive and quick.

The steal pudding keycaps are cool but not quite pudding caps in my eyes. The stealth bit means nothing shows on top of the keycaps when the keyboard lighting is off. The letters are printed in a smoky color that blends into the black top. When the Chroma lighting is on, the letters light up. The bottom half of each keycap is also smoky-transparent, so it gives the illusion of a pudding cap, but does not allow as much of the lighting to show as a true pudding cap does. I swapped some of the stealth keycaps for regular pudding keycaps and the difference is very noticeable. I mention this because I cranked the Chroma lighting to its highest brightness when I had all stealth caps, which contributes to lower battery life. Maybe it’s just me, but if I have backlighting on a keyboard, I want to see it.

text:
I have the White version of this keyboard from Nacodex, with Blue Switches. I have to admit, I was mainly drawn to the keyboard for the PBT Pudding Keycaps. I love pudding keycaps because the translucent sidewalls really show the RGB backlighting. If I have a backlit keyboard, I want to *see* the lighting, y’know?

The white tops of the keycaps makes the rainbow backlighting pop even more. Visually, this keyboard looks great. The backlighting turns off after 1 minute of inactivity.

The default lighting mode is a solid rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple. Pressing FN \| switches between the other modes available. To me, most of the other lighting options were gimmicky. One is no backlighting, and the keys light up as they are pressed. Another is rapid breathing. One more is no backlighting and the row lighting up when a key is pressed. And so on. For me, those options are more distracting than having a solid rainbow, or the other sorts of effects I can create with keyboards that have software.

The instructions say there is a Mac mode. As far as I can tell, the Mac mode turns the Alt key into the Command (⌘) key, which is very strange for muscle memory. After a few minutes I switched back to Windows mode, which uses the Windows key for the Command key, like most keyboards do when used with a Mac.

The top row looks to be the F1-F12 row … but it’s not. It’s actually default to be 1, 2, 3 etc. -- but the printing on the keycaps shows F1, F2, F3, etc. This tripped me up the first time I used the keyboard.

I wouldn’t recommend this keyboard for an office environment due to the noise. I’m not complaining about the noise, just mentioning it in case this is your first mechanical keyboard.

Connecting the keyboard via Bluetooth was very easy, I simply turned it on and held down FN + P for pairing mode. When using the backlighting, the keyboard battery lasts for about 5-6 hours. The space bar flashes to indicate when the battery is getting low. The included USB cable is USB A (computer) to USB-C (keyboard).

I am not currently gaming, so I used this keyboard for a lot of writing. I didn’t notice any lag connected via Bluetooth. The standout parts of this keyboard are the rainbow backlighting and the pudding caps.

title: Afterglow Wireless Deluxe Controller
text:
I wanted a glowing controller for my Nintendo Switch from the moment I bought it. But the options haven’t been great, not until the Afterglow Wireless Deluxe Controller was released.

I like this controller a lot. I’ve tried quite a few, including Nintendo’s Pro Controller, but the Afterglow is my favorite. Not just because it glows, but because it feels nice in my hands. I have small hands, so I want a lightweight, easy to hold controller. The Nintendo Pro Controller felt nice, but I didn’t like the matte finish on it, nor how that finish felt against my hands after playing for a while.

The Afterglow controller is compact and lightweight. It has a plasticy finish that I like. The A/B/X/Y buttons are quite clicky, with some resistance behind them. The joysticks are taller than the ones on the joycons, so that takes a bit of adjustment. The big button on the back of the controller is a bit weird, but it can be disabled.

Lastly, the Home button is really close to the X (and the + is really close to the Y). I’ve accidentally hit the Home button more than once in the middle of a FPS match, which isn’t ideal. And I have small fingers!

There are different glow modes: set color, fade in and out to set color, cycle through all colors, and react to movement of joysticks. So there’s a lot of customization and color options. The controller looks the best in the dark, but it’s not too shabby in the middle of the day, either.

So, even though I have a few small quibbles with the button placement, the lighting is honestly enough to make up for that.

title: Razer Kraken Kitty Headset
text:
Okay, so, I’m a total dork and love things that glow. I couldn’t put the Razer Kraken Kitty Headset on my head quickly enough -- glowing cat ears? I almost wish I was a streamer, so I could show them off!

The headphones are very comfortable. They’re heavier than other pairs I own, but I don’t notice that when wearing them. The headband is padded. The ear cups are too, fitting comfortably over the ear. The headphones stay in place without squeezing my head too tight, which is important for me, as I get headaches when headphones are too tight. The headset has measurements on each side, so you can keep track of what is the perfect fit for you.

One: changing the color from the default Razer green requires Synapse 3. Synapse 3 is still in beta, and only runs on Windows machines. I only have Synapse 2 on my Mac, which is my main computer for using Discord while I game.

Two: the cable is not removable. I had hoped to get an adapter and make the Kraken Kitty a Bluetooth headset, but then I’d have a 4 foot cord hanging off my ear. The cable is a strong braided one (like all Razer devices), but I do worry that it will wear out, or I might run it over with my chair. Then I’ll be stuck with a headset I can’t use anymore.

title: HyperX Alloy Origins Core Tenkeyless, HyperX Red Linear Switch
text:
I’ve been using the HyperX Alloy Origins Core Tenkeyless Keyboard for a few weeks and I love it!

I have the Linear Switch (HyperX Red) version. This is my first time trying linear switches. The first few days, I felt like I was typing on the softest keyboard ever. I personally like how buttery and responsive it feels, but finding the right switch option is really one of those things you have to try yourself. I did notice that it’s easier to “bottom out” the linear switch versus say, a Cherry MX Blue switch.

I have a light hand and don’t do a ton of button mashing with the games I currently play (Warcraft, Paladins, SDV), so the Origins Core has replaced my daily driver, the HyperX Alloy Elite RGB (with Cherry MX Blue switches). I do miss the volume rocker on the Elite RGB, but that’s all I miss.

The Origins Core does have function keys (FN + F#) for volume, media control, and light profiles.

Getting back some of my desk with the Tenkeyless version is another plus, too. The keyboard is small enough that I actually would travel with it, if I were going somewhere for a few days. The USB cable is detachable, which makes it easier to transport.

I use this keyboard for both writing (at least 2-3 hours of typing a day) plus gaming. I like that HyperX has built angles of adjustability into the keyboard feet. I can have a 3°, 7°, or 11° angle. The keycaps are a little slippery during extended gaming sessions, but this hasn’t bothered me enough to replace them.

The keyboard itself has a good build feeling to it, and it doesn’t slide on my desk, even during intense moments.

I did try HyperX’s NGENUITY software to make my own custom lighting profiles. The software is only available on Windows, but the keyboard can save 3 profiles to its onboard memory. I switch between Windows and Mac, so I was excited that I could customize the keyboard on my Windows machine, and be able to use those light profiles on my Mac without needing the software. NGENUITY allows a LOT of customization; I spent a few hours playing with the different lighting options. I like NGENUITY more than Synapse.

I have one little quibble. I wish the lighting for the caps lock key was on the key itself, instead of above the arrows. But that’s a tiny little complaint, it doesn’t interfere with my use at all.

I recommend going with the RGB version; you can always set a solid color. The RGB lighting is so much fun, and I dare I say -- it’s pretty!

title: Razer Basilisk X Hyperspeed Wireless Mouse
text:
[[VIDEOID:4c2e9d2f7b0e6a0691a91cb5e893b6c]] This is a review for the Razer Basilisk X Hyperspeed Wireless Mouse.

For comparison purposes, I also use a Razer Basilisk 16,000 DPI Optical Sensor (wired) and a Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum (wired) on a daily basis. I don’t love the wired Razer, as I’m not a fan of the scroll wheel or the design of buttons 4 and 5.

Right off, I noticed that I liked the scroll wheel on the Razer Basilisk X. It doesn’t have as much resistance as the wired version does. It’s a little clicky and has some resistance, but not so much that I revert to using my laptop’s trackpad, as I do with the wired Basilisk.

The left and right buttons are nice and clicky. The side buttons stick out a bit more on the Basilisk X than on the wired Basilisk, which I prefer.

I have small hands and found the Basilisk X comfortable to use for hours at a time.

Synapse 2 on my Mac could not find this mouse. Synapse 3 on my Windows computer did find the mouse. This mouse is only compatible with Synapse 3. On Windows, I was able to customize the different buttons.

There’s no RGB customization, as the Basilisk X is the less expensive model. I was sad to see the Razer logo doesn’t light up; yes I’m a dork who likes glowing peripherals.

The mouse can be used either wirelessly or with Bluetooth. There’s a switch on the bottom to switch between connectivity types. The Basilisk X uses one AA battery; to help with battery life, I put the switch on BT to keep from accidentally waking the mouse if I don’t have the dongle plugged in. The USB dongle can be stored inside the battery compartment. It’s very small and difficult to remove from a USB port once inserted.

In contrast to other battery powered mice I’ve used in the past, the Basilisk X’s battery compartment is on the top of the mouse. The top pops off so easily I’m worried that it will pop off while I’m using the mouse, especially during an intense moment in a game. All it takes is a little pressure in the right spot, and bam, off the battery lid goes. I really don’t like this.

I don’t have a scale, but there’s a noticeable weight difference between the wired Basilisk and the wireless Basilisk X. The Basilisk X feels very lightweight in the hand. It’s almost a bit too light for me; I notice the difference every time I switch between the mice.

title: E-YOOSO Mechanical Keyboard, Outemu Blue Switches
text:
I’m not an expert on mechanical keyboards (that’s a rabbithole I don’t want to go down, or I’ll be building my own in a week), but I do love them now that I’ve switched to using one on a daily basis. My daily driver is a HyperX Alloy Elite with Cherry MX Blue switches.

I’ve put this E-YOOSO mechanical keyboard to the test for about three weeks. The switches are Outemu Blue Switches, which is a knock-off of Cherry MX Blue switches. I definitely noticed a difference between the Outemu and the Cherry. The Outemu are a little noisier and don’t feel as smooth. I feel more resistance when I type on the E-YOOSO keyboard versus the HyperX one. Over a few hours, the resistance adds up.

Of course, the HyperX keyboard is more than double the price of this one, but the E-YOOSO is lacking in some basic features that I’ve become used to. There’s no attached wrist rest, and I really feel the lack of it. Muscle memory keeps my wrists up as if there was a rest under them, which gets tiring. There are no multimedia or sound controls on the keyboard; I really miss that easy adjustment when I’m mid game. The keycaps are basic plastic, without any texture. What you’d find on a normal cheap keyboard, and again, this is a matter of preference, but the keys are slippery. Not great for gaming.

The silver screws on the keyboard continually catch my eye. This is a minor thing, but I wish the screws were flush with the plastic case rather than sitting above it. I’ve snagged my fingers on the screws a few times. The USB cable is plastic instead of braided.

The lighting options are preset, you can cycle through them via the FN and INS keys. I do like that the keyboard includes options without needing to download additional software, but for most people, the first mode (steady rainbow) will be the default. If I’m gaming in the dark, marquee or snake are useless. Another minor quibble, but I really don’t like the orange row of the keyboard, I wish another color had been chosen. The orange just doesn’t fit with the other colors, in my opinion. It’s too similar to the red row right above it.

I do like the dust resistance; I’ve had the keyboard sitting out for three weeks and haven’t noticed any dust building up on it.

The Logitech was my preferred mouse for a long time, but I’ve been using the Corsair almost daily instead of switching. It’s good for general use as well as gaming.

One of the biggest pluses for me is that Corsair’s software, iCUE, runs on Macs. I can customize everything, including the lighting, make macros, change the DPI, and probably other things I haven’t found yet. There’s a lot of options to explore in iCUE, but I think it’s pretty intuitive.

I like the hand feel of the mouse. I have small hands; this mouse is comfortable to use for hours at a time. Obviously, everyone has different preferences, and I’m quite picky myself. Hand feel is impossible to test when buying a mouse online. But Corsair has designed this mouse to have three different thumb grips. My Logitech mouse has adjustable weights, which requires a little fiddling. Changing the grips on the Corsair is super easy: they snap into place. Magnets keep the grips on and make a quick switch out easy, if I think I might want a different one when playing.

I also like how the scroll wheel feels. It reminds me of a little tire, with its tread.

The mouse is lacking buttons for serious gamers. Aside from the usual left/right click, there’s only forward, backward, and DPI up and DPI down. I also have to say I don’t notice any difference between the Corsair’s 18,000 DPI versus the Razer’s 16,000 DPI or even the Logitech’s 12,000 DPI.

title: Logitech G935 Wireless Gaming Headset
text:
I tried the Logitech G935 Wireless Gaming Headset for about two months before writing this review. I wish I liked the headset better, but after testing it, I’m still on the hunt for the perfect headset.

Currently I do most of my gaming with multiplayer Switch games, such as Splatoon 2. I have to use Discord on my computer or phone to talk with friends while we play. But I also want to hear game sounds, so the option to have dual sound inputs is what really drew me to the G935. I connected the headphones wirelessly to my computer and used the 3.5 mm cable to connect to my Switch. A bit messy, but I was willing to accept that if it worked well.

But it didn’t. No matter how many sound settings I adjusted, my voice was muffled when talking. I had better results using a normal pair of headphones and the built-in microphone on my computer!

Not to mention, finding the proper button I want to use when wearing the headset is difficult. I have to feel and count the buttons, which takes my attention out of the game and performance suffers. I suppose I’d develop some muscle memory if I used the headset for longer, but I still feel like there are too many buttons. And the volume rocker is at the bottom of the earcup, so if you take the headphones on or off, it’s really easy to change the volume and not be able to hear or get a screech in your ear.

Comfort wise, I tend to get headaches if a headset is too heavy and/or tight. About an hour was my limit for wearing the G935, or I’d have a headache from the weight of it. The earcups are actually pretty comfy and well padded, the headset is just big and I wouldn’t recommend if you have a small head.

Sound quality is good, one of the better parts of the headset. But I couldn’t find a way to adjust the volume on one source and not the other via the headset if I did dual inputs.

I just wasn’t thrilled with the G935 headset. At the level it’s designed for, I would have expected Bluetooth connectivity instead of a wireless dongle, better button design/layout, and better comfort overall, not to mention clear voice quality.

title: Faulty dongle, alright sound.
text:
I really wanted to like these. I have a high end pair of the a50s that I love. Kiddo is not ready for something that pricey, but he would be better off with a wireless headset for distance learning. He has to get up and get papers and such that the wire has become an issue. When these popped up for review I jumped on the opportunity.

Fit and Feel:
My first concern was unnecessary, they fit my 8 year old on the smallest size just fine and are light weight so he isn't bothered by them. My husband was able to adjust them out to fit his head as well, so I would say these fit a wide range of head sizes. They really do make you look like a Transformer as another reviewer stated, but at kiddo's age that was a plus not a minus. If they weren't bright white it probably wouldn't be so noticeable. He liked the soft ear cuffs, I found them to be okay. Not super plush but not super cheap feeling either. While being light for him was a plus, I found the headset to feel a bit plasticky and flimsy for the price range. He and I agree to disagree on that one.

Sound:
I like that he can still hear me when he has them on. These are more of a muffled "open" headset than a noise blocking "closed" headset. If you want to block out the world around you, these are not for you. If you want to still hear people talking and what's going on around you, these are good for that.

Sound was just okay. A bit tinny but in this price range most are going to be. At least they aren't over done with artificial bass to make up for it. If you like a rich bass check out Sennheiser, but expect to pay a bit more for it too. The mic was okay sound wise. It didn't pick up much background noise, but it did oddly clip off your last word in both Zoom and Discord. That might be a sensitivity issue on those programs end more than the headset, but it was odd that it did it with both. Our other headsets didn't. I love the flip up mic, I've heard enough people eating while not on mute to wish that it was a mandatory feature :)

Connectivity:
Here is where much of our issues stem from. I was willing to go 4 stars up until this point. But, the dongle is a train wreck. First of all there are no included instructions on how to use it and most of the online instructions are for the transmitter version not the dongle. So you will have to dig a bit to find instructions how to set it up. That is unacceptable in my opinion. It is not just pop it in and use your headset, there is a process...

Also, the dongle plug is too loose to stay in the usb port securely. It jiggles in his laptop, my computer, both of our usb hubs. I popped it into the PS4 and while slightly tighter still looser than I'd like. It also sticks out a bit over 2 inches when plugged in and easily gets knocked out. It also constantly loses its settings and is a royal pain in the behind. Most likely we got a dud, perhaps trying to get a replacement dongle would fix the connectivity issues, but in all honesty it's just too big to have poking out the side of a kid's laptop.

TL;DR
Faulty dongle and flimsy plastic feel make this mid-range wireless headset a bit of a dud. Sound is tinny but okay, mic is fine and flip to mute is amazing, battery life was as expected. Fits an 8 year old all the way up to a full grown man. Bulky but light weight. If it weren't for the faulty dongle, 4 stars considering the price range.... as it came... 2 stars.

text:

The only time I got any static was adjusting the volume when testing for bass, so the drivers were being stressed. Otherwise the volume wheel didn't produce any static.

If you want full noise cancellation these aren't going to get you there. I was still able to hear external noise if it was loud, like someone calling for me. They also didn't create that weird negative pressure that some noise cancelling headsets create, which was a huge relief. These are very comfortable to wear, not too heavy but not flimsy light. The ear cups are a standard size, if you have large ears and struggle with headsets in general, you may struggle with these. But I would not call them smaller than average. They were a bit warm though. So if heat is something you are looking to avoid, I would say switch to an open set instead, those are better ventilated although they don't do anything to block outside noises.

Overall this is a great headset that performs well above it's pricepoint. Which is surprising since Alienware anything is notorious for being super overpriced, lol.

title: Quality sound and an impressive Mic
text:
I used my Sennheiser Game One's as a comparison. In their heyday they were in the $250 range (although they are half that price now, oh technology why do you hate my wallet so much). Anyway, I figured they would be the best set on hand I could test against. Both sets were tested on my system with a dedicated sound card (soundblaster Z) and on my hubby's system without a dedicated sound card. I tested for PC use only, so if these are for an xbox keep that in mind.

Need for dedicated soundcard: First off, while the Senn's require the soundcard to pull enough power and not crash my computer, the Astros proAmp thing either compensated enough to not need one, or this headset is fine without a sound card. Either way, I did NOT need a dedicated soundcard for the Astro's.

Overall sound quality: ok the Senn's sound slightly richer. Not above and beyond but the sound seems "warmer" and more immersive. I'm not saying the Astro's were bad, they passed all the sound tests I ran with flying colors, pulling in a wide range of super low bass and super annoying high frequency. I'm just partial to the Senn's, but the Astros were excellent in their own right.

Microphone: Ok this is where the Astros shined. They isolated the noise better, voice was much clearer, and they triggered Discords auto-enable flawlessly. My Senn's often clip the start of my words even on the highest sensitivity.

Muting: Going with the Senn's on this one, flip mic to mute is just awesome. Astros have an inline mute, that you slide. When muted the LED lights on the proAmp turns red which is a nice visual to know you are muted. Flip up mic is more of a preference, but I’ve heard enough drama in discord from people forgetting to mute than it’s a life choice more than a preference :P

Fifth, comfort: Senn's win this one with a caveat, they are a lot warmer. All that super cush comes at a price, they make your head hot after a bit. The Astros weren't as squishy soft, but they are better ventilated and lighter.

Conclusion: Compared to my Senn’s I say they average out to being equals. Sound is great, the mic is amazing, and all the replaceable parts on the Astros incase they wear out make these a really great set. The only real negative is the instruction sheet. IT IS AWFUL. Seriously they wrote it in like 3pt font in light grey. They have a diagram on one side that is rather pointless and HUGE, then the actual instructions on the back are super tiny. If I were writing a review for instructions alone this would be 2 star review. Thankfully its for the headset, so I’m only dinging them one star for the terrible instructions, lack of cush on the padding, and the price point. For $250 gaming headset you gotta hit all the categories out of the park. These did well, but my Senn’s are now half that price and comparable in performance.

title: Good first gaming mouse, especially for its ease of use
text:

The least sensitive is for precision, sniping the zombie on the building across the way, that sort of thing. I like how intuitive and accessible these are, for rapid switching on the fly.

I find the low setting also works well for software developers if you need finer control when laying design elements for a UI in a tool like Visual Studio. On that score, a friend and fellow developer said the mouse "felt weird". I'm used to gaming mice, so it seemed fine to me. There is a little thumb rest (this is very much meant for a right handed person) and above that rest are the forward/backward buttons. Lights are on the scroll wheel, the sides, and the logo on the back. The right and left buttons show no separation to show that they are buttons making for a sleek design. The ample red and black cable echoes the colors on the mouse.

If I had any complaint, it's that the forward button is textured and the back isn't. Given how they are positioned, it's not for any type of tactile clarity, so I don't see why they don't match. It's a small point.

title: Awesome wheel
text:
This is pretty much the sweet spot between a basic wheel that lacks force feedback and a top of the line wheel that costs more than a console. It clamps to the table (and do clamp it, or it'll go bouncing around if you crash into something).

It is fully wired. You need to plug it in for power, and the cord is pretty short so you may want an extension cord, and you plug the wheel into the USB port on the PS3 or PS4, so you may need a USB extender if you're far from the TV. I'm playing at about 80 inches from the TV with no issue, but that's close to the limit.

The force feedback is adjustable, at least if you're playing Project Cars, and it's a good idea to flip through the options to find the one that's right for you. It emulates a semi-automatic car with gear shifting paddles behind the wheel. Project Cars at least responds to that. Since I've never driven anything but an automatic, I'm basically flapping them around trying to get a sense of what they do. The wheel is comfortable to hold and turns easily enough, but with a little more resistance than a real car. The pedals are big, close enough to the size of the pedals in a real car as to make it hard to notice the difference. If you are playing on a hardwood floor the pedals will slip around. Get a welcome mat to put under them when they are in use and they will stay put, this assuming you are attaching the wheel to the table and not going all the way with a frame setup. The pedals are responsive and adjustable. In the default configuration the break offers more resistance than the gas.

The PS3/PS4 switcher is fairly hidden in the front behind the wheel, as it should be given you will be using that switch least of all. You have full controls for both, including a dpad, options, share, and the triggers (but not the bumpers L1 and R1 that I've seen) right on the wheel. Project Cars (can you guess my favorite PS4 racing game?) recognized it with no configuration required.

Overall this is a lot easier and a lot more fun than racing with the controller. I'm having a blast. Now if only I could stop crashing into the walls.

title: Fabulous headset.
text:
The sound quality is remarkable. It levels the volume a bit, which I like. I've played a few games (cough AC Unity cough) where the background noise can be loud and then the dialog drops inexplicably. This makes it all a bit more even. The tonal range, bass to treble, is quite good. I noticed no distortion. You can hear yourself in the headset, which I find important. It is very good at blocking out external sound, so don't expect to hear someone calling to you from the next room.

One thing to keep in mind, the microphone can sort of kind of go in backwards, and it's nasty uncomfortable if you do that. It should be set up such that the mike is on the left hand side. I have no idea if it works the other way. I didn't want to deal with that. I do know it seems to click in and it stays. I wouldn't think it should make a difference in terms of comfort, but it does. Even when using them without the microphone, having them not be backwards makes a big difference in comfort.

I found these to be snug, but comfortable. They adjust easily. The mute button is the only button on the right front, so it is easy to access. I would have liked a visual indicator if the mike is muted, but that's a small thing. Again, remember to shut off the chat feature on the Kinect if you want to be able to speak to someone privately (or to not annoy your teammates with the blare of an air raid siren, if you're in a neighborhood like mine that has one -- no air raids, just a peaceful siren to herald in the calm of the weekend).

These charge on USB and they charge fairly quickly. An indicator light on the earpiece tells you if they are charged, and if they are on. And of course the XBox will show you on screen to whom the device is paired.

I know it's not supposed to work with a hub, but I had a spare and I needed this and a keyboard to go into the same port, so I experimented. I used http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00H0PLQHO?psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00 as the hub and http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B003SVSJ1K?psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_search_detailpage as the keyboard and mouse. I then went into Kinect and turned off the Use Kinect for Chat feature. I tried first a Skype call (call testing service) to keep things simple, and that worked. I then tried it in game, and that worked too. I put them in the port on the side towards the front, not the back port--no choice because the back ports are used for external drives but work mentioning as that has given my trouble in the past with the keyboard and I suspect the headset would fare no better. So if you aren't getting a good signal, try that port.

I tried one more thing it's not supposed to do, and it doesn't do it. It doesn't work with the PS4. Unusual, since normally any headset with a 3.5mm connection can work with that. It will function as headphones, but it cannot detect the microphone. If you want one headset for multiple systems, this isn't it. If you want a truly excellent headset for the XBox One, this most definitely qualifies.

title: Underrated, don't miss this fantastic game
text:
This is the true successor to Black Flag, the real Assassin's Creed of 2014.

It almost feels like Unity was where the pencil pushers focused to make sure it has everything the nex gen should, by the books, it follows all the templates, and they pretty much left the Rogue team to do what they wanted. That's how it comes off anyway.

This is perhaps the best Assassin's Creed game yet. From Black Flag, you retain sea battles, navel forts, and whaling. We see a return of building up districts by investing in renovating properties that we first encountered with Ezio. Game play is pretty much as you'd expect from this series, no major divergence from the franchise there.

The story is top rate. Shay starts as an assassin, disenfranchised perhaps, but loyal to the cause. He's a contemporary to Connor, and we see Adewale a few times in the game. Over the course of the story, he sees the unintended consequences of the assassins' actions. He sides with the Templars, not because he believes in their visions of world domination -- and the modern day storyline reminds us that they are the bad guys, this is not a good vs good scenario -- but because he wants to stop the destruction being unwittingly wrought by the assassins.

History is still the playground, and we meet some amazing historic figures, the primary one being Benjamin Franklin. We're running around the colonies during the American Revolution.

title: Pickup is weak, sound field is amazing
text:
It comes with a USB cable to update the controller. I found that odd, but convenient. I can always use extra cables. The adapter has controls to increase game sounds, increase chat sounds, mute the microphone (it lights up if the mike is muted--a very convenient feature) and it can turn up and down the volume as a whole. The audio cable is standard, so you can use it in anything else that works with a headphone. The microphone retracts well enough to be invisible if you don't know to look for it. I used it for a bit with my 3DS and it worked fine for that. The audio cable is permanently attached, and I do not like that design choice. The cable is the single most likely part to break (worse for me because my cat chews these cables, but true in general). A port with a swappable cable would increase the lifespan of these headphones, and would offer choices in terms of swapping to a longer cable, a shorter cable. A more modular design is always a better choice.

It's a good size for a female. The microphone is well places (more on that in a bit) and the headset fits well and is comfortable. It's lightweight, comfortable, and easy to wear for long gaming sessions. The padding was soft without being annoying or sweaty. The ear cups don't annoy the ears the way some can after a long while.

As I said, the microphone sits well. It sits exactly where other headsets I have used sits. For me at least, position isn't a problem. The problem is that the pickup is lacking. If I speak at a normal level--and here I admit to being fairly soft spoken-- it doesn't fully pick up my voice. It echoes in the headset, and does that very well. It reminds me of the studio setup I had back when I was podcasting It's that kind of quality echo back. That's my largest issue with these, and the reason they lose a star. They might have gone to three stars but for the sound field.

The sound field is astounding. I had to keep taking the headset off to see if I was really hearing through the headset and not the speakers. The sounds are directional and adequately distant to give the audio illusion of space and positions in space. I have never heard audio this good from headsets in this price range. That's where this headset truly shines. The sound quality, the range of base and treble, and the sound clarity is impressive as well. In fact, if you're looking for a set so that you can watch shows or play without the noise bothering anyone else, and the mike isn't an issue (or if you naturally have a loud voice) you are going to be hard pressed to find anything better than these.

title: They wimpified my assassin.
text:
When you first start the game prepare for a long install. This game has been patched, re-patched, and patched again to knock out the bugs, and there are still bugs. In the first section, before even the welcome screen (which is granted something like an hour into the game) I managed to crouch behind something only to have a clipping error trap me there. I had to go in the world map then back out again to refresh the screen layout so that I can move. But that's not that bad. Most of the bugs are gone, and those clipping issues are a running part of the franchise.

There is a companion app with a whack of micropay transactions that is pretty much a required part of the experience. Many chests won't open until you solve a ridiculously easy puzzle in the app. Easy, because the things you're looking for don't move, so you can just remember where they are for the next try. That's a little worse, especially because not all mobile platforms are supported. At the time of this writing Windows Phone (tiny install base, granted) and the Kindle Fire (very large install base) are not supported. If the thing is mandatory, it should work on all platforms. The app also allows you to send out your assassin's on assignment, similar to what Ezio was doing in Brotherhood, except it made sense for Ezio to do that. He was pretty much leading the assassin's at that point. Arno isn't even an assassin when he starts. Also, the forgot the initiation rite from Ezio's time or else it changed past all recognition. The new one is really weird.

Also required is the multiplayer element built right into the single player story line. I mean, you can ignore these things but not if you want to fully complete the game to 100%.

The upgrades are tied to helix credits that you can buy, more microtransactions, which can get kind of annoying especially since they start at $20 and go up to $100, but are, at least, optional. Really optional. Like if you don't buy air assassination, you can still perform an air assassination, you just have to guess when it will and will not work as the option doesn't show up in the UI. It's as if they made the decision to implement the "you have to buy this" feature late in the development cycle, so the programmers just hid it from the interface. You can also do leap of faith before Arno learns it. In fact, you have to do it before Arno learns it.

If anyone was wondering if we lost the modern era stuff in this game, worry not. It's still there. Pretty interesting stuff too.

Arno is wanted, so much so that if he is seen in a restricted area, no matter how many other random people are loitering around, he'll be pursued. So with this in mind, he walks into a police station and randomly offers to help with the crime problem. The only cop on duty isn't all that concerned, neither with a most wanted fugitive standing in front of him, nor with such an odd request, but a bored prisoner sets him to solving murder mysteries. Why? Because they wanted murder mysteries in the game. They're not bad murder mysteries. They just don't fit in at all.

The worse part, is that Arno is the single wimpiest assassin in the entire brotherhood. Eagle vision wears off in a few moments, and needs to recharge. He can't escape battle and heal over time. Like Ezio, he needs healing bottles. Unlike Ezio, he can't find doctors all over the place. He can't counter and do an instant kill. He just gets some extra blows in and if he does it wrong he's off balance instead. His attacks do a lot less damage than any prior assassin. What he gets instead is...he can crouch. Yep, we're giving up unlimited eagle vision, healing over time, and a deadly counter-attack for crouching. Oh, and he can pick locks. So basically we're trading in an assassin for a cat burglar.

If you can, bypass this one and try Rogue instead. Rogue is the real A.C. game out this year, a true successor to Black Flag. This one...had potential for true greatness and gave in to mediocre gimmicks instead.

title: Amazing!
text:
I am in love with this console.

The graphics are amazing. I love the look of the games on this system. The sound is impeccable. We run it off a 7.1 surround system, and I've had moments where a twig will snap behind me, or a beast will roar off to the left. It is a bit more precise that I'm used to in how it handles locating sound between speakers, by firing both off but not at the same volume. I really love that.

The controller is so comfortable. I had some problems early on with the rubber coming off, but each time Sony was great about quickly replacing the controller. The audio jack on the controller means even the most basic headset can be effectively wireless for gaming. I did not think I would like the touchpad, but now I love it. It has an accelerometer, so for Infamous: Second Son, when you are using the controller like a can of spray paint, you have to turn it sideways and shake it. And the embedded speakers are such, it sounds like a can of spray paint being shaken. The PS3 controller always bothered me a little that it is too easy to inadvertently push down the left thumbpad (so it thinks you hit L3) when you are trying to run around. I've yet to encounter that problem with this one, not even doing the various rundown sections of Assassin's Creed: Black Flag.

Sharing in-game video is quick and easy. It works so well, and so fast. I didn't think I would use that, but it turns out I kind of like sharing awesome moments on Facebook. I'm very much a solo gamer, and the library for that is still very impressive.

If you have PlayStation Plus, your games are backed up online. When I upgraded the hard drive, which is ridiculously simple, I just redownloaded my games, already in progress. It picked up where it left out without a hitch.

For stability, for elegance, for performance, and most importantly, for incredible game play, I give the PS4 five stars.

title: Great for the PS4, okay for the PS3, not so good for the Vita.
text:
It has good audio prompts, like "Charging Battery", "Powering On" and "Powering Off", so you are clear on what it is doing, which is cool.

It can pair to the PS4 two ways. You can plug the Optical cable into the USB dongle, plug that into the USB port, and go fully wireless. Or you can use the enclosed audio cable plugged into the PS4 controller. Both are easy to set up. Both work.

For the PS3, you need to plug the Optical cable into the USB dongle, plug that into the USB port, and then go monkey around with the settings until it finally works. That one will work, but it is more of a pain.

For the Vita, or any other media device, it should be simple. You just plug the enclosed audio cable into the headphone jack, turn on the headphones, and you're good to go. Only after a little while it says "Automatic shutdown enabled. Press the power button to cancel." If you press the power button, it says "Automatic shutdown disabled". What it does after that is up to a coin toss. It will either tell you it's powering off and then proceed to do so, or it will stay on. I've yet to figure out the pattern. I would have assumed that I did not press the button, or that it did not register, were it not for the audio prompt that automatic shutdown was disabled. I might have blamed it on the battery if it didn't happen less than an hour after a full charge, and right before staying on for an additional 45 minutes.

It has little blue Turtle Beach logos on either side that glow red while the device is charging, blue when it is charged, and flashes blue when it is in use. I would have preferred a stable light to the flashing, or even no light to the flashing. If I can hear noise, I know it's on. The flashing is just annoying. It has separate volume controls for each earphones and microphone, and audio presets such as "bass boost", "bass and treble boost", "vocal boost" and "natural sound". I favor "vocal boost" for most games and videos, though some games sound better with "natural sound".

They are good for noise cancelling, and the sound quality is excellent. In "vocal boost" mode, videos level (the voices are not drowned out by the special effects) which I very much appreciate. Turtle Beach is known for excellent audio equipment, and the sound quality on this is flawless. Were I judging it by sound alone, it would be five stars.

The microphones attaches and detaches easily, for use as a gaming headset or just earphones. There is a mute button on the right ear, that is quite easy to get to. The buttons are spaced well enough, and distinctively enough, that they are easy to use while you wear the headset.

They are comfortable when worn on the head, but when I wear them around my neck they get grabby with my hair, which is, for me, the biggest negative.

title: A worthy mouse with good build quality
text:
The Rat 6 mouse seems to be going for the customization market, but where it really excels is in simple build quality. The weight, smooth precision parts, and mechanical functioning of this mouse make it fell less like a peripheral and more like a piece of tactical combat gear. The buttons are well placed, it slides smoothly without catching, and the sensor does its job very well.

Perhaps my favorite feature on the Rat 7 is the small rocker switch behind the scroll wheel which can be used to raise and lower the mouse sensitivity (pointer speed) on the fly, which nearly makes the precision aim button obsolete. These aren't uncommon features on a gaming mouse these days, but they're implemented well.

I'm used to using an ambidextrous mouse and switching hands often. This mouse can be used left handed without much difficulty, but you lose access to some of the buttons and features when doing so, most notably the horizontal scroll.

I previously owned a RAT 7 and really loved it, but after a couple years it failed on me. First thing to go was the braided cable, which started to short out when parts of it were moved. I hate braided cable. Eventually, I dropped it and was surprised to find one of the buttons had broken from a short fall. In the end, if you use your mouse frequently, it's worth getting a nice one, but the really high priced ones probably aren't worth the premium.

Overall, more than worth the price difference between it and the lesser mice on the market.

title: So much fun! However, not a ton of crossover appeal to adults
text:
I'm a big fan of the Just Dance line of games, because I love getting exercise while playing. So I was excited to test out this version for kids, especially since I have a little one who will hopefully be able to play with me in a few years, and a niece who is just the right age right now.

What I loved about this is that unlike in other games in this line, the dancers on the screen are actual kids! Usually, we get some weird cartoon character with improbable fashion choices, and when I see them moving on the screen I think to myself, "of course you can do that move, you're not a person." In this game, you get to watch actual kids of different ages doing the dances, sometimes they are dressed up in silly costumes, and sometimes dressed to fit in with the theme of the video. Watching real people do the dance moves increased my enjoyment of the games dramatically, and I wish they had that option for all of the grown-up games.

The song list is fantastic for kids, and my niece was familiar with most of the songs. There were also a lot of old-fashioned favorites that I was familiar with, so we had fun together. However, most of the songs have that overly cheerful tone of most children's media, and after about a half hour, I realized that I would never voluntarily choose to play these songs over any of the songs in the grown-up games. Of course, I'm an adult, so that's to be expected, but you should be aware if you are an adult wanting to play this game, you will probably not find the song choices ones that have a lot of intergenerational appeal after the first few plays.

That said, they are great picks for kids, and the gameplay itself is a lot of fun. I'd say if your kids are young enough that you do not want them exposed to songs such as "promiscuous girl" which is an example from another Just Dance game, I would definitely choose this game. If you are comfortable with the content of the other games, I would definitely choose those, because the songs are more complex and interesting.

text:
I have the Nyko Dual Charger Station in White and have been reasonably happy with that brand, but when I saw Amazon had created their own reasonably-priced line of chargers, I was all excited. I love the AmazonBasics batteries and other items, and to find a black charger station at a low cost was great!

Unfortunately, this has two major flaws that the other charging station brand doesn't suffer.

One, the Wii has to be ON for this to charge. And the Wii makes noise when it is on. So in order to charge my controllers when I am done playing, I have to put up with the whirring of the Wii for five hours. And sometimes the Wii inexplicably shuts off before I'm done charging, which makes it a production.

Second, you're supposed to take the controllers off when you are done charging them. None of the other brands make a fuss about this. Is it truly critical? I can't tell. When I left my controllers on for a couple days, they still worked after and hadn't lost their charge, so maybe that's not important. But they make it very clear in the instructions that this is a key Thing We Ought To Do.

The other complaints I have are ones that other dual charge stations also have, like having to take the silicone sleeve off. So that's no biggie, I'm used to it. But having to have the Wii on to charge is what really makes this dual charging station kind of annoying.

It's attractive and the lights glow nice colors (blue while charging, green when done), but were I to purchase a new one, I'd go back to the Nyko brand just so I can turn the Wii off when I am done playing.

text: [[VIDEOID:46fef64578a45aef7c837552a437df4e]] This game is a blast to play on the balance board - you turn the board sideways so it resembles a small snowboard and it's easy to imagine you are shredding down the slopes, doing tricks and having a blast. I love the soundtrack and often when I don't even feel like playing, I'll play just so I can listen to the tunes. Any exercise from this game is moderate - it seems good for the legs, but doesn't tire me out (but then I am a landscaper so I'm already reasonably fit). Recommended.

title: Awesome - can unlock songs while just playing normally, good song variety
text:
I'm thrilled with this latest DDR game. I own all the PS2 Dance Dance Revolution games and I love to work out a few times a week with DDR. The last few games before this one required you to go through some kind of stupid dance master mode or something to unlock songs- so I was thrilled to find that you can unlock songs, dancers, etc just by playing normally in game mode.

Two annoying things in this one:

You can't shut off the dancers

The announcer is dire - really, really bad. Luckily you can shut him up in options.

I do love that there is at least one good rap song in here, and quite a few oldies like Dub-i-Dub and Butterfly (a new remix). There's also just generally a good variety of songs. There's an interesting clubhouse reggae song that I was particularly happy to see.

I have played four nights now with a person with very different musical taste than I have, and we both enjoyed it a lot and found songs we wanted to replay each night.

I'm giving it five stars because of the simplified unlock process and the fun variety of songs. Yay for X!

title: Fun and catchy but not the best of DDR
text:
The good:
Fun, catchy songs that I immediately enjoyed playing.
Easy unlock process - you just play in free play mode to unlock songs

The bad:
Game level is a bit easier than other DDR games - I usually play standard to heavy in DDR, and with this game, I have passed every song on heavy/ expert on my first try. They were complicated enough to hold my interest, but I don't feel at all challenged here.
Only about half as many songs as a normal DDR game, graphics are clunky
The dancers, as always in DDR (I just turn them off)

For the price I found it a worthy buy - as a regular player I get bored of the same songs all the time, and so any new game that helps me mix up my workout is much appreciated. But it certainly isn't up to par with the other DDR games, much as I am enjoying playing it.

However, I could see new DDR players really enjoying this, because the music is catchy and accessible and the steps aren't too hard.

If you are a regular player, know that this is a fun diversion that you will enjoy for a good while, but isn't going to become your challenging new favorite.

title: I like a lot of the songs, but hate the unlock process
text:
I have all the other DDR and DDR-type games for PS2, and am enjoying this one so far, though I really hate the Stellar Master Mode, which you are forced to play to unlock new songs. You can get points to purchase new songs from playing the normal way, but you unlock songs to purchase by playing the Stellar Master Mode, which features all sorts of odd challenges, like strange arrows or arrows that move in odd ways. I play DDR by freshening up my instinct and so retraining my instinct to follow odd arrows is not any fun for me.

Then a lot of the songs are a bit too easy for me. I am not a great player by any means, so when I can get an A on Heavy (or Expert as they call it now) Girls Just Wanna Have Fun on my first try it is a bit disappointing. I'd like to have something to work towards!

Still, if you are a fan of the series this will give you some fun new songs to play! But if you are new to the series I'd get DDR Extreme 2 or DDR Max 2 - those are my favorites.
