title: Sailor Moon meets Pokemon
text:
Take a clueless magical girl, throw her into a world populated by critters that kinda resemble Pokemon, then add a few staples like dungeon crawling, and you might end up with Moco Moco Friends.

The basic gameplay is pretty simple. Go explore dungeons, fighting and collecting Plushkins. The dungeon part of the game reminds me somewhat of Rogue, but at a very basic level. The overworld consists of a shop which I've yet to use. There's a garden to grow materials you'll need for various upgrades. The sewing shop turns those raw materials into necessary components, and you'll use those in a third building to train, evolve, etc, your Plushkins. The towns "people" will sometimes give you quests, and over the course of the game, you'll unlock other NPCs.

As simple as it is, I find it charmingly addictive. I'm up to chapter 20 now, and I think I'm getting close to the end. The difficulty slowly ramps up once you get into the higher teen chapters. There are a few things which I could point out, but they don't reduce my score. Mainly the repetition and tedium of doing the same thing again and again. Go into a dungeon, which so far, typically consists of no more than 6 rooms and I've yet to see anything bigger than three floors. Fight some Plushkins on your way down to the boss, and collect materials Once you beat the boss, you're taken back to the overworld, where you'll repeat the process. Some dungeons are story-based and some are special timed dungeons that give bonuses to material collection or experience.

The game keeps the original Japanese voice acting but there is English text and there are a few funny anime-style references thrown in. Some of the interactions are genuinely funny. One of my favorite reactions is Moco's face when her Plushkins are hit in battle. The Plushkins don't die. They're just stuffed animals and you kinda beat the stuffing out of them during the battle (yes, you can actually see the stuffing popping out as they take damage). When the Plushkin faints, you might have a chance to befriend them once the battle is done.

Given the nature of the game, it makes me wonder why the original publisher didn't team up with some plushie manufacturer to create some unique tie-ins.

title: Meh
text:
Edit, two months later. I'm dropping my original three-star review to two-stars. I was adding a new stack of cards to the folio when the spine decided to break. See attached photo. It did not fully break off, but it reflects the quality of the product. After this, I decided to get a real trading card binder for the same price. I finished the job by tearing the now-falling-apart folio completely apart and used the now-useless covers in the binder's front and rear display slots.

It's a soft-cover folio. Each page has four slots in the front and four in the back. The pages are FIXED. You cannot add (or remove) pages. There are 14 pages in total, so at 8 slots (4 each side) per page, that gives you 112 slots. I figure this will fill up pretty quickly, necessitating another folio. The pages are not marked in any sequence, so you have to sort them in whatever order you wish. The only possible positive I can give is that it has the AC:HHD branding on the cover. But for functionality and usability, I'm figuring any collectible card case would work just as well (or better, if it were hard-bound). Overall, for $10, it gets a big "meh".

title: *New* Nintendo 3DS
text:
I have an original Ambassador 3DS from the 2011 launch, long before they introduced the XL models. When the XL models did come out, I did not upgrade to the XL, because I had already gotten used to the form factor of the original 3DS. I carried it everywhere. I don't carry a bag, so it was always in my pockets. Not too big, and not too heavy, it was not uncomfortable.

When Nintendo announced the *New* generation, I was excited, but that excitement quickly diminished as they indicated their intent to only release the XL version in the US. Well, Nintendo can sell me a game based around an Italian plumber and I would buy it, so with the prospects of a regular sized 3DS looking dim, I reluctantly upgraded to the *New* XL model. It WAS big, and took a very long time for me to get used to the size. I don't have large hands, so I ended up getting a bit cramped, and forget about carrying it in my pocket. I would need a belt and suspenders to keep my pants up, it was so heavy. I could barely use the new C-stick because I felt like a 2-year old trying to learn piano when my fingers just didn't reach that far.

Nintendo does a U-turn and decides to release the regular sized *New* 3DS, so what else was I to do? I "downgraded" from the XL, and I'm a happy person now. I'm still amazed at Nintendo's original intent of a non-release, but at least they finally appeared to listen to us fans and we got what we've been wanting.

As for the *New* 3DS itself:

I've done a system transfer a few times now, and either it's becoming second nature, or they've streamlined it very well. The transfer process is a fairly painless walkthru, and afterwards, you move the SD card from the old to the new; the old gets wiped to factory defaults, and when you turn on the new, you'd never notice a difference. I exaggerate. Who could not noticed going from a brick sized XL model to a comfortable regular one? But you get my point, right?

This version came pre-shipped with three Happy Home Wrecker top faceplates, so I installed the Isabelle faceplate. Installing the top faceplate is tool-free, it just snaps in. The bottom faceplate requires a small phillips-head screw driver, but you still need to remove the bottom to install the SD card even if you are not swapping the plate. Right now, there are not many faceplates available outside Japan, but from my understanding, the Japanese plates fit the international models, so if you find a good cheap exporter, you should be good.

You will still need a 3DS charger, as they've stopped shipping those with the *New* generation. I dunno why. Packaging is a bit smaller, but it certainly doesn't endear brand-new customers who find out their shiney new handheld needs to be charged with an unsupplied charger. Unlike tablets or non-Apple phones, the charger is not any USB variant, but there appears to be several USB-to-3DS adapters altho I've not used one myself.

The stylus is smaller, and just as cramped as ever, so invest in a pen-sized one if you can. It's worth it. I actually use a retractable ball-point pen with the ink cartridge removed.

Both versions of the *New* generation have improved on the 3D aspects, so whether you like the XL size or regular size, that alone is something to consider. I barely used 3D mode, and I don't know how, but it works significantly better so that I'm starting to turn it on more often.

I can't comment on battery life, since I've not played very long, but there are indicators that it's about 4 hours. My original 3DS was upgrade with a Nyko PowerPak which gave it beefy battery life with minimal additional bulk or weight, so here's hoping that Nyko will have a new version out soon.

title: Animal Crossing: Happy Home Wrecker
text:
So as everyone should know, this is an Animal Crossing spin-off. It's not a main AC game. That means they took the universe of Animal Crossing and made a whole new game. No fishing, no bug hunting, nothing like that. You basically decorate. But there is a little bit more than just that. You end up building the town, with a hospital, cafe, boutique, etc, and all to your choosing with the pretty vast Animal Crossing catalog (furniture, wall papers, even gyroids, and insects even if you don't catch them).

I've built all currently available buildings, and remodeled one. Not sure if there are more after that, or if it's just more of the same. This is a bit concerning, because right now, as cute and fun as this game is, I'm worried about longevity and replay. I have well over 350 hours logged in AC:NL, and I doubt I will achieve that here.

The designing is interesting. You select items from the catalog and place them however you wish, within certain limitations. It's much easier to move things (unlike the pull/push in AC:NL). Each job has an overall task. Like Dotty wanted a two-toned room. Villagers will give you visual clues how much they like the items you give them, and some of them will provide a few basic pieces to start with. But it's more fun designing the town. e.g., my schoolhouse has two classrooms and a hall, so it's a lot of tun to pick themes, even if they are obvious.

There are still a lot of good points to the game. Miiverse is fully integrated in the game, as in it now has an in-game button. No longer pressing Home, and logging into to Miiverse. Yea, it's a small thing, but it helps streamline connecting and is less distracting. There is the Happy Home Network. After you've done a job, you can upload your designs for the world to see (and rate). The standard 3DS in-game camera (L+R) is still present, and it seems as if they've made it easier to change camera angles.

I guess biggest hoo-ha of the game was the Amiibo cards. I got ONE card in my game (Lyle). You basically activate NFC and tap the card to invite that villager to wherever you are. Right now it seems pretty simple, so I'm not sure how deep that goes. I'm ordering a few more cards, so I'll just have to wait and see.

Unlike AC:NL, days are not real-time. There is no in-game clock/calendar. You can do one job per day. If I have one complaint it is with the save feature. If you're in the middle of a job and wish to save, you can't. You have to stop the job. To save. you go back to the office and write a log, which ends the "day".

Given the current price, I'm torn. Unless you are a die-hard Animal Crossing fan or just need to play the latest games as soon as possible, I might wait until the price drops a little. It's not a bad game overall, but it might be a little different than anticipation or expectations.

title: Project Mirai DX
text:
I played the demo, so I was sure I knew what to expect, but it turned out to be a whole lot more than the two songs from the demo. More than I can possibly cover in this review.

For starters, the main function of the game is the rhythm game, where you play different songs with different characters, at different difficulty levels. If you've played any rhythm games before, the fundamentals will be familiar. Here, you can chose to use "tap mode" or "button mode", where you either touch the screen, or press the A/B/X/Y buttons, respectively. Since I'm a bumbling oaf, I figured button mode would be the easiest, but it turns out I like playing with tap mode better.

When you start the game, you choose which character you want to be, and the style of room. I chose Miku and the green room, but you can change that. The game uses StreetPass, so make sure you have an open StreetPass slot (Nintendo really needs to increase that). Since I've only had the game for less than a day, I haven't tagged anyone, nor have I used the AR cards. Dunno exactly how many AR cards there were, but seems like about 10.

When you play songs you earn points so you can buy new decorations for the room or outfits. There's some mini-games you can play. So far I've played Go, which you activate while in Hang-out mode. There's also a Tetris-style game on the main menu. You can collect different different stamps for accomplishments. You can take photos in game, which are saved to the SD or post them to Miiverse in the usual manner (there's a new Miiverse community for the game).

In the interests of brevity, I'm going to cut this short, but there are plenty of other things I haven't mentioned. If you like rhythm games, or just like Miku or the Nendoroid Vocaloids in general, this is a fun game so far with plenty to keep me occupied.

title: Farming Simulator 2014 for 3DS
text:
I've never played a game in this franchise, but it appears there are several versions for various platforms. The 2014 version seems to be a stripped down version of 2013 adapted for mobile devices (3DS, PS Vita, iOS, Android). This review is for the 3DS version. The closest comparison would be the PS Vita version. The Android version may be cheaper, but contains the dreaded "in-app purchasing".

This is a farming simulation, and that's pretty much what it is. You plant seeds and grow three basic crops. This is not a social game like Harvest Moon. This is a good game if you just want to drive tractors and manage how to most efficiently tend and sell your crops. When I say "tend", that's usually a matter of trying to schedule everything so you don't have any idle machinery. Once you plant and fertilize, you just play the waiting game.

It's a fairly fun game with little depth. You can set it down and pick it up at will, watch TV or do other stuff while waiting for harvest time. As a sim, there's no ultimate goal, altho there are trophies for various deeds, things like how many hectares you've harvested. There are easy to finish timed missions, usually in the form of "find the lost something".

There are a few things in the 3DS version which could be better addressed:

It could use information on the types of equipment available. You're presented with the name of the equipment (Krone Big-X) but no idea what it's for. Have a device nearby with internet access so you can search the wiki's, which is almost mandatory.

Hiring workers is nice, and allows you to move on to other tasks, but you do need to keep an eye on them. They'll get stuck on fences or rocks. When you want to sell a harvest, you have the manually drive to the point of interest. And let's not even talk about how hard it is to backup a tractor! Seems like it all these should be a matter of course to adapt the AI for these things.

Cars are eye-candy and serve no purpose. Roads, too. You just drive the shortest route and traffic be damned. I like to park my tractors in the road to create massive road jams, which seem to periodically clear up automatically. You can bump into cars and force them off the road. Sometimes it's fun to play a bit of Mad Max with the cars, but they'll eventually get back on track. Maybe an option to disable traffic would be helpful.

There is no multiplayer, StreetPass or SpotPass, but there is a Miiverse community. But in all seriousness, I'm not sure what they could present for those types of scenarios anyways.

title: Harvest Moon: The Lost Valley
text:
Since the game came out less than 24 hours as of my review, it's hard to make an in-depth review. But since I see non-helpful reviews lashing against this game because "it's not the real Harvest Moon", I thought I would share my experiences based on my current 6 hours of play-time. I'm quite aware that this is a Natsume-developed game and this might be considered a variant of Harvest Moon rather than a main series game.

Those who decry it as a "Minecraft meets Harvest Moon" probably have not played either this game or Minecraft. The blocky terrain is the only similarity to Minecraft. The concept of the terrain is interesting, and it gives you a broader style of gameplay. The terrain shape also seems to have implications in how your crops grow.

Unlike the most recent Harvest Moon, A New Beginning, there is very little hand-holding. You spend about 30 minutes with the first harvest sprite who teaches you basic terrain and crop management. After this, the sprite gives you a fairly easy first quest, then you're kinda on your own. Explore, plant, and do the normal things. I don't know what triggers some events, but there seem to be some events that are triggered based on what/how much you've planted so far.

Terrain management takes a bit getting used to. You trigger management mode by pressing Y, and then using A/B/X/Y to dig, raise, etc. Once you trigger terrain management, your screen is highlighted with a 3x3 selection, but only the differently colored selection is the one you operate on. You'll find yourself moving around quite a bit, either to position your selection marker, or to move terrain blocking your view. You can press the L and R shoulder buttons to rotate the camera, and press L+R simultaneously to place the camera directly behind you.

Tool selection is somewhat context-sensitive. After you've used terrain mode to prepare the field, you press A to choose an operation. Facing a prepared section of field, that will allow you to plant seeds. Approaching trees will let you chop them down. So it seems like you don't need to manually select your tools any more.

There are plenty of Harvest Moon features, beside the farming. You have stamina which you need to be mindful of, but you get lots of it. I've not been at risk of fainting yet. Time passes rather fast, about 1 real second is 1 in-game minute. I'm suspecting that as the game progresses, you'll need to make standard Harvest Moon types of time-management decisions. I've only met a few NPCs so far, but they kinda plant themselves in my yard, rather than a town proper like HM:ANB. Since I've not yet woke up the Harvest Goddess, which is a key plot element to unlocking the rest of the seasons, I'm hoping that a real town will eventually open. There are stairs to the left of your house, but they're blocked off and only NPCs can use them.

The 3D in the title is a bit of a misnomer. Most (if not all?) of the game is in 2D mode (you can tell because the 3D status light is off), so I suspect the 3D part of it is rather from the view of the character, which is something isometric view: that is, the camera floats behind the character, and as you walk around the world, the camera can (and will, of it's own) rotate to view different perspectives.

The camera... This is why the game gets 3-stars. It moves on it's own. You'll be walking in your field, and it'll rotate around. It doesn't appear that you can modify the camera behavior, and hopefully this is something I can learn to deal with. Natsume used a similar technique in their recent game Hometown Story, and altho it is not as disruptive, it is still somewhat unnecessary.

I've been anticipating this game for a few months now, and will definitely be playing it more. I'm not 100% certain I am enamored with the game, as I've yet to hit that "sweet spot" which tells me "Keep playing!".

title: Fantasy Star
text:
I'm 19 hours into the game and just finished the main story. This game is just that addicting. In a fun way. Even with the main story finished, there's an enormous amount of content to explore, and that's not even considering the DLC. I can easily see logging over 100 hours.

If I have any issues with the game:

People talk too much. They talk and talk and talk. Mostly during the main quest lines, and at times you'll wonder if you're playing an RPG or a visual novel.

Once you trigger a main quest line (and that also considers Live quest lines) you're sorta stuck in that arc until you finish it. There's a few points where you can take a break, but for the most part, if you need a break, just close the cover rather than waiting for a natural pause.

Luckily, the main story is not hard and the game's general progression will level you appropriately. I finished at level 25, and feeling cocky, I visited some new areas where some monsters took 50% of my health in two hits, so the difficulty is not so much in the main part, but post-game. And I haven't even touched multiplayer yet!

And finally, one of those few games where I was compelled to watch the cutscenes. The game lets you skip them, but I didn't, they were just beautifully done. Overall, I really want to call this a "masterpiece".

title: Hometown Story
text:
Even tho the game is created by the same person who created Harvest Moon, try to keep in mind that this is not a Harvest Moon game. Why mention the obvious? I've seen several comparisons to HM which makes me wonder if people consider this a HM title. It's not, altho it shares many similarities, but keeping that in mind will give a proper mindset when playing this game. No preconceptions about HM, etc.

I'm having an OK time with the game so far. I know from reading the Natsume forums that as you get more into the game, the more the town will build and become alive. I have a few issues with the game which hold me from posting a full 5-star review. Actually, I'd like to post this as 3.5, but since we can't do half-stars here, I'll round up.

Character customization is good. There was enough starter customization options to make me feel like I was picking my own character, rather than a cookie-cutter. Yet not too many options to overwhelm and put me into that endless second-guessing mode.

The tutorial, such as it is, is very short, and once you get past that, well, you're on your own. This is the hardest part of the game so far, the sheer learning. The town is huge, and there are many NPCs, and trying to absorb all this is a bit daunting at first. I guess they wanted to get out of that hand-holding style so common. Well, back in my days, when we got a game, we played it first without reading directions or having popups leading you to the next objective. This is kinda what I feel right now. Once free of the tutorial, you might want to spend a few days in the shop before venturing out, when a few key cutscenes occur, and just to settle in. There are also a lot of cutscenes, but you're used to that, right?

I won't go into deep depth of the game play, but will just touch a few points.

Music is good. Altho I can see why others might say the shop music might drive you nuts, the song is long enough and non-repetitious that I still enjoy it.

On the map you can find NPCs, but they're not labeled, so it seems you have to remember their faces. When an NPC asks for something, there is no log, so you've got to either rely on memory, or use a notepad.

My main issue is with camera angles, which change at bizarre points and make it hard to tell where you are walking. I've ended up watching the lower screen, which displays the map and a directional pointer, but that hinders me from looking around for resources (as well as just enjoying the artwork). The map is zoom-able, so you can view your current zone or zoom out to see the whole town. If you click on certain spots on the map, it will give you a direction cue to follow, so you don't get (too) lost. You can also highlight an NPC to bring up a direction cue, but some of the map controls are also a bit strange. Sometimes when trying to highlight an NPC, I don't actually highlight it, and end up zooming in or out...

Overall it's a quirky little game, but nothing that should be terrible once you acclimate to those quirks.

title: Pokémon X
text:
I've got six badges so far, so I feel like I've seen enough of the game to make a review based on actual game-play rather than preconceived notions. I've only been playing Pokemon since HG/SS, so I'm definitely not a genwunner. I'm also not into competitive battling, so I won't really be talking too much about that, or things like the new fairy type. Those are topics for discussion on forums, not a game review. Since most of the changes are the online features, I'll probably discuss those more than anything else.

For starters, yes, it is the same as every other Pokemon so far. The same introduction, pick your starter, battle random trainers and gym leaders, collect badges, defeat the champ. The same limitations of having a party of six, with each having a max of four active moves. If you stop and think, everything else is gravy: story, graphics, music, etc. The fundamental mechanics are the same, and I think that is quite frankly the majority of the reason for the franchise's staying power. You can pick up any gen game, and knowing your basic types, weaknesses, etc, you'll know how to play.

A lot of the changes in this generation are based mostly around the online features, some of which were only in their beginnings in BW/B2W2. But you no longer have to find a Pokemon Center to participate in the online functions, they're all right on the screen. You can turn the online functions on and off at will.

Probably the most interesting is the PSS, the Player Search System. Like most native 3DS games, this game integrates with the 3DS friend codes, so you no longer have to manage separate friend codes. You just add their 3DS code to the 3DS friends app, and then you can see their status in-game. Now while you're in game, you can see their status: player profile, badges, and other things. You can battle, trade or chat with them. Pretty much like in the old Union Rooms, but not as limited as the Union Rooms were.

Over time, you'll see people being added to the PSS, under the headings of acquaintances and passerbys. Acquaintances are added as you interact with other remote players via the global trade, battles, etc. I'm not exactly sure how passerby's work, but I think they just are random people who appear on your screen; again, you can interact with them in all the same manners. One thing I enjoy so far is the "wonder trade", which is a random trade matchup: you chose which Pokemon you want to trade, and it'll find someone in the world, and you get what you get. You might get trash Pokemon, or you might get something good.

Beyond the online features are all the other changes to the game. Music is awesome, no longer grating to the ears (altho I'm a chiptune fan, you can only listen to the Pokecenter music for so long without wanting to stab your eyes out). The graphics are fantastic, altho I do not play in 3D mode. The avatars are nicely customizable. After a long-winded review, I'll just close with that I think this is a great addition to the franchise.

Post-game edit: I beat the champ in about 5 days, less than 25 logged playing. This is by far the easiest version I've played. Each gym, elite and champ, I was able beat in one attempt. I never felt it necessary to rethink my team, go back and grind up, or anything of that nature. I also played straight thru with my starter, Fennekin, in slot one. She was KO'ed a few times, but I never considered retiring her. With Exp Share, even my HM slaves become viable.

I'm still exploring post-game play, and since I have tried to refrain from strat guides, I don't know how extensive post-game is yet. So far, I've found a side-arc of working in a detective agency, and found daily jobs at a hotel. I found two stationary legendaries to catch, and ran into one roaming legendary but do not know how to catch it yet. I did not find anything similar to BW2's Join Ave, or the little and big stadiums, with their daily battles, but I'm probably not searching hard enough.

title: Etrian Odyssey IV: Legends of the Titan
text:
I hadn't heard of this game, or seen any reviews, but when I saw it on the new releases, I decided to pick this up on a whim. Sometimes such impulse buying can get you burned, like the recent SimCity release. But this game is certainly not one of those.

It is a nice mix of classic dungeon crawling using some of the newest technologies. If you're not familiar with dungeon crawling, basically you start out at a base town with a few services (buy, sell, etc), and then venture into a dungeon, but there is more than one dungeon in this game.

Also similar to some of those old school crawlers, usually you can only save the game while in town. You can make restore saves, which get deleted as soon as you start playing again, and there are a few special save points in the dungeons. But if you die in this game, you won't be doing the typical save/load routine. And yes, you'll die. And probably often.

The game is a bit difficult. There are two settings, normal and easy, but I am playing it on normal. The overall story is just to go out and explore, but don't be reckless. Recklessness will ultimately harm you, as will complacency. There are even a few early encounters that (try to) teach you the detrimental effects of being complacent.

Different than many modern games, where the dungeons are side-notes and the maps are fully revealed, where you can beef up and go nuke anything that moves without worrying about dying. So don't get trapped into EZ mode thinking here.

There are a few other features in the game that make it unique:

Primarily is the mapping system. If you've played any of the classic dungeon crawl games that did not have mapping systems, you might remember the old pen-and-paper maps we'd draw as you explore the dungeons. While the game has an auto-mapper feature, it's by no means perfect. You'll use the 3DS stylus to draw walls, make iconic notes, paint water, and so on. The maps are saved even at the dreaded "game over", so that particular hard work is not lost. Get used to mapping, it's necessary, and actually quite fun and enjoyable. Get used to spinning around in a 360 degree circle, and checking to make sure there are no secrets.

Oh, how I wish we had this kind of mapping system back in the days of the Bard's Tale!

Somewhat related to the mapping system is the auto-play. You can place various movement icons on the map (left, right, up, down), and press "START", and the game will automatically move in those directions. Kinda like a macro, but not a fully automatic. You can map out a circular patrol pattern so that you can keep walking around the dungeons waiting for random encounters, without having to keep pressing buttons. I know some players will frown on such "auto levellers", but try it. It eases the grinding which seems to be inevitable in these kinda games.

Another nice feature is the content delivery system. The developer blog posts QR codes to unlock items, quests, and so on. So far, there are only two such postings, but I hope they continue doing so. You use an in-game feature to access the QR system.

Like a lot of newer 3DS games, they try to incorporate StreetPass, which is interesting, altho since I purchased my 3DS during the initial release in January 2011, I've only gotten a single Mii Plaza StreetPass tag. But I'll still hope to see if I get other tags. Apparently you can acquire new characters in this manner.

Finally of note is the music and the graphics, which are also just as good. The graphics are nicely drawn, also evoking nostalgia for hand-drawn graphics, instead of perfectly rendered 3D models. The package I picked up even had a CD of the OST; dunno if the version being sold on Amazon does as well, since it does not specifically note it.

All in all, if you like old school hack-n-slash dungeon crawling games, you'll probably like this game. If you've never played one before, why not give it a try?

title: Burned
text:
The short version: don't buy this game.

Any innovative features are buried under the fundamental flaws that exist in the game. I only wish I waited a week after release, but now I'm out $80 with nothing but a not-so-warm and happy feeling that I've spent my money on a product which implies my endorsement this type of system, and by purchasing the game, I've contributed to the mess that is the video games industry by spending my money to support online-only DRM.

Out of the almost 2,000 reviews here, various gaming blogs and other news sites, if you're not already aware, this game has the 100% necessary requirement of online play. If your internet is down, no game for you.

Basically, you're leasing this game, and only under the good graces of EA. If they decided to shut the game down, you can't play. No online, no play. Servers overloaded, no play. This is NOT an MMO, where you are logging in to a server to play a game, this is DRM (digital rights management) which is the authentication method used to verify the license of the game.

Oh sure, they'll eventually fix it, and they've already promised us a free game, currently unidentified, from the EA catalog, but don't be surprised if it's some kind of bargain-barrel game. But what they HAVEN'T promised is a method to fix the online-only DRM, so their promise of a free game is just to dangle a carrot in front of us in the hopes that we'll forget how thoroughly they're burning us.

The DRM method used is the new trend in video games, and the only way to express your dissatisfaction is to NOT buy the game. Compare this to video games ~10 years ago, where you got a CD, and you can install the game at any time. Nope, even if you got the physical media for this game, you might not be able to play this next year, or whatever. I can pull out my old Doom or Quake games, each easily over 10 years old, and still play them today.

Social features of this game aside, this is NOT an MMO (I know I'm repeating myself). 100% online is not a requirement for a game like this.

Save your money, send a message, don't buy it.

title: Harvest Moon
text:
I've only played the original DS release of Harvest Moon, and this one feels rather different than that original version. Now, it's been a few years since the original DS version was released, so memory might be a bit hazy, but A New Beginning has really grabbed me in a way that the DS version did not.

I find myself losing track of time. It's one of those "wait, just one more thing!" games. When I look up to see a couple of real-life hours has passed, I consider that to be a good measure of the game's ability to keep me engrossed. Not that it's a very hard game, or super in-depth, but the in-game time clock is always running, which is part of the drive.

There's even a multiplayer option which lets you meet up with 3 other people to trade a surprise gift (one gift trade per session), milk their cows, and a few other things.

I don't really use the 3D option, other than a few minutes at a time, but for the majority of my game-play, it is turned off.

While I have no major complaints against the game, but there are a few quirks to point out. Nothing that deters me from plating the game, but just things I wish they had done in other ways...

The introduction was extremely slow, which can be very annoying. For a few reasons, I decided to restart the game after playing thru to Spring 20, but realistically, I don't know how many people will decide to restart, so that may not be an issue. Even so, be prepared to spend a bit of time on the intro, none of which can be skipped. This also applies to almost every cutscene, in that you cannot interrupt them, speed them up, or just skip them.

Player movement control is achieved solely by the 3DS circle pad. The crosspad is only used for camera options. That may sound like a small thing, but when most other games will work using either the circle pad or the crosspad, it might take a little bit of acclimation before you stop zooming the camera when you meant to move...

And while not really a design flaw or quirk, but in-game time moves, and moves fast, and seems to always move. It appears to be about 1 real-time second per in-game minute. There are plenty of times I find myself wishing time would slow down. Some times, you may find that you might not be able to accomplish every single daily goal. But is overall a part of the game fundamental mechanics, needing to plan and strategize to make the best of each day.

Overall, no regrets in buying or playing, and find it quite fun, and in an odd way, rather relaxing after a day of real-life work.

title: Worth every penny
text:
While I haven't done any real time comparison tests, I've had my Nkyo-powered 3DS off the charger for 9 hours now (I don't use the dock), and it has only consumed one bar of the battery meter. I'm running White 2 with the C-Gear turned on. Playing it 15 minutes here, 30 minutes there, etc, only closing the lid when it's time to take a break. Using the original battery, the 3DS would have been long dead by now. I would comfortably say this can at least double the battery life. Since it's only a week or so old now, only time will tell if it continues this performance.

It does add some weight and thickness to the 3DS, which can be noticeable over lengthy gaming periods. Couple that with sharp edges of the 3DS (unlike the smoother edges of the DS series) it can cause a bit of discomfort. On the positive side, the bottom of the battery is a rubbery non-skid material which does make it slightly easier to grip, and sits on a table-top without fear of sliding away.

The battery is really easy to install. Just four screws, pop off the back lid, pop out the old battery, and insert the new battery. While the included tooth-pick style screwdriver is a nice gesture, don't use it. Any game geek or computer nerd worth their salt should have a precision screwdriver set; if you don't have a set, ask around. You don't want to strip the already-easy-to-strip screws, so be careful. If you're not comfortable with this, find a friend (the same one you borrowed the precision screwdriver from).

Be careful how long you take, because many games are time sensitive, and if you take too long, the clock will reset. I did not notice this, and when I tried to sync White 2 to the Global Link, it detected a time change and placed a hard-wait of 24 hours on me. I think I saw a discussion here how to quickly pop it out without losing the date/time.

Finally, not sure if it's worth noting, but my 3DS is one of the original NA releases (Ambassador Certificate), so the original battery might have already been approaching its end of life anyways.

title: It's OK as DLC
text:
This is a _very_ short campaign. Before going into the campaign itself:

Installation was much easier than installing the original game. Probably due to the fact that, by now, you have the Origin client installed, and the DLC installs thru that. Once installed, it does NOT show up on the main list of games, and the order receipt shows "no serial number necessary", so it was a little confusing at first how to actually PLAY the DLC. It doesn't appear in the main menu under "Downloadable content".

Once the DLC is installed, you "Continue" an existing game, and you'll trigger a new quest to start playing the DLC. You have to be level 10 to trigger the quest, but if you've finished the OC, you should more than meet the requirements. This is rather an interesting method to activate the DLC, and I liked it.

I was level 40 (the max), have most of my skills maxxed, and a nicely outfitted character who migrated right into the DLC campaign.

This said, consider the rest of this review to contain possible spoilers.

As I said, the DLC campaign is very short, and most of it revolves around building your new keep, which is a very sweet residence indeed, a miniature town. In between running the restoration quests, you complete the main story quests for Dead Kel, as many of these quests will intersect. So you'll be in the area anyways.

One word of warning, and a definite spoiler, once you begin the final Dead Kel quest, going into his dungeon, make sure you have enough inventory space to loot every chest and pile, because once you vanquish Dead Kel, it looks like you cannot return.

I didn't log how many hours I played until I defeated Dead Kel, but it was certainly less than 10, and probably something you can hammer out over a weekend. As I said above, since I was maxxed out on character, at no point in playing did I get that "oh crap" feeling, where I was in over my head. title: Excellent fun
text:
I liked this game enough that when my free 30 day trial ended, I opted for the monthly subscription.

I'm no stranger to MMORPGs, and there's no real need to list out those which I've tried, but this one (WoW) seems to fit a lot of my personal desires in a game.

For starters, my machine is fairly up to speed: An Athlon XP2100+ (overclocked to 1.8) with 512mb of RAM, and a GeForce 420MX with 64mb. The only possible source of horsepower problems are with the video card, which is definately underpowered. In the big metro cities, where a lot of activity happens, I get some lag because my video card is not able to handle it fast enough.

I also play games for my own personal enjoyment. I don't power-game, power-level, whatever. I haven't read any of the guides to quick advancement. I'm a newbie, and I like it that way, because I discover the game on my own terms, and there is an enormous amount to discover.

The interface is fairly easy to use. Point-and-click. Left and right mouse buttons trigger different actions. Lots of keyboard shortcuts, so that you can really play with both hands on the keyboard. Related to the interface are all things like character analysis; inventory, skills and quests management. All these are easy to bring up, and fairly obvious once you start looking at them.

The death system is also nice. You can easily die, but there's no devestating consequences due to a misjudged situation. Other games I've played have dire death system: you can loose EVERY item in your current inventory, including money; you can loose massive amounts of experience points even to the point of loosing levels. Some of those other systems are so horrific that it's not unheard of to reroll a character even after one death.

Here in WoW, death is unavoidable. But when you die, you can either rez at the cost of XP (never loosing levels); or run back to your body and rez at no cost. You will rez at reduced health, and you may rez in the middle of mobs or even a PvP battle, so there is still risk involved. You might even die in a place where you can't rez. All in all, a good way to handle dying.

For now, the game is mostly quest-driven, and advancement seems to be much easier if you quest more than grind. Maybe at higher levels you'll need to do the grind, or maybe you're more into the PvP thing more than exploring the world. Whatever you like, WoW seems to have enough for everyone.

Others have talked about how gimped some of the classes are (the warrior), but again, since I'm not driven by power-levelling, that doesn't seem to bother me. I play as a warrior, and have won and lost my fair share of duels, so at a low level, it all really depends on how tactical you are in playing.

There's a lot more that could be said, but there's no room for it. Try the 30-day free period and see for yourself.

title: Great addition
text:
There's a lot of things I think make this expansion pack worthwhile. Just another game to play, that alone would be a deal. But you can sort of "pick up" where you might have ended in NWN:OC or SoU.

I haven't had any crashing problems, and have a general run-of-the-mill system: XP2100+ with 512mb, XPSP2, DMA133 hard drive. The only thing that might be considered sub-par is the graphic card, which is an older NVidia MX420 which I've had for about three years now (64mb). But even with the video, I get good response, except in those areas where there are a huge number of scripts running, such as one battle scene near the end. luckily, those are few.

Other than that, the plot is fun, and full of unexpected twists and turns. But it allows you to follow those plot twists, such as betraying your allies. The ultimate goal seems to be the same, no matter which way you play it.

Graphics and sounds are fine, as in the original NWN. They did add a lot more cut-scenes to HotU, tho, which can get kind of annoying. Some of the cut-scenes add depth to the story, but some are just seemingly put there for eye-candy.

There's also lots more puzzles in this expansion. Some are fun, but one in particular got extremely tedious very fast. I knew exactly how to solve it, but I had to wait for in-game timing events before I could move on to the next step. I honestly cheated at that point, and just solved the puzzle. Otherwise I'd probably waste 30 or so minutes.

You can start HotU with a new character, and you'll immeadiately level him up to level 15. I'd really recommend that you play straight from OC to SoU and then HotU. You get a good feel for your character, his strengths and weaknesses. It's easy to take your newly made level 15 character and assume invicibility. I ended the OC with a level 15 half-orc barb, took him thru SoU to level 18, and ended HotU around level 22. Quite a bit of growth in there. Besides, I'm an XP hunter and level monger, so I like that kind of stuff.

title: hack-n-slash maybe, but still great fun!
text:
I like this game a lot. Forgive the length of this review - this is a long game, which has a lot of elements.

For starters, the sounds are excellent. The voice-overs are a little goofy; I get a little tired of Tomi's "hokey-dokie!", but the sound effects are very nice. The music is simply outstanding, and very well written. I especially like the musical trigger, which changes the soundtrack when you are going into battle.

Visuals are outstanding as well. There should be enough eye-candy to satisfy most critics (weather effects, shadows, and a wide range of item art).

Game control is generally straight-forward. There is a tutorial which walks you thru the basic game mechanics. But really, most RPGs have the same generic features - character development, inventory management, maps and notebooks, and so on. It's not too hard to figure out to press "i" to bring up your inventory screen, or to click on an NPC to talk to them.

Camera control is a bit tricky. There are three modes - chase, top down and driving mode. The game defaults to chase mode, which automatically rotates the screen. I found myself getting a little queazy, as the screen would rotate, so changed it to top down mode. All that means is that I have to spin the screen manually.

You might need to spend some time in screen rotation and zooming, due to the way the game sometimes puts plot items right underneath another object. I often end up clicking on an avatar and getting a dialogue box, rather than examining the item I want.

As a small side note, there are WAY too many crates/barrels/boxes in the game, in places you don't expect to see them. A lot of them are locked, and a lot of those are trapped. It gets to be tedious, because you really want to search all the areas, in case there is a signficant plot item.

The campaign is pretty big. It's divided into four "chapters", but they're fairly longish. I've finished the OC (official, or original campaign) and the SoU expansion pack. I really don't know how long it took me to finish. I found the SoU expansion to be a little more fun in some areas, even tho it was a lot shorter. The SoU adds visual effects to plot items, and henchie inventory control, among other things.

It is kind of linear in play, and personally, I like that. In most non-linear games, I have a tendency to dawdle around or simply get lost without knowing what to do. The main storyline is fairly straight forward, but there are still a lot of side-quests you can tackle along the way, if you get bored of the story.

Others have said the game is too much hack-n-slash, but I like that. In all my RPGing, I always select the generic fighter type. So in this game, I chose a half-orc barbarian. I don't choose my character types based on lazyness. I know a lot of people would say choosing the big dumb brute is the easy way. But when you think about it, if you have to wade into five or six mobs with just your brute force, taking direct blows, it's just another style of strategy, which is the style I've been playing since the old C-64 Bards Tale games.

In any event, there are a huge number of items to find in the game - weapons, armor, magic items. Gold abounds. I was a little worried at the start of the game, trying to hire a henchman for 250gp, when all I had was 50gp in my pocket. But as soon as I started adventuring, that turned into a non-issue. The game-world is big enough that it does take a bit of time moving around from place to place.

I haven't played online yet, and am franky probably not going to even try. My online gaming experience was spoiled years ago thanks to Diablo, Battle.Net and wide-spread cheating. I know these newer games have methods to control stuff, but honestly, quite a lot of people I meet online are just plain jerks. I guess anonyminity tends to make people less polite to strangers which they'll never meet personally.

title: Great fun
text:
I purchased this game a couple of years ago, after the initial release. For one reason or another, I ended up getting rid of it. But I just had to re-purchase this game. It was a little cheaper this time around, considering the game has been out some time already.

My decision to purchase this game, twice, should reflect how much I enjoyed this game.

I personally like to play a "free" activity, and my favorite is to take the steam engine on the Northeast Corridore tracks. When driving any of the trains, play with full manual controls for the best effect.

The steam engine has a slightly steep learning curve, but it's definately worth it. Twisting the valves, opening the firebox, shovling coal, all these things (when done manually) can lend a great sense of realism to the game. To the point where I can imagine myself sweaty and grimy, sailing ~60mph trying to keep this infernal contraption from derailing! And yes, make sure you turn derailments ON, and switch to an external view as you realize, with horror, that you just cannot make that curve...

title: Almost perfect but the flaw is huge
text: I really like games that have no absolute set in stone rules no timers nothing you have to do in a specific order just a wide open land to explore and things to do as you want and on your own time. Yes I am a big animal crossing fan but when I read about yonder I thought maybe this could be a very fun change and I was right.  But I have to say I honestly have a love and hate relationship with this game. I absolutely love 99% of everything about this game but the 1% that I hate is something that drives me absolutely crazy. This game runs on a cycle of day and night but unlike animal crossing that is literally changing with an actual clock, Yonder’s day and nights cycle so quickly that you can’t even finish a task before your character is whipping out a lantern so you can see in the dark and yes it’s nice that that is automatic but you do miss a lot of details in the dark and if you are traveling you can easily become unsure of where you are and how you got there for the next time. I haven’t timed the day and night cycles but it is extremely quick and it is really hard for me to like this game and I am even tempted sometimes to set the game down during the night time cycle and just play during the daytime cycles but again that’s just frustrating. Apparently I am not the only one with this complaint because I did look up online to see if there was anyway you could change those settings and that seems to be a huge complaint with this game. title: Buy only if you want FOV
text:
So I have a pimax 5k, and upgraded to this 8k. And it is a noticeable upgrade in SDE and resolution. The upscaling mode works great. because if you can run the 5k, you can also run the 8kx. I've also owned other headsets: Samsung odyssey, Oculus Rift S, HP Reverb. Now I gotta say that the 8kx's FOV cannot be beat. It's the reason why i stick to pimax. However, the FOV is the only advantage. The contrast, color vibrancy is admittedly slightly, barely worse than any of my other headsets. It was actually noticeably worse actually, before the latest pitool update which allows you to adjust the backlight brightness slider. Set it to 90 and now vibrancy isn't an issue. Is the big FOV worth the double price tag and slightly less vibrant colors? You decide. But for me, it's worth it. I've tried to enjoy myself in the rift S and reverb, but I just couldn't lie to myself: the narrow fov is way more distracting than the slightly less colors of the pimax.

Also I guess I'll complain about the lenses of the pimax. they're ok, that's it. I don't know how oculus does it, but even with the rift s's lower resolution, it managed to get rid of the black void between pixels that comes naturally with low resolution. it's got an anti-aliasing film on it or something, which is what pimax needs to make it magical. But as of now, it doesn't.

Also, the cable that I got was giving me problems: I would shake it and loose the image, and the headset LED would turn red. Oddly enough, the problem went away. However, when I plug in a pair of headphones into the headphone plug, there is a very loud buzzing electrical noise in the background. It tells me that there is still something wrong with the cable. I have a workaround for the buzzing for now: plug headphones into computer output jack instead. But I worry that the rogue electrical signals could fry the headset in time.

And lastly, the default audio that comes with the pimax sucks, as it floats above your ears and sounds very nasal.

title: best of the best.
text:
Why all the hate? This is the ultimate perfect mouse. Super light, decent accuracy, but most of all...11 programmable buttons!
I've been looking for the ultimate mouse for years and years, and let me tell you I've spent a small fortune just buying mouses left and right looking for the perfect one. I've had the mad catz mmo5, mmo7, rat5, rat 7, razer naga, razer hex, high end logitech mouses, and several steelseries mouses. they were not cheap. This one trumps them all, razer sux but I love their nostromo.

Right before I got this mouse, i thought i had the perfect mouse; the steelseries WOW wireless mouse which is identical to this one. I don't play WOW, never have, but I liked the idea of having 11 programmable buttons for other games. The wow wireless unfortunately only has 10, the gold edition is 11!! Wireless was cool and all but the wifi was giving my hand a major radiation burns which is insane so I had to let it go. I'm glad I got this gold one because its wired and that 11th button is programmable...it also runs on the same software! so I did not have to reconfigure anything.

Pros:

Ergonomics- Super comfortable, super light, and all the buttons in all the right places. The pinky/ring finger button is absolutely fantastic. It causes less confusion when you can spread buttons between all your fingers instead of just 2. I don't know why Razer doesn't do it and they suck because they refuse to. Sure razer got a mouse with more programmable buttons but trust me, in the heat of battle your thumb will be too slow to hit them all in succession, nor accurately since the buttons are all clustered up. You will have to think for a split second for each button which makes you even slower. Also its so uncomfortable to hit the back buttons with your thumb. Then in comparison... madcat mmo7, the best of the madcat mouses also sucks. It is flat, you will get cramps and it is so uncomfortable to use, the mouse is angled towards the right so your fingers will have to stretch just to click the left mouse button. The buttons on the madcat is also flimsy and you won't know if you pressed it or not, also they break so easily. Then the thumb buttons are so clustered that when you hit one button you hit them all. Also the thumb joystick on the madcat is a joke, not enough room at all to move it. I loved the thumbscroll though, thats the only highlight of the mmo7.

Software- Steelseries got the best software for this gold edition mouse. Lots of auto profiling buttons, and easy macro creation! Razer synapse sucks in comparison because you MUST log into the internet to use the mouse, and it is super buggy. And there is a limit for profile creation, even though they moved to the cloud for 'more memory'? WTF?! All those gigs of cloud storage and I can't make more than 10 profiles in razer synapse?!! Something smells fishy here. Logitech software is a joke, no autoprofiling, and their mouse buttons are software programmable which means it wont work in all games. The mmo7 software is decent and pretty easy to use though, no complaints there.

Looks- Okay, I don't play wow and I hate the wow logo on the mouse, but it still looks pretty good. The madcatz mmo7 takes the cake in looks, and the razer doesn't look too shabby either but looks don't mean much when compared to functionality and comfort.

polling rate- okay the polling rate for the gold edition mouse is pretty low, 1khz. But I've had other mouses with higher polling rate and i notice no difference at all.

Overall, this gold WOW mouse is the best of the best. Better than even the 2nd place, the steelseries wireless wow mouse. But some may prefer that for the wireless if they are not allergic to extreme wifi signals. It can be better, perfect actually, if it had that thumbscroll like on the mmo7 but i ain't complaining. This mouse is still the best. I seriously don't know why people hate on this mouse. I have tried them all, many mouses over 100 bucks but none can compare to this one for only $50.

I guess I should be happy that this mouse gets so much unwarranted hate though, because it drove the price down so low that I'm going to buy 4 more for backup.

title: bad controls, storyline, and repetitive.

The best thing about this game is the graphics and the complexity. The customization of characters is amazing for a vita title, you don't see much of that. The multitude of weapons, modules, and upgrades you can do will keep you busy for a long time.

However after a while it gets repetitive. You start noticing that there are not that many enemies, you fight the same ones over and over and over. The world is also super tiny, your quests will make you run through the same tiny world over 1000 times. Also the storyline is just standard, nothing special and nothing memorable. Music is also generic. You also cannot customize the button layout, which is lame and it takes a long time to get used to.

My biggest gripe though is the aiming system: target lock for melee sucks, doesn't work for crap except the first hit because you will be going through the enemy and lock will break. And if you're using a ranged weapon, you can't shoot AND aim at the same time unless you have 2 thumbs, thanks to the inability to configure your buttons. Also there is a lag when you aim and it always makes me over/undershoot my targets kinda like a s***ty fps game.

Pros: It has a decent storyline with some touching moments, and the characters are very charming. The artwork and graphics is just amazing, I can't complain there. The battle system is very straight forward in battle, but the skill and class system is very good and addicting. There is just so many ways to customize a fighter that you'll spend dozens of hours grinding your characters for that perfect combination of skills and class. Then there are those skills that only certain main characters can have, but you can have them pass those skills down to a child of your choice and make even better skill combos. This system reminds me a bit of final fantasy tactics, with its many combinations of fighting classes and secondary skills.

Okay now for the cons:

Although the story is pretty good, it's not on the level of epic-ness like the great classics such as Final fantasy 7, tactics, Xenogears, Chrono trigger etc. It's just not memorable and there is nothing that will make you remember the game years from now.

My biggest gripe though, is that even though there are lots of DLC's, the main story/game is too short. For a game with such a great battle system, I wish I could grind out my classes doing the storyline battles (like in FF tactics for example). But no, the game ends before your soldiers even begin to use the customization system to its full potential. Seriously, it just leaves you thinking 'What the eff..'. So if you want to fully unleash the potential of the class/skill system, you must stop playing the storyline and just do a bunch of mindless battles on the side. A LOT.

So overall it's one of the best rpg games of this generation, but not at the levels of the greats. Which is sad because there are no rpgs this generation that compares to the great classics. I would still recommend this game because although it's really short, you can beat it in under 15 hours (that's really damn short for a strategy RPG), it's still a very fun and engaging ride.

For a regular old gaming mouse, though, I'd probably go with something from Redragon, but if you need these extra buttons this is actually a really great mouse.

text:
5 MONTH UPDATE: Changed to ONE STAR. Now the thing has a double-click issue. Started noticing it a few weeks ago where 1/10 click registered twice. Today EVERY CLICK REGISTERS AS A DOUBLE CLICK. I've read some trouble-shooting items from their website...reset the mouse, checked polling rate in settings in iCUE, etc. This mouse is functionally useless. Piece of junk, and I wasted $80. I can connect through USB and keep my iCue settings, but iCue doesn’t detect the mouse when connected through Bluetooth. I feel like I wasted a LOT of money. I was able to reassign all the buttons I wanted to change and I disabled all the silly lighting effects...set up a default profile that works with what gaming I actually do. Corsair needs to scrap all the "CUE" stuff and start over.

title: a great game sabotaged by its own developers
text:
Valkyria Chronicles is a terrible game dressed up as an excellent game. It seems at first to have all the tactical enjoyment of a computerized Squad Leader (Avalon Hill's masterful tabletop WW2 game) and a great roleplaying element and story. I was very happy for the first several scenarios. After that, the game falls apart and becomes a chore of tedious cutscenes and deathtraps. The player learns that the advice given by the game in mission briefings is designed to make you fail. The quasi-scientific theme becomes corrupted by inappropriate fairy tale elements. The vast array of solid tactical mechanics is ditched in favor of chaotic scripted events that will have you wasting hours of time on "bang, you're dead!" endings to long scenarios. There is no autosave. Thete are numerous lengthy cutscenes that cannot be skipped, and it will wear on you the 10th time watching the same cutscene giving you wrong information.

This is a case of no coordination on the development team: fantastic core programming, great story. Then an incompetent level designer/programmer undermines the game's goal by making it about luck and repetition. Then an editor decides the essentially deep story that is a clever metaphor for WW2 in Europe needs mages and winged farm animals stapled to it. A five-star game was pillaged of all its worth before it hit the shelves. Don't buy it.

title: An ideal game for the right kind of gamer
text:
Much has been said in these many reviews. Disgaea 2 is a brilliant tactical strategy game that doesn't take itself too seriously. You will feel justified in using any means possible to accomplish your goals: Nobody else in the world has a conscience, so why should you? Of course, when I say "any means possible", I am not including cheats like restarting the game over and over until a random treasure is exactly what you wanted. I think you know what I mean.

I usually hate games with bad stories or bad voice acting. Disgaea 2 is the exception. The tactical play and the mechanics are SO GOOD that even I don't really care about the airheaded plot and blase voice acting. I recommend playing the game in Japanese and using the English subtitles; The Japanese voices are less irritating than the English voices.

Disgaea 2 is a game about leveling up. Yes, that's what I mean. It is a hardcore look at the concept of "level ups" in RPG's and tactical fighting games, and it zooms right in on that one concept. Not only do your characters level up, but their skills level up individually. Not only that, but every one of your inventory items can level up. Not only can every item level up, but the people living in your items can also level up. Yes, I said people living in your items. They are little, cartoony smiley faces representing the individual skillset that your particular item has. You can trade, combine, and upgrade these people between items and between characters. The sheer mathematic of all the things you could possibly do with your adventuring party is simply staggering. You may find yourself equipping 20th level opera glasses. No, really -- opera glasses. One of my characters has a pair that are of "legendary" quality.

This game has a sense of humor. But even if you don't have any sense of humor yourself, the balance and design of the mechanics are incredibly good and will rivet you to the game, if you are a fan of turn-based, tactical fighting.

Parents: The violence is all of the animated, non-bloody variety. It is akin to the old TV series "Batman", in the sense of animated "POW" and "KABLAAM" effects. That are not taken seriously. Still, if you are opposed to violent video games, fighting IS the core of the action in this game, and you might want to steer away. I myself let my kids play freely. There is virtually no sexual content, though a few of the tiny, cutely animated figures appear to be scantily clad. A couple of these female figures also have a (barely visible) effect of their breasts bouncing as they move. Also, there is one hilarious exchange in which one heroine criticizes the bust of another heroine. But in the scope of scores of hours of gameplay, these are tiny, isolated, and superficial references. I rate the game as "clean", and it is free of vulgar, tacky, or insulting references. The scripting, while boring, is almost always grammatically correct. The gender relations depicted in the game are bizarre and sometimes reversed, but overall they are healthy relationship, taken in the ridiculous and strange setting of the demon world. Speaking of "demons", they are mentioned everywhere. Demons come in all shapes and sizes. Any other game would simply call them "monsters", so the demonic reference is only a name, nothing deeper. Still, if such references are offensive to you, beware. Beyond that, I cannot think of any anti-Christian or religiously disrespectful themes/images in the game.

I will not admit publicly how many hours I've logged in playing this game. The number is huge but still much smaller than some of the people who've written detailed analyses of the game's mechanics and programming. And since you can play any kind of monster that you have defeated in battle (you can make new characters of that type), I'm likely to log many more dozens of hours before this game is retired to a box, assuming it ever is.

Incidentally, I have also played Disgaea I (Disgaea: Hour of Darkness). And while you will appreciate certain story points more if you've played it, it is NOT necessary to have done so. I think the sequel is superior to the original, which doesn't happen often. I would even go so far as to say this one IS superior to the sequel, discounting the opinion of anyone who thinks otherwise. The streamlined mechanics and game balance simply can't be ignored. If you own neither game, I suggest buying the 2nd game (Disgaea 2: Cursed Memories) first, and then search for the 1st one if you really are interested in the nostalgia of the two-part series.

Hope this helps your decision.

title: A wonderful, complex strategy/RPG game
text:
I've been having lots and lots of fun with this game. It has its shortcomings, but at its heart, it provides very hard, engaging, stylish gameplay for a dedicated player of video strategy games. Some of the concepts are unusual, and the complexity is fairly high. The presentation style is anime graphics. Scenes of combat are non-realistic, cartoony affairs that I enjoy watching and interacting with. The story text is well-written, although the story itself is nothing to shout about. The clever, sometimes outlandish, characters are more interesting than the plot line.

I have read several player reviews (on various websites) that mention the difficulty of grasping the game rules. I did not have that problem, but that is probably for the following reasons: 1) I was warned by reviews before I bought the game that its mechanics were a bit odd. 2) I have played Riviera, Fire Emblem, and Advance Wars. This game is a sort of fusion of all three of those games, though it is greater than the sum of those parts. 3) I've played other games involving collecting and playing electronic "cards" as a part of the combat. These factors combined, I was ready for the game.

It does seem to be getting very difficult as I proceed through the chapters, but I respect that. ;) For devoted fans, it's a must-have!

title: unique charm and gameplay without the gore
text:
It's fair to say that Steambot Chronicles is unlike any other game you'll have played, and it's probably best suited to fans of eclectic games. It is a fusion of game styles using elements of a sim-type game, a few economic principles, vehicle combat, roleplaying story, with some emphasis on musical performances. In other words, it's hard to define by normal game labels.

The game is not a big-budget production, and I would not want to pay full price for it. But as a collector of off-the-wall or niche games, this one is a perfect addition to my library. It makes me laugh, keeps me curious, and is usually relaxing.

You can only play as a boy character, a teenager who has lost his memory during a cruise ship accident. The technology is early 1900's, in a fictional country similar to the US. However, this world has developed the splendid Trotmobile, a sort of 19th century robot that requires a pilot. Your trotmobile can be used for commerce or combat and is the focus of the game. However, you will also spend a good deal of time meeting people, running errands, and raising money to support your other habits.

The game should not be taken too seriously, partly because is intentionally light, and partly because it's a bit choppy in places, and you'll be disappointed if you depend on every plot twist to make sense, every action to have a logical result. But if you can take the story with a grain of salt, it is wonderful and very charming. The graphics are not first-rate, but they do have a unique style and simple charm.

Technical prowess is not one of the game's strong points. There are sometimes load lags, as you pass into new territories, which seem unreasonably long. The camera work is sometimes choppy, and the camera angles are occaisonally frustrating. I find myself able to forgive these weaknesses for the sake of playing in this game world, but it is something to consider, if technical finesse is important to you.

Parents: Language used in the game is almost completely mild (there will be the occasional minor expletives). There is no graphic sexual or violent content. There are mild references to romance, as dating is a part of the game. There is also violence, as you'll be clubbing and shooting mechanical opponents fairly regularly, but it's all within tasteful limits, in my opinion. I would let a small child watch me play without any worries. A lot of girls might like this game, so it's a real shame they didn't allow for a female lead character.

The reviewers here critical of this game should probably be playing a more mainstream, less artful game. This game is for the rest of us, who enjoy a break from the dull, repetitive products that come from the major game houses.

text:
I love this game. Interesting characters, tons of choices, and if you're not so good at driving (like me!), you can walk or fast travel. Nice. The game takes place in the future, fifty-seven years to be exact, but it's very relatable. If you live in a big city, I think you'll agree. I found the controls easy to learn, in the way Death Stranding, for example, was not. Although I'm not a fan of the music, the radio can be turned down. I like that you can choose to help the cops (or not). Just like today, law enforcement is "outgunned, outmanned, and out planned." The lighting, general atmosphere, and sound effects work to increase tension perfectly. If you're a fan of robotics you'll enjoy building your personal arsenal of mods. The weapons are useful and if you don't get too far out of the city you'll have no trouble completing quests.

Sony has gone above and beyond to make amends by releasing at least three patches with more to follow. Each patch improves the graphics and the gameplay. I own a basic PS4, and I've experienced zero trouble with this game. Before you throw your hands up and dismiss the game, ask yourself how long has your PS4 been sitting in its own dust? How hot is it getting after hours and hours of gameplay? Check the space on the hard drive. I bet there are games there you haven't played in years. Clean it up, and if the game still doesn't work, then it's time for a new PS5. I think I'm close to needing one because the disc drive is failing.

I don't understand why Sony would release an unfinished game, although it's hardly a new phenomenon. But they are making amends. This game is fun and to me, it's a new experience. Now, go forth V and stir the pot in ways that make it most fun for you.

title: Some new, mostly old
text:
So it's time for another pokemon game. Truth be told, I'm not a huge pokemon fan. I played red/blue when I was in high school and had very enthusiastic friends, but after that I meandered through the series, I've played most of them up to this point but mostly just trying them out without really dedicating myself to finishing/collecting everything.

So Black/White is pretty much your standard pokemon game. You start out with friends/rivals getting starters from the local professor, you quickly meet the 'evil team' and are turned loose on the world to go find the 8 gym badges so you can become the pokemon league champion. Standard cut and paste from every other pokemon game, though I did appreciate that they cut out a lot of the exposition and got you started on your way pretty fast.

And there's a whole new cast of pokemon to catch and battle. Honestly, I'm a little disappointed how thoroughly new everything is, not that it's a bad thing, but I kind of liked the older generations for introducing new versions of older pokemon by means of 'young' versions, or new evolutions. There are more than a handful of new parallels to match older generations, a new 'pidgey', a new 'caterpie', and others. The designs run the gammut from cute and charming to big and badass, to uh, well, things like Trubbish, whose name really speaks for itself ;9 But that's pretty typical of any pokemon generation, there's good designs and... not so good. You pick your favorite starter, and then fill in the rest of your team with whatever you like or whatever you need for the next gym/story event. As always, what you can catch/evolve/etc is balanced (somewhat) around what you need.

The story is very linear, in that there's actually more of a story instead of a string of random events as you progress along. Unlike some earlier games, you *have* to complete the gyms at the time you encounter them, your progress will be impeded in some way until you've beaten the gym. To balance this somewhat, you no longer need gym badges to do anything except keep control of your pokemon, any HM you receive such as strength/cut/fly/etc can be used immediately. Not that it means much since most of them only lead to extra items rather than new areas like way back in Red/Blue.

I will say that it brings probably the creepiest pokemon villain ever to the table. N is basically a pokemon fanboy that has a legion of minions to do his bidding. From the get go he gives you these long winded speeches about friendship and destiny and changing the world and how all the pokemon are his friends. It's downright creepy, so he's quickly a villain you hate to run into.

So far (and by that I mean I'm only about halfway through the game) my only major complaints are that I'm just not seeing a lot of the new mechanics that were introduced in the older games. Some of these are in the online component (berry farming is only accessible via gamesync, which is not working until Nintendo of Japan can get it's servers up after the earthquake crisis) but one has to question the reasoning behind developing parts of a game to *require* connecting to a specific domain when some of those parts would function perfectly fine offline. Dunno I haven't gotten to try the gamesync function yet so it's hard to say. Just seems silly to release a game then not have part of its functionality available for another 2 months after release (and longer now, with the delay). Or other features, like being able to add beaten trainers to a list and be able to re-challenge them later on, that seem to be just missing from the game. Perhaps it's just me, or maybe I'm missing something, but usually the idea of a sequel is to build on what you've brought before. At it's core pokemon is the same game its been for 15 some years plus, but its the periphery that's changed considerably and it seems like Nintendo isn't running with some of their good ideas from the past.

Anyway, if you're completely new to pokemon it's an excellent game to get started on. If you're an old fan of the series that is content with what's come before, it's also an excellent game. If you're someone that is expecting a complete revamp of the series however, looking for a new model that shies away from series conventions, this really isn't for you and expect to be disappointed.

All in all, I find it pretty fun.

title: Step down
text:
I liked F, and I adored F2, but this is rather a disappointing entry. It can do in a pitch, but if I really wanted to enjoy the experience, I would go back to F2.

For one, the song selection is rather lacking. Not only there aren't many songs to begin with, I can barely point to just one song in each category that I enjoy. For another, the lack of songs that are not by Miku is felt even more than it did in the previous games. There is only one sole song for Rin, Len, and Luka, although they are at least partake in a couple of ensembles. Meiko and Kaito do not have any songs of their own, and they have even fewer ensembles.
Because in order to complete the game you have to grind with them in each section, and the vocals do not get switched for each song, you can't help but to have a mismatch between vocals and the modules. It is particularly annoying using Kaito's module with Miku's voice. If everyone had at least one song in each category, or at least the vocals were switchable, it wouldn't have been nearly as painful.
On the flip side, I suppose it did make me switch the modules around than I did before, but, yeah, they really need to start treating all the vocaloids more equally. Miku does have some decent songs, but I do find her voice to be tiring.

It is easier than the other games, I'd say. It is possible to set the game mode the same way that F and F2 were, which keep track of all hits and misses (but you can't unlock new modules that way). But, in the story mode, as long as you clear a particular voltage for the song, you can pass even the most difficult songs, even with extra challenges, quite easily, as long as you have a suitably outfitted module, it doesn't even display the number of notes missed unless you explicitly prompt it.

I did enjoy the plot and the medleys, though.
