title: A "poor man's mario Kart" that's superior to it's idol
text:
This is a game that every Wii owner should have.

In a lot of ways, it's what I'd consider a "poor man's Mario Kart": it's got crazy cartoon racing, lots of opportunities to screw up or battle your friends and opponents, and a lot of over the top action, it just doesn't have the name value of it's big brother. However, this one offers a lot of advantages over it's more famous competitor.

Price: This game costs less than $10. You can't beat that, especially when Mario Kart hasn't come down from it's $50 price tag, even two years after it's release.

Controls: Where Mario Kart was a little sticky on the controls, and not very forgiving for average to beginning players, Excitebots is perfectly good for beginners and young children. Moving the bots is pretty simple, and the controls are highly responsive, and even if you stink, the game is very forgiving following multiple crashes.

Variety: Mario Kart is going to trump this game in terms of variety of Karts (most of the Excitebots "cars" are pretty much exactly the same), Excitebots blows Mario out of the water in terms of what you can do while racing. You'll get powerups in much the same way, but you can also play a tambourine, make sandwiches, collect rings, hit bowling pins, and more. It's fun to try and figure out how best to handle these minigames, and it's one of the only games where you'll ever kick a field goal while trying to play a song in the middle of a race.

Bonuses: Like many Wii games, you have a lot to unlock. This is both good and bad. It's good for replay value, but it does limit your options if you don't play it regularly on single player mode. I've beaten the game on single player mode with the regular difficulty, and played many times with others, but I still don't even have enough stars to have purchased all of the cars. The game balances this with good online play, decent two player (though the game plays split screen vertically, making these races much more difficult), and a few different bonus games which require a lot of precision.

If I have any major complaint about the game, it's that the cars are basically all the same. They have different "ratings", but you won't notice much of a difference, though the "Spider" car is very, very good. We actually decided to ban the use of this one, but all the others basically do the exact same thing. Also, on two player mode, you only get the two players cars, which unbalances the bonus for winning the race. These two gripes are pretty minor at the end of the day, and I really think that this is one of the best games out there on the Wii. Tragically underrated.

title: Vulgar Variety, but too many serious issues
text:
It's hard to review a game like this because there's so much going on. Complete about half of the single player campaign, and you'll start to see what I mean. Dancing games, shooting games, "skill games" which usually force you to have impeccable timing, "sports" games which involve you shaking your wiimotes as fast as you can, and a whole lot more.

If I were judging on variety alone, this is an easy 5-star game. Big, big mistakes keep me from rating it highly.

The first major problem with the game is that you have to unlock EVERYTHING. Even two player mode. And the only way to do that is to play the game in single player mode. For what is primarily a party game, this is absurd, especially since playing on single player gives you a chance to get a handle on the unusual timing and other aspects of each game, and you'll maintain a healthy advantage over your opponents. Some might not find this to be too problematic, but if you want to play with a group, you have no option other than to spend lots of time playing on your own, or repeating the same minigames over and over as a group. If you get to unlock two player mode, which is very easy, you'll only have access to the four or five games you have played through on single player mode. It's silly and annoying to have to do this, and it really sucks a lot of fun out of the game.

The second problem with the game is the difficulty level of some games. Dancing is really easy - everyone gets a near high score on this. Then there are games like cow tossing, or pig racing, which you have to play dozens of times just to come close. There are a LOT of "wagglefest" games, where you and your partner just shake the wiimote as rapidly as possible, often for a minute or more at a time. These are especially frustrating when you fail them on single player mode, because after a single try, your arm will really hurt (especially the carrot juice shooting game). Making this even more problematic, we noticed while playing that the game is not particularly responsive to movement of the controls, particularly with the nunchuk. The slow response times make some of the difficult games nearly impossible.

Finally, the game is party friendly, but two people never get to play the same game at the same time. This is not a problem with some of the minigames, but playing with four people on dance modes is very aggravating, since each person must play the same song every time. Other games require you to do something for a long time, and with four people, it can take a good ten minutes or more to complete a single round. This is an annoyance more than a legitimate complaint, since this is certainly a design decision. Some games simply wouldn't work on a small screen that accomodates multiple people, while others would be very crowded if more were to join in.

Parents of younger children might find some of the games a little on the vulgar or too violent side, but this game is aimed more at teenagers or adults, so it won't be a problem for most. If you don't want your young child exposed to pretty consistent bathroom humor, however, this is not a good choice.

title: Some irritating features, but overall great
text:
This is a throwback that is overall very well done.

The good:

Multiplayer - It's amazing to think that over the umpteen different Mario releases, on all kinds of platforms, that this is the first time Nintendo has managed to allow both players to play at the same time. And it's great fun, because you can compete, or you can help each other out, or you can do both at the same time. Totally awesome.

Gameplay - It's SMB3 with a whole lot of cool graphics, better suits, and more hidden stuff. Who won't appreciate that?

Level Design - This is a core component of gameplay, and one that should not be overlooked. The level design in this game is probably the number one thing that really makes it stand out. Every level has something unique about it, which makes it unique, memorable, and interesting. At no point do you feel like you're rehashing an old level, or doing something over, just with a higher difficulty. And that's a great thing.

The Bad:

The Save System - You can only save in a real slot after you've beaten a castle. You have a "quick save" option, but there's only one of those, so if you play in a household where multiple people are playing at the same time, you won't be able to really utilize this well, since you'll overwrite each other's slots.

Mario's Abilities - Some will label this as a positive, but sometimes I think Mario can simply do too darn many things. One of the things that I've always liked about SMB games has been they're simplicity. You run, you jump, and you collect powerups. In this game, you can pick up and throw stuff, you can jump in the air and stomp, you can do a spinning punch manuever, you can do a hop-skip-jump move that makes for really long jumps, and in multiplayer, you can press 'A' to encase yourself in a bubble if you're about to fall in a pit. All this is available to you before you get any powerups whatsoever. It's not impossible to learn it all, but it is a little complicated to have it all thrown at you without...

Tutorials? - You have tons of abilities, lots of stuff to explore and collect, and the game throws even more at you when you progress. But there is no simple way to learn all this in-game before being thrown into the mix. There are some tutorial videos in the mushroom castle, but they only show you what to do, not what buttons to press in order to hop-skip-jump or to pick stuff up. Also, I'm still not sure what I gain by rescuing toadstools...is it just the extra life? Is there any reason for me to collect giant coins other than to unlock more videos that I don't really have an interest in watching? A single, simple in game tutorial would solve most of these problems.

Level of Difficulty - I don't have a major problem with games which are too easy, but I think this Mario is very easy. It might be one of the easiest ever. By the second day, I was already on World 4, and I had already gotten all the big coins from all but two stages. I'm feeling like my $40 of fun might be done in the course of a few more days.

Overall, my gripes are minor. This is a really fun game. It seems a little expensive to me given the difficulty level, so expert gamers might want to rent it before buying, but this is a really good addition to any Wii collection.

title: What a joke
text:
This game is a joke. It crashes frequently, the character models are sloppy and pixelated, the cutscenes are jumpy, the voice acting is stale and often buggy (multiple characters talking at once), and the story is...yeah. It's something about an evil wizard and the demise of the elven race, and it's so stereotypically bad that you'll lose interest in that aspect of it before the opening cutscene of the game is done. And the translation is pretty laughable too. I'll admit that I didn't get far into the game, but if it were a book, I definitely wouldn't have read through chapter 1. Pretty bad all around for me.

But as this is a strategy game, and not an RPG, the story takes second seat to the game play. There isn't much to say about that either. The game play makes you feel like you're playing a boardgame. With yourself. If you've ever played computer monopoly, you'd know what I mean - after a few games, you simply want to throw in the towel from boredom. There's not much to it without interaction, and it shows. And in Elven Legacy, you're in the same situation. The computer always reacts the same way, and it balances it's lousy AI by simply tripling the number of troops they send at your forces. It feels unfair at first, but eventually you start to realize that without doing that, the game would be, if possible, even more simplistic. Yeah, you need to use some advanced tactics, but once you figure out a few things, it's easy to wash, rinse and repeat to dominate missions. After a few 3 or 4 hour turns, with a few crashes thrown in for good measure, you'll be quite over this one as well.

If they did anything right, it's that they did include a fair number of units for you to play with, a couple of special abilities (most of which seem really weak, but at least they're there), and a few bonuses that can be unlocked if you are willing to put up with the already enormously tedious gameplay.

You move your coarsely pixelated units around a map that functions pretty much exactly like it would have 15 years ago, and you do battle. In short, if this were released in 1994, I might have been impressed, but today, it not only feels clunky and outdated, but it looks it too. A game like this is simply not acceptable in 2009 and beyond, especially if they're not going to take the time to make sure that it actually works on most machines. They had a good premise of bringing back the old style of gaming, but if it is to work, you're going to need to do a little better than this.

title: Hitman Series
text:
For such a price, it's hard to argue, but at the same time, I think you have to be somewhat of a masochist to really like these titles.

For starters, there is very little in terms of tutorials, and for games this complex, some tutorial aspect is pretty much necessary. They all kind of drop you into a world and expect you to be able to utilize all the different parts of the game as if you were an expert. In Silent Assassins, for instance, it took me over a week to figure out how to beat the very first real mission because of the "strange" behavior of some of the AI (which took me a while to figure out). Now, yes, there is a tutorial, but all it teaches are the very simplest aspects of movement and combat. Does it help you understand how enemies react? No, and unfortunately, that's the #1 most important aspect of the game. There seem to be a whole lot of little idiosyncrasies about how enemies react to your presence that make it very, very difficult.

Then there is realism. For a series of games that prides itself on realism and tactics, why is it that your enemies can take such enormous amounts of damage before dying? This eliminates a whole barrage of different possibilities, because a good 75% of the weapons that you'd want to use for sniping are effectively useless if you can shoot someone in the head, they survive to be able to shoot back and take cover, and then they call all their buddies to come at you. If you get shot in the head, you should die. Simple. But because of this design decision, there isn't much of an option for sniping out the guards or taking a similar, non-linear approach that would probably pay dividends in real life. Even though there are usually two or three ways to beat every mission, you must conform your entire plan to the specific actions the game wants you to take in order to beat every level.

The game's AI is also based on a series of checkpoints, which feels very unnatural. For instance, in the first mission of SA, you deliver flowers to the front door of the mansion. You are then, presumably, to sneak upstairs when all of the guards in the room turn their back, but if you so much as move a muscle in any direction, even in sneak mode, they will turn and shoot at you, unless they have walked past a certain point. Now, I don't know about you, but if I turn my back on an expert assassin, I would expect him to be able to sneak upstairs if I turned around, particularly if he was trying to do just that. I found that the other two games in the series were a tiny bit more forgiving, but they all suffer from this at some point or another.

Granted, I didn't play very far into any of these games, but I see the same issues prevalent throughout, and they eventually made me put the whole series aside with frustration. As I said above, for the price, it's very hard to argue against this bundle, and certainly, these games have their fans, but I think in terms of playability, there have been an enormous number of games that have come out, both recently and from a long time ago that not only rival the Hitman series, but far surpass what they can do. I'd take any of the Thief games (also by Eidos), or Assassin's Creed over these any day of the week. To be honest, you're probably going to get more playing time out of Assassin's Creed if you do a good job exploring it than you will out of all three of these Hitman games.

title: Not much to it really...
text:
This game seems to be trying to be a hybrid of Doom's FPS nature and Diablo's RPG qualities, but set in space. It seems like it's got some promise, except that it isn't much fun once you blast your way through the first couple of stages.

There's nothing to really look forward to as you progress - not much in the way of weapons, upgrades, or anything that's particularly exciting. Sure, you might find an assault rifle, but it works exactly the same as your other guns, and you might be in the Life support module of the ship rather than the Crew Quarters, but really, all there is to tell you the difference is a slightly different set of enemies, and maybe one different background object to look at. There is no loot - you grab parts that help you upgrade yourself, your guns, your little robot companion, and which also allow you to make useful stuff like grenades and med packs. It's an OK system, but there should be more - I should have to find SOMETHING other than parts, be it ammo, or other types of armor and weapons lying around - because at the end of the day, that kind of customization is essential to a game like this.

Upgrading your character seems to be the ideal place for a game like this to thrive - I mean, Diablo was really just about creating the most buffed out character you could make, but in this, you won't notice any of the character upgrades you're purchasing doing much for you. What does it really mean that my "attack rating" goes up 4 points? It doesn't seem to mean that my guns do any more damage, and your character is automatically laser accurate as is. When I fight other bad guys in most games, and I up my strength for instance, I can almost always see that giving me some kind of advantage, usually in changing the amount of damage I deal, or in the amount of inventory I can carry. Here, you get nothing other than a number, which claims to have gotten better. Your guns and your fighting skills stay basically the same, and you wonder just what you're doing this for anyways. This is the nature of many games in this genre, but here, it feels especially poorly done, perhaps because this is really all there is to look forward to at the end of a long space-dungeon tirade.

The cybernetics side of things seems like it should be cool, but it doesn't really do much either. Just like before, your cybernetics make very slight adjustments to your characters meaningless statistics, and sometimes open a few more options in your skills tree. They made some attempt at making the game feel more open with the cybernetics affecting your "humanity" rating, but in reality, all this does is limit a few of the higher options in your skills tree, and it has no other effect on the way that characters interact with you, or in what ending you get (although there is one alternate ending for 100% human characters).

Controls are clunky also. The camera pans using WSAD and you control Seth through the use of your mouse, which is much more difficult than it should be. Your guns vary in usefulness, but some are particularly unresponsive, particularly those with limited range. With one gun, which is called something like the "sonic rifle", you can't shoot at long distances, which is fine. What is not fine is that if I click to fire on an enemy outside of range, and Seth needs to move closer, you have to stop holding down fire, or your character will stutter in place, doing nothing, even if the enemy does move in range (I should mention that holding fire is always an option with every other gun, even this one, but for some reason, it breaks when the enemy is outside of range).

You also get equally generic special combat abilities, but just like before, it's hard to say that you really want any of them other than a few (I like the one that defaults to Num1 and Deadly Strike), and when you use them, you can't hardly see what they do that's different from simply shooting a bad guy. Deadly Strike, for instance, sends a small beam of space-stuff out that hurts your opponent. Um...that's what guns do, isn't it? There would be some usefulness to it if it were significantly more powerful than a gun, but by the time you're in the third level, it's probably about even. Animations for these are slow, and sometimes seem to skip entirely, which makes them even more questionable.

Overall, I think this is a game that falls flat where it could have been a real mega star. With a little more thought, and a little work on the mechanics, they have enough ideas here to have made a real winner. Unfortunately, this one seems a little half-finished, and that's a real shame.

title: Charming, but...
text:
As far as adventure games go, I'm looking for one that has intuitive but challenging puzzles, a solid story, and isn't particularly repetitive.

Drawn is OK in so far as intuitive puzzles go, but I did have a few "what the heck is this about?" moments that were easily solved by the help system. If you find a particular puzzle too challenging or boring, after fiddling for about a minute a "solve puzzle" button will appear that instantly moves you on to the next scene. That said, I never had to use it, and I can only imagine that most adult gamers would have to use it to solve the pictures in the cave puzzle, and most would probably use it there only if they do it wrong and then realize there's an order to it. Other puzzles are pretty easy. The only time I ever found myself stuck was in searching for the gong ringer because it's very small on the screen.

As far as story goes, Drawn was a winner. I say was because the end of this game is completely unsatisfying. It's basically a blatant setup for a sequel, and not much more. There was good build up, a lot of mystery and intrigue, and then it just kind of dumps you off very unceremoniously. Lousy job editors.

Many puzzle/adventure games are very repetitive, requiring you to memorize particulars or re-solve puzzles as you go through the game in backtracking. Thankfully, Drawn isn't like that at all.

So in so far as I'm concerned, Drawn scored a 1.5 out of 3 in terms of things that I'm looking for in a game. Not so hot, but to be completely fair, the story was pretty good for most of the journey. Add to that a very short playing time, mine was only around 3 hours (almost 45 minutes of which was searching for the stupid gong ringer), and you have a game that I think most intermediate game players could finish up in an afternoon, which is both good and bad. For me, I wanted more, especially considering how blah the ending was, and the way that it was just kind of dropped out of the sky. There was plenty of room for expanding the game just a tiny bit to come to a satisfying ending.

I can see this game appealing to many gamers, particularly those who don't really want to be that challenged by the gaming experience. As far as I'm concerned, it's OK, but there are lots better.

title: A 1996 experience in 2010
text:
This game would have probably been considered groundbreaking back in 1996. The graphics, the little animation and music there is is also quite lousy. But fortunately, I'm kind of a sucker for nostalgic, older-feeling games like this, and I can overlook these issues when I'm playing if the gameplay is good.

Unfortunately, it isn't.

Most of the puzzles in the game are pretty easy, but there are more than a few "what the heck do I do now?" moments in the game stemming from the fact that the most human interaction you get to drive the story along is a few telephone messages. Then there are a couple of puzzles that made absolutely no sense to me whatsoever. The package at the door was a great example. I picked up a package, and I wanted to open it, but couldn't. So logically, I scoured the grounds for a razorblade or knife, or just something to open it with, figuring that was why it just didn't open itself. No, in fact, I needed to "use" the package with the table, and then I could open it. I doubt that would be most people's first reaction, and in fact, I only came to that by chance when I was searching for my knife. For much of the game, I also carried around a dead rat with me figuring that it had to be used for something to help me get through the game; nope, I needed to use the rat with the toilet to get...nothing. Wow.

As for not being able to pick up things until needed, I thought that was a decent way to build the game since there are literally hundreds of different things you can grab in the game. It was a little annoying, but at least it made inventory management doable.

The game also includes a helpful hotkey that highlights the different clickable elements on the screen to help you figure out what you can and cannot do, but since the pointer changes as you mouse over things, I thought that was a wasted attempt at a hint system.

The story is OK. It's interesting to see that it's based on a historical text, but unfortunately since it's foreign to me (and I would assume anyone), the game has to make up for it with LOTS of in-game text. By the end of the second chapter, I had read at least 5 magazine articles, five or six paper letters, a deed, 2 diaries, about 15 emails, and a legend that, to be honest, wasn't that clear, so I had to go back and read it again. And none of this is related to the puzzle solving, it's all story based. There is a lot of reading to be done, and by simply having one or two characters appear throughout the game, or maybe even just have a single telephone conversation, much of it could have been avoided.

Overall, I think this is a barely playable game that will only appeal to hardcore puzzle/adventure gamers who have a lot of time on their hands.

title: The camera...
text:
I see all these great reviews about this game, but very few people mention the #1, so-huge-I-can't-possibly-review-the-game-without-mentioning-it camera problem?

This game is a whole lot of fun. The character development system is (at least for me) totally new, and it works to give you a more well-rounded character, allowing you to spend experience as soon as you get it if you need to. The story is pretty interesting, and the game is by no means easy. To me, this game is very similar to Neverwinter Nights, and if you liked that, you'll surely find Drakensang to be a good game for you.

However, there are some quirks to the game system that tend to make this one of the most difficult to play games I've ever met. It's not that the game is really hard in that battles are difficult, or quests are too obscure, it's just feels like developers often went to great lengths to ensure that their game packed in lots of annoying quirks. Looting animals is a great example - you loot them the first time, then you get something, let's say a rat tail. Then if you have a character with sufficient skill, you will be able to search more, and you'll get leather strips or something. So in essence, you have to search every dead animal twice just to get all the stuff out of it. There are a few other things like this that are unnecessarily annoying, and they are frequent enough to be a bother.

Another problem that I've noticed with this game is that it is incredibly linear. There is no problem with linear RPGs, but in at least half of the conversations in the game, you get only one dialog option, particularly in the beginning of the game. It would be nice to be able to voice something other than the get-through-the-game-as-a-polite-gentleman option. This is also a problem with character creation; granted, there are a good 15 or so classes to choose from, but all the characters of one type look exactly the same, so you can't do any customization. In addition, some of the characters simply will not get you through the harder difficulty levels of this game, the archer for instance. One would assume that Archery is a great skill to have if you're actually adventuring through this game, but in practice, you start every difficult battle about 5 paces from your enemy, and by the time you've strung your bow, the bad guys are already bashing your head in with a club. And it's not like it's just this way with a few fights, it's a constant problem that never seems to stop. In the end, you can build an archer character and beat the game, but your archer will start to act and feel much more like a warrior than a true archer.

Then there is the #1 problem with the game - the camera. Because this is a game with an over-the-shoulder camera system, it automatically presents a big problem if one of your party members is fighting, and another is up a flight of stairs or around a corner. When this happens, you are only allowed to target on things you can see, or if you're lucky, that the camera can see around a bend. If you are on the bottom of a staircase and your party is fighting on the second floor, there is little way for your characters on the first floor to pilot themselves around the staircase and up to the fight without manually controlling them the whole way. And then what do you do with your spellcasters who need attention? Even in non-fighting situations, it can be a bother when you can't position the camera correctly while exploring the world map, and you end up looking down upon your main character, where you can see maybe twenty feet around them. Of course, you can spend time adjusting the camera, but after a while, it just takes a lot of time to fiddle with it, and sometimes, it just isn't worth it.

Like I said, Drakensang is a mostly quality game, and hard-core RPG fans will love it, but it's major flaws are too much for it to overcome.

title: The endless hallway into hell
text:
You like hallways?

If you can answer yes to that simple question, you'll love Doom 3. If you, like the majority of people, think hallways are really not very interesting, then you're going to absolutely hate Doom 3. And with good reason: 90% of the game takes place in one long, dark hallway. The major differences between levels usually consist of the difference between ramps and flat ground, or catwalks versus regular ground. I played about 75% of the game, and I remember walking out to the surface of Mars about 3 times. I remember about 3 levels that were not hallways. They were short. I am currently on level 34 out of 40, and I'm about ready to put this one away for good.

Level design aside, the entire game suffers from being incredibly long and repetitive. The same bad guys, the same boring guns, the same little hidden areas, everything (in fact, there's only one new gun in the entire game, and it's ammo is so limited you can hardly use it). Every single time you see a dark corner, you might as well load up your chainsaw and just start walking forwards. You could do it the proper way I suppose, by switching from flashlight to revolver and blasting, but why? You'll run into the same 4-5 zombies and one dark-orange-demon-guy, pick up some random ammo, and wonder why you spent so much money on this damn game.

Overall, one of the most disappointing games I've ever played, because the graphics, even 6 years after it's release, are pretty darn nice. Unfortunately, that's the only good thing I have to say about it.

title: Ahhh, Just Gotta Love That "Click!"
text:
Mechanical keyboards. There's nothing better.

You're instantly lured in by their siren song of "clicky keys."

So obnoxiously noisy, but you welcome it. You love it. You need it!

OK, that's a little much, but if you've ever used a mechanical keyboard before, then you feel me.

If not, then get ready to be freed from that mushy, muted excuse for a keyboard that you're using now.

The cat daddy of all mechanical keyboards is, of course, the IBM M model. If you've used one of these guys at any time over the last 30+ years, then you know what a quality mechanical keyboard is like.

Those things are like boat anchors. Heavy & huge, but oh so clicky.

However, this keyboard from FIODIO is so well made (& has some awesome extras not available on the Model M) that the IBM will soon be a faint memory.

Measuring just 17" long X 5" wide, this keyboard has plenty of room to stretch out on, but without taking up a ton of desk space.

And even with its compact stature & being constructed of ABS plastic, this little guy is still heavy enough (at 1lb 8oz) that it won't get pushed around on your desk.

The keys sit high, are well placed, & are thoughtfully arced. They also have a nice, long travel distance.

And, as you (& your neighbors) will quickly learn, this keyboard makes a lot of beautiful noise.

This can be attributed to the "blue switches" (although I'm not sure who the manufacturer is) installed under each key cap.

Blue switch keyboards are typically the most "clicky" keyboards you will find (outside of the Model M). There is an audible "click" about halfway down the key press before the key bottoms out on the keyboard frame.

So you get both an audible & tactile response which is very satisfying & helpful while typing.

If you've never owned a blue switch keyboard, then be prepared. It's noisy, but so worth it! (however your family may disagree).

Be warned that this is a WIRED keyboard. So you will need a free USB port. However, the keyboard instantly auto-detects (under Windows at least). So no drivers required.

You also get built in RGB lighting which is also programmable.

I haven't messed with trying to record any lighting preferences. Honestly, the keyboard looks very slick with the default lighting it ships with. But the option is there if needed.

As well, with RGB you instantly have a back-lit keyboard for typing at night. So the RGB lights not only look cool, but are also functional.

I haven't used this unit for any gaming. But it is being marketed as a gaming and/or office keyboard. However, for office use (many hours per day in my testing), you will have no issues.

You will also get a FUNCTION (FN) key that has presets for multimedia controls (mute, vol down, vol up, etc..) plus lighting adjustments.

And lastly it's spill-proof. Which is a bonus to everyone with a drink at their desk & too much stuff in their way.

So there it is. Overall, I'm extremely happy with this keyboard. If you're on the fence, give it a shot. I don't think you'll be disappointed.

title: THis is a follow up?
text: THe original "The Strike" was one of my top rated Wii fishing games.  After getting used to the way it works it was fun and enjoyable.  My only real complaint with the original was that it was too short.  I was able to buzz thru it in a couple of weeks (playing a couple hours a day).  I ordered this game cause I wanted MORE.  Boy was I let down.  This game is not nearly as good as the original.  The stuff that really worked well in the original are all but gone.  The graphics are a HUGE step backwards (unless you like all your fish to look like overstuffed coach potatos). THe few improvments (radio stations on the boat, a GPS with waypoints, and the ability to have the fishfinder and gps mini map going at the same time) don't even come CLOSE to making up for what was lost (challanging and rewarding mini games, line tension graph when fighting the fish, the ability to still drive the boat when the large GPS map was called up, the fish proximity indicater when scouting, a drag that was adjustable on the fly, the fish stamina indicator, interesting and informational load screen facts, a casting meter indicator, different types of casts, and fish that looked, well like fish).  Yea this game is a let down (especially as a followup).  You basically play the same lakes (plus 2 bonus lakes) in reverse.  There is no "reputation" points to be earned, and no matter how carefully you scout, the fish are not there for the tournemant (but do reappear in later tournements)  Basically your not going to win the tournament your fist time out (it takes me to the 3rd tournement each time).  I have found a few gliches where fish, lures, screen shots, or boats hang up and if your participating in NPC challanges you can basically win just by having a livewell full of fish before the challange even starts (oh and occasionally I win a challange that I never even was aware I was part of- a nice bonus but again a bit buggy).  THe bottom tournament ticker is a waste of time and a distraction (don't worry YOUR name will never appear on the ticker- but you will know when dale trickle catches a 0.9 Lb smallmouth.  uggh what a waste of resources).  The grizzled old "tour guide" that you get when starting out in amatuer mode is a bit of comic relief (especially if you have been listening to non country music and suddenly turn it on for him!).  He offers such worthless advise- and I wish there was a way to toss him overboard (thankfully he doen't ride with you on a tournament- but will make comments on some of the fish you catch).  Load times are still painfully long (like the original) and the controls are similiar enough.  One other gripe is that the Motion Plus option really screws things up (as another reviewer said "do they even test these things out before hand?").  Turn off the motion plus option and the controls are much more stable.  Heres the real kicker.  If Bas Pro SHops putsa out another version- I will have to really think twice before getting it- this one was an embarassment and I hope BPS really thinks twice before putting their name on something so disappionting (to be fair the original game was great and I did get this one used so I don't feel totally ripped off).

title: Works well but NO RUMBLE
text: I got this as many others have because the wired controllers force me to sit to close to the TV.  Now if your looking at this controller for a PS2 then you are either on a tight budget, love those old school games, or old like me (lol).  I don't have high speed internet service at my home, so the "new" generation games really aren't for me.  I love my PS2 and have a ton of games for it, so I'm happy.  The only thing really missing was the ability to NOT have to re-arrange the living room every time I want to play a little GT4.  We also have a Wii and I really started to get spoiled by the wireless controllers, but there just are not any great racing games for the Wii (Need for Speed is ok, but too much time spent street racing and avoiding the cops- just not my cup o tea).  Well after a particularly intense GT4 session I got my recliner tangled up with the contoller cord and pulled the PS2 off the shelf (no damage thank goodness).  I came to Amazon just to see if a wireless controller was even an option and was shocked to find so many! After reading all the great reviews (good and bad) I settled for this.  I'm glad I did!  This controller is well built (well as well built as any others I've had, and I've had at least a half dozen over the years), and pretty comfortable in my hands.  I like the "longer" handle design as it fits my hands and my play style better (YMMV).  There are no sharp edges or funky seams to mess up the feel.  The analog sticks are cushioned nicely, and appear that they will hold up for the long run (most of the controllers I use get retired because the rubber end on the joystick gets ripped off from too much turning on GT4).  These are as good as my current wired controller (that has lasted over 2 years, but has a stick point when moving the stick to the right, I've tried to fix it, lube it, file it, oil it, sand it, grease it, graphite it, and every other conceviable solution with no avail!).  The sticks have no sticky spots and really awesome centering springs (strong, but not overly so).  The buttons are a bit smaller, but have a positive feel and also no stickyness.  The start and select buttons are positioned a little higher on the body, but it only takes a couple tries to get used to them (plus you really don't use them that much anyway).  Battery life has been acceptable so far (3 hours on new Rayovac Alkies and still going, I mainly use rechargables but none of mine were charged so I still need to test them out- I expect 2 to 3 hours on them).  I really love that I can turn the controller off, go do something else, and come back, flip it on and have it connect and work immediatly!  Now I can let the dog out, eat dinner and take a bathroom break without using up battery power!  I also paused my game, switched the controller off, took out the batteries and put them back in, switched the controller back on and was instantly connected.  No need push the reconnect button everytime I need to do something else!  Range is outstanding (15 to 20 feet at least) and I even can play with the contoller under a blanket (for when my hands get too cold)with no loss of signal.  There is NO lag, no funny glitchs, no delays, or other problems.  Honestly the only reason I took off one star is that there is no rumble feature, and the discription states that the unit is fully rubberized (I really wasn't expecting it to be fully rubberized, but thought maybe the handles would have a rubber grip to them).  All in all if your reading this then you are in the market for a cheap wireless controller for an old school game.  This fits the bill and really works as well as anything wired.

title: If you like fishing....
text:
First and foremost if you hate to fish- then avoid this game. Its all about fishing. I've only played it for a short while so far, but I can tell this is gonna be a fun game. Graphics are better than expected (especially the fish themselves and the water scenes). Controls are easy enough (even without the wii pole). Hint you dont have to revolve the nunchuck in a circle- just bounce it up and down when reeling- works the exact same. The game also has a real sandbox feel to it (even if you CAN'T fish off your hotel room balcony)and you don't feel limited or confined like so many of the other Wii fishing games (Rapala fishing esp.) The pop up hints get in the way after a while, but they can be turned off. So far I've ignored all the other characters except the initial fishing tutor, and the hotel girls. There are a lot of different "quest" fishing challanges so you should not get too bored. There are also a lot of different areas to fish with different quarry at each one.
This game does have a few downsides that stop it from being 5 stars. No Mii support is a real bummer. You can customize (to a limited extent) your stock character- but I really believe they could have tossed out the clothing shop and just allowed you to play as your Mii (I mean isn't that the reason you bought a Wii in the first place? so you could use your own creation as a player?). There is WAY to much talking in the game (well reading actually). I find I'm pressing the A button so fast that I often miss what is being said (ok lazy on my part- but I really don't need to hear the same schpeal each time I cash in my fish). Camera angles are sometimes messed up when walking around. This could be user error but I have not found a way to change the camera angle when I'm walking around.
All in all if you enjoy fishing (either real or video game) you will get a kick out of this. The game is a lot of fun and JUST misses the mark on being one of the BEST Wii games out there.
update after YEARS of playing I still stand by my original thoughts. I have completed just about every aspect of the game and own my own cruiser, have the top tier aquarium, caught every species, and am only missing a dozen S level fish. I keep coming back and playing this. It is really enjoyable even if I maxed out my points (999999999 or something like that) I even bought every lure, piece of clothing, and every piece of tackle. The game is still fun, and I started another character, just to start it over and work throught it again. It has good play value even after many hours spent playing.

title: Cheap materials, does not last. Falls apart while it still looks "brand new".
text:
Very disappointed- this brand came from the recommendation of a friend and at first they seemed like a good quality product, but two pairs of these and both broke suddenly in the same way after a few months of use, the plastic "arm" between the headband and earpiece cracked at the screws and split apart. The first pair, I assumed I must have cracked somehow by jarring it and not realized it, the second just abruptly snapped in the middle of use (as in I heard a loud pop and something smacked me in the side of the head). I am by no means a vigorous user and usually sit fairly still playing games, this is clearly a design flaw (the plastic where the screws socket is thin and apparently very brittle based on how it breaks apart) as they were not even extended/flexed to the max at any point and after the first pair I was deliberately careful. I went to their website and they spend so long going on about "misuse" and "wear and tear" that I just gave up and didn't even bother filling out a support request, I doubt I'd get any satisfaction out of it.

title: Counterfeit Firmware and dangerous 3rd party charger!
text:
The PSP 2000 series is great when purchased brand new, but be carefull with second hand ones that might be modified or have 3rd party components!

I have the same model of PSP that was straight from the factory so as an original owner, I know what the real thing is. This second hand one stated that it might come with aftermarket parts and accessories which is understandable, but it should at least have legitimate firmware. Counterfeit firmware, also known as custom firmware, can potentially "brick" the unit. While it can allow you to run stuff that the PSP would not normally be able to run, it can also damage your PSP and crush compatability with genuine firmware and accessories. The PSP that I received is incompatible with accessories like the PSP camera because it has fake firmware. If you try to install genuine Sony firmware that is safer for you PSP and allows you to use different accessories, the counterfeit firmware prevents you from doing it. I have to use weird downloads inorder to downgrade the firmware and install genuine Sony firmware. This can be risky if done incorrectly and should have been done while it was being refurbished!

If an item has counterfeit firmware and is incompatible with genuine accessories and genuine firmware, it does not "function like new". Ebay is safer for second hand things like this. Amazon Renewed does have hit or miss success on other units as well. Like the Amazon Renewed Sony PS2 that destroys every disc you put in it. A new PS2 or certified refurbished PS2 does not reck your disks.

The charger that this PSP came with was not the original charger. This would normally be understandable except one problem, the charger it came with gets REALLY hot, weighs nothing, feels cheap, and does NOT have any safety marks whatsoever. The aftermarket charger isn't even UL Listed!

Summary:
The PSP 2000 is best purchased factory sealed in the box but that gets REALLY expensive. This refurbished one is great when you have the genuine charger that won't burn your house down. The refurbished PSP definitely isn't as nice as my 100% original PSP 2000 and doesn't come with the factory installed apps like Sensme Channels, but it does everything else just like a new one. The only thing it doesn't do is support PSP accessories like the camera and allow you to install genuine firmware without having to worry about "bricking" the PSP. You can fix these issues with online downloads but it is risky when done incorrectly and should have been done prior to selling the unit. The only reason I'm giving this refurbished one 4 out of 5 stars is because losing the camera compatibility isn't much of a loss, plus I'm in a pretty good mood. Everything else, including games seem to work well so far. I will update this review if anything changes.

title: Why could they have not just expanded on the first?
text:
Dynasty Warriors Gundam 2 is deffinitely not what I had hoped for. I played the first one, and really like it. In fact it is the only Dynasty Warriors game I have played through to completion (All characters maxed, all maps beaten, all objects unlocked, etc...). Unfortunitely, Koie decided to make changes and they all hurt the game.

Pros:
1) More gundams and characters to choose from. They have added a lot of new suits for you to play as and that is really exciting and cool.
2) They expanded on the mission mode, which in the first game was fairly small.

Cons:
1) The Gundams "Special Attacks" which expanded on them selves the higher level you were in the first game now are just longer. So, there is nothing new and cool to see, it is just a long attack or a short attack. Lame!
2) Thye added Giant boss badguys. You would think that this would go in the "Pros" category, sense it looked like a cool addition. But like many other things in this game they messed it up. The Giant bosses, are very tough and take a while to defeat. But the game ends up sticking NPC's in the battles with you that act like dumb NPC's. This leads to having to replay boss battles over and over, because key NPC's die during the fights because they run straight up to the bosses and get killed. This is probably the most frustrating thing about the game. After replaying levels 5-6 times because the NPC dies, you just don't want to play anymore.
3) Everything is locked at the start of the game. There are only 3 training missions open to play in Mission Mode at the beginning, with the others unlocked during Official Mode. So, when you get fed up dieing to Giant bosses in Official Mode, you have nothing to go back to to just have fun.

I was really looking forward to this game and had it pre-ordered about 2 months ago. But now I wish I had never gotten it. It was a really big let down, and cast a dark shadow over the whole series. I would not reccomend this game, unless you really want to try your hand at some pointless difficulty.

title: I put stock in focus groups, developers, and experience.
text:
Mortal Kombat has proven that it doesn't take a good game to get critical acclaim from many sources including the media and a few kids down the street who value goofy animation over substance. There's no accounting for individual tastes...
But for general impressions, it's probably a good idea to at least consider the impressions of focus groups and professional developers who have years of experience catering to the same demographic. It's not just marketing witchcraft and catchphrase mumbo-jumbo, it's something that a handful of us have earned multiple college degrees to better understand. Many focus groups of all demographics have been recorded, at great expense for some smaller developers, to get accurate impressions of the audience. Yes, there are no 6-year old female electronic entertainment developers in the field, but many of use take great measures to empathize with the needs and desired of our audience as best as possible.
If you can appreciate dated graphics, a shallow interface, a plotline and premise that can be summarized in about 5 words, and repetitive gameplay (and that's completely acceptable, particularly for those who rent games, play game infrequently, or have limited exposure to games, which is actually a rare thing for this current generation male or female) by all means follow your heart.
Still, from the standpoint of many professional (though obviously not perfect for everyone) reviewers who have the good of the consumer in mind... it would be unfair to the majority, who might expect more from games they purchase, if these points weren't made before they invested.
Perhaps rent this game, play it for a weekend (IMHO there's about 6 hours of gameplay in here before it becomes old to even the most open mind) and see if it's worth buying.

title: The SNK legacy lives on!
text:
King of Fighters Dream Match 99 (KOFDM99) is my current favorite of all the King of Fighters titles (though Garou:Mark of the Wolves is my favorite SNK fighter overall), and that says a lot.
Basically, KOFDM99 is really the Dreamcast version of the Neo Geo game of KOF98:The Slugfest. This confuses a lot of people. KOFDM:99 and King of Fighters '99 Evolution (which is the real KOF99) are two totally different games.
KOFDM99 has just about EVERY character that ever appeared in an official King of Fighters game. That's a whole 38 distinct characters, if you're keeping score. This is the definitive King of Fighters title, and probably the best for 2-player competitions.
KOF99:Evolution and KOF2000 have their merits, but because of their smaller rosters and modified style, they fall a little short of KOF:DM99. While KOF:99E has better effects on the DC (KOF2000 has yet to be ported), KOF:DM99 still holds it own. The graphics easily take on the like of Capcom's greats like SF:Alpha 3. Obviously it doesn't have the pizzazz of the newer 2D DC fighters, the gameplay and character design has always set SNK apart from Capcom or Arc Systems (makers of Guilty Gear).
SNK has always had the most colorful roster, each character distinct with their own robust (if sometimes disturbing) personality that fuels the game. Coupled with good animation, great music, and top-notch controls (minimal learning curve) anyone who considers themselves a 2D fighting fan NEEDS this title. King of Fighters may not be as popular as Capcom's titles, but in Japan it's still one of the most popular series around and for good reason. KOF:DM99 continues the legacy of excellent SNK fighting games.

title: An OK Product
text:
First of all I have to say I don't know why some people are confused about how many screen protectors come in this package. It comes with two. Not two of each, two total-- one for the top, one for the bottom. You also get a cleaning cloth and a "Soft Card" which I assume is to get the air bubbles out, but it doesn't say. Works well for that anyway.

I was a little curious as to why it did not come with instructions, but I guess the process is easy enough to figure out.

I used the cleaning cloth to get the DS screens clean. I peeled the backing off the top protector and laid it on the screen going from one side to the other, smoothing the air out as I laid the film down. I used the "soft card" to push the air out from the edges of the screen. I was satisfied with how it looked.

Then I did the same for the touch screen. Despite thinking I had laid the protector on perfectly straight, one of the corners did not fit exactly. I pried the screen up with my fingernail and peeled it off. This was my BIG MISTAKE. Pulling the film off resulted in so much static that very small fibers were attracted to and stuck to the film. Unfortunately since the backing is covered in adhesive (as opposed to being a static cling), it was impossible to remove the very fine particles that were now stuck to the protector. I did not notice this, however, until I laid the protector back down on the DS. Where ever a piece of fuzz was, an air bubble had formed around it and I was unable to push the air out.

The bubbles were VERY noticeable on the dark screen of the DS when it was not turned on. When playing a game however, the bubbles were hardly if not at all noticeable.

The next day I decided to pull the bottom protector off and rinse it under the sink. I used a dab of soap and rubbed very lightly. I expected the adhesive might get ruined in the process but it doesn't appear to have been. I was able to wash the majority of the big fuzzies off. Reapplying the film showed improvement, but there are still one or two small bubbles. I can live with it though.

In conclusion ...

- make sure you wash your hands and clean the screen very well before applying these things. You might consider using a higher quality cleaning cloth that absolutely will not shed.

- once it's down, DO NOT pull the protector up again (with the intention or reapplying it).

- applying the screen slowly and firmly, going in one direction will eliminate most air bubbles.

Three stars out of five. An OK product. I have had no sensitivity problems, and I just hope it does its job!

title: Hey Rocko let's race!
text:
Very good kart racing game. Sorry but I do get tired of MK sometimes after playing all itterations for years. I'd hate to add up all those hours....
This game controls well....I used a wired controller and played on the tv. You cant reconfigure buttons or use gamecube controllers. It wont take long to get used to it though.
Colors are vivid, tracks are good and good length. They also are not too wide or too narrow. But the magic of course is the characters! I was quick to unlock Heffer because he is my favorite. In this game you also unlock crew members and chiefs. They actually let you customize the gameplay....Muddy Mudskipper lets you go through slime really fast. You get to make different combos to make a really unique ride. I dont know how many combinations there are but its a LOT. Different ones can do things such as act as a magnet to suck up coins, add extra boosts, extra items, etc. This alone should keep the game fresh and fun for a long time.

The cars do feel different. You can change the wheels, engine and tail pipes to change vehicle stats such as speed, drift, handling, etc. Parts are unlocked to be bought with your coins collected and won. You can really change up the looks of a vehicle with paint schemes and they arent limited to specific characters so Spongebob can have Ninja Turtle paint on his vehicle. I dont think weight matters like it does in MK.

I ran through the cups in medium, all manual control in about 4 hours, taking short breaks, placing first fairly easily. The credits roll when you place 1st in all cups in any speed. But parents, dont let a kid fool you and say they beat the game and are done with it if the credits roll....I have also done several challanges and a boss "fight" and have only unlocked or accomplished 18% of the game on about 5.5 total hours playtime.

Theres a battle arena that would be awesome with other players in the room but you can play it alone.

So...is it as polished as MK? No. The music is lacking....i would like to have had show theme songs. Sound effects are great....slime sounds slimey! The game looks fine--really good most of the time. I did experience some disappointing lag at times and they need to patch that. Its bad when it happens and theres no excuse for it. Thats the only gripe i have.

I think this is good for fans of kart racing games, its not perfect but its similar to MK but ....I think its 28 different tracks and even though thats a lot less than MK, its unique tracks make it a decent game. I cant attest to online play....i tried several times and didnt get a match....in other words, no one to race. Of course, this game just came out though.
This is a good game for kids, a family or people like me who love the older Nick chatacters and Spongebob. There are newer characters as well. Its FUN and thers a lot of humor in the pit crew items. Fun--That is the most important to me.

Easy 8 out of 10

title: What....no quarters??
text: I did grow up in the 70s and have my original Atari and games.....I wanted this for being portable and a lot of games in one cartridge.  Tempest, Black Widow, Red Baron, Yar's Revenge, Combat, Asteroids and Warlords make it worth the money to me and there are lots of other great games on here like Centipede and Millipede (both console and arcade versions!)  Real Sports Baseball is still fun and several other sports titles are tolerable especially having grown up with them in a time before great graphics and ultra-realism. Spent a lot of hours with those sports games back then.  Tennis is still challenging....amp up the speed.  Most Atari games have lots of settings you can mess around choosing the right ones for you. Yes, there are several games that are 2 player only, as some people have stayed/complained, some sports games....but others of the same sports can be switched to one player on the "virtual Atari" console before starting the game.....just like they used to be.  I have no idea what people expect for their money.....back in the day Atari carts were usually 30 bucks.....and I can't begin to add up what I probably spent on Tempest alone in a dirty, stinky arcade back then when everybody smoked including the kids and you had to stand up to play instead of lounging on your couch.  So.....I can't complain about having all these great games on a good portable console for a lot less than I used to spend in the arcade back then.  Sure a few games are duds but they were duds back then, too. I did change the settings to get rid of scan lines.  Crystal clear is awesome to me...scan lines weren't even fun back then.  Some of the paddle games like Breakout are barely playable without a legit paddle controller...Circus, Circus is practically impossible but these few problems are not a deal breaker for me.  I can play it on my old system.  I can see how people used to modern gaming may not love it or even like it but honestly, you weren't the market this was for.  If you can't play Combat with a friend or family member and not laugh and get super competitive....lol....sorry for ya.  This collection needed Pac-Man, River Raid, Frogger......several others but this is fine.  If you had told me I could sit on my sofa and play all these games for 30 bucks back in 1979.....I wouldn't have believed that at all.  Enjoy these great games!

title: Ninjago is a guilty pleasure and I love this game!
text:
Original stand alone story and gorgeous graphics make this game very good. It is a little on the short side to actually just complete but as with other Lego games, replaying missions and getting everything takes a while. I think this is one of the better Lego games, especially on a hand held. The music in it is excellent and there is a lot of variety. The controls are very tight and the game mechanics work well. This game has two save slots, which is nice if you'd like to start the game over with out losing all your progress or if another person wants to play the same cartridge. Also, "dying" in a level doesn't cause you to have to start that level again from the beginning....you just continue to respawn as your coveted stud count continues to drop with each "death". I think this game is probably over looked by adult gamers who are fans of Lego games or even of the Ninjago series and that's a shame because this game is excellent.The character count is massive and can be confusing for someone who is not very familiar with the show but that adds to the challenge. My only complaint at all is that if you want to replay each level on free roam IN ORDER from the story mode, you'll probably need to look that up and write it down then proceed. The reason is the story mode sends you to so many different areas of the map, in no memorable order that it would be sort of hard to remember the order. Or you can just use that second slot to start a new game forgoing all your hard earned characters. There is no real open world free roam---you fly from "level" areas on the dragon. There are a few goals to be met while flying but nothing major so the dragon really just moves you to levels you can choose after beating the game. This is not a let down since the only Lego game I know of with a decent free roam open world stage on the 3ds is Lego City.

I think the controls of this game and the difference in each of the playable characters make it excellent.

text:
If you are a fan of these franchises you can't go wrong. I've played for about 7 hours now and love it. I got the starter kit, The Scooby Doo pack and the Back to the Future Pack.....will definitely get a Ninjago fun pack tomorrow.

The gameplay is really fun and if hearing things like Batman say, "We aren't in Gotham anymore.", when he lands in Oz just thrills you to the core, this game is for you. title: I like it but there are issues
text:
This game is definitely a quality release. If you played the first one, you'll be impressed how much the circle pad improves gameplay and the total improvement in graphics and gameplay options is dramatic. Everyone likes to compare it to Pokémon for some reason and I just don't feel it is at all similar other than your collected vivosaurs battle. The battle system is fairly in depth and engaging as you actually "push more buttons" and make more choices while in the actual battle. There is a stadium mode which is a fresh, nice touch but again to battle online the person must be in your friend list and have the game of course. The bone buggys are a fun addition and customizing them adds depth. I played this game for 7 hours so far and I am not overly impressed yet I never felt my money has been wasted. If you like dinosaurs or huge beasts that battle, this game will fulfill that for you. It's a good solid game for what it is but you should make sure this is the game for you before purchasing. I think it is one of those "E" for everyone games that is actually better suited for younger players yet I am not pleased with the "stereotypes" of the NPCs....in fact I am slightly offended by a "fat" character who is clumsy and "rolls around" on the ground due to his "round" appearance. And no, I'm not over weight myself, I just feel this is disparaging content in an "E" for everyone, 10 and up game---in this day and age. I also feel the female character who only likes "cute" vivosaurs and pretty colors is an offensive stereotype and I kept on wondering what on earth the programmers were thinking with the NPCs. I guess they are supposed to be humorous but I find it offensive as well as disliking almost all the other NPC characteristics. If considering for a very young player, there is a LOT of text and a child would need to be able to read to really get full benefit of the battles and vivosaurs collected. The gameplay is fun, the excitement of exploring and excavating and battling is pretty good. To get full benefit of the game I think you need someone to play with, locally or online.

there but I don't see much charm or lasting appeal after the initial play through unless you have someone local or online to battle and excavate with.

title: major eye candy that functions perfectly
text:
I've reviewed a couple of other Pokémon games and gave them high scores. Yes, I am a fan of the series. I average about 400 hours per game even though I'm no pro. Pokémon Omega Ruby is fun. It's the most fun I've had with a Pokémon game since Soul Silver (my favourite), and it is the best looking to date. I thought X was mind blowingly awesome but all the little improvements in this one, even minor things like how great reflective surfaces look, how tree lines have more detail and depth, how Pokémon attack animations look amazing is enough to push this game to the top of my list. This is not a stale remake but of course it follows tried and true Pokémon formula. It's a better game over all in every category than X with tons of content.

A FEW things I really like:
DexNav
Pokedex (homage to the GBA is awesome and the dex functions really well and is fun to use)
Graphics--true improvement in every aspect, even NPC models are a delight--battle animations are magnificent
2 different bikes that actually function completely differently--mach and acro
Pokemon Contests---while not as fun as Pokeathlon it's still great
Transferring Pokémon from other games considering they are "newer gen" Pokémon
Secret bases--customization is awesome
*Also, it's faster to heal your Pokémon with nurse Joy...battle animations have been amped up to be faster. Other than sneaking up on Pokémon, the rest of the game things can happen faster, including how fast you can go on the bikes.

To be fair---here are two things I really don't like--
1. Music--it sounds great but when changing areas, entering buildings, especially going into battle, it often seems like a jarring change instead of a smooth transition...it seems pretty major to me and is very annoying, maybe I'll get used to it
2. Not being able to customize your character is a step back for a game that took SO many steps forward. Even if they had limited the options, there should have been character customization options. People who play hundreds of hours get pretty tired of seeing the same character.

Wish--still wish Pokémon could follow my character. Simple but very great thing about SS.

Note....these Pokémon don't suck as some people want to continue to say. People who say this often continue by saying 1st Gen are the only Pokémon they've cared about. Every gen has great ones and some stinkers. Well, this game is set for you to catch them ALL.

Whether you played the originals or not, there's enough familiar content and new content and improvements that this game, like Heart Gold and Soul Silver gets to stand out on it's own as a major contender for best Pokémon game ever. It is just a sheer delight to play and Game Freak went above and beyond to give us another super great quality gaming experience.

(I didn't mention online play because I don't do that until I've spent around 50 hours on the game. Writing this review I am only about 30 hours in)

I hope you enjoy Pokémon Omega Ruby or Alpha Sapphire as much as I am

"Break it, see what's inside" is stuck in my head forever, now. This was a main reason actual critics panned the game....I thought, "It can't be THAT bad.", well, it really is.  Playing the Robo Knight levels is the only break you get from the other rangers yelling....but Gosei yells.  I have no idea how the creators/producers thought this was anywhere near acceptable during testing.  And...the actual game is just pretty broken.  The rangers are often facing the wrong way and it's difficult to make them turn back around.  It's possible, but it feels like a control issue instead of a proper challenge.  The game play is nothing new from previous PR games on handhelds....beat the throngs of bad guys, collect some things, fight a boss who usually flees to be fought again.  The Zord fights are probably the only thing I did like but then, that's why we keep buying these bad games, right?  LOL.  Zord fights look pretty good but none of the graphics in this game are 3ds quality.  PR Samurai and PR Super Legends both for DS are much better games, with the latter blowing all the others away yet it still isn't great.  Card scanning could cause a mental breakdown.  If you're willing to try it, it's VERY difficult to get your lighting set up right for the cards to scan and there's very little pay off.  I tried to scan 80 cards of which 30 scanned....I did briefly see a screen indicating the rangers had skills and health upgrades but it didn't say how much or even if it was permanent and I never say the screen again.  Classic scenes rewarded for card scans are simply pictures....as you may know if you scan the cards with your ap on your phone you actually get short corresponding segments of "film" from the shows, which is wonderful.  There is NO excuse for that not happening with the game as well.  I can see that small kids would like the game just because it's PR.  But this is one Mega shiny turd with bad graphics, bad controls, repetitive game play, little reward or pay off for accomplishments, no co-op even locally, not the tv ranger's voices (no excuse for this), and that "vocal support" truly is the ruination of the game--unbelievably bad and super annoying. I've heard debate that as long as the games are E for everyone, they will be awful but that is absurd as there are lots of E for everyone games that are excellent.  It comes down to them doing as little as possible relying on the name to sell the game.  If you feel a need to own every PR hand held game ever made, as I do,  then you've already bought this and know it's not even as good as older GBA PR games.  If you want a good Power Rangers game....or just a playable game, don't waste your money.  Take a step back and forwards and buy Power Rangers Super Legends 15th Anniversary.  This game turned THAT game into a much better game than it was originally.  Buy it instead or even PR Dino Thunder for GBA.

title: A review from someone who is actually playing it....not just saying my kid likes it...and a bit of comparison to the 3ds version
text: Love it.  Great graphics, fun modes and lots to do. Terrific voice acting and characters.  I have the 3ds version and the portal works fine with the PS3.  The console version really is a whole lot better than the 3ds version but the 3ds version is more of a platformer, you can store two Skylanders and just swap them out by tapping their icon on the bottom screen and they can jump.  Other than that, the PS3 version is a much more immersive and richer game.  I think this is a game for the whole family to enjoy and I have played a heck of a lot of games since 1978.  Infact, it sort of reminds me of old fashioned Diablo type dungeon crawling (and some Skylanders have similar type abilities) but most of the adventuring takes place in well lit areas and even though the NPCs are cute they are not "sticky sweet" or too childish for adults who just want to experience a fun game. I love the bright colors and the little details like ice forming on the ship...or little puddles on the deck.  And it is FUN. I like buying the character updrades in this version as that is not an option but is automatic in the 3ds version.  Skylanders transferred from the 3ds retain their LEVELS but not their upgrades.  Hats in this version actually have a purpose and can effect stats in many different ways such as making a Skylander faster or better defensively.  In the 3ds version hats just sit on their heads and look cool...lol....no effects at all.  I waited for this version and the figures to become a little more affordable and honestly, it's one of those rare times I wish I had just bought it on release day because it's that good and would have been well worth the price. Finding new figures in the stores is almost impossible now. Good news-- It's ok to buy Skylanders used if you want to or don't have a bunch of cash....this version has an option to reset the Skylander so you can do all its stats, leveling up yourself.  Also...the best thing about BOTH games....you really only have to have 1 giant and a Skylander of each element to play the game effectively and enjoy all the parts.  So...I think that comes down to your giant and 7 of the other elements.  And since you can use Skylanders from the original game, there's lots to pick from and enjoy.  Of course, you'll want more than 8 but it's like eating an elephant---ONE bite at a time will get you there :)  At first I thought the figures were a horrible gimmick idea but now that more and more games on any system are requring you to pay for additional DLC...this is really cool since you have a figure and a game character to show for your money spent.  There's no online mode for the battle arenas....that's the only thing I don't like about this game. I've been fairly dependent on online for quick games with other people for several years so no online battle option feels like a step backwards in gaming.  Other than that, i think the concept is amazing, the game plays very well, the modes mix it up, replay value is strong for each level and for each figure you collect.  I think it's superb and would think anyone who likes games could enjoy this nearly perfect game.

As with the other games in recent past, the split second timing needed for reversals is a little too difficult to pull off with any regularity so it feels like hopeful button mashing frenzy. title: Better than running away with the circus!  Magnum Opus to the MAX!!
text:
I'm not going to claim to have been a fan since Red and Blue. I started late with Fire Red and have played all the ones thereafter. I'm not going to say I bought it for my kids and they love it. I'm going to just tell you WHY it's enjoyable for adult gamers and go over a few of my favorite new features since I'm 15 hours in to the game now.

Pokémon games can be played on as simple or hard a "level" as the player chooses. By this I mean a person could easily "beat" the game simply by raising stats on a handful of Pokémon and just pummeling everything else with lower stats to pieces, totally disregarding type match up mechanics. This is what a lot of kids or inexperienced players do. I did it also with my first game so I'm not criticizing anyone choosing this path at all. For a much more in depth, time consuming experience to last hundreds of hours you can really learn type match ups, move sets, seriously EV train, only use Pokémon that are beneficial to the team (even if you don't LIKE them), etc. Either way YOU want to play or somewhere in the middle of those descriptions it SHOULD be a very enjoyable experience and well worth your money. I think this game is for anyone who wants a good game to play.

I love the new PSS system. It is so much easier to find people to battle, trade, friend, etc.

I also like the voice chat for friends. I was actually surprised how well it worked today.

The sheer business of your bottom screen now really lends to the feeling of constant movement in this game. It's almost overwhelming compared to the previous games. In fact, you'll be working hard multi tasking on THIS game....training several ways or enjoying fairly fun mini games with pretty good variety. I really liked Pokeathlon in Soul Silver so I'm glad to see some mini games I actually enjoy choosing Pokémon to use in, again. Pokémon-Amie is a nice change of pace too....so far I like it but am not sure I will have much interest in it weeks from now. I could be wrong, though.

The sound is superb. The graphics are super great...I mean I just can't say enough nice things about the over all presentation. Even the menu works much more fluidly. I loved repeatedly making Panchams faint....their cry just cracked me up for some reason. You'll find plenty to like in this game. I can't tell you what it would be like to a person who had never played another Pokémon title before....but...part of me wishes it was the first time I'd played one because this is definitely Game Freak's magnum opus. I want to hug them each because they really did a lot of things the fans asked them to implement....this game is a love story from them to the fans. It is perfect. 11 out of 10

title: Better than the others
text: I have played a lot of PR games on GBA....and two on DS including this one.  I actually loved this game and think it is better than the newer Power Rangers Samurai.  It really didn't get good game critic reviews and I can't figure out why.  A lot of critics said the levels were bland....well....on the show, the fight scenes ARE in bland areas and this has been the case with every single PR game ever.  There are many rangers with different moves to "unlock" or use. That part alone makes this game much better than Samurai which is more platformer than fighter since there were very few moves available to the rangers and kick moves are non existent.  There are SO many fighting moves in this one it's easy to forget some.  Both ds games have advantages and draw backs and we fans really haven't gotten a GOOD game but I think this one trumps the others.  I love the ability to toss a baddie at the screen or straight into the air to pummel him in combo attacks. Replay value?  Sort of---you CAN go back and replay missions for better bonuses and scores. If you have to choose between this or Samurai, I suggest going with this one as it feels more complete as a "fighter"---not perfect at all but a big improvement over other PR games and the story is not a rehash of a season but a blend of seasons and rangers with a fresh plot.  Just a better experience all around. Parents who have complained their 3 year old...five year old...etc. can't progress in either game..., both games are rated E for everyone aged 10 and up because reading skills are required to "learn moves" or advance through the games.

text: I wanted this for Decap Attack, Sonic, Altered Beast and the Streets of Rage so I feel like I got my money's worth.  Super portable...easy to hookup.
