Of course, if you have the original system, stick with that.  If you sold yours long ago (like I did) or never had one, this is a good way to go.  I had no problem with the controllers after I positioned the system at a higher level on the coffee table by just sitting it on some stacked books.  The range is NOT great on the wireless part but you CAN plug in a controller if you have one...or two.  I had just one cart, Road Rash and it plays very good on this tiny little system. The system itself is not much bigger than that original cart and is ultra light weight.  This is about convenience of not having tons of cartridges laying around but it sure does play them nicely if you want to use them.  Is it the same quality as the original system?  No.  Is it effective?  Yes. I mean, really...are you going to devote the hours to retro gaming you did when it first came out?? If you ARE then you might want to find a really clean original system. I'm not sure what people really expect for 40 bucks these days but this is less than the price of one new game and for WHAT it is and ISN'T, I give it an 8.5 out of 10. text: I bought this for a LONG train ride and played about 5.5 hours straight before I was tired of it for the day. Not bad.  I'd read mixed reviews and finally just broke down and bought it since I am a pretty big Pokemon fan.  Well, the button mashing is extremely repetitive as others have clearly stated. This to me was a significant source of annoyance and so far, I haven't found much use for the touch screen as everything can be done with the buttons.  That's not really cool for a touch screen system in 2012.  The game DOES look great in 3d and the story is ok for a Pokemon spin off game.  The bad thing is my favorite part of the game wasn't even gameplay....it was watching my Mii friends walk by looking in the Pokemon store window while my Mii was standing there looking in.  I thought that was a really cool thing for some strange reason and I liked seing my Mii friends integrated into a game if only as strolling NPCs.  Personally, even though the games are pretty different--I think the Pokemon Mystery Dungeon ds games are more enjoyable if you are an older gamer. Of course those games get mixed reviews too but I liked them and found them to be much more absorbing, pleasurable and colorful.  I can see why Rumble Blast would appeal to much younger children as there really is no strategy or memory skills involved and it is brimming with cute Pokemon.  Bad investment....no.  Great game?  It's an ok game.  As usual, I found my truth to be on middle ground with all the reviews I had read.  This is a time-killer game to me since you can pick up and play and not have to concentrate much but it looks beautiful and hey...it's Pokemon.  I suggest buying used...I would have been happier with button mashing at a 20 buck or less price point.  Certainly not the worst game I ever played but far from being a MUST play game.  Good luck, enjoy.

title: Disappointed
text:
I really don't see why Valve would even sell this disc package, as none of the games are actually on the disc. You have to download all of them. So really all you're paying for is the piece of paper with the activation code that comes in the DVD case. There are four games in this package, each requires a download of around 2GB ~ 4GB+ to install.

Ok, I should have known better. I'm one of the many people that even today who don't have high-speed broadband. I live in a rural area that isn't served by any of the regular ISPs. So I make do with dial-up and a cellular 4G MiFi service. Sure the 4G is high speed, but I'm limited to 5GB a month. So to get just one of these games, I would have to use up the bulk of my monthly data plan, or spend $10 per GB to buy extra. Which is why I ordered the physical box package, so that I wouldn't have to download anything. It really makes me a bit angry to find out that this disc was intentionally created by a company without the actual content on it. I could understand if they were just doing downloads to save the cost of a physical package (DVD & case), but they're not.

I'm sure these are great games, but since I haven't been able to play one, I'm just giving them an "OK" rating. Maybe some day I'll be able to download them and come back and give them a real review.

At least the activation code did work, I see from reading some of the other reviews that is not always the case.

title: Classic game
text:
Back in the mid 1990's I worked for a small engineering company, and for a time you could tell when it was 5pm without even looking at your watch. That was because the sound of keyboards being pounded began to echo through the engineering department. Myself and seven other engineers would start playing Descent right at 5 o'clock and continue to do so till late into the night. It was a great game.

I never got around to playing the version for the original Playstation until years later when I had bought a Playstation 2 console. Just recently I purchased one of the new Playstation 3 slim consoles, and I was under the impression that the PS3's could not play Playstation 1 or 2 games. But a couple weeks ago I was reading a thread in the Amazon Video Game customer discussion forum and someone there mentioned that you could in fact play PS 1 games in a PS 3. I tried playing the original PS1 Silent Hill game and it worked! Finding that out I went and browsed the used video games here on Amazon looking for some old classics to buy. Descent Maximum was the first one I ordered. Got it in about a week later and have been playing it since.

The game play is as I remember it - with the exception you're playing against the game itself and not other people. Being an old PS1 game, playing it on one of today's 42" television leaves a lot to desire - the graphics are really blocky on a screen that size (still playable though). So I ended up moving my PS3 and connecting it to a smaller 24" monitor, which suited the low-res video resolution better.

Descent Maximum is very similar to the PC Descent II game - you have similar tunnel systems, weapons, and the addition of the guidebot to lead you to objects and locations. Like the PC game, you can rotate your ship 360° in any direction (which at the time made some people a bit queasy). There are six worlds to play, each with six levels (36 total). Blowing up the reactor on the first level when I played this PS1 disc for the first time brought back memories.

There are a lot of fun old games like this out there - I'm glad to find out that I can still play them and will be looking for more.

title: Great Game!
text:
I was a bit surprised when I was offered by the Vine program to try this game. I haven't really played any video games in awhile, and when I did it was mainly First Person Shooters. I did play some of the Rayman games back in the days of the Sega Dreamcast (which I still have around here somewhere), and I remembered they were pretty fun.

Playing Rayman Legends is great! I had forgotten how much fun platform games were to play. The game is really easy to pick up (control-wise) and the graphics are fantastic. There have been a lot of improvements since those Dreamcast days. The levels are challenging - but not to where you can't figure out what needs to be done or how to do it.

I didn't get to try any of the online features of the game as I don't have a fast enough internet connection to do such things. Still, the stand-alone games are tremendously enjoyable by themselves. And the mini-games are great when you don't have time to play - although they are addicting and it is easy to sit down to play for 20 minutes or so, and then look up and find you've been playing for well over an hour. That's mainly because I tend to replay levels and games trying to do better than I did before, there seems to be something I miss or did wrong. But the thing is, I don't seem to get frustrated when that happens - the games are that entertaining.

Since playing Rayman Legends, I've also went ahead and ordered the previous game in this series - Rayman Origins. The reviews I've read say that it is just as fun as this new one.

I would recommend this game to everyone - young / old.

title: Works for me..
text:
Just got this gizmo this week-end and have been playing around with it. I thought I might share some thoughts on the experience.

First off this isn't my first experience with a Pinnacle product. Years ago I bought one of their miroVIDEO DC30pro video systems and had a horrible experience with that. It didn't work, and I got zero support from the company. The only positive thing from that experience was the support I got from the company I bought the board from - they worked with me for about a year to figure out what the problem was (the board was apparently incompatible with the chipset that my system motherboard used...). Needless to say, I've been wary of buying anything made by Pinnacle since then. But last year I saw an announcement for this Video Transfer gizmo in the newspaper - and since then have wanted one - especially after seeing video online of it demonstrated at some electronic show. I've held off buying one main because of my previous experience and about half of the reviews I've read on it have been a bit negative. I finally gave in and ordered one, I figured if I didn't like it I could either send it back or give it to someone.

Anyway, got this in yesterday and in the package was the device, a cable set (standard RCA video, r/l audio cable), a power transformer, a quick start guide, and a slim manual. One end of the gizmo has the power connection that the transformer plugs in, and the two USB ports (one standard USB - the kind a thumb drive plugs into, and the other is the "D" shaped plug - the sort you find on the back of most printers these days, in the manual there is note stating that this port is for future use, so I'm guessing its not functional at this time). On the other side of the gizmo there are the connections for the video inputs. The standard RCA connectors and an S-Video connector. On top there is a single round button, one side controls the recording mode (good, better, best) and also acts the power on/off switch. The other side of the button turns on/off recording. There are many led lights - some near the connections and some arrayed around the button. These light turn red or blue depending on what the device is trying to tell you at the time. Commonly, red means the device is recording and blue means that things are done or ok...

Hooking this device up took some thought - as there are a number of different ways to do that. First you need to consider what sort of video input that you are going to record. I first hooked this up to an old VCR that I had laying around (connecting to the RCA outputs) - but then realized that doing that, I couldn't "see" what was being recorded - so I wouldn't know when to start / stop the recording. I corrected that, by running a cable from the VCRs "F" connection (the old screw on antenna cable connection) to an old television. One other thing to do before starting - you need to go to the Pinnacle web site and download the latest firmware upgrade and put it on your flash drive before powering the device up. The instructions on how to do this are on the website and it's pretty simple to do. Be sure to unzip the file first....

Right now, I'm just copying some old vhs tapes, so hooking up to the vcr works for me. And with the vcr's tuner I can also record the occasional television program off the air (least till the switch to DTV goes into effect - then I guess I'm going to have to connect to one of the converter boxes).

I've transferred over a number of tapes last night - most home movies created with a camcorder but also tried an old commercially made documentary. I'm recording to a 4GB thumb drive - and recording at "Better" mode. So far the quality of the output is what I expected it to be - pretty much the same as the vhs tape itself. One snag that I ran into, I want to use these digital copies on my Sony PSP - but when I tried putting one of these files on one of my memory sticks and playing it with the PSP - the PSP didn't recognize the file (DoH!). Going back and reading the manual (yeah, I know I probably should have done that first...) I found out that there are three recording modes - one for iPODs, one for PSPs and another for other devices (PCs). Each one is a bit different than the others (and there are the three quality levels for each, good, better, & best). The device automatically chooses which mode it uses based on the device you hook up to it (you get to choose the quality though). So by using a thumb drive, it made my videos into the Other format. No big deal. I have Corel's VideoStudio installed on my computer and I was able to load the files into it and save them out to something that my PSP could use. I could just plug in my PSP to the device, but then it would be tied up while it's recording. Converting the files isn't that big of an inconvenience. If you don't have any video editing software - there are a number of reasonably priced packages out there other than the one I'm using (although I've been very happy with this Corel package) and most of these will convert to a format friendly to either PSP or iPod or both...

So to recap - I'm pretty happy with this device. It seems to do what it claims to do, allow me to transfer video to either my PSP and/or to my iPod.

title: Nice concept - if it worked...
text:
Just got this in today and so far it's not working.... (shipping was fast though!)

There wasn't a very detailed description of what this gizmo is, so I'll attempt to provide some information. This unit is a "cradle" (that much was given), but it is also being billed as being a "charger", which in my opinion is misleading. This unit has no charging function in itself - to power this unit you will need to plug a charger / transformer into the unit (transformer not included, guessing you're expected to use the one that came with your PSP).The power is transfered through the cradle to the PSP. This disappointed me, as I planned on using this as a charging unit for when I took my PSP to work - so I didn't have to haul my charger with me.

The unit has some built in speakers, but I have not been able to get them to function. The only instructions included with the unit, is what is printed on the back of the box. The instructions are for the function of the three controls/outputs on the back of the unit.

* AV OUTPUT for AV output
* Play/Charge/OFF - Slide to play your PSP console, charge PSP console or turn the speaker function off.
* LED ON/OFF - Slide to turn the blue LED on or off.

The LED lights work (and look nice), and the switch for turning them on and off worked. But I haven't been able to get the speakers to work. I thought it might be a problem with fitting the PSP console to the unit - you have to fit the console over a 1/8" headphone plug and a power plug and press the PSP down onto these plugs. I believe I got the PSP fully attached, but I'm not sure if I did or not - like I mentioned the cradle's speakers didn't work and I really couldn't tell if I was getting power to the PSP or if it was simply running off its own battery. The cradle also allows you to tilt the PSP a bit so that you can adjust the angle of the screen.

I plan on keeping the unit I received and seeing if I can get it to work - worst case scenario, I'll disassemble it and see if there is something I can fix (which I know will void any warranty and make the unit unreturnable). This unit is a bit on the cheaply made side, I wish someone would make something like this that was a little more heavy duty - like they do for the iPods. I'm giving it at least two stars as I plan on keeping it - if I ever do get it to function 100%, I'll come back an append my review.

Other than this, it fits the Switch very well, and seems to protect it. May even hold it if there was a slim case on the switch. Would recommend if storing the A.C. charger that came with the switch was not a concern.

title: Addictive fun
text:
This game was pleasantly surprising even though it's fairly simple. My husband and I, who are old enough that we used to play Zork on our Apple IIe when we were first married, found that we would spend hours every night after dinner glued to the Wii working our way through this game. The puzzles are difficult enough to be engaging but not completely impossible, the story line is ok, the graphics are decent and detailed, and navigating through the game is made easier by the use of a point and click map. We were sad when it ended. In this game the storyline is less exciting than the puzzles and figuring out how to use things. In that way, it reminded me of Zork all those years ago, although I recall Zork being even more inventive in its use of objects to solve problems.
The only complaint I have about the game is that the collection of 'postcards' seems more important than it is. In the end, if you play it, collect them for the fun of the collecting because they don't have much value other than that.
Overall, a really fun game that a family could enjoy together. But watch out because it's easy to spend hours in front of the TV doing this.

title: Sadly disappointed
text: My husband and I just completed this game and I wish I could say it was because we were enthralled by the amount of game play or puzzle action it provided. Instead, I have to say it's because we like to finish what we started. The impression we get of this game is that the programmers had to rush to get it to production and abandoned any hope of creative programming about halfway through it. It's less of a game, and more of a story line with things you can do to entertain yourself... at least until about halfway through when you have run out of things to actually do and end up simply wandering around the game platform hoping for encounters with characters. And there are no shortcuts to take you to places faster. How hard would it have been to include an interactive map where you could point to a destination and it would take you there? Apparently too hard for these programmers. Or maybe that would have just made the game too short because you can waste an incredible amount of time wandering around in this game, doing nothing. I can just hear the brainstorming that went into creating this game: "Okay, guys, we now have the story line and the gamer cannot mess with that until the end of the game, but the game is too short. Let's throw in a couple of seemingly important tasks to distract the player from the fact that they are actually doing nothing to solve a mystery! How about a parachute to nowhere? Or a radio that does nothing? You know what? The story is set around WWII, let's throw in a little meaningless Nazi teaser." I hate to give a bad review to something, but, really, if something is going to be advertised as a 'game', I'd like to see a little more finesse in how it allows the player to interact. Otherwise, just advertise it as a walk-through experience, which is more accurate. I'm so glad I didn't pay full price for this game, which is completely not worth it. If you are curious, save your money and rent the game.

title: Great update on a beloved game
text:
My husband has always been a huge fan of the Zelda series, as well as myself. It was our childhood growing up and now has developed into something truly amazing. We played the Twilight Princess back when it was out on gamecube and then on the wii, but the new HD version for the Wii U is really amazing. The graphics have been cleaned up, a lot more than I expected, and there have been some nice updates. The Poe lantern allows you to find the Poe in the day time, so no having to wait so long for night time just to hunt it in that time. With no sun song, it makes a difference. You can find it and then you will know where to be at night.

Another update that is interesting is the addition of the Hylian stamps, each letter of the alphabet. This of course is a necessary addition for anyone who would love to learn more about the world we grew up in. I feel like Epona is a little harder to steer, more like a real horse, so it does change a few of the things in game, but nothing that would be too much to handle. The game also works with the amibo characters, so that is a fun little addition if you have any of the Zelda characters at home. Over all it is still the story we all love, just updated a bit and has a few extras.

title: Premium design but doesnt fit properly with Elite strap installed
text:
This is one of the coolest charging dock for Oculus quest 2. Even though the charge station looks very elegant, some serious design change needs to be considered for this product to be popular.

Pros:
- Charges headset and controllers all at the same time
- No need to replace batteries often
- Elegant design
- Over charge protection
- Over voltage protection
- Over current protection
- Short circuit Protection
- Magnetic charge pin so you can remove the headset
- Controllers charge status
- 18 months warranty

Cons:
- Actual usage of magnetic charge pins are not useable due to design. Unless you remove the controllers first, you cant remove the headset from the charge station. So this magnetic charge pin doesnt really add any purpose. I have to use both my hands to place/remove from the charge station.
- Charge station has indicator only controller charge status. You still have to check the headset charging status from the left side indicator in the headset.
- You need to replace controller's original battery cover with provided metal spot on cover to make it rechargeable with station. Because of this, you cant install any grip/sleeve to your controllers. I feel this is a design drawback. Most of my games I need my grip for the controllers and without the grip/sleeve it starts sweating and controller becomes slippery!
- Controllers doesnt sit properly in the station when you have the lanyards installed. Need extra push to sit fit and start charging.
- Major disadvantage is the placement of charging port for the station. It is placed in the rear side of the charge station (circled in the attached photo) and if you have Quest 2 Elite strap installed then it doesnt sit properly as the charge port/cable is blocking headrest of the elite strap. So the headset doesnt sit and wobbles in the station.

Considering all the good features it has and the value for the money it is one of the best charging station if you can live with the cons mentioned above!

title: Impressive Sound and Value
text:
The sound impressed me right out of the box. I connected the headset directly to my PC and was pleasingly surprised at the clarity of the highs and the richness of the lows. The low end could use a bit more boost overall but more about that below.
The PS4 and XBOX crowd need not spend the extra money for the mixing console because you can't use it. The headphones plug directly into your controller as they normally would. Although the sound quality and braided connecting cable are quite nice for the price!
The Mixing Console has some heft and is sturdy enough no to wiggle much from where its place. There are no instructions in the booklet for using it but it is fairly straightforward.
There is a place to connect the headset with the mic (TRRS Connection) and a standard headphone jack. They can both be used at the same time. Nice feature.
The inline volume and mic control worked smoothly with no crackle and the microphone itself stayed reasonably where it was put although you couldn't get it very close to your mouth .
Once the driver is automatically set up from Windows (no download necessary) you can select the EQ that you prefer by a short press of the EQ button on the left. I found that "GAME" mode seems to be an overall winner for best overall quality. "MOVIE" mode boosts the mid range (center channel). "MUSIC" mode seems a pretty well flat EQ. "BASS" mode loses mode of the high and just boosts the low end. I stayed away from that mode because it compromised the clarity too much and "GAME" mode provided plenty of low end to be satisfying.
Overall, for the price, this model from Amazon Basics is a definite winner which I would place as a contender as one of the better Gaming Headsets in the budget category.

title: Very Pleased - Build Quality is Fantastic
text:
Reactions to this mechanical gaming keyboard:

* Keyboard is a pleasure to use - the key presses travel well and feel great.

* Clicking is definitely noisy - this is true for all mechanical keyboards but this one seems a bit louder than average.

* The wire has a cloth mesh around it - pretty common in higher end pc peripherals and this one looks nice.

* Comes with a cover in case you transport it a lot - don't have to worry about stuff breaking it or getting in the keys.

* The keyboard's USB cable is detachable which is nice for storage.

* The textured keys are a neat novelty. If you play a lot of FPS games or MMOs you may really appreciate having the textured keys so that you can place your hand correctly.

Additional thoughts:

Full disclosure, the HyperX Alloy FPS mechanical keyboard is my first and only experience with mechanical keyboards. Thoughts, in no particular order.

Build quality & hardware: The build quality of this keyboard is superb. The specs list that the keyboard has a solid steel frame, and I believe it. The entire thing feels very weighty and solid; there’s no give to the frame at all and no plastic squeak. The keyboard is very portable (I’ve brought it between computers in my apartment and back and forth to work) and has a detachable cable. It includes an extra charging port for … something? The port works as a pass-through; the male end of the USB cable has two connectors though you’ll only need to use one if you don’t plan on using the extra charge port. I’ve used it as a convenient place to plug in my mouse. The port isn’t particularly high amperage (0.9A with a standard USB 3.0 port, as compared to 2 or 3A with modern phone chargers), so I wouldn’t suggest using it to charge your phone or tablet. Overall the keyboard feels extremely sturdy and the build quality is excellent. The aesthetic is very loud – read: 'gamer-y' black with red accents – but doesn’t look too out of place so long as you don’t enable the goofier light modes and stick with the default key caps.

Extra features: Advertising for the keyboard touts it’s 100% anti-ghosting “game mode”. For those of you not in the know, ghosting is the problem where some keyboard keys don’t work when multiple keys are pressed simultaneously. Microsoft has a great write-up to explain the problem. I don’t expect to make use of this feature; I don’t play fast-paced games where this has been a problem. Still, it's a novel solution to a problem that would be infuriating should you encounter it. On the keycap front, HyperX includes some additional contrast color and textured keys (WASD, 1234) that can be swapped in if desired. They even include an installation tool that worked well. Ultimately, the keys were hideous and I didn’t find that the texture was helpful for my use case; I chose to revert to the default keys.

Mechanical keys: This is my first experience with a mechanical keyboard. The HyperX Alloy FPS uses Cherry MX mechanical keys. I wasn’t sure what I’d think about these, but now I believe the hype! I’d expected to tinker with this keyboard a bit before putting it into storage, but it’s become my preferred keyboard in the house. The travel distance feels just right, and the “click” that comes with each button press provides the perfect amount of feedback. That being said, this keyboard is loud! It’s not an issue if I’m just playing games or reading the internet, but my family members have requested I switch to a different keyboard if I work from home while they are in the room.

Overall experience: I’m very pleased with this keyboard. The build quality is fantastic and it’s very satisfying to use. title: Parts of This Game Are Fun, But Prefer Others in the Series - Here's Why:
text:
Some thoughts on ASSASSIN'S CREED UNITY:

* I played the PS4 version.
* I do not have the same frame rate issues that others are reporting.
* I think it's not one of the best of Assassin's Creed (AC) games. Having played most of them, I like Black Flag, the Assassin's Creed 2 games, and AC1 better, but like this more than Assassin's Creed III.
* This game pales in comparison to Shadows of Mordor and Assassin's Creed Black Flag.
* The movement in this game is often erratic. I always find that I get more comfortable with the movement in these games as I play them, but I think this game is particularly bad.
* The game feels buggy and glitchy overall. The animations are not as fluid as in other AC games and Shadows of Mordor, NPCs behave weirdly reasonably often, clipping, etc. However, I did not see any gamebreaking crashes or bugs which made me restart a mission/reload the game.
* Combat is about par compared to previous games in the series, but much worse than in Shadows of Mordor.
* Paris is a good setting for the game. AC gameplay benefits from the city streets, as opposed to open terrain, as in much of AC3 and Black Flag.
*In previous games, I really enjoyed the Abstergo/future storyline, but in the more recent games have stopped caring. The plot is overly convoluted and there's very little advancing of the narrative going on.
* Arno is a decent enough character though, and I enjoyed his storyline, but I wish that the rich history of the French Revolution was brought into the game more.
* Paris seems too chaotic, there's too much random robbing and looting going on. It can be distracting, and you'll get random events occurring during (at least some of the) missions, which can get in the way/become problematic.
* Did not try the multiplayer missions.
* Integration with the web games leaves something to be desired, in my opinion. I have heard that they are not very fun, and I'm not really interested in participating anyways. Am bummed that I have to do this in order to unlock some of the game's content.
* In short: if you haven't played Shadows of Mordor or Black Flag, play those first. If you like both of those games and still want more on a current gen console, Unity may be what you're looking for. Just don't set your expectations too high. I enjoyed playing this game - just not up to the quality of some of the previous games I've mentiioned.

title: Rattling and binding are hard to overlook
text:
Razer Huntsman Mini 60% Gaming Keyboard: Analog Optical Switches - Doubleshot PBT Keycaps - Chroma RGB - Onboard Memory - Portable 60 Percent Form Factor - Detachable Type-C Cable - Classic Black

I really wanted to love this keyboard. There are tons of reviews on Youtube and Reddit about all of the features this keyboard has. It's great to be able to customize the pressure on the keys to simulate joystick movement. It's not just that, you can customize the sensitive and actuation for individual keys. Even further you can have different commands at separate actuation points on a single switch. Rad! But.......

Not all games support the analog controls on keyboards. I play Destiny and could not get this function to work. The speed, Actuation points and separate commands at actuation points worked great. You can spend loads of time customizing and tuning the actuations until it feels just right for you. This is all adjusted through Synapse, arguably one of the most resource hungry proprietary apps out there. I already use Synapse for my mouse and headset so it's fine.

I don't think individually stabilized switches are it though. OMG the rattling! This keyboard makes the worst sounds and is terribly loud. It feels and sounds so cheap. You wouldn't guess by hearing it or looking at it all of the tech it has. The feel isn't great either. If you hit the keycaps just a bit off angle it binds and makes a loud click negating any nuance to the actuation points you've spent so much time tuning. Honestly, for all of the cool tech this keyboard has the binding and rattling were just too bad to overlook.

Oh, also artisan keycaps won't fit over the switch stabilizers.

I wish it had an indicator on the headset, but not worth knocking off any stars though. Overall sound quality when listening to Spotify is superb for a gaming headset. It doesn't quite keep up with dedicated headphones in the same price-range but they more then makes up for it with the other features. Music is still very crisp and clear. In game sounds (Minecraft and StarCraft 2) are emersive and it's easy to discern which direction an aggressive mob is coming from to react quickly, the surround sound is definitely on point.

The microphone is very clear on Skype. The people I have called have noted that there was very little static and my voice came through crystal clear. I have not used it in any voice chat apps as I usually just game alone or with my children in the same room, but I would assume the same quality there as well.

The range on the headset is more then adequate as I was able to walk to my kitchen to grab a drink without losing signal. They did drop out while I wore them to check the mail, but that's understandable. Getting them to re-connect was very fast(switch them off and on on the headset). Not sure if I would ever need a longer range on a gaming headset.

As far as comfort goes, the longest I've worn them continuously for has been around 3-4 hours. They where a pleasure to wear for that amount of time and I'm sure they would be comfortable much longer. To be completely wireless, with a 15 hour rechargable battery, they are amazingly lightweight. The height adjustment is very easy to set up with indentions that seem to click in place. Although these tend to move a little when putting them on or taking them off. This hasn't been an issue so far once they are on and comfortable, but I could see this being a weak point in the long term.

As far battery life, I haven't been able to test the full life of the battery. The claim is 15 hours, but if I'm not wearing them, they're on their dock charging. One thing that is annoying is how they won't seem to charge unless they are hooked up to my laptop. Would be handy to just be able to plug them up to a ac adapter to charge while I take my laptop to class or work.

The buttons and volume placement being on the right ear piece is well thought out and easy to access without looking. This is especially true with the volume wheel on the bottom side. On the fly volume adjustment is easy and effortless.

The build quality leads me to believe that these will last a long time. I could see the charging on dock feature failing after a lot of uses, but even then you can plug the headset up to the dock directly. The available mod kits available on Amazon look like fantastic replacements for when the muffs or the top pad get worn out to keep them going longer.

Overall, 4.5 stars.

title: Great game, poor online experience
text:
I'm conflicted about how many stars I should give this game. As for the game itself, we love it! My two oldest boys and I have been playing it almost every day since we got it. We even bought an inexpensive bass guitar and another cable so we can play two-player. The game is a lot of fun and I do think it can teach you many of the basics of playing guitar and develop some of the 'mechanics' of playing. Playing the songs is, of course, fun (and it doesn't force you to play songs you don't want to), but the 'arcade' games are fun and helpful, too, teaching the fretboard, chords, and scales.

The only downside is the connection to the Ubisoft servers. It worked flawlessly for the first few days we had it, but we've been unable to connect to the servers for many days in a row now. I've just spent a few frustrating hours last night and this morning trying to figure out the problem and have not been able to. Ubisoft support, while prompt, has been less than helpful. There are two reasons you'd want to connect to the servers, to use their Uplay service to track progress and to purchase new songs to learn. Fortunately, you can apparently buy songs through the XBOX Live store as well, which is what I was looking for. I don't care so much about the online tracking of my progress...

So, 5 stars (easy) for the game, drop one star (and maybe more) for the issues with connectivity and support.

title: Educational....
text:
This is a simple game and it doesn't take much to play it. You don't have to think too hard, either, but when not playing the "Top Trump File" can be read to learn more about who/what is on the card. I don't see it being something anyone would want to play on a regular basis, but for occasional play, it's a nice way to spend some time with others and it manages to easily get some education into my children's day. It also helps to pass the time if boredom is there. Even when not playing, it's fun just to look through the cards, at least to me.

To play, someone deals the cards to the players face down. The players then pick up their cards, so only one card is visible. The player to the dealer's left starts and picks any stat on their card to call out. The other players call out that same stat and the best number gets all the cards, which then goes to the bottom of that person's stack. The winner of each round picks the next stat for the next round. The game ends when a player has all the cards, and they win. This can take awhile to play, so the directions have instructions for a quicker version, too, along with details about what to do if 2 players both have the best stat.

Depending on what set it is depends on what stats are included. The "Greek Myths" set has Strength, Magic, Terror, Audacity, and Top Trumps Rating. The "Ancient Rome: Gods and Emperors" set has Strength, Legacy, Terror, Popularity, and Top Trumps Rating. The "Washington DC: 30 Things to See" set has Cost, Visitors per Year, Year Established, Visit Time, and Top Trumps(Must See). They all have a picture of some sort, along with more information about the person/place/etc.

title: Great clicking sound and amazing build quality!
text:
I would honestly rate this a perfect 5 stars were it not for the keycaps and the not so bright RGBs.

The keycaps are made from ABS and only the main characters are shine through, the special characters are just printed on which don't show up with RGB lights. One major downside to ABS keycaps is that they tend to get oily really quick. After a few hours of use, the keycaps began to get very shiny and slippery, which detracted from the all black color scheme and annoying when gaming. I ended up swapping the keycaps with PBT double shot keycaps (Monoprice + Razer) to get the ideal illumination and shine through. See pictures of difference.

Being the owner of half a dozen keyboards, this one really hit a sweet spot. The media keys are really good and the volume dial is amazing. They don't feel as amazing as the ones in the Corsair K70/K95 ones, but they are decent. The software is also really good and lets you go pretty deep into the RGB light customization and effects. Comparing the Razer software to Corsair's CUE, Razer's software is miles better than Corsair CUE. CUE often crashes and resets macros mid games, sometimes completely freezing the keyboard or mouse (one of my main reasons to switching to Razer KB). I've yet to experience a single crash with Razer's software (use it for some of my Razer mice and capture card).

The green switches are similar to blue switches with some notable differences... Using my Corsair K70, E-Element, Motospeed, and Redragon keyboards with blue switches as a reference, the green switches feel a bit crunchy. Its not necessarily a bad thing as it feels slightly different from Cherry Blues, but still clicky and satisfying. This feels more similar to Outemu Blues (found in E-Element, Motospeed, and Redragon), but less clicky (less loud). Cherry Blues sound more like a type writer, Razer greens sound like your finger tips are smashing lays potato chips, and Outemu Blues sound like you are smashing a stack of lays chips per click (much louder, louder than Cherry Blues).

Now the brightness was another thing that didn't blow my mind away. I had heard that the 2017 and 2018 Blackwidow RGB keyboards had really bright RBGs. Using my pictures as reference (max brightness), they are not as bright as Corsair K70 or my other RGB keyboards. Not a bad thing either, personally. Since my desk is next to my bed, the slightly less bright RGBs make it easier to fall asleep, whereas others (Motospeed, Redragon, Ajazz) are sometimes blindingly bright at night.

Also, if you are wondering whether you should get Greens or Orange switches, I would highly recommend Greens. Having have tried Oranges before (friend's KB), the Oranges feel like gimped Brown or Black MX switches.

title: That thing has been serving me well and it feels amazing to hold
text:
First initial impressions: Photos Attached - EDIT: Added comparison to my Corsair M45

My old PC mouse is a Corsair M45 Raptor. That thing has been serving me well and it feels amazing to hold, but then I decided to take a chance with the Venus for my laptop (Asus R516U).

This thing is amazing to hold. The ergonomics are slightly better than the Corsair M45s as it has a pinky rest, if you are a paw grip. The 12 side buttons personally for me are somewhat easy to press if you can figure out how to move your thumb. Most reviewers I've seen complain that they have to pull the tips of their thumbs way back to reach the last two rows, but if you instead swivel your thumb to press the last 2 rows with the back of your thumb they become quite easy to press.

The mouse itself is all soft plastic with textured finish. The center top glossy part is where your palm sits and I guess it is made so that your palm sweat glides down the smooth surface. I don't really know the purpose of the glossy top part but it feels good to the palm. My only concern is that the texture finish will probably wear out and turn back glossy. This happened with my Corsair M45. The side plates on that thing are made of the same material as the entire surface of the Venus, with same texture too, and those wore out over time. Now they are glossy and can probably see that happening to this mouse as my fingers and palm rub into the surface. We'll see!

The light show is also amazing and can be changed on the fly with Utechsmart's software. The only colors that don't seem to change is the small dpi LEDs as those are permanently red. You cannot change individual colors, like for each button or section of the mouse; You can only have it set to one color. The other only color options is either pulsing with various speed levels, and non-pulsing, as in just permanently on with varying light intensity levels.

You can program Macro keys into your mouse and assign them to each button including the DPI buttons. Personally I got this mouse for AutoCAD as I'm taking an engineering class for it and the macros help me switch tools on the fly. You CAN set buttons to functions such as erase, etc by typing them into the Macro Manager(records and saves).

You can also customize the DPI profiles for each LED level. Haven't really used this, as DPI 2 & 3 (2000 & 4000) are good to me. BTW you get 5 DPI profiles. The first one is with all LEDs off, the second one starts on the first LED and 5th one ends at the 4th LED. Kinda strange, but cool that you get 5 profiles.

title: It's a blast, but more bang for your buck with Fallout 4
text:
I've been anxiously awaiting a next generation Battlefront game for years--not just as a casual gamer, but as a Star Wars fan since childhood. I'll raise a little rabble and agree that the omission of Galactic Conquest or a deeper single player campaign is palpable, but that doesn't stop this game from being a really fun (albeit spawn-die-repeat) online multiplayer game. The variety of game modes adds a lot of replay value, as does the points/upgrade system.

The graphics are absolutely gorgeous, and it's no hyperbole when I say I'm living my childhood dreams when I play because of the beautifully immersive worlds and careful attention to the smallest details to place players inside the Star Wars universe, whether players battle on-foot or take to the sky. Adding to the depth of the experience, music throughout the game relies heavily on a remarkable and appropriate original score to complement the standard John Williams fanfare.

Fanboy accolades aside: You should probably buy Fallout 4 first. Despite the great job they did building a fun and beautiful game, EA definitely deserves the ire they've drawn from customers regarding how they're handling the release of DLC. The game isn't nearly deep enough for the $60 price tag, only for EA to tell customers that to get the "full" experience, they'll need to pay an additional $50. If they continue developing and publishing the franchise, I hope they'll invest in packaging the value a bit better for the sake of their customers (but hey, there's profit to be had).

As for the special edition system, I couldn't have asked for a cooler reason to buy a PS4. It's a great collectible for a fan. I paid the price of a standard PS4 and essentially got the game free.

Enjoy.

title: OK controller. Motion controls do not work on PC. Edit: Left joystick broke.
text:
Edit: No joke, only a few hours after writing this review my left joystick has started bugging out. When I hold forward, the stick seems to sometimes think I'm only pressing it about 90%-ish the way forward, making movement inconsistent and making a game like Dark Souls practically unplayable as it thinks I'm walking instead of holding forward all the way to run at normal speeds. I was gonna deal with the controller in its less-than-perfect state, but now looks like I have to return it.

Original review:

This is not necessarily a bad controller, but I have to say it's not what I was expecting considering what people say about 8bitdo. After using it for a little over a week now, I have some thoughts. I'll start with the good.

Pros:
- The back grip buttons are very nice to have, and feel great to press. Nice and tactile -- not too clicky, not too mushy.
- The profile switching feature has been very useful. Being able to have set profiles, and switch between them on the fly, is pretty sweet, especially for reconfiguring the back buttons.
- The charging dock is sweet. I never have to worry about the batteries dying, and it's just a nice little stand to place the controller on. Magnetized so I don't have to worry about making sure it's seated properly.
- The ergonomics are pretty solid, with one minor exception I mention in the cons section. Specifically, claw grip feels very comfortable which cannot be said for certain controllers (looking at you, Dualsense). The controller also feels nice and light.

Mid:
- The value is.... okay. If you compare it to an Xbox controller, you're essentially paying $20 more for back grip buttons, profile switching, hall effect joysticks, more compatibility, and the included dongle + charging dock. Seems like a pretty good deal, except for the fact that the Xbox controller has markedly better build quality and slightly better ergonomics. So while it may seem like a really good value, there are definitely some trade-offs you're making by going with the 8bitdo. The xbox controller just feels better to use, honestly.
- I didn't want to put this as a con, as it may very well be something specific to my system (and it's not a huge deal anyways), but after closing the controller configuration application -- without fail -- my PC starts to hang up and I have to reboot. I have zero idea why this is happening, but again not a huge deal as I've only had to use the software once or twice so far.

Cons:
- Motion controls do not work on PC. I have to say it feels pretty scammy to advertise the motion controls and not mention that they just straight up do not work. That was a big part of why I bought this thing in the first place -- I've gotten used to it on the Steam Deck, as it's a great way to add a little more precision to traditional analog stick aiming (and I just can't get down with the little trackpads). Really disappointed that isn't an option, even though it was advertised.
- The shoulder buttons are honestly garbage. They just feel super mushy and sticky, and they're a little loose so the controller rattles when you shake it as a result.
- The back grip buttons need to be placed higher IMO. I have big hands and even then it's still a rather uncomfortable stretch for me to be in position for both the back grips and the shoulder buttons.
- The d-pad is also rather mushy-feeling, especially when you compare it to the Xbox Series controller which has a super nice and clicky d-pad.
- Connectivity is pretty good, but not great -- there have been a couple of instances where it's just randomly disconnected, and I'm sitting a mere <2 meters away from the dongle with nothing blocking the way.

Overall I think I'm gonna have to look elsewhere for my next controller. It's not horrible, but considering 8bitdo's reputation, I was expecting something a lot better. Probably a better idea to just save up and get an Xbox elite controller IMO, at least if you're a PC gamer like me.

title: Great keyboard for the price, but the K70 beats it.
text:
Pretty great keyboard for the price, especially considering the lighting options and USB passthrough. Those are both great features, but there are a few things I don't like about it:

1. Lack of dedicated multimedia buttons. Not a big issue, but from a casual look at the pictures, it looked like there were dedicated multimedia (volume up, volume down, mute, email, etc.), but there aren't. You can do FN+F Keys for volume and such, but it really just isn't the same. There are only two buttons in the top right, one for brightness and one for locking the Windows key (very useful). Again, not a huge issue, but it still would have been nice to have at least volume buttons, or even better, a really nice volume wheel like the K70 has.

2. USB plugs. The USB plugs are pretty awful. They have this really bright yellow accent, and it's just horrible. I would recommend plugging the keyboard into the back of your computer.

3. The spacebar. Some people may like this, but I think it's awful. It's all textured like the WASD/other extra keys that come with it, but unlike those keys, the spacebar is pretty much a "sucks to be you!" type of deal. The keyboard doesn't include an extra, non-textured spacebar, and that really sucks. It's very uncomfortable IMO, but then again, you may like it. I just hated it.

I know it sounds like I don't like the board, but I really do. Here are the things I loved:

1. Build quality! Corsair is renowned for having great build quality in their mechanical keyboards, and this is no exception. Although it is all plastic on the outside, unlike Corsair's other boards with their nice stainless steel finish, the plastic is actually very sturdy. It's got a nice texture compared to some other plastics I've seen on mechanical keyboards. It would have been nice to have the stainless steel, but for the price, it's fine as is. Little to no flex as well.

2. Lighting. The lighting software (Corsair Utility Engine) is great. It has nicer presets than the K70 RGB did (at least, when I had it), including a "visor" effect, reactive typing, and more. It's all customizable, and while it's not 100% user-friendly, it's a huge step up from what it was when it was first released for the K65/K70/K95 RGB boards.

3. Feel. The switches feel awesome. I got Browns on mine, and they feel really nice, and sound great too. I'm a bit heavy-handed, so I like clears more, but these are fine and I very rarely trip on them. I'm not a super fast typist at around 75~80 WPM, but these are fine. It's also nice that they offer Blues, Browns, and *shudders* Reds.

4. Look. Nothing much to say here, but it is a very well-designed keyboard from an aesthetic standpoint. Aside from the fact that it doesn't have a standard layout (Grr!), it really looks great.

All in all, it really is a great keyboard for the price. Full-size, Cherry MX switches, really great custom lighting, great quality, all in one $110 package is a great price if you have a hard budget. I would recommend getting the K70 for just about $10 more though, if you can sacrifice $10 and no custom lighting for better build quality and dedicated buttons.

title: Super linear slightly interactive movie more than RPG
text:
My best advice is to make a good tub of popcorn before starting. The first major phase of the game is more cut scene than game. And even after you get into the meat of the game the flow is broken up by yet more cut scenes at least every 5 minutes. Some are fairly brief conversations between party members, but more often than not I was begging Square Enix to let me get back to actually playing the game. Final Fantasy's known for its extensive use of cinematic sequences but at times I was weary of watching a $60 game more than actually playing it.

If you've read people describe the lack of an open world, as-linear-as-it-gets gameplay, and lack of any choices whatsoever and are wondering if it's true just waiting to read someone say how they're exaggerating just stop now. It's all true. The landscapes are beautiful but one glance at the map reaffirms that sinking suspicion that you're on train tracks. The layout is beyond obvious as well. If you see a dead end on a map it's a guarantee there's a "treasure chest". Nothing is hidden. There is no room for doubt at all. Your characters might as well walk themselves and you moving around the map is a mere formality.

To me, the biggest redeeming quality of actual gameplay is long boss battles where extensive use of the Paradigm Shift system is a requirement for winning. It still annoys me that I cannot control my characters, but at least they have a fairly decent system of playing director. You will learn quickly that efficient paradigm shifting can turn an impossible encounter into a relatively easy one. However, only a minority of the game is spent on long boss battles.

If you're looking for any semblance of a traditional RPG I'd suggest you look into [[ASIN:B002I0J4AM Star Ocean: The Last Hope International]]. I'm regretting not spending the $50-60 on Star Ocean and waiting to get a used copy of FF13.

Final Fantasy XIII really could of been so much better. Maybe I expect too much of a retro feel, but I honestly think they completely ignored so many of the things that made Final Fantasy such a successful series that it will disappoint most RPG enthusiasts.

title: Works with Yamaha Clavinova CVP-509
text:
The TRENDnet Wireless N Gaming Adapter TEW-647GA allows you to connect devices with an ethernet plug to a wireless connection on your own wireless network or wireless internet router/modem. Typically, this is not used for laptops or desktops (for which you would use a USB or other wireless adapter that you can configure from the laptop/desktop). Instead it is used to connect "dumb" devices, like some game systems, other hardware, or in my case, a Yamaha CVP-509 digital piano.

Because "dumb" devices don't have a way to configure a wireless connection, you first have to set up the TRENDnet Wireless N Gaming Adapter TEW-647GA on your desktop or laptop using the downloadable or CD-ROM based configurator wizard. A warning to Windows users: when you first run the wizard, some Windows configurations will pop up a warning that asks how you would like the wizard to connect to the network. If you do not choose the least restrictive option, you will be unable to configure the adapter. The configurator will lead you through several steps. The exact series will depend on how you want to connect to your network. After it has finished configuring the adapter, it will instruct you to unplug the adapter from the desktop or laptop and plug it into the "dumb" device. If you were successful, your device will now be connected to the internet, so that you can download games or connect to other players online (or, so that you can download music, piano radio, or piano lessons as in my case).

I had some problems in getting the configurator to work. Each time, the configuration failed, without any advice on how to fix it. Although the TRENDnet support site did not seem to offer any searchable solutions, a Google search indicates that this is a known issue that can be resolved by contacting TRENDnet customer support.

title: A micro-managers dream come true
text:
This game was recommended to me by a friend who also loves real time simulation games. Next to the Simcity franchise, this is one of the most popular and well-received RTS games out there.

A little backstory... I started playing Sim Theme Park (1999) back in 2000. That was (and still is) a very fun simulation game. One of the best in my opinion. I feel the mixture of real-world accuracy and fun gameplay (even though very cartoony) was executed perfectly by the developers. Furthermore, the overall aesthetics and art style of the game are very appealing to me.

RT3, however, is a jumbled, overly-complicated mess in my opinion. The UI does not flow well, and the item menu layout makes it difficult to manage your park. Most importantly, there are just way too many options to play with! Everything (and person) in the park has a full-range of options to tweak... enough to make an OCD person go absolutely nuts, lol. I fully support real-world accuracy in these games, but I also understand that it's still a game, and I want to have fun playing it. And the developers definitely went full-tilt making RT3 as realistic as possible. Some people will no doubt love this, but I think that most people coming from Simcity or Sim Theme Park will find the game far too micro-manage-y.

The sandbox mode is fun, but since money is not involved, you quickly lose motivation playing it. What's the point if you can build anything you want, immediately? The campaign mode is not what I expected... I was thinking it was more along the lines of Sim Theme Park or Simcity where you start with a lump sum of money and an empty park, and you build your park from there, managing it along the way to keep a positive cash flow. Instead, the campaigns are somewhat preformed, giving you a basic park that you 'take-over' management of. Not very exciting in my opinion.

Overall, the game is not as fun as I had hoped for. If they allowed users to let the park run more autonomously (perhaps an 'auto-pilot' mode if you will) with the ability to tweak various items if needed, that would be better. Or, as an alternative, provide advice to the user on various aspects of the game (i.e. people find admission prices very cheap... people are not satisified with the quality of ice cream offered... etc). In it's current state, however, I don't want to go through my 5 hot dog stands and adjust the amount of mustard on my hot dogs.... and have to guess what the best selling price would be based on the insignificant amount of financial data the game provides real-time. The concept is great, but they just strayed too far in to the weeds without providing enough framework to allow the player to adequately adjust all of the options.

Those coming from Simcity- or Sim Theme Park-style games beware... you probably won't enjoy this one.

title: Makes the difference in driving games
text:
Love it, but I'm already thinking of moving up again. I bought this on sale to replace my first wheel, a Thrustmaster T80. I was wearing out T80s after about 2 months. Fortunately the manufacturer stood behind them enough to send me new ones. I've had the Logitech G20 for over 6 months now and have had zero issues. I use this with a PS4, and my game of choice is GT Sport.

As for the force-feedback part of it, it is fun being able to feel the curbstones in the corners. It is even more fun when you feel, in the wheel, when the car gets light after cresting a hill. The pedals are much nicer than T80 set in that I get just a little "feedback" (not force-feedback) from the rubber bumper under the pedal. Some folks take the bumper out, but I left it in and rely on it. I can always press into it if needed.

If you are thinking about getting your first wheel, I think the G29 is great. The T80 may be half of the price of the G29, but it is not even a quarter of the quality and durability of the G29. That said, just having a wheel and pedals alone makes a big difference in game-realism over using the joystick controllers (and for me makes a difference in overall time). I was quite content with the T80 until it started failing, but I was also already wondering if force-feedback was worth the extra money (it is).

One star off only because the force-feedback, while very nice, feels a little gritty. I'm guessing the more $$ we spend, the more realistic and smooth they feel.

title: Good idea, poor execution
text:
I bought this controller because I thought it had a layout that just makes sense. Hold your hands out in a neutral position, and look where your thumbs lie. They're both pointing forward in the position of where the analog sticks are on this controller, like the Wii U controller but with a USB connection. It's a shame that it kind of sucks, though,

Pros:
+The layout really does work. For games where a lot of the time you're control movement and camera at the same time, it works great. like it better than both the Playstation and Xbox layouts.
+The rubbery coating on this feels fantastic, I wish it was on everything. Feels very high quality. It also feels very solid and has a super long cord.
+Has three buttons on each shoulder: the trigger and two bumper buttons. I never found myself needing a second set of bumpers, but they aren't in the way so it doesn't hurt to have them.
+Interchangeable analog sticks of different heights. A nice touch, though the default one was the only one I found usable.
+The buttons, in general, are decent. In particular, the triggers have a nice, analog feeling resistance to them. The other buttons don't feel particularly good or bad, which is a feat for third party controllers in and of itself.

Cons:
-This is the big problem: the analog sticks. They're more or less unusable. What they've done was, they gave the sticks an area of high resistance, surrounded by an area of low resistance. The idea was to make it so that in an FPS, you can aim precisely with the area of high resistance, and then if you need to, turn around very quickly using the low resistance. It doesn't work. What ends up happening is that the area of high resistance isn't big enough. You'll be trying to aim, then the stick will slip into the area of low resistance, and since you aren't expecting it, will go all the way to the rim of the circle.
-The sensitivity setting is messed up. If you set it too high, the game will start detecting button presses that you didn't push. I'm not sure why this happens, because the sensitivity of the analog sticks should have nothing to do with any of the other buttons, but it does.
-The shape of the controller doesn't really fit human hands. It tries, you can tell where they added lumps and bumps to try and be ergonomic, but they just aren't placed right. It doesn't feel good in the hands, which is a shame because the rubber finish does.

It's a neat curiosity, but don't get if you actually want to play games with it.

title: You get what you pay for
text:
It isn't the original, nor does it have the pricetag or rarity of a USB version of the original Sega controller.
The build quality is not that of the real thing. It will creak and groan a bit when you squeeze it. I do not think it will give up on me tomorrow, though it probably won't last years and years like the official controller from back in the day.

However, that does not change the fact that in its own respect, this is a great controller.
The famous Sega d-pad is emulated quite nicely here. It's smooth, responsive, accurate and tactile. It's been a while since I've used my real Saturn controller but this does feel just right; it won't disappoint you. The face buttons have a great on/off, low travel, digital feel. The only complaint I have about the feel of the controller is the shoulder buttons. They're passable, but they require a lot of force, hit with a hard clack, and are difficult to push rapidly. Though obviously not an original design, the layout is still one of the best ever created.

If it breaks, it's cheap enough to buy another one. While it's still living, this controller will feel like the original and serve you well.

Turns out when plugged into a PC these are a modified XBox controller so it has full compatibility with PC games. title: It's just kinda meh at first, but it gets better.
text:
(Updated below)

So they mass announce that Far Cry 3 Classic won't be released for 2 months, TODAY...why did we pre-order this version with the season pass? It makes no sense. People apparently wanted to play the iconic predecessor to this game first (because that's what people do to get revved up for a new game or even movie release, they run through the predecessors which is what the FC3 Classic inclusion in the Season Pass was marketed for). The Ubisoft website and press materials I saw gave the impression that FC3 Classic would be a day 1 item. It wasn't until after the pre-orders shipped out yesterday that we learn that it's at least 2 freaking months away. Garbage. FC5 better be good. If it is, I'll update the review. Ubisoft, on the other hand is still a 2-star company. You'd think I would have learned from dealing with their shenanigans over the last few high profile releases but Far Cry is such and awesome series I got suckered in. Never again Ubisoft.

Update #1 - So after spending some time with this game and ignoring the Season Pass issue above, I have to say, the game is thus far pretty weak compared to the rest of the series. Weapons are okay, I guess, but nothing better or that we haven't seen before in this series. Combat is okay. The world is gorgeous but the people in it are far too generic (they've always been that way but FC5 feels like there's more of them so it's like you're reminded of it more often). Ubi could have killed off about 60% of the population assets for this game so that encounters feel a little more unique and that might have been fine.

But my biggest issue, and the reason why I'm leaving the 2 star review for now is that the game itself doesn't draw you in the way the rest of the series does, particularly the most acclaimed installments (3 and 4). In those 2 games, your role was one that almost anyone could identify with; you were trying to save your friends and family or honoring the last wishes of a loved one. Most of us have family or people we care about and the content and story were enough in both instances to draw most players in on an emotional level (and the reviews bear this out). In FC5 you're a random law enforcement officer and there's really no emotional incentive. The villains don't do anything to provoke emotion to the extent that Vass and Pagan Min did (not to mention the other bit characters and mini-bosses in both FC3 and FC4). There's not much to care about and because of that, the game feels empty. If it wasn't a Far Cry title, this might not be as much of an issue except that the gameplay and scripted events force you to act as if the game is Far Cry rather than some random shooter wearing a Far Cry hoodie.

Update #2
This game gets weaker and weaker. Repetitive combat, forgettable characters, lame store, silly air combat you're forced into (crop dusters are stupid, seriously, I have a .50 caliber rifle, farm planes should pose no issue). I just can't get into the game. I'd rather play FC3 again. This one is just dumb. I'm not even sure I'll last long enough to complete it.

Update #3
The game eventually does pick up some if you stick with it. There are a few events later in the first 2 story arcs that I did that started to draw me in some. John Seed's arc ended up pretty decent and for the first time I felt like this was in the Far Cry realm. Jacob's has been pretty decent so far, though one thing I don't like that there are a number of forced game sequences where you're captured (seemingly at random) that you can't escape or have any control over. These are necessary to the story arcs however the captures are just oddly timed and could have been better thought out as to not interrupt the player during play outside of the story progression. Either way, the game picks up about 1/3 of the way through and for the first time for me it became a game I wanted to play every night. Upping the rating to 3 stars.

text:
Right now, this is probably one of the top 5 "must haves" for the Wii. FPS-type games used to be frustrating and clunky on consoles, but now that the Wii has arrived, it opens up a whole new level of control that's often as good as, and sometimes better than a simple keyboard and mouse combo like you would find on a computer.

The controls in Metroid Prime 3 are great, though not quite as fluid and exact as those found in Resident Evil 4 (another definite "must have" for the Wii), but that's not a fault necessarily as the controls are designed around a different set of objectives than you'd find in RE4. I'd say that it should take around 10 to 20 minutes to get familiar with the controls and maybe a total of an hour's play time to get totally proficient. That's not a particularly steep learning curve, and those more familiar with FPS games on the PC will likely cut those times down significantly.

The graphics and settings are done particularly well; though some might complain that the PS3 or the Xbox 360 games all look better, I haven't really come across any that actually PLAY better or are more entertaining, but to each their own I suppose. Each location is distinct from the others and the soundtrack helps to build the overall feel of each world. The story is well paced, though not quite perfect as it does get a little lame or cheesy sometimes. This does not detract from the overall feel of the game however, most people will be too busy searching for suit upgrades, engaging in fast-paced combat and completing objectives by solving some rather creative puzzles to even notice that the story is predictable and a little dry at times. Overall, the whole package comes together to make a stunning game that's good for at least 20 hours of entertaining play-time the first time around.

I personally did not find a whole lot of replay value after I finished the game (whereas I'm still playing Resident Evil 4 even though I completed the game a few weeks before I started Metroid Prime 3), but the options to rerun the game on a higher difficulty and unlock bonus content (sadly, none in the form of extra game play or mini-games that I could find) will keep hardcore Metroid fans and gamers that insist on completing every facet of each game they own busy for quite a while.

My one and only minor grip is that I took the extra time and effort to obtain 100% completion so I could get the continued bonus endings (one for 75% and one for 100%) only to be rewarded with two snippets that were short and uninspiring. Of course, that's just my opinion, the actual ending that everyone gets regardless of completion percentage is well done and closes the game well. Overall, Metroid Prime 3 was a great game experience, easily one of the best I've had in the last 10 years,

title: A great innovation to gaming
text:
Since there are already over 750 reviews for this product, there's not much I can say that hasn't already been said. The main thing I want to focus on here is that this system is FUN. People seem to complain a little about the graphics, but I'm not purchasing a virtual art gallery, I'm purchasing a gaming system.

I used to be hooked into the perpetual upgrade cycle of hardware that exists on the PC gaming front, but somewhere along the way over the last 7 or 8 years, the industry became more about eye candy and less about the actual game. If you look at most of the top 10, 20 or whatever number of all-time game lists, you'll see games that are often way behind the graphics curve. Most of them are lacking visually simply because they're older games (i.e. Diablo or Half-Life for the PC), but the main point is that they're fun and they leave the player with a memorable and entertaining experience. All the eye candy in the world simply cannot make up for a game that lacks that. There are plenty of gorgeous games with no content to them, and shelling out $400 or more for systems to play the latest in games with cutting edge polygon counts, textures or rendering is akin to throwing down hundreds of dollars on a mannequin that looks exactly like Jessica Alba in the flesh.

Not that there is anything wrong with the PS3 or the Xbox 360, but there's a reason why the Wii is outselling everything else; it comes down to fun (and price). Yes, there are crappy games on the Wii and a lot of really fun games on those other systems, but in my opinion, when the Wii developers get it right (i.e. Metroid Prime Corruption, Wii Sports, Resident Evil 4), the experience is far beyond what you can get from games on other consoles. If you're enjoying the gameplay to the fullest extent, most people don't even realize that the graphics aren't perfect.

The lower graphics tech is part of what keeps the system's price down, which puts it within reach of just about anyone with a job and the ability to save money. Personally, despite still having both a high end desktop and laptop PC suitable to run the latest whiz-bang games coming out, I haven't even looked at either of them for games since I purchased my Wii...I spend my time playing the Wii or looking at the release dates for the next Wii game that I can hardly wait to play. And coming from a former PC game and hardware-junkie, that says a lot.

title: A pretty keyboard, really nice response time, lacks tactile feel to the keys.
text:
I like this keyboard, and to make it simple if you don't want to read more, it's worth the money if you want a higher end keyboard. But it's not something I ever felt I really needed out of my setup, and it doesn't make a massive impact for the type of gaming I do. Onward to slightly more details.

So the keyboard itself has very bright and very pretty RGB lights on it. It's gorgeous, and very well lit. The material underneath the keys is metal, and the keys themselves are a nice plastic with the lights. It has a good weight to it, though I do wish I still had a num-pad on the side. The keys are very light weight to press, they click very easily, and make a fair amount of mechanical noise. I like the noise, some other people might prefer their keyboards more silent with less noise themselves. The only real other issue other than the num-pad I have with it, is the lack of tactile feel of the keys. While they are mechanical, when I first used it, there was little assurance I was hitting the correct keys, as it's really easy to hit the wrong thing on them. I found myself hitting the windows key unintentionally with the bottom of my hand when playing a game with WASD. Not a massive problem, the more you play with it, the better you'll get and the less mistakes you'll make, but it's something to think about. Corsair made a good offering with this keyboard, and for roughly $99~125 dollars, it's a good keyboard that will likely last a very good long time. But keyboards aren't something you have to spend alot of money to have work a while most of the time. My old 30$ logitech keyboard, although kinda gross after years of use, worked perfectly. Oh that's another advantage here, it's easy to clean the keyboard as there's no trim around the keys. So a can of compressed air will clean the underside of the keyboard easily. I recommend it, but I have to take a star off.

title: A great wireless headset, not a good mic, and it is small. Perfect for me though.
text:
NOTE: I got this for review purposes, but I am not endorsed by the company. Just provided this. Also, to explain my situation of use, I own a Blue Snowball Microphone, so I do not need headset mics. My head is on the smaller side, so keep that in mind.

I've owned a few Logitech headsets, and honestly, I've always found they feel great. However, usually in my experience they've lasted maybe a year, then the cable is tangled and the headset dies, because the cord never is of good quality. Maybe good sound, maybe good mic, doesn't matter if it doesn't last. I was hesitant to even get this for review, but I decided I wanted a wireless headset for the first time, and that was always the failure point of Logitech headsets, the cords. So without a cord to fail, why not?

When it arrived, I didn't even think it was a headset. Got it out, it's incredibly light. The plastic on it feels good like Logitech plastic does, but like I said, light. It made it almost come off as cheap at first. Charged it up, plugged the USB wireless connector in, turned it on. It fits my head perfectly with plenty of room extra for me, but most headsets are big for me, so I don't think everyone could use this and fit well. I play for hours at a time, up to over 8 hours of Youtube and Gaming, I've never once ran out of charge. It's light enough it's not ever uncomfortable for me after wearing it so long. I have had to turn it back on a fair few times after it's been running for hours, it does disconnect, but it's a very mild issue usually. Comes right back.

Sound quality is good, but I'm not an audiophile, I can enjoy music on it perfectly. Microphone quality on it is not great, friends tell me it sounds like a Xbox Mic, but that's why when I'm at my PC, I'm using my Blue Snowball. When I'm in VR, I'm using my Oculus Mic. Noise cancellation on it is...eh? I mean, sure it does muffle some noise, but I would not at all call it a true noise cancelling headset. I would say it isn't noise cancelling. Maybe a 2/5 at best at that.

Overall, I do recommend it, if you have a smaller head, and want a good wireless headset that is lightweight, made for long playtime. I would not recommend it if you're planning on using the microphone on it constantly if you're looking for a good mic though. Is it worth 80$? Maybe. It really depends on you, I think it can be, I would have to think long and hard and weigh my other options first. But I might have chosen this too then.
