title: A nice carrying case, with good and very useful accessories.
text:
This is a really nicely built case for the Oculus Quest 2. Remarkably so. I personally also own the Oculus branded Carrying Case, but it's really not nearly as easy to carry as this one. Let me get into why I like this one in some ways better and worse than the other, as well as the accessories included.

1. The case itself, and why I like it more and less than the Oculus Case
The case is not a hard shell case, so it's very nice to feel. It's not rough, it's made of a mesh. One side is stiffer than the other side with the backpack sling, which there is only one of the shoulder straps, which I rather like. It's comfortable to wear, and the pack is not terribly big, but certainly big enough for all accessories. I do wonder if it'd fit an elite strap, but it certainly fits the standard straps, which are better really if you're travelling anyway for general purpose. It pretty securely fits the headset, but I will say it does not secure the controllers nearly as well unless you use the pouches instead to store them. It's also significantly cheaper than the Oculus case, only 30$ versus 50$, and has more room for what you might want with it. With it being softer though, it does make me wonder if it'd be okay if it was dropped, as with the oculus case, I highly doubt the Quest 2 would even be scratched.

Pros:
-The case has a nice shoulder strap that feels good to wear, and feels secure. Much better than the genuine oculus's hold strap which is not wearable.
-The case has more room for all accessories to the Oculus case, and the headset has a dedicated X pattern harness over the top of the compartment to secure it neatly.
-It's cheaper than the Oculus branded case, but not cheaper in quality.

Cons:
-It's less protective of the Quest 2 if dropped, due to the soft mesh material on one side, and the stiffer material on the other.
-It doesn't secure the controllers nearly as well, and there is less indication of the correct way to put in the controllers.

On the accessories, all of them are either really handy or just a nice addition even if not used.

-They have a silicone cover, much like Oculus is handing out right now due to their Foam recall, but this one has a nose hole to block light. This is much better than the real Oculus Silicone Cover in most cases, especially given that if you need to see the outside world, it has passthrough, you dont need to look out the nose hole like in other headsets.
-They included a lens cover made of silicone. This is handy if you want to take out the headset in sunlight, but don't plan to use it. You have to keep the lenses out of sunlight, and you may want to keep dust off of them. This helps to do both things, plus it keeps scratches off of the lenses by keeping particles that you may wipe off from causing those scratches.
-There's some decorative eyes. They have a Panda, a normal set of eyes, and some weird looking connected eye. It's a nice touch, though if you would like it or not is personal preference. I like the Panda, but I'm not particularly interested in decorating my Quest 2. They look pretty good, and honestly, it's a nice addition even if you don't use a single one.

Overall, I really recommend this headset case. If you plan to go places with it, I recommend this over even the actual Oculus branded one, because it's an actual carrying case, not just a protective shell to keep everything together. They included actually useful and well made accessories, that are as good as first party produced ones, and the only accessory they added that you may not use is stickers that don't really feel like they added to the cost of the case. They feel like a nice touch they added without jacking the cost because they added something. Very nice of them. I think as long as you're careful to not drop it or hit things with the case, this will work beautifully.

title: A great headset, made better by increased capacity for no additional cost over the old 64GB model.
text:
I now own 2 Quest 2's, though one I immediately gifted. I got my first in November of 2020, and ever since have enjoyed it immensely. It's not just a gaming headset, it's a media device, it's a relaxation tool, a workout device, and of course a solid gaming headset. There's more to it than just playing games, which is why I can recommend it to so many kinds of people. Let me explain why that is.

The Quest 2 is first off, a lighthouse free device. No set-up of little boxes to see the headset in the corners of the room or on the ceiling. It uses Cameras on the headset, and a virtual boundary that you draw when you start up the headset. You do have to confirm the boundary or re-draw it every time you turn it off and back on all the way, not just let it sleep, but that's a minor issue. Tracking is not as solid as a lighthouse VR like a Steam Index, HTC Vive, Etc. but very usable. There are times where it's a problem, mainly sniping in games like Hotdog's Horseshoe's and Handgrenades, but that's a minor issue. Plus many slight imperfections in tracking are being accounted for by game developers such as Anton of H3VR to make the experience with Camera tracking better for more precision with less precise tracking methods.

The media playing of the Quest 2 is very good. You can pull up 3 browser screens at once surrounding you in normal Quest mode with tabs open in each one outside of the active tab. I've had no issues related to compatibility between the Quest 2 Browser and any site, especially when you can request the Mobile or Desktop version of the site if it doesn't work on one. I have not tried putting files directly onto the Quest 2 for playback, so I can't speak on that. The screen on the Quest 2 is very crisp (though not 4K by any means) to where I don't have any issue watching a movie on it with the normal resolution.

Comfort wise, I think this is one of the main drawbacks of the Quest 2. The stock strap is good, I used mine for a long period, and still go back to it for certain use scenarios. However, it's not as secure as I want for movement intensive games like Beat saber, even if it won't fall off. Ever since replacing the strap, I've had less headaches with the Quest 2. It also can strain the eyes, but I personally have less issues with that than most. I've played on a Quest 2 for 10 hours straight, and my eyes felt slightly bothered. Not saying everyone can do that. They also recently added a Silicone cover to all Quest 2's or the ability to request one for your Quest 2, which feels much better than the foam alone. The foam to me felt like sandpaper after only a short period, and that cover feels like what it should have been before. Some people will have issues with the Quest 2 using a 3 position IPD, which will change how well you see the lenses. It's a "three sizes fit most" type solution to IPD adjustments. Some people will fall outside of the range of the IPD, or even in the right range won't be perfect, but I've had no issues in the default 2 position it is shipped in. It's also easy to set that position, just slide the lens left or right. Controllers feel good, and should fit most hands, they also only use 1 AA each and last for over 10 hours easily.

For gaming, there's 2 different answers to how well it does. I'm breaking it up into two sections as a result. If you're not planning on using your Quest 2 for gaming, please skip this entire section.

By itself: The Quest 2 is solid, though it has many limitations. It is not a replacement for a gaming computer, but it can operate many games completely stand alone. SuperHOT VR is one I personally play only on the Quest 2 by itself, and it's been out a moment. You can get many solo VR games on the Quest 2 app store, but some will have graphical downgrades over the PC versions. One example of a game doing this is Onward, a Military Sim shooter, which had to be graphically downgraded on Quest 2's to be compatible to play on the system, but still be capable of playing with true PC players. Many may also look to play VRchat on the system, while I recommend the experience, Quest users on the game are unable to see PC avatars or go to PC worlds, which is a shame. Understand that by itself, the Quest 2 is limited somewhat by it's capabilities, but many developers are designing their games around it, or for compatibility with it. It will be a good amount of time before the Quest 2 becomes an unsupported standalone system.

Oculus Link: While the Quest 2 has problems running many games by itself, or have to be downgraded to deal with the processing power, it doesn't have to stay that way. Oculus and aftermarket companies have Oculus Link cables which are USB-C charging cables that are designed for high data transfer rates for a smooth experience. They are also intended to connect your computer to the headset, to use the computer's processing power to play games, rather than the Quest's. As a result, this allows you to play all PC VR games on the Quest 2. However, this hinges on your computer being able to run VR games at all, and at a smooth enough rate to make it a worthwhile experience. VR ready PC's are not cheap, but if you're already trying to play the latest intensive games at high resolution, your hardware already is likely up to the task to play in VR. Even some less powerful PC setups can be fixed to make the experience better, rendering then upscaling to the desired resolution, or other methods. This can make a game much more smooth, less taxing on the hardware running it, and more enjoyable. What you will need to run the games is far beyond the scope of this review, and you may want to consult someone who knows about computers to ask if your setup is powerful enough to run VR. Also, the Link cable needs to be secure, one tip I have is to use a strap, usually included with VR cables, and strap it to the side of the headset neat where the charge port is. This will keep the cord from dangling straight down and occasionally disconnecting the link. Also with the stock strap, run the cable through the middle of the headstrap, then to the charge port then use the individual strap, so the cable runs down your back, not your side, helps to keep you from being twisted up. One other downside is the Link does still use battery life with many setups due to the power being sent to your headset being lower than the usage, still can get many hours of play at full charge, and able to go again the next day for just as long. I don't know much about using Air Link or Virtual Desktop for wireless Link connections so, I can't comment. I tried, it didn't work very smoothly for me.

Final conclusion or a TLDR: This headset is likely one of the best headsets for entering VR, for any reason. Watching movies on a big giant virtual screen can never get old to me, or meeting friends "face to face" on a game using the Link function, or hitting blocks that fly past me to a song's rhythm in beat saber to exercise a little in doors, whatever I use it for, it works, and well. It isn't the best VR headset out there, but it is the current best Standalone VR headset to date. Capacity wise, 128 GB is fine, but with too many games, you may run into storage problems, but seeing how everything on the Headset is digital, things are easily deleted and re-installed as needed. Resolution is nice, comfort is acceptable with some issues but minor, and the quality of the build is good. At no point have I ever thought I wasted my money on this, if anything, I wish I had gotten it sooner. Oh one other feature I want to mention is that due to it using cameras to see the outside world for tracking purposes, you can also look outside of VR without ever taking off the headset. Through passthrough, you can see the outside world in Black and White. Very handy feature that I believe all headsets after this one need to include. For the price, this is an easy sell, highly recommend buying this headset, and going from there. If you're looking for the best of the best VR PC headset, this isn't that, but it is a great entry level PC headset, that won't steer you wrong. Mine hasn't let me down, and shows no signs that it will.

title: A good fightstick for someone on a budget.
text:
I've wanted a fightstick for a few years now, but I've never wanted to muster the over 60$ most good fightsticks cost. However I've also been told that cheap fightsticks are not worth picking up. This one came to me for review purposes, so I finally gave a fightstick a shot. This one is solid. Here's why.

This fightstick is maybe not the best quality material wise overall, but where it counts. The buttons feel good, as good as old arcade units at least. The stick is fully responsive, and 360's are not hard to input. I do have to get used to how it feels, but that's true of any new control type. The area for your other hand to use the buttons has a different material that feels softer. Very nice touch for resting your hand on. What's also great is that this stick can be upgraded if desired, not that I think it needs it, but a good thing for someone wanting to get into an arcade fightstick. I think for the price, my minor complaint of the overall build quality being a bit plastic-y, lightweight, and only using suction cups, are really nitpicks. I certainly recommend this one for a starter fightstick, to make sure you're into fighting games and wanna up the experience a bit.

title: A great gaming mouse with alot of buttons, but lacks in some quality
text:
I like this mouse quite alot, it replaced my Logitech G203 mouse as my main gaming mouse. The main reason is I like the shape more, it's more accurate, and those extra buttons are a really big plus for many games. I do have some problems with it, it's not nearly as easy to program the DPI adjustment, and it's not mounted at the top on a button like the G203 for easy DPI changes. It's a switch on the bottom of the mouse, making quick snappy DPI changes for sniping to normal run and gun gameplay not really viable in game. It's not as easy to change the light settings on it either, but that's a mild complaint. The plastic is a little thinner than the G203, despite the fact that the G203 is a cheaper mouse by 40$.

Overall, I think this is a very good gaming mouse, and there's a reason it took over as my main mouse so quickly. But I just wish it were made a little more sturdy, and had some design changes to make that DPI claim more useful rather than just a selling point. I do recommend this mouse, but I would consider how often you will use the additional buttons versus wanting a better build quality. Also, this mouse is not heavy, some people like their mouse to be weighted, this is not.

title: A very nice and well put together headset!
text:
Note: I received this item for free, and as a result I may be biased, however I have no obligation to review this favorably for the company. I tested the headset to be as critical as possible, but please understand I still am not 100% unbiased.

This headset is really nice feeling, and I actually prefer this over my main headset. I normally use a Corsair Void Elite headset, and yet while it's more expensive, I prefer this headset. It has nice audio quality, is noise canceling, and looks really nice. Handling it, it doesn't feel quite as nice as my Corsair from a material's standpoint, but it feels better to wear.

Audio:
I find it has very nice bass compared to my Corsair which lacks in bass, and this headset can go decently loud. The volume knob is on the right side of the headset, and is very easily adjusted, I prefer this over the normal wheel design. Treble is acceptable, and I have had no issues with listening to music, or playing games with the headset audio wise.

Microphone:
While I could have lumped this in audio, it's important to review it separate. I have been told this headset sounds better than my Corsair, but the difference is not massive, it is acceptable audio quality. I do have a complaint here though, this headset has no button mute on the headset itself. To mute the headset, you must put the microphone up. Pretty common feature on gaming headsets. However, the way they did it is have a similar knob to the volume that almost locks in place at the bottom. It's very stiff, and you can't really get a good hold on it one handed. I would much rather have a button on the back of the headset over a twist, though I am sure that over time, it will get less stiff.

Comfort wise:
As said before, it's noise canceling, and is an over the ear headset. Feels really nice, and the mesh is very supportive. It can easily fit on most people, as it also does not use a stepped adjustment for the size, so it can be very snug on a person if you want it to be. For me, I did not have to adjust it much to fit me, and it fits like a glove, which is perfect. I could easily make it more loose on my head though if desired. One complain I do have on the comfort is the cord length, it's not long. I would greatly prefer a longer cord. It is a rubber cord, so it's not likely to get permanently twisted and tangled like my old Logitech headsets did with their mesh cords.

Overall: I am very impressed with this headset, I went into it thinking it would be nothing special, and far worse than my Corsair headset I spent 70$ on. Instead, I got a headset I prefer in most regard over it, and is cheaper. I will likely use this headset as my new gaming headset for the most part, and if it ever gives me any trouble, I will update this review. Also side note, I do wish they packaged a 3.5mm splitter jack so you can connect it to dedicated microphone and headset ports, thankfully I had one from my corsair that uses the same thing as this headset, a single 3.5mm. I would prefer if they packaged that in the headset, but those splitters are cheap, so it's a very mild complaint. All my complaints are mainly nick-picks, as this headset just is really good for the price. Cannot recommend it enough if each one is as good as mine.

title: It's a mixed bag, but not actually bad.
text:
Okay so I'm going to start off with what I liked about it.

Liked: I think the actual build quality, like how the plastic feels, is solid. You dont need to go into this thinking it's like a real shifter, because it isn't, its not high end, it's going to be plastic-y. But it is some very nice feeling, thick, and just good quality plastic. It has a good arcade-y feel to it, but it is a liked and disliked part about it for me, you can throw the gear lever very easily. The push down reverse is a very nifty function, and really does make it so you dont go into reverse by accident. the two locking pieces work very well for securing it to a desk, just like the wheel, and it doesnt go anywhere.

Disliked: It is a bit difficult to get into the right gear sometimes when you try to do it quick, in project cars 2, I had 2 instances in the same 2 races in a similar spot, where going from 5th to 6th I tried to put it into 6th, and ended up not throwing it far enough and just going into neutral, losing me a ton of time. There is no feeling in the shifter unlike a real car, this goes off of the arcade-y feel, it feels like a fake car. It feels alot like the way you think a manual works, without ever driving one, if you get what I mean, you know the motions of how to do the shift lever, you know what to do, and when you do it without the gear lever, you think its effortless. Its the same feeling as this, but when you get in a real car, you feel the transmission doing work, you can feel the resistance when you go up or down, even in neutral, its very different, yet very similar to what you think it should be. It doesnt have a sequential mode, which means alot of games will force you to have to use the paddles, when really the gear shifter would be so much better.

Overall, until i get more experience on it, 3/5 stars is my rating, though I think 3.5/5 is more fitting. For the money, you cant get any cheaper shifter that is actually a real H pattern shifter that is brand new, without it being an unused private seller's. i personally wish I could have had the G27 shifter that had buttons and a sequential mode, but it is what it is.

Side note and something to consider with this review: I had to wait nearly if not a full week to get the item, when a 2 day shipping order was put in, my wheel came in faster than expected, but my original shifter got lost somehow. This may have negatively hurt the review as I am not 100% unbiased.

title: So Much Fun!
text:
(XBox 360) I`m a casual RPG gamer, and I`m enjoying this game immensely. I`ve played for 20 hrs so far, mostly doing side quests, so I expect I`ll be playing at least another 100 hrs to finish. Great value!

Reckoning has been compared quite a bit to Skyrim, but I think a more fair comparison would be to the Fable franchise or to World of Warcraft. The art & animation are definitely closer to these two games (very colourful and magical looking), and the fighting is similar to Fable only much, much better.

The fighting and weapons in Reckoning are fantasticly fun. You don`t have to choose a class (warrior, rogue, mage) but instead can blend and change between a couple or all three. You can pick up an use any weapon in the game, regardless of how you`re playing (so if you`re playing mostly as a warrior, there`s nothing to stop you from picking up a staff and rocking that for awhile). You can allocate your skills and ability points to compliment your favourite way of playing, and if you decide to try something else, you can unwind your fate, and change! On top of this, there are some super cool weapons that I`ve never seen before like chakrams (a pair of circular boomerang type magical blades) and faeblades (long daggery type thingies that are more of a medium range blade).

As I haven`t played much of the main quest line just yet, I can`t comment too much on the story, except to say that there have been lots of subtle clues to imply that *SPOILER* the fact you were brought back from the dead is having far reaching repercussions on everyone you encounter and interact with. I`m intrigued, and looking forward to more.

As for the game stability, etc... I`ve played for 20 hrs without a glitch or crash. The glitches I noticed in the demo have been resolved. Also the load times between areas seem very fast- faster than Fable 2 & 3, and much faster than Dragon Age 1 & 2.

Say all you like about the story, world design, or similarities with other games (and while you do, consider the similarities in the fantasy genre of any product- be it a game, a movie or a book), when it comes down to it, a video game is meant to be FUN. And this one is... incredibly so.

text:
I must say, I am blown away by how nice this keyboard is for the price. I got this originally to be a to go keyboard and to work on my server at a remote location (which has a keyboard with a broken spacebar now), but this now became my main keyboard, replacing my Cooler Master TK Quickfire Pro with Cherry MX blue switches. I love how these keys feel and sound heavier (perhaps because they're supposed to mimic green switches). I also found I like this keyboard layout better than the one that combines the 10key with all the delete/home/etc. keys. This keyboard also requires you hold down the FN key to use media keys, which I prefer over the other way, or like my cooler master, the FN key has this awkward lock implementation.

Onto the negatives, I like that the keyboard feet that fold out have rubber grips, but one side doesn't stay in place when the legs are tucked in, so I have to always have the legs out which is fine by me since I do that anyways. My last gripes are that the media keys on the function keys aren't backlit, there is no indicator light for the meta key lock, and I wish they also offered a less gamer font type. They should really consider making one of these boards with a more vanilla font.

Conclusions: Just get this keyboard. Ignore the Cherry MX Blue/Green switches, after using them for years, I'm not coming to this keyboard thinking I'm using cheap, crappy switches. This keyboard is a total bargain. The switches are rated at I think 50M clicks, so lets hope that's true. But even if it was half that, I'd buy this keyboard again. Oh yeah, and the keys are loud, expect that like you would with other blue/green switch boards

title: Challenging and Fun
text:
I was a little nervous when I ordered this game. I wanted something fun, something that would get my heart rate up, and maybe even teach me some dance moves, but I'll be perfectly honest -- I'm out of shape and I have no rhythm. This is why I don't dance publically but love the wii -- an opportunity to embarrass myself in the privacy of my living room to my heart's content and nobody knows it but me. I have a short attention span, so have long since grown bored of Wii Fit, DDR, Wii Cheer, and a couple of other exercise programs barely worthy of mention.

Why was I nervous? Quite simply, because a few reviewers reported that this game wasn't for people who didn't already know how to dance. For that reason, I had this in my shopping cart for a month before I cliked "buy". Too bad I didn't get over my wariness sooner.

To the naysayers: I see your point. This is not an easy game or an easy workout. There aren't easy on-screen guides with 4 possible places to stomp your foot. With a wii mote in each hand and your feet on the floor, you are expected to follow all manner of footwork from the basic to the complex. The tutorials works like this: slowly, feet only, for 3 moves, then slowly, hands and feet, for 3 moves, then normal speed. Wait! I wasn't ready. Rewind! Yes, I definitely felt that way the first few times I went through the routine.

But I wasn't looking for easy. Did I really expect, with my flabby thighs and embarassing upper arms, that I would smoothly glide into salsa moves in an afternoon? No! I expected to have to work for it, and that is precisely what I have been doing for the past 2 weeks.

It is worth noting, to those who can't keep up with the routines, that at the end of every routine you have the option of going back into the routine to work on indidividual moves. This option sends you back into the workout video and allows you to play a small segment in a loop, over and over again, until you decide you're done with it. Three slow moves not enough? Just go back into the turoial and repeat to your heart's content. It took me a few days to realize that I had this option, so I wanted to make sure to mention it.

That said, the game does do a pretty poor job of helping you figure out what move to do next. This is particularly true during the cardio boxing routines, where they tell you how to punch as they are throwing it. Um, two second's notice, please? That's one of the reasons I knocked off a star, but before I get ahead of myself, let me just do the pros and cons:

Pros:

*A great workout
*Fun latin dance moves
*Fun cardio moves
*Entertaining workout games such as dodging bulls
*A personal trainer to help you choose daily workout programs that gradually step you up from trainee to pro
*Good music
*Practice mode that allows you to select any part of a workout to retry over and over again, until you get it right

Cons:

*Some difficulty following the moves, especially in cardio boxing
*Only 20 songs
*The way this game determines calorie burn has to do with how many correct moves it detects from your wii mote, which means that if you are only using one remote (such as in 2 player mode), it counts about half the calories burned as if you're using both remotes.

I recommend this game if you want a fun workout, even if you aren't in great shape. If you're a lumpy couch potato, you might want to start with Wii Fit and try this when the cardio in that game fails to challenge you (which won't take long), but if you're determined and up for a challenge, there's no reason that this can't be the right game for you. I've only had the game for 2 weeks, so it's hard to know what kind of staying power it will have, but I have a short attention span...anything I stick with for 2-3 months is a good purchase for me, and I'm definitely not even close to being done with this one.

title: Well made controller--may not be for you
text:
This is a well made controller that cannot replace a dual shock controller, but it can make a great complement for fighting games or a solid controller for Genesis emulators. The quality is there. Not $100 amazing, but nicer than the typical OEM or third party controllers. It's wired, which can be seen as a positive, especially for folks looking for low latency (handy for fighting games). For games where you need to use the d pad, it's much much better than what Sony provides. That's more of a knock on the standard controller than a compliment for this one, but you get a great d pad. Likewise, the buttons are more responsive than the mushy oem buttons. These two factors along with the revised layout makes it more of a traditional fighting d pad arrangement. As someone who grew up with old school arcade games, I prefer an actual digital stick vs a d pad, but otherwise, it's a great feel.

The upsides are there, but console games tend to be made for the console's oem controller. The d pad and front buttons work different, which can lead to some games not registering inputs the way you'd like. Most games work well without issues, and anyone could appreciate the snappy responsive feel of the buttons. I'd suggest checking out a couple YouTube reviews using this and the specific games you wish to play before buying.

text:

Kudos for multi device compatibility and various inputs. I'm hoping the days of separate TB devices for PC, Xbox, and PlayStion are over!

Traditionally you needed a system (could be Windows, Linux, or Mac) running steam to be the client (plus a Windows PC host with appropriate hardware for your games). It it could run Kodi or something, I'd understand. For now, it's a $50 one trick pony. Note there's no controller, so it turns to closer to $100, though you can use that elsewhere too.

It's not bad, not do I recommend avoiding this. Just know what it is.

title: Good, but not "Premium"
text:
I've used plenty of Turtle Beach headsets over the years--both wired and wireless; designed for the PC or consoles; no frills designs and those designed to "up sell". This is the first lower end wireless PC headset of theirs I've tried. It lacks the polish of the i30 and i60, though to be fair, it also lacks the price of those models as well. It looks like a cross between the Recon 320 and Z300 models, and it's priced in between those models as well. For some reason Turtle Beach decided to put the word "Premium" in the title of the product. It's not. The i30 and i60 are premium. This is budget. No shame in that, but it's rather disingenuous. The build is plastic, and not always the good kind. The wireless is OK, but can drop or have other issues near WiFi sources. I think these only operate at 2.4ghz rather than use the dual band approach of the real premium devices. That being said, when the wireless is working, it works great. As with all of my TB wireless headsets, I cannot hear any static, cracks, etc... Robust battery life and a rechargeable battery is another positive shared with other TB headsets, and the simple controls is a plus over the i30 or i60. I wish the mic was removable (again one of TB's the premium features you'll find in a Z300 or i60), and I didn't try it. In general, I've had good luck with their mics in the past FWIW. This isn't a bad headset, and at the right price, it's a great value. At $130, you may want to look for a Z300 refurb or closeout instead.

Pros:
* Clear wireless
* Good sound (nothing special, but you don't wish you were wearing something better just because of the sound quality)
* More or less comfortable
* Rechargeable battery with good battery life
* Simple controls (the i60 and the like are a bit complicated)

Cons:
* Drop offs in challenging wireless environments
* It's not premium (plastic build, basic features ...)
* Price seems a tad high. I can see $75-100 as a better fit

Meh:
* DTS
* Superhuman hearing
* Sound modes
* "fully wireless" = entirely true, but so are all wireless PC headsets (partial wireless is more of an Xbox issue)

title: This is what you want--just be sure to download the right version of Dolphin and set to mode 4
text:
I lost my Wii in a divorce back in 2011, though at times I missed it. I didn't miss having another power brick; I didn't miss finding a home for another gizmo; and I didn't miss component cables. I've been HDMI only since then, and while there are some adapters that let you use a Wii via HDMI, this allows me to use my HTPC to run the Dolphin emulator. Dolphin is free (as in speech), works very well, and though it works with any controllers (can emulate Wiimotes or GameCube controllers using anything that works on your PC), it allows you to use authentic (or knock off) Wii controllers. Wii sensor bars are a misnomer, as the bar does no sensing (the Wii remote does that), but they need power for their USB emitters. Wireless sensor bars work, as do any number of other solutions, but this is among the best. That's not the magic bit, the reliable Bluetooth connection for Wii remotes is what's special. There are other solutions, but not cheaper nor easier. This is what you want.

Setting it up is kinda easy once you know what to do. It took a bit long to figure out what to do, so let me help you. Note I didn't bother with the included CD for a variety of reasons (notably I don't have a built in drive on my machine).

* there is no driver required nor available. Try as I might to find one, it doesn't exist.
* there is a firmware update, and as it's tiny and easy to install, we'll start there.

1) Download the firmware update at http://www.mayflash.com/support/download/ (look for W010
Wireless Sensor DolphinBar MAYFLASH DolphinBar)

2) Unrar it (need to do this twice) and run updater (note sensor bar not plugged in)

3) while holding synch, plug sensor bar into usb port (a good quality extender should work, but unpowered hubs not recommended)

4) after plugging in and releasing synch, option to install firmware will pop up; Update firmware (take a second, as it's tiny)

5) there's a hardware switch for above and below TV placement on the back of the bar (never seen one of those), so fill that out. Also change to mode 4

6) Make sure your copy of Dolphin is a recent one from dolphin-emu.org (not dolphin-emulator.com--that caused hours of issues!)

7) Pair Wiimote(s) and everything should work with default settings. You may want to verify "continuous scanning" is enabled on the controller settings (I believe it was defaulted to on).

* note that the Wii Remotes will automatically turn off in time, but using the power button will turn it off sooner.
* all accessories (classic controller, nunchuck, etc...) should work
* four controllers should work
* I got 90-95% OEM Wii sensor bar performance (it has a harsher cut off than I recall, but when pointed at the screen, it works great).
* remember that Dolphin like a Wii has a software setting for above/below TV placement
* the cable is disgracefully short, though it does kind help in cable routing, as you basically run the extender cable to the TV and plug this in there. I had no issues with a quality (though only $6-8) USB 2.0 extension cable. There are reported issues with unpowered hubs.

My biggest hardware issue came from not knowing what mode to use (If everything else wasn't so good I'd deduct a star). 1&2 aren't really for gaming. 3 kinda works, but it's not what you want. Choose mode 4. Note you can change modes with the Wiimote (press home and the D pad--each direction corresponds to a different mode). The biggest issue overall is downloading from the wrong site. It's latest version wasn't recent and simply wouldn't work. Use mode 4 and a recent version from dolphin-emu.org, and you should be fine!

title: Turtle Beach's best efforts, though they still have room for improvement
text:
I've used a gazillion Turtle Beach headsets (X31, X32, X42.XP400, XP510, PX51, Z300, and a few wired ones). I generally love the wireless (zero static) and the fit. These do well in both regards, and they upgrade the appearance, build and functionality from all of these.

The presentation when you open the box is amazing (especially since I got these as warranty replacements/free upgrade for the Z300). You really feel like you're opening up $300 headphones. The look is angling more for the Beats/lifestyle headset crowd more than the gaming scene, which is fine by me, as I tended to remove the boom mics and use headsets as headphones for TV, movies, and music. The marketing and manual is very clearly geared for Mac/iPhone users. There's no mention of Android (worry not, these pair with any modern Bluetooth device) and Mac comes before PC in the instructions. I use these with my work PC and my Samsung Galaxy Note 3 btw.

Taking these out of the box, you immediately appreciate the comfort and fit. These definitely are the best fitting Turtle Beaches out there. The weight is just right, and my enormous head never feels squeezed in. The plastics look better than they feel, and all in all, it's not quite up to $300 headphone standards, but the aluminum is a nice touch. Swap out aluminum for the plastics and you're hitting the mark. The leatherette earpads are a bit of a challenge however. They feel nice, and the shape works well for me, but they tend to cause sweating, even after just a few minutes. It's a trade off of sound isolation vs breathability. There''s a clear mute indicator (a nice touch) as well as dials for headset and chat volumes, as well as a somewhat difficult to use surround control (still the best of the Turtle Beaches I've used). The headset itself has a bunch of buttons, in an oddly symmetrical array on both ears. Once you get used to it, they work better than other TB headsets, and it's easier to adjust sound modes (I never do that anyway). What I liked most is an upgraded voice indicator system to let you know about pairing, Bluetooth powering on/off, etc... Plus it pairs much much faster than my z300, XP510, PX51, etc... The Bluetooth is amazing btw. Sadly the wireless is only almost as good. It's static free as always, but like my z300, there are occasional pairing (with base) issues that I never have with the XP/PX series.

Speaking of XP/PX series, like the z300, these are lacking in their versatility. The base station only takes USB in, which is great for a Mac or PC, but it doesn't take RCA, 3.5mm, or optical. If these had an analog in (the headset has a 3.5mm in, but that kinda defeats the purpose) as well as an optical in, then these would be the undisputed king of TB headsets. They're by far the best for Bluetooth and a computer, but they cannot hook up to a receiver, gaming system, optical out from your TV, etc... like the XP/PX series.

Amazing presentation/unboxing
Nice look and above average fit/finish (though I'd like to see less plastic for $300)
Phenomenal Bluetooth (audio--I never tried these on a call or Skype)
Great (but not perfect) wireless (no hiss or static, but had a couple pairing issues)
Amazing comfort, save for the sweaty ear pads
Wish the rather nice base station had additional input options

I really wanted to give these 5 stars, and in the end I did albeit with reservations. The price would be right with a couple changes (or cutting $75 as is). That being said, I really like these. The amazing Bluetooth will see these used while traveling, and these give me serenity at my desk, which is kinda priceless.

title: Great audio, but could use some tweeks
text:
I love the audio on these headphones, as I've loved the audio on several other recent 5ghz digital headphones ([[ASIN:B006W41X1S Turtle Beach Ear Force X32 Digital Headset]], [[ASIN:B006W41W4Q Turtle Beach Ear Force XP400 Dolby Surround Sound Gaming Headset]], and [[ASIN:B007ZZ6OW6 Corsair Vengeance 2000 Wireless 7.1 Gaming Headset (CA-9011115-NA)]]). It's crisp clear and generally devoid of any issues. These and the other above options sound way better than any of the 2.4ghz or 900mhz headphones I've ever used.

I also like the confortable fit, removable microphone (I primarily use these for TV/movies/solo gaming), and general fit and finish. Setup is a breeze, Bluetooth is a plus, and the multichannel sound comes in handy (and works rather).

So what's wrong? Well, wrong is a strong word, but the buttons can be confusing, the power button takes a while to turn on (longer than the 3 seconds it's supposed to), the various modes are hard to access, and there's only one input (one digital). On a $50-100 devices, these are all acceptable. For a $250 device, the power button should be more sure, the modes should be easier to access (admittedly they're nothing special), and there should be at least two digital inputs. I'd give up some of the audio modes for a second input or better ergonomics. Also, while the fit and finish are good, it's not great or luxurious, which I kinda start to expect in this price range.

Pros:
great audio
decent range (then they just die)
good battery life
rechargeable batteries
TOSLINK passthrough
Bluetooth
removable microphone
nice packaging

Cons:
difficult ergonomics
only one input (one digital and one analog, but cannot select)
pricey (cheaper options get you the great audio)
fit and finish could be better for price

Compared to the cheaper [[ASIN:B006W41X1S Turtle Beach Ear Force X32 Digital Headset]] you gain a rechargeable battery, Bluetooth, pseudo surround, an optical input/pass through, and a nicer base station with removable power cord (after having a bunny eat through one, I appreciate that).

All in all these are great headphones (I don't chat when I play games, so I cannot speak about that aspect). At the right price, these are a great option, but otherwise I'd tend to recommend the X32 or one of the other options. If you're still using staticy old school wireless headphones or interference prone 2.4ghz ones, try one of these 5ghz digital ones out!

title: Surprisingly good with a silly flaw
text:
The good news is that this controller is way better than a Wiimote in a plastic wheel. It's honestly a great solution for driving games without the bulk, hassle, and cost of a full fledged wheel setup but better than the standard controller or the aforementioned Wiimote setup. At first it was a tough transition from the standard controller at first, with oversteer being the biggest issue. In time my times improved, mostly by avoiding the wild spells of oversteer turning into a complete loss of control. As an added bonus, in Forza my corners used to score mostly 1s and 4s, where now I routinely get 2s and 3s (plus the 1s and 4s). I'm guessing it's showing a greater deal of consistency, and I know passing and drifting is way easier. Would a full wheel setup be better? Definitely, but it would take way more room in my living room. With this, I can throw it under the couch or whatnot.

The bad news? Well that's baffling. I understand the lack of analog sticks, as the wheel replicates most of that, but the wheel has no should buttons. That's a huge loss for driving/racing games, as these buttons often are used for shifting. Hell, even Microsoft's own Forza series uses it extensively for setup. I couldn't even change the setup (to reduce the oversteer I mentioned above), as you need shoulder buttons to tab over. Frankly I cannot fathom why Microsoft didn't find some place to put the buttons. Even a crappy location is better than nothing. The light up ends are gimmicky, and I'd rather have should buttons. Other than that, ergonomics aren't great. It's not a huge deal, but, it could be quite a bit better. Do know that this wheel isn't compatible with rechargeable battery packs, the charge and play kit, or and voice chat capability. Frankly it really doesn't seem like a 1st party effort. It does work beautifully wirelessly however.

text:
This game shows off all the creative ways the WiiU can combine motion, tablet use, and traditional joystick/button controls to make fun, innovative gameplay happen. What holds it back, and I think holds the WiiU back these days, is that it is deceptively cute. Everything is cartoony (in a very enjoyable way) but this can make some people (I imagine teens and older adults like myself) wonder if they are really the intended audience. However, once you play through the first several stages of these cute games, things get difficult quickly! I think to take these games to completion would be pretty hardcore. If you only play the first few levels, then you might think they are too casual and childish.
It's too bad because I think Nintendo has really great hardware and this game collection shows it off well.
I will second what many have said here: the Luigi's Mansion game is the most obvious winner for my wife and I.

title: deceptively cute - deep and clever
text:
This is a hard game to define. It is close to real-time strategy, but instead of fighting an army you are fighting creatures, puzzles, and environmental obstacles. You are also fighting the clock, because at the end of an in-game day you must round up all your pikmin lest they be eaten by their natural predators. You are also dealing with prioritizing your resources by deploying Pikmin and explorers on different tasks. That's right, there is multi-tasking in this game. You need 15 Pikmin to carry that fruit, and in order to grow Pikmin you need to defeat that insect and carry it back to the base with another 10 Pikmin. All before the day runs out. So while hardcore detractors might see it's pretty and cute design and write Pikmin 3 off, anyone who has played it into its intermediate stages knows this can get hairy.
But it is always fun, whether the joy of discovering a new area or defeating a difficult beast, or hauling home a couple giant fruits. And it feels good to explore a pretty environment (various types of natural settings with plants modeled after real Earth species) with a cute cadre of explorers and Pikmin.
If you are one of those hardcore gamers, you have to go for 100% completion to see all the extremely unique and clever game design that goes into this title. Once you have all the gameplay elements unlocked, use your WiiU game pad to find tempting dark spots on the map and venture in prepared for serious originality and challenge.
If anything is "casual" about this game it is the overhead perspective (making it easier for non-3-D game experts to control) and the emphasis on using your brain rather than your hand-eye coordination (most of the time). But I have to put casual in quotes there because there is nothing casual about being clever, and some of these situations required a few re-starts before we had a solution.
In short, really fun, deceptively cute, just complicated enough to keep it challenging and engaging. Totally worth it.

The only negative has to be that the aiming process can be off at times, but one gets used to it by the time the game really gets into full swing.

title: Bright and invigorating - in a dark room at night, it helps you concentrate as well as being fun (no shame in that)
text:
After 20 years of doing computer programming full time I finally realized that I'm not nuts in wanting a fun keyboard. Once I got the keyboard, I found that it actually looks just as cool in person as it does on the Razer website. I work late at night and turn off all the lights and I have found that it really shifts my mood to have the lights on this keyboard.

After a while I do grow tired of the constant wave lights, but there's a simple icon on the taskbar that allows you to instantly shift modes, so I find myself shifting into the slow change mode a lot of the time, which is more mellow but still improves your mood. In this mode, all of the keys have the same color, and the color slowly changes through a cycle - very slowly, in good pacing with hours' of work. Sometimes, though, I want the wave lights back. There's no doubting that with the wave lighting effect pulsing across the keyboard about once a second in a dark room at night it changes your mood and makes you feel a bit more like you're a character in a Phil Dick novel than a boring computer programmer.

Believe it or not, the 'slow change' mode (as opposed to the 'fast wave' mode) is also invigorating, because you may not realize it until you have one, but your unconscious mind's eye becomes accustomed to whatever the keyboard color is as you routinely glance down at it while thinking not about the keyboard, but about your work. To have the color always be different when you glance down gives a mental jolt of invigorating stimulation that, in my dark room at night, makes life on the computer ... just seem pretty cool, even in 'slow' mode.

Regarding the keyboard itself - of course you need a ten keyless type of keyboard for serious work (blue keys, brown keys, bla bla bla, you can read about all that elsewhere) and - I do have my personal favorite - after trying many different ten keyless keyboards, some with brown, some with red, some with blue - I had a real revelation one day when in frustration I looked down at my keyboard thinking the thing stunk after once again missing the key I was trying to hit - and realizing that the actual physical layout of the keyboard was identical to another one of my ten keyless keyboards I'd purchased that I thought I loved (I have a bunch of keyboards around as I tried to find the best one). So I swapped out keyboards and started using the other, identically-laid-out one, but it had clacky, loud, clicky keys. Suddenly the keyboard felt like a whole new design. No missed keys (well, rarely). No frustration (well, not much). I could have sworn it was a different physical keyboard layout. I even put the two identical keyboards side by side from different angles with a ruler and stared down at them with squinted eyes just to confirm that they really were identical in terms of physical layout, weight, shape, etc. - and they were. The ONLY difference was the blue vs. brown keys. So what I learned is that the body pays attention to more than the keyboard layout as it becomes unconsciously familiar with the hand motions used with the keyboard. The sound and tactile feedback impacts your unconscious motor brain. You really have to find which style of tenkeyless you want - soft, or clicky.

Fortunately, Razer's chroma has both soft and clicky (the soft is called 'Stealth'). I use the clicky. But in terms of the colorized effects, which is what this review is really about - super 5 stars. If you're at the computer all day - or if you're a gamer - why not have fun at your %^*^ machine? Actually, I found out that the color effects are more than fun - they help your concentration level. And the colors effects are strong - really bright lighted colors. Really highly recommended.

(The only downside is that you cannot see the key symbol for the 'shifted' version of the keys which sits on the lower part of the number keys. In the dark, this means you either have to remember that the * symbol is Shift + 8, or else you have to really squint down at the keyboard and try to use the colored glowing light of the keyboard itself reflecting off the walls to get a tiny vision of the dark symbols on the keyboard beneath the bright glowing numbers to remind yourself if you're hitting the right key while pressing Shift - and sometimes I just continue to get it wrong. But this is a minor complaint.)

title: Short but sweet and super replayable
text:
I finished this pseudo-single screen arcade action platformer when I first sat down to play it. It took me an hour or so. If you get good you can probably do it in twenty minutes or so.

You play as disembodied head Taco, who is apparently a lunar octopus. She ran out of fuel and crashed to earth, and needed to fuel up... by catching a bunch of fish and turning them into fuel. Unfortunately, the cats of earth have other ideas, and commandeer a UFO of their own to collect fish first and also attack you.

Every stage but the last boss consists of you trying to steal fish back from dastardly cats, including sleeping ones. You have to navigate a maze of platforms to get around - and don't touch the spikes.

Music and visual style are gorgeous and a perfect fit for the gameplay.

It's all very simple and all very charming. The price tag is steep but if you play this competitively with friends it will definitely prove it worthwhile.

However, it will take you a while to get good, and you'll enjoy it the whole way. Controls are simple, with just jump and dash, but it definitely feels more modern than the sorts of single screen platformers that inspired it. Particularly the way your dash move swerves up at the end has more in common with Celeste or Gris than it does Rainbow Islands.

The good ending is apparently pretty difficult to get, so that should add another level of challenge and replayability.

title: Stone cold classics and some underexposed gems
text:
This collection contains more stone-cold classics for my money than the pack-in volume 1, but no surprise delights quite like Aquaventure. If you hate the 2600 era, I can’t really recommend it, but if you are open to really early games, these are pretty rewarding. Now, these are all first-party Atari games, and first-party Atari games are rather infamous for not pushing the envelope on graphics and complexity the way Activision did. Third-party games were the lifeblood of the 2600, so I hope we see some of them eventually.

It’s the 7800 games make this a really outstanding value for me and force me to bump up my score to a 5. Awful sound chip aside, the 7800 games are all gems, and their presence alone would make me pick this cartridge up for a measly couple sawbucks.

Let’s talk about each game on offer in brief.

Asteroids (7800) - hands down my favorite version of Asteroids, even including the arcade game and Super Asteroids. It’s fast, agile, fun, and it looks good too. I’m looking forward to trying out the Lynx upgrade to this when the Lynx collections arrive.

Yars' Revenge (2600) - while Activision is the king of the 2600, this is my single favorite game. The gameplay loop is incredible, with the perfect balance of attack and defense. It might feel fiddly until you get the rhythm, but I promise it’s worth pushing through until you do.

Millipede (2600) - while I prefer the pure and simple Centipede to the overly complicated Millipede in the arcade, I prefer this quite a bit to the 2600 Centipede. The additional layer of gloss on the graphics and the additional complexity of the ruleset makes for a more satisfying home console experience.

Basketbrawl (7800) - this is NBA Jam, many years before NBA Jam existed. It even has powerups like Tournament edition. It isn’t quite as entertaining as NBA Jam - especially in the sound department - but it’s still great fun.

Centipede (7800) - the closest thing to the arcade version people had at home for many years. My favorite home version of it.

Solaris (2600) - arguably the most beautiful 2600 game, and a darn fine forward scrolling shooter on a system that had many worthy entries.

Sprintmaster (2600) - top down racing like I long to see on the Evercade, but I just can’t get used to the controls. Very impressive graphics for the system, though!

Submarine Commander (2600) - a hidden gem of the catalog, this combines fast action with an interesting rhythm and good strategy. Spend some time with it if you never have!

Haunted House (2600) - the original survivor horror game. You need to find scans of the manual to play this, if you don’t already know. It’s still fun, but can be bewildering.

Planet Smashers (7800) - this is a really interesting take on the vertical scrolling shooter, with bosses reminiscent of Phoenix. It is HARD, though. The graphics are very 2600-esque for a 7800 game. The fact that 7800 games have a reset button on the keypad is really unfortunate.

Bowling (2600) - I can’t explain why, but this early bowling sim is really fun. I think it’s the wish fulfillment aspect of being able to spin your ball the way you want at any time you want as it rolls down the lane. Different modes take this ability away, but why?

Desert Falcon (7800) - I do not care for the 2600 version of this Zaxxon clone at all. But the detailed and funny 7800 version made me a believer.

Radar Lock (2600) - very reminiscent of Solaris in graphics and gameplay, but not quite as fun. It required using the second joystick to change weapons, and I haven't figured out how to do that yet...

Human Cannonball (2600) - It's like playing Scorched Earth with one player, except you have to catch the shell. Weirdly meditative. I've spent a lot more time playing this than I can explain.

Street Racer (2600) - The two-player games on here are the perfect way to experience being an only child in 1978. The uncontrolled second player almost beats me every time.

Air Sea Battle (2600) - A little bit more fun than Street Racer, but it's still a two-player game without two players.

Realsports Tennis (2600) - It's not Activision's Tennis, but it's pretty good!

Dark Chambers (2600) - Very advanced survival horror for the 2600. I haven't figured out how to play this again yet.

Wizard (2600) - an unreleased prototype where you have to seek out an invisible enemy. The enemy doesn't seem to move in either game mode, which makes it a little too easy and repetitive to be fun.

text:
Note - I got this as part of the premium bundle.

I am much more acquainted with Data East's arcade output than their home ports, so this has been really interesting to explore. I'm still trying out everything, but so far Magical Drop 2 has absorbed most of my time. The NES Burger Time is off from the arcade version in frustrating ways, but maybe I'll get used to it. Joe and Mac 2 is good as ever, and Side Pocket is weirdly addictive. Burnin' Rubber, aka Bump'n'Jump, is probably my favorite title here.

Karate Champ has not held up well. Fighter's History is not a patch on Street Fighter II, but for a system with few fighting game options so far, it's one of the best. Bad Dudes and Two Crude Dudes aren't quite as sublimely over the top as their arcade versions, but they're still a good laugh and really fun examples of a genre that I'm not great at. Midnight Resistance, a spiritual successor to Heavy Barrel with tons of Contra influence, is new to me; I'm enjoying it a lot.

I wouldn't have bought the system for this collection, but I'm having a lot of fun with it nonetheless, especially for the "free" game with the premium edition!

title: Interesting games from a sadly forgotten publisher
text:
EDIT: well, in the fullness of time, I’ve spent more time with this cartridge than any other except the Piko one, so I’m awarding it an extra star. Rad Gravity and the Brainies did not seem like games I would pour hours into originally, but save states do enough to sand down their rough edges that they’ve become real favorites of mine.

The Interplay collections were part of what sold me on the Evercade, so it's been a little surprising that I haven't enjoyed them more. They are smaller than most collections, and they have games that have more nostalgia value than modern-day gameplay value. The Interplay vaults are large and deep, so I hope they excavate more gems in the next set of releases. But for the price, this is still a very worthwhile purchase. Let's go game by game.

The Adventures of Rad Gravity: This initially unassuming game, which I thought was an enhanced C64 or PC port initially, is quite good. It's a combat-heavy, exploration-heavy platformer with puzzle elements. It's not exactly a Metroidvania, but it's kind of in that vein - maybe a Metroid Man. The difficulty is pretty punishing at first, but once you get used to it you’ll get far with minimal save state scumming. I recommend spending quality time with this - it goes really unexpected places with some really great graphical design choices in a hurry! My favorite thing about the Evercade is discovering great games I’ve simply never heard of, and this is near the top of the list.

The Brainies: This puzzle title from Titus, which starts with a bizarrely sexy cinematic, is a rather standard block-pusher, except in this case the characters themselves are the blocks. It has something in common with Chew Man Fu on the TG16. It's really weird, and frustratingly makes you play a tilted Mode 7 world after making you look at a top-down map that would be more usable - which costs you time from the extremely rigorous clock! It's pretty fun after you get used to it, but I recommend save-state scumming to make the rough edges in the original game less of a problem.

Clayfighter 2: Judgment Clay (get it, get it, like Terminator 2 lol now you understand the humor involved here): significantly worse than the original, missing some of my favorite characters, and just plain not very fun. It looks much less clay-like than the first game. It is one of the fairly small number of actual fighting games on the console thus far, so there's that.

Claymates: The far and away best title on the compilation, this is a stone-cold classic with a strong Kirby vibe and really great level design and gameplay. It is a little floaty for my tastes, but it's easy to get past that and enjoy this for what it is. I'd probably have bought the compilation for this alone, and been quite happy with it at that.

Earthworm Jim 2: If you loved Earthworm Jim, but wished it had a lot less actual platforming substance and a lot more random weird one-off levels, you'll love Earthworm Jim 2! For me, it's a definite step down from the original in terms of substance and fun. It's interesting and fun in its own right, but it feels like they collected all the gimmick ideas they didn't have time to implement in Earthworm Jim and added a few platform levels to string them together. This is as far as I am aware the only official rerelease of the SNES version, which had different background art and the ability to change weapons vs. the Genesis version.

Prehistorik Man: This Titus platformer isn't quite as fun as the Joe and Mac series or the Bonk series, but it's very interesting and quite beautiful, at least in the early going. It's very hard, quite complex, and a bit too fiddly, and thus very much in line with the Euro-platformer philosophy that the Evercade so far specializes in. I don't expect to finish this game, but I'll enjoy what I can from it. (As an aside, what WAS it with the 90s and cavemen, anyway? Fully 10% of the Evercade titles, Atari collections excepted, seem to be caveman-adjacent.)

title: An oasis for classic gamers looking for something new - Premium Pack is the way to go
text:
Evercade is the only video game company on the market who is actively curating interesting collections of games with surprises for even wizened classic gamers like me. So let me state my bias here: if this were the same quality as the cheap knockoffs available far and wide, with only the custom cartridges to distinguish itself, I would still give it a four-star review.

Happily, that isn't the case. This is a very solid, very comfortable, even premium experience. At first I was surprised at how large the unit is, probably halfway between a Game Boy Advance and the Wii U tablet. But due to the size and the dedication to comfortable curves, it's much more pleasant to hold than a 3DS, a Switch, or the like. You'd have to go back to the OG PSP to find a handheld that fits so comfortably in my medium-sized male hands.

The Sega-like D-pad disc and the face buttons are perhaps softer than many of us are used to, but I quite like them - the face buttons have a lot of travel and a satisfying enough click, making for maybe less immediate feeling than, say, a Switch, but a similar degree of tactile feedback to a Genesis controller. The shoulder buttons have no throw and are very clicky, which I like except when I accidentally press them.

There are some negatives. The screen could definitely be nicer. It's similar to the original PSP screen, but people's expectations have heightened in the last ten years. It looks really nice to me, but the view angle etc. leave something to be desired. Usually I'm looking straight on, so it's not something that bothers me. Some of the carts (particularly Atari 1 - maybe it's the first to be produced?) are too tight. There is an instructional video on Evercade's YouTube channel on how to best get the too-tight ones out, but it's not that hard. This didn't really bother me, either.

Now, onto the games.

Atari 1: I was kind of irked to have this packed in, as I've bought umpteen Atari compilations and first-party 2600 single player games are not the highlight of the 2600 library. But I was really pleasantly surprised. The 2600 games are all actually playable - helped out by the inclusion of prototype games like Aquaventure and fan games like Yars Return (not half as good as the original, but plenty good). Yes, these have been released elsewhere, but they seem more attractive on a cart with 20 games vs. a Switch app with 120. Some home ports of arcade games, notably Gravitar, are extremely impressive and at least as fun as the arcade. The 7800 games, though, are really where it's at, with the amazingly wacky Ninja Golf, the impressive motorcycle racer Motor Psycho, the odd rail shooter Alien Brigade, and the criminally unknown Food Fight.

There are downsides. The Atari arcade ports mostly don't do the original games justice. If I had been in charge, I wouldn't have put the hilariously awful Tempest prototype on this cart, but it's worth a laugh. I don't know why they included the middling 2600 Desert Falcon when the far superior 7800 version is on Atari 2, but whatever. It feels cheap to include only one Swordquest game, and not having the manual available makes it hard to succeed.

DON'T MISS: Food Fight, Ninja Golf, Motor Psycho, Yars Return, Gravitar, Aquaventure, Double Dunk.

Interplay 1: One of the smaller collections, but one of the most attractive to me. I spent a lot of time with Battle Chess, Boogerman, Earthworm Jim, and Clayfighter as a youngin', so I looked forward to playing them again. Battle Chess is agonizingly slow to me now, but it's still pretty fun if you can take a deep breath and relax. Clayfighter has not aged well, but it's still reasonably funny. Boogerman has always been a very solid platformer buried under puddles of snot, and it still is - if you can stomach the "humor", the gameplay is pretty darn good. And Earthworm Jim is a stone-cold classic after all these years.

I was very interested in the Titus games I never played before. Incantation is a gorgeous platformer with an extremely small viewport (think Bonk). It's a little fiddly, but I'm having a good time with it. Titan is an all-direction Breakout takeoff, except you can slow down time and have to shepherd the ball all over the place. It's a very interesting takeoff. I don't know how long I will enjoy it, but I've found it really rewarding so far.

DON'T MISS: Boogerman (seriously, it's solid), Earthworm Jim, Titan.

Data East 1: I am much more acquainted with Data East's arcade output than their home ports, so this has been really interesting to explore. I'm still trying out everything, but so far Magical Drop 2 has absorbed most of my time. The NES Burger Time is off from the arcade version in frustrating ways, but maybe I'll get used to it. Joe and Mac 2 is good as ever, and Side Pocket is weirdly addictive. Burnin' Rubber, aka Bump'n'Jump, is probably my favorite title here. I wouldn't have bought the system for this collection, but I'm having a lot of fun with it nonetheless.

DON'T MISS: Joe and Mac 2, Burnin' Rubber/Bump'n'Jump, Magical Drop 2, Bad Dudes, Side Pocket (no, really)

Don't stop with the pack-in cartridges, though - buy more! My personal favorite compilation so far is Piko Interactive, which is stuffed with great games and a lot of totally interesting RPGs. Other highlights are Interplay 2, Atari 2 (with Desert Falcon, Basketbrawl, and lots more), Technos, and "modern retro" mavens Mega Kat Studios. And finally, though they're no longer available on Amazon, the EU-only Namco cartridges are amazing and worth the import. I'm so excited this system exists, and I can't wait for the next wave of cartridges in the fall!

title: An amazing game pad!
text:
I ordered this gamepad to use as a second player controller for my Neo Geo mini, but it's so marvelous that I'm tempted to order another to use with an adapter for general retro console use. I was really on the fence about getting it - I don't know when I'll see my coworkers again, much less if anybody will want to stand close enough to play two player on this tiny screen. (There is an HDMI port, but it's hard for me to use.) I didn't know what to expect of the weird thumbstick - whether I would like it at all - or what the build quality would be. After all, it's an inexpensive pad compared to a lot of other "modern retro" pads.

As soon as I pulled it out of the box, I had a good feeling. The controller is incredibly solid and weighty. I like the Retro-bit Genesis and Saturn controllers, but they feel weightless and flexible compared to my memories of the originals. This one, by contrast, feels like it weighs as much as an Xbox 360 controller - a good thing in my book. It's solid as a rock; it feels like I could stomp on it on cement without so much as scratching it. (Note: I am not recommending you do this.) The buttons are clicky and responsive.

I'm terrible at fighting games, but this pad makes me feel almost competent. Pulling off sweeps, 4-6 moves, or 623 / 421 moves feels incredibly natural. I've always preferred Sega/NEC disc-based d-pads to Nintendo-style pure cross d-pads, but this is a new evolution.

My only complaint is that the Neo Geo is a four-button controller, so this won't work with many SNES or Genesis games. Which isn't a fair complaint. But if somebody were to clone this with shoulder buttons, I'll be first in line to buy it.

Until then, I'll keep using this on any game that will allow it. It's a marvelous pad and an amazing value. Don't miss it.

title: Amazing build quality and screen, a great time for the Neo Geo fan and newbie alike
text:
The Neo Geo's library is strongly weighted towards genres that I rarely play and am not good at - fighting, run-and-run shooters, shmups, beat-em-ups, and sports games - and is remarkably heavy on sequels. That said, these games are some of the most finely detailed games of their era - the Neo Geo was a heck of a pixel-pusher. I've never had so many Neo Geo ports together in one package before, and having them all in one place makes for an amazing overview of a console I never got to spend quality time with.

My favorites of the bunch, Fatal Fury, Samurai Shodown II, Blazing Star, and Metal Slug, come through with shining colors, but I've actually been having a lot of fun with less familiar games, like Puzzled, a weird Tetris variant, Last Resort, a spectacular shmup, and Top Player's Golf, a really great golf sim. (And I hate golf.)

It's great to have all these games in one unit that's about the size of my coffee mug, and it's faintly miraculous that the screen and sound are so great. The unit is built to last, with a great tiny joystick and great feeling buttons. (I know a lot of long-time fans hate the button layout, but I understand why they changed it - with most games using A-C, it's more comfortable on the fingers this way.)

I have and love the Retrocade Tempest machine, but it cost twice what this does and only plays one game. I have the NES, SNES, and Genesis minis, and have the TG16 mini on order. I may like those games better, but in terms of value and flexibility, none of them are a patch on the genius of this lovely little inexpensive machine. Even if you're a Neo Geo newbie, maybe especially if, I suggest you give this a try.

title: Fantastic game, frustrating rough spots
text:
The good news: Picross DS is a worthy follow-up to one of the best brain-teaser puzzle games I've played, [[ASIN:B00004TMGP Mario's Picross]]. The bad news: despite a host of great new features, they've actually left out a great feature of that 14-year old title and even damaged the design (though only slightly).

Picross DS keeps the same Sudoku-meets-Minesweeper gameplay of the classic game, derived from the popular paper puzzles called nonograms. You are given the number and order of colored cells in each row and column of a grid. By logical deduction and good guesswork, you must figure out which cells should be colored in and which shouldn't be.

Easy and Normal puzzles are time-limited and serve as an introduction to the game; Free Mode puzzles have no timer or warning that you've misplaced a tile. Free Mode is the bulk of the game, and a more satisfying way to play. There are a few minigames as well (a pair of "whack a square" games and a "reverse drawing" game, and possibly others), but these are rather dull and not the point. A change for the challenging: the largest puzzles here are larger than any I've played before.

In gameplay, you can either use the stylus (good for smaller puzzles, frustrating for large ones) or the d-pad and buttons (better for large puzzles, slower in competitive play).

Which brings me to one major addition: online and local wireless competitive play. You and another go head to head to finish two puzzles. I haven't put much time into this mode yet, but it doesn't intuitively seem a big draw - Picross has always been about contemplative mental exercise to me.

The next addition is more exciting: a "Daily Picross" mode, meant to test your speed at small puzzles randomly chosen. Five modes are available, only one of which is unlocked at the start. This mode has a great deal of potential and could bring some longevity to the game once it is finished.

The next major addition is one I've wanted for a long time. A puzzle editor allows you to create your own puzzles, either cell-by-cell or by automatically generating a puzzle from a free-hand sketch. I don't like the automatically-generated puzzles I've done so far, but I may get used to it.

You can share the puzzles you create via local wireless or over the internet, and download puzzles made by others. Nintendo will be releasing multiple puzzle packs that provide puzzles from previous Picross games as well.

This would all be perfect except for two changes made to the basic presentation:
- Mario's Picross had three save slots, to allow three people to use the same cartridge. This game has a single save slot - you can't really share this with a friend or a family member. Expect to buy one per person - at least it's cheap.
- More gravely, the picture you uncover by solving the puzzle is now displayed, both as a small icon on the puzzle select screen and at full size on the top screen. This hurts replayability - there's little point in replaying a puzzle if you know what it looks like. I have not completed Free Mode yet, but a full random Time Attack mode, as the earlier game had, would go a long way towards making up for this last problem.

While the former problem can be ascribed to Nintendo's desire to sell more copies of the software, the latter is simply strange. Nevertheless, the additions make this a superior title to its excellent predecessor and a downright bargain for its budget price. Highly recommended for those who like thoughtful, contemplative puzzle-solving.

title: One of the better classic compilations
text:
Taito Legends is a hard compilation to judge. It -- like Midway Arcade Treasures 1 -- mixes early, mid, and late 80s games, and it's just odd to have Electric Yo Yo on the same disc as Operation Wolf. There is, admittedly, a lot of filler -- the old lightgun games don't do well without a lightgun, the scrolling shooters are mostly forgettable, and three Space Invaders games might be too many for one compilation. However, the games span many genres (single-screen and scrolling shooters, adventure, puzzle, action) and the really good games are, well, really good.

Buy this compilation for:
* Space Invaders
* Jungle Hunt
* Bubble Bobble
* Rainbow Islands
* Phoenix
* Colony 7
* Zoo Keeper
* Elevator Action
* Plump Pop
* Rastan
* Super Qix
* New Zealand Story
* Plotting (aka Flipull)
* Tube It

The presentation is great. A lot of attention went towards this package, and it shows.

While there are glaring omissions (Japan and Europe got two compilations, with a total of around fifty games overall), it's a solid compilation. In any case, for the price, it's a steal.

title: Namco does an anthology right
text:
Namco is the king of the unsatisfying anthology. On the original Playstation, Namco released six volumes of Namco Museum (five in the US), each with a small number of games -- although the interface and extras were fantastic, and without par. They released 16bit and N64 versions without the interfaces. They released two Game Boy Advance installments: one with the essentials (Ms. Pac Man, Dig Dug, Galaga, Galaxian, and a really crappy racing game) and one all Pac Man. They released a terribly stingy package (with just the same old games again) across the current generation of consoles.

Then this game came out in Japan. It contained arrangements of the same old games (though thankfully Rally X returned to favor), but was still stingy at only seven originals and four arrangements, especially considering how many times some of us have bought these games!

However, the American version adds ten new obscure (Motos, Grobda, the excellent Dig Dug II) and not so obscure (Rolling Thunder!) games to the mix, substantially increasing the value. While some of these titles are just this side of awful (Druaga and Dragon Buster, I'm looking at you) most of the added titles are quite enjoyable if a bit slight. Rolling Thunder, a very substantial game that had never been included on a US compilation until this one, is a killer addition. (For what it's worth, Namco released the bonus US content as Namco Museum Vol. 2 in Japan. Some things never change.)

The arranged versions are a mixed bag. Though I love the original Galaga, I find the arrangement pretty intolerable. The art style is garish and ugly and the gameplay is less focused than the original. I can't comment on Pac Man. The arranged Dig Dug is a very interesting remake, plenty worth playing and the best on this compilation. The Rally X arrangement just adds a few powerups and spruced-up graphics.

Now that this has hit a new budget price point, it's truly an essential part of the PSP library. Even if you don't like Pac Man (and I don't), you'll have at least a sawbuck's worth of fun with the games here.
