title: Tons of bang for your buck:  months of play on console, plus ONLINE games, APPS, and more!
text:
We got a full year of play out of each of the previous Skylanders games, which is great compared to other games where we can zip through it in one or two months max. We are Skylanders veterans in our family, but you don't need to have played any other Skylanders games to jump in and enjoy the heck out of this newest offering from Activision, Skylanders Swap Force. It's called "Swap Force" because the "swappers" (not all characters are swappable, as there are regular characters and lightcore character that light up on the portal and in the game). But the "swappers" are characters where the top and bottom are connected by magnets, giving you the ability to make new combinations by taking any top and putting it on any bottom, for a new character! This aspect is SUPER-thrilling to the kids, and they have been counting down the days since last year when it was announced.

The game itself, if you have not played it, involves chapters (levels) which are in different areas of Skylands, a magical realm full of exciting characters, presents, magical keys, hats that give your character special abilities, amusing but tough enemies and bosses, puzzles and mini-games along the way, secret areas and beautiful scenery. In Swap Force, which is the third in the series of Skylanders games (Skylanders Spyro's Adventure was the first, and then Skylanders Giants was the second), the Swap Force characters were tasked with protecting the magic in Skylands. Well, technically they protected the volcano that supplies the magic in Skylands, but one day a huge eruption from the volcano blasted them into two pieces! Now, as in all Skylanders games, you get to be the "Portal Master" and choose which Skylanders to put on the magical portal (that comes with the game and plugs into your game console) to save Skylands.

There are 16 swappers, giving you a total of 256 different combinations. But, at about 15 bucks each, you don't have to worry about getting all 16. The starter kit comes with two swappers, Blast Zone and Wash Buckler (plus a new version of the character Stealth Elf, which is way cool too). We decided to buy only two more swappers, at least for now, and that gives us 4 swappers with a total of 16 combos. You can ignore the marketing and, well, call me frugal, but after going through two previous years of spending a small fortune trying to collect all of the Skylanders, we made a budget and decided we would get the starter kit and two additional swappers, plus one light core character. Everything else they want can go on Christmas wish lists. It is somewhat of a parental mini-game to track down highly sought-after and rare characters that are released in very limited edition, and even in limited stores (the big stores that carry the Skylanders characters have their own "exclusive" characters that are only available in their particular stores).

One thing that is really important to know for choosing which additional characters to get is that there are eight different "elements" in Skylands. An element is basically the area of specialty for that particular character, or for that particular geographical area of Skylands. The elements are: Fire, Water, Earth, Life, Air, Tech, Magic, and Undead. If you have a character for each of the 8 elements, then you can access special sections within the game that need that elemental character to enter.

A HUGE bonus to the Skylander line of games is that you can use any of your characters from the two previous Skylanders games and play them in the current Skylanders game, Swap Force. So if you've played Spyro's Adventure or Giants, hang onto those characters because you can use them in this one, which helps with having the different elemental characters to access the special sections in the game.

Portal of Power? It's a round pedestal connected by USB to your console. It lights up and looks really cool, and you can put your Skylanders on it to send them into Skylands to play. (ahem, I mean, to SAVE SKYLANDS!!) You can put up to 3 items (2 characters and a magical item) on the portal at a time, and it's a lot of fun to watch them join the game, with their own amusing catchphrases. The Stink Bomb swapper says, "Clear the Air!" The swapper Grilla Drilla says, "If there's a drill, there's a way!"
We love to play it in two-player mode, it's cooperative play, and a lot of fun. Adults and kids alike in our family enjoy it.

Difficulty setting: You can choose between Easy, Medium, Hard, and Nightmare levels of difficulty, which makes it adaptable to all ages. My youngest likes to go all the way through on Easy, then try the other difficulty levels for sections of the game. The Hard and Nightmare levels make it fun for the older kids and adults.

Experience: I can't believe I didn't mention this earlier, but one of the biggest perks of playing Skylanders games is that each character stores its experience, upgrades, power-ups, gold, and other data right in a chip in the base of the Skylander! So you don't have to rely on your game system to hold all of that, because each character stores its own data. Guess what? This means that when my son went over to his friend's house to play the Skylanders games, he could take his characters over, and still have all of his upgrades, etc. on them. They have had a blast bringing their boxes of characters back and forth to each other's houses to play...and it doesn't matter what gaming system they have, either. We played on our Wii, but his friend had the Skylanders games on his Xbox. How amazing is Activision to have all this worked out? And Vicarious Visions is the inventive developer.

New to the Swap Force game is that the characters have the ability to jump, which really opens up all kinds of new possibilities. Jumping isn't just for the new Swap Force characters, but somehow the game developers made it that all of the previous Skylanders from the previous two games now have the new ability to jump as well

The graphics are gorgeous, the cut scenes are beautiful and fun to watch, and it doesn't take long to get the hang of playing this very very fun game.

I highly recommend it, and my only caveat is you may want to budget from the beginning. I helped my kids figure out which swappers to buy so that they would have one from each element. Of course, we have our last two years of Skylanders to use as well, so if you are new to Skylanders, I definitely recommend a budget. It's important to mention that these games are very kid-friendly, and you won't find anything disturbing or violent in them that would scare a child. That's one of the reasons we love it.

But honestly, my friends, this game will provide tons and tons of enjoyment....in addition to the gameplay on your console, there are also online games that go along with it, as well as apps that are part of the franchise. I mean it when I say we got an entire year of game play out of each of the previous two Skylanders games. We are a gaming family, and Skylanders is absolutely our favorite game of all time. Get one and jump in! You won't regret it.

title: Wholesome fun for the whole family, tons to do within game!
text:
Highly recommend the Skylanders Giants game. We got it the day it came out. Even though we could have gotten the Portal Owners game, we were thrilled to buy the one that came WITH a portal because the Skylanders Giants portals PLUG IN to the game console, instead of using batteries (yes, even rechargeables will drive you mad replacing them constantly). Just a side note: the original Skylanders game, the XBox version had a plug-in portal, but the others all used 3 AA batteries.

My 8 year old son pointed out that I'd never have to change batteries in the new one, as well as saying we could use our battery one as a backup if the new one broke. (proud mommy)

The Skylanders Giants game: you can use all of the characters from the original game. Of course there are many different types of new characters that your children are convinced they need: ones that light up, the Giants ones, Series 2 ones (which is the same one as in the first game, but modified slightly to make the child want the new one, too!) And there are new regular-sized ones for the Giants game as well.

It's so fun, even for adults, and there are a zillion layers in it. So many different ways to enjoy the game, mini-games, etc. I'm astounded and delighted that there are games like this out for my son and his friends.

It reminded me of when I was young, and got the Final Fantasy game for the first time. And you realized then that there was so much more to do than the basic video games ever prepared you for.

Just my two-cents. It's very fun, the levels, characters, mini-games, even the art in the game, it's all amazing. Besides buying the various characters, you can also buy add on worlds. I've been distressed that my son's 7 and 8 year old friends are playing Call of Duty type games. I'm so glad that there are wholesome games like Skylanders around so my son can enjoy being a kid and killing little bouncy froggies for now, finding gems, doing puzzles, playing a very addictive stone card game, earning money, buying upgrades (that you get to choose from, not just live with, doing battles and hero quests, and so much more that you may get so lost in the game that may or may not stay up late a couple nights "checking the game out." ;-)

Last year we went all out in what we jokingly referred to as the Ultimate Skylanders mini-game, that's when the parents run from store to store, or online site to online site, in order to track down the various just-released or hard-to-find Skylanders, especially when Activision was caught off guard by the HUGE interest that didn't match up the with the inventory.

We set a budget on it this year, though. And whatever we get, we get. But the game itself is so much fun, and has so much to offer, that we would highly recommend it. Hope this helps someone.

title: A must get for Co-op, but has its problems
text:
In some ways I feel bad about giving this a 3 star since it has lots to be said for it and in fact is a must get for an adult looking to play a co-op game with their child.

I won't talk much about the good things, because lots of other reviews cover those, instead I'll concentrate on the problems.

1. You can only save at the end of a "mission". I understand that in the 1980s there were memory limitations, but in the new millennium, there is no reason not to be allowed to save anywhere in the game. Especially since some of the missions are long, fatigue would set in for my child and sometimes we were running into her bed time.

2. There is no camera control. You have to take what the game gives you and sometimes it is tricky lining things up.

3. Parts are too hard. I know this sounds hard to believe about a game with unlimited lives, but you do get docked points every time you die (at least until later when you gain enough money and complete enough unlocks to buy "extras"). It's frustrating to build up a bunch of points and then see them all drained away because you come to a section where the enemy is throwing grenades every five seconds. Some of the jumps are difficult too, especially with the lack of camera control.

4. They don't really take much advantage of the Wii-motes. You do get to use the remote for whipping, which is good, and you can use it for digging, which is kind of lame, but for a game that involves so much hand to hand fighting, I'm really surprised they did not include the remote for fist fighting, it seems like a natural.

5. The battles are repetitive and do not call for much strategy. This is really more of a puzzle game. I had fun playing this with my daughter, but I think I would have gotten bored quickly playing it on my own.

6. There are some glitches that can prevent you from moving forward. Again, since you cannot save in the middle of a mission, that means replaying the whole mission over again.

Still, in the end, after a bit of a rough start, my daughter and I had a fun time playing this together. This was especially true once we were in free play and had bought the "extras" (some might call them cheats). So I would still recommend it as a good co-op for playing with your child. Yes, it is violent, but in that Lego parts flying way. In fact, one other small problem is that I would now like to show my daughter the actual movies, and she would like to see them, but they are too violent for her age.

title: It is an interactive movie
text:
I will start out with the apparently heretical statement that I was not a fan of the earlier final fantasy games. I am a big RPG fan, but please don't shoot, maim or otherwise attack me, because it is true. I found them all to be overly melodramatic, meandering, very predetermined, and frankly too much to sit through until the end. However, Final Fantasy X has hooked me.
That is the great thing about the PS2. I have tried several games that never interested or whose predecessors have failed to entertain on my PC or the PS one. This game falls into this category.
The major improvement is in the voicing and the movies. The story moves along with incredible cut scenes and plot exposition. No more reading along with out dated graphics and long load times. There is more room to wander for those of us who like the side quests. The battle system is much improved over the "real time" system, and now leads to more strategy and thinking during battles, not just fast paced button pushing and hoping for a good outcome. Yes, it is less realistic, but this is a game. The grid system for leveling up is major improvement, and you can spend considerable time weighing the pros and cons of each direction you can pursue and which locks to use up your key spheres on. Another place for fans of increasing the strategy.
All in all, the game can be tailored to whatever the player prefers. It can be fairly fast if you plow strait through to the end and (like I did) feel that the prior games got a bit tedious, I did it in about 45 hours. But, you can spend days traveling around with the side quests and some get extremely hard, and I have not completed them all yet.
To keep this short and not delve into all the technical stuff that most of us honestly don't care about, I will put it this way. The game is beautifully done, the right mix of gameplay and melodrama have been met, the controls are adequate and easy to learn, the strategy can become challenging, the music and movies are tremendous and the battle system is probably the best on the playstation 2.
All in all, this is like watching an interactive movie. It is challenging enough for the adults and entertaining enough for the kids. For PS2 RPG fans it has set the standard.

title: Surprisingly good quality for the money.
text:
My family was coming to stay with us for a week and having played both co-op and battle modes of Guitar Hero III at their house in the past, we decided we needed a second guitar. I assume, like anyone reading this, there's some price sensitivity to the official Guitar Hero guitars, and that's why you're checking out this one.

I got this for ~$20 on Amazon when it was on sale. I think that's very reasonable for the controller. The buttons are a touch "splashy" to the feel, but they are quality. I wish they had been shaped a little bigger because they are actually not only rounded on the corners, but they don't activate well from pressing just near the bottom... you have to get the whole button usually. In this regard the delivered controllers with GH3 are slightly better. But it's not nearly enough to deter me from saving some money, and it does work, just takes a little getting used to. My Sister-in-Law was actually impressed with how well it works. The whammy is firm, and very responsive as is the strum bar. I'd say they are at least the same quality as my original, and the whammy bar seems better built.

The face plate has an inordinate amount of screws to change them out, but it's nicely done. I got the White one for the Wii controller and it has a pink plastic insert.

All-in-all, it's a solid quality item, and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for multi-player action in Guitar Hero 3.

I got the Wii version and it REALLY should have included some hardware to allow it to be used with Rock Band. I personally find the Rock Band controller better than this controller and the original GH3 controller as well. The neck isn't as fat or rounded, making the grip more comfortable... I wish this controller had opted to clone the Rock Band controller fit and buttons, but for what it is, it's really nice.

The only real "decent" alternative if you are looking for some bang for your buck is to get either the Aerosmith Guitar Hero special edition, or perhaps now that it's available, the Guitar Hero World Tour. We already had Rock Band, so the latter didn't make much financial sense given how often we play.

One caveat, this system does say to check their website for future compatability. I'm guessing that means with future Guitar Hero games, but maybe there's a chance it could support Rock Band in the future, but that seems rather unlikely.

Pros:
Solid quality Construction throughout. Already took something of a beating!
Responsive controls
Far cheaper than most controllers
Interchangeable face plate.

Cons:

I had to reach out to the company for them to "reprocess" the warranty of a supposed item that was damaged in transit as opposed to them automatically. In addition, I now have to wait an additional 2-3 weeks for a new controller. This means that warranty process of replacing a controller (which one can purchase from Amazon and have delivered in 1 day) would be 5-6 weeks. Note you do not have to send the defective controller back to them so that wouldn't even be an excuse for delay on their end, either. Perhaps I'll update my review with an additional star if the company actually follows through expeditiously but from what I am seeing thus far, that doesn't seem to be in the realm of possibility.

title: Defend your people and your hut...or else!
text:
Pixel Junk Monsters is a fun defense/stragety game.

You are Tikiman. One day, his town has become overridden with various, dangerous monters. You must keep them from reaching the hut and killing his flock. If all survive at the end of the level, then you get a rainbow. You must get 7 rainbows to move to the left side of the map, where new worlds await you.

Each level is different. It will describe each level and what you should do.

Towers cost money to build. You need to think carefully about where to place each tower, so they will have the desired effect. Most monsters will leave behind coins and blue gems. Gems are needed to buy a new tower. But you must hurry to collect the coins and gems left behind. They WILL disappear on you if you're not fast enough. Sometimes you can find coins and gems through the trees.

The most difficult part of the game is figuring out which towers will kill which enemies. Each enemy is different and not all towers will do the same thing to every monster. For ex: Canon towers don't have any effect at all on flying monters. They don't even fire. Arrow towers are helpful, but still not good enough. You need an airgun tower, and alot of them if there are a lot of flying monsters.

There are four different colored flags you can upgrade your tower to: Blue, yellow, purple and black. You can upgrade each tower to its fullest, which is black and gold. The tower will have a black flag and a gold base. This is the most powerful. Blue is the weakest. You can use the blue gems to upgrade quicker. You need the correct amount to do so. Standing directly in front of a tower and dancing will slowly upgrade your tower, but it takes longer. It takes longer with each color.

This game is extremely addictive. You can become obsessed with trying to get 7 rainbows to get to the other side of the map.

title: Just another interactive novel...
text:
There's not much game play on your part at all. You just basically read what the screen shows and tap the A button constantly. This game is a cross between Unsolved Crimes and Hotel Dusk, both for the DS.

In Jake Hunter, you choose which actions you want to do, but after you do that, it's just more reading. I love reading and mysteries, but this game was a little TOO much reading. It felt like forever until the next action or scene.

During the game, you'll be asked to complete a list of questions that concern the case or reveal your answers to the suspects. If you get the reveal answers wrong, the suspect will look at you like you're crazy and tell you to think again.

Occasionally, you'll see the "think" option to the left. This is just to refresh the details of the case and you don't get a game over or anything if you get a question wrong. You just go back to the beginning of the "test."

Sometimes you can't leave a location until you've talked to someone a couple of times or looked around. If you get stuck, there is this cool hint system where Jake will smoke and think at the same time. It will give you an insight on what to do next. In some instances, you play as Jake's assistant, Yulia. In her hint system, she'll run her fingers thru her hair.

The graphics were decent. Actually, they were pretty cool for such a tiny game.

The music was the best feature, I thought. There were three or four different tracks that I remember. One of course, the evil, spooky music when some big details of the case surface when interviewing. The main track for Jake's office, which is upbeat and reminds me of the old school original nintendo games. (I miss the simpler times)

This game would be ok if there was a little more action involved on the player's part. A couple of things to mention: One: you can't die or get game over so you don't have to save that much. No matter which question, answer, or person you choose to interrogate, you cannot lose. Also be warned there are multiple spelling and grammar mistakes in this game. I know it sounds petty, but for a game, I think that's pretty important, to be able to spell and make the game understandable to the players.

Overrall, this game would be good to play on a rainy day.

title: Satechi® Edge Wireless Gaming Mouse 800 DPI, 1600 DPI , 2400 DPI , 4000 DPI with 500Hz Return Rate (Electronics)
text:
The Satechi Edge is a fantastic wireless mouse. As the price of a good wireless mouse is usually substantial, I was surprised by how much product I got for so little money. Compared to other mice I have used in the $20-25 range, this Satechi has superior precision, comfort, built quality, and versatility. Whether you are looking at this for wireless gaming or just for an all-around good wireless mouse, the Edge deserves your consideration.
---------------------------

MY NEEDS & WHY I PURCHASED THE SATECHI EDGE
I need a precision mouse for work-related activities when working documents at 4000%+ zoom where mice with high res’ make life much easier. Mac functionality and the ability to locally adjust DPI settings are huge pluses. Finally, I need a mouse that is comfortable to use for long periods and reduces fatigue. The Sentey Lumenata is the wired mouse I have come to use for my desk setup. This Satechi Edge is the mouse I use when running my computer through a TV or when on-the-go.

I have owned Logitech mice for over 15 years. In the past few years, I have become increasingly less pleased with their hardware quality and software support. While I have had many great Logitech experiences in the past, the high hardware costs, the poor OS X support, and the fact that there is a lot of competition has made it the time to move on to other brands.

Having owned this mouse for a few weeks, I can now say for sure that this was the right wireless mouse for me. It gives me mobility for situations where I need wireless functionality, but it still has plenty of performance capability.
---------------------------

THE DESIGN
The Satechi Edge is a mid-sized wireless mouse capable of variable resolution. It can function at 800, 1600, 2400, and 4000 DPI with a 500 Hz polling rate (that can be adjusted to 250 Hz.) Rather than using Bluetooth, this uses a micro receiver that operates at the 2.4 Ghz bandwidth. Using two AA batteries, this mouse works well with alkaline, but best with high-performance NiMH cells, such as the eneloop professional. The range is advertised as being 98-feet and max accel as 20Gs.

This mouse has seven buttons, and these buttons can be programmed for variable functions, using both 4 DPI profiles and a standard video-view profile. The DPI is selected using the color-coding. Unlike some other gaming mice, this means you can adjust the DPI directly on the mouse, and without having to use proprietary software (which often requires setting up an account, an active internet connection, and the installation of software on your machine…something which many users aren’t very fond of.) Using internal memory, the mouse remembers your last DPI setting when powered down. This mouse does NOT feature customizable X and Y axis resolution.

On the bottom of the mouse are two switches. On one side you have a slider that you can select off, on, and on with lighting. On the other side you can select a polling rate of 250, 500, or enter video view mode. This final mode defaults some commands for the purpose of media viewing.

On the thumb-side of the mouse, there are your back/forward buttons, along with a gaming button to the front-left where your pointer finger rests. On the top you have the scroll wheel and the DPI button. Pressing this button changes the color of the scroll wheel and lit logo, which corresponds to a change in DPI. The scroll wheel has a solid up-down clicky scrolling, but does NOT have horizontal scrolling capabilities. This mouse has a LED-lit scroll wheel, and the rear logo is also LED-lit.
---------------------------

WHAT I LIKE
This mouse has great ergonomics. It fits the average sized hand quite nicely, and the button positioning works well with the grip styles I use. The buttons themselves have very solid feedback (especially for a $25 mouse), and the rubberized side traction does a good job at improving grip with longer usage. Compared to a regular mouse, I find this design reduces my hand fatigue and wrist/finger pains.

The design of the USB micro receiver is also nice. Like Logitech, a micro receiver is now used. It is compact, easy to transport, harder to accidentally damage, and can be left plugged into a laptop even when on the go.

While this mouse has a power-saving firmware that is pretty aggressive, it is nowhere near as aggressive as the power save used by Razer in the Orochi, and unlike the Razer there is not a long wakeup delay because this mouse uses its own USB receiver rather than Bluetooth.

I also like how this mouse has given me flawless performance with Windows XP, Windows 7 U, Windows 8.1 Pro, OS X 10.8, and OS X 10.10. The mouse was plug-and-play on all of these devices, and the mouse control programs I already own allowed me to customize the unit’s settings.

I also really like how I can configure DPI settings without needing to use a company’s proprietary software. I do not want to have to set up a user account or require an internet connection to adjust settings. With this Edge, I don’t have to.
---------------------------

WHAT I DO NOT LIKE
The advertised range of 98 feet is a bit of an overstatement. In the best of conditions inside of a lab, this may work but not anywhere else. There are tons of 2.4 GHz signals just about everywhere, and some USB 3 connections can cause interference with some 2.4 GHz signals. This can cause a major drop in signal strength (and in some cases signal reliability.) I get about 10 feet of solid performance when I have positioned the USB receiver to point in the direction of the mouse. However, if I go much beyond that I will occasionally get ‘skips’.

If Satechi went to the 5.8 GHz bandwidth or added a port to the mouse so it could be used in a wired mode, I think that would make this product even better. If you are setting this up in an area with tons and tons of signals already flying by, you may have range issues. In some cases, this is easy to fix with a desktop setup buy purchasing a USB extension cable so that you can relocate the sensor closer to the mouse.
---------------------------

USING THIS MOUSE WITH OS X
If you just plug this mouse into a Mac, it will work but with limited functionality. The left and right click will work, as will the scroll. If you want to use the other buttons on this mouse, a mouse control program written for OS X is the easiest method I have found thus far.

So I am currently using this on OS X Yosemite with SteerMouse. This OS X mouse control software program is basic but reliable. It will allow you to customize the buttons, commands, speeds, acceleration, etc. It is a paid program, and some free programs of this type do exist.

---------------------------

CONCLUSION
Overall, I am very happy with how much product I got for the money. It was about $24 delivered to my door, and I like this mouse as much as other mice I own costing more than twice as much. Obviously, one limitation when gaming is the fact that it is wireless, and how the absolute best precision is almost always with a wired mouse. So the big question here is if one would prefer the wireless functionality over more advanced features, higher resolution, and potentially more consistent performance. While that is a personal call, if you decide to go the wireless route then I highly recommend considering the Satechi Edge.

This is a great mouse for both Windows and Mac users alike and having had such a great experience with it thus far, I highly recommend the Edge.

title: OUTSTANDING!! -- Precise, Versatile, Solid Build, Comfortable, Affordable, Works Great with OS X!
text:
[[VIDEOID:81fc746e896d652d27313403dc1cad6d]] The Sentey Lumenata Pro is a fantastic mouse that is not only great for gamers, but also great for anyone looking for a precision tool. Whether you are into gaming, graphic design, data visualization, architecture, or just want a really good mouse, the Lumenata Pro is probably a great match.
---------------------------

MY NEEDS & WHY I PURCHASED THE LUMENATA PRO
I need a precision mouse for work-related activities when working documents at 4000%+ zoom where mice with high res' make life much easier. I also need a mouse that can execute macros stored in the mouse's own memory, including when being used in OS X. Finally, I need a mouse that is comfortable to use for long periods and reduces fatigue. Subsequently, I cannot speak in detail on gaming specifics, but some of my experiences will likely still apply to your needs.

I have owned Logitech mice for over 15 years. In the past few years, I have become increasingly less pleased with their hardware quality and software support. OS X support could only be described as `abysmal' (I kid you not it took them 9 months to update their own software to work with 10.10, and during that time their mice did not function correctly or at all on Macs, yet they continued to sell their devices as "Mac-compatible".) So despite many great past experiences, it was time to move on.

So when shopping for a precision mouse, I more or less checked out gaming forums. Gamers need mice that are well made and functional. A mouse that works well for gamers will work well for my general needs. Browsing forms, I came across Sentey. Surprisingly, their products in the $25-35 range were rated as well as many mice costing twice that or more. So I chose the Lumenata Pro.

Having had time to use the mouse and customize it for my needs, I can now say that this was a really, really good purchase.
---------------------------

THE DESIGN
The Lumenata Pro is a mid-large sized mouse capable of providing a resolution ranging from 200 DP to 8200 DPI. This mouse has DPI presets as well as the ability to customize DPI settings for the X and Y axis individually in 200 DPI increments. While it is easiest to customize X and Y axis using Sentey's own software program, you can do this using buttons directly on the mouse itself.

Technically this mouse has 13 functions. The buttons/functions are as follows: (all can be customized except the left click)
-left/right click
-scroll up/down; scroll side/side
-scroll click
-forward/back buttons on thumb side
-programmable gaming buttons (2) front opposite side
-mode toggle on top/center
-FS button on top/center to change DPI
-DPI preset toggle, bottom thumb size

This right-hand mouse has strong side contours and a soft rubberized surface to improve ergos and give you the best grip. The Teflon coated feet allow this mouse to glide smoothly (especially when paired with a good gaming mat.) The braided USB cable is more durable than a standard rubber coated cord. Size-wise, I have average sized hands and this mouse is perfect for me.

The center LED has a toggle switch to change the color of the light. Each color represents an individual profile that the user can customize to their needs. If you play different games or programs and need different mouse settings for this, you can set up different profiles and toggle to the different settings as needed. Once programmed, you do NOT need to be connected to the internet or Sentey's program to change these settings as they are stored on the mouse itself and can be toggled using the `M' button.
---------------------------

WHAT I LIKE
Beyond everything else, this mouse is precise. On both OS X and Windows 8.1, it works flawlessly. When working documents that are a few thousand zoom, the ability to dial back the settings for precision is great. The ability to make my X axis faster than my Y is great because it makes me more precise. The rubber coating gives great traction even if your hand starts to sweat from prolonged usage, and the ergos reduce fatigue. The heavy duty braided USB cord is still flexible enough to avoid being obtrusive, and the USB connection is USB 2, an advantage since USB 3 can interfere with 2.4 GHz signals in some instances.

I also like how this mouse did not come with any accessories that I will never use but pay more because they are there. Cases are nice, but I would prefer to buy a mouse without these extras and save a few bucks. So I really like how Sentey offers one version of the Lumenata without anything other than the mouse/paperwork/CD.

I have called Sentey a few times to ask specific questions. I have actually spoken not to general customer service reps, but the product designers who engineer the hardware. I am guessing they are a smaller company as this is a rarity these days, but it is really nice because I get direct, true, and up-to-date info. (For example, they told me how Sentey is now working on a program that allows their mice to be controlled via a smartphone or tablet.) This to me is really nice because I am using this mouse frequently with OS X and am experimenting with ways to make this mouse work best with OS X, and now I can literally pick up the phone, chat with an engineer, and discuss my ideas...and because of this I have gotten this mouse to have 100% functionality with OS X Yosemite!
---------------------------

WHAT I DO NOT LIKE
I have virtually no dislikes here. With that said, it should be noted that due to the use of the soft rubber finish, the mouse DOES easily show fingerprint and oil markings. title: ~~FANTASTIC Keyboard~~ Well made, affordable, versatile, easy-to-read, great feedback, & perfect LED intensity to improve vision
text:
This Azio Levetron is an awesome keyboard. Well made, affordable, and versatile, this keyboard is a good fit for many different tasks/needs.

I do want to note on two things:
1) I am not a gamer so I cannot say exactly how well this keyboard works if purchased solely for the purpose of gaming. I purchased this keyboard for work and home usage. I did so because I like LED backlit keys as well as the feedback gaming keyboards provide.
2) I have only used this keyboard for a short period, and so I cannot speak to long-term reliability. I will update this review down the road to report back on how the keyboard holds up.
------------------------

MY NEEDS & USAGE
I recently purchased a Dell IPS display so that I can run it as a secondary monitor next to my 15-inch MacBook Pro Retina, as this allows me to run Windows 8.1 via a virtual machine on the display, and OS X Yosemite on the MacBook’s display. As I use software that runs better on one OS over the other, this allows me to run whatever software does best in what OS. It also gives me easy access to legacy OS’ if I need to test something like code.

I have apple’s wireless keyboard and think it is excellent. However, it favors mobility over performance. I find gaming keyboards tend to do the opposite…they are built for heavier usage, heavily favor accessibility and performance, and use features that make this possible (I own an unusually large amount of gaming gear.)
------------------------

DESCRIPTION: THIS KEYBOARD
This keyboard is the Azio Levetron L70, a wired, entry-level gaming keyboard that is LED backlit via blue colored LEDs. You can toggle these LEDs on and off, but you cannot change the color or the intensity.

The layout of this keyboard is pretty standard, plus it has a massive volume knob and a switch dedicated specifically to turning the LEDs on and off. Each side of the keyboard has an LED light. The keys themselves used oversized letters, and these markings are clear so the LED light can shine through. A removable palm rest is included and the cord length is about 5 feet. The bottom features non-skid, non-marking rubber feet as well as retractable feet to increase the angle.

I have used this keyboard with: OS X 10.10 Yosemite, OS X 10.8 Mountain Lion, OS X 10.7 Lion, Windows XP SP3, and Windows 8.1 (current build as of 2015.) They keyboard works reliably on all of these, but note that this is technically a Windows keyboard and so with OS X you may want to use a keyboard control suite to modify some of the commands.

The interface used is USB and it works on both USB 2 and USB 3 computers (can’t speak to USB 1.1 as I do not have computers that old anymore.) It does NOT seem to generate the harmonic distortion that some USB 3 devices can which can result in interference with 2.4 GHz signals.
------------------------

WHAT I LIKE
The light intensity is perfect…bright enough to see when lights are on, but not so bright that it is an annoyance in darker environments. Another LED backlit keyboard I had was so faint that the LEDs did not really increase visibility.

The lettering used is very large, making it easier to see and making it better display with the LEDs. If someone has trouble seeing most keys, this is an outstanding choice.

Typing itself is comfortable, and I find the palm rest makes typing even more comfortable. Like many other gaming keyboards, you get more pronounced feedback than the standard free keyboard that comes with desktops. I strongly prefer this feedback when typing as I find I can type faster and with fewer errors. Also like many other gaming keyboards, I find that the physical force required to push a key and have it register is very, very consistent. With keyboard without this consistency, it is easy to subconsciously start pressing certain keys with more force than others, and this can result in more mistakes while typing (least for me anyway.)

The cosmetic fit and finish of this keyboard is outstanding for the price. The numbers are neat, the patterns are sharp, there are no sharp spots from molding overspray, and the keyboard wire is quite beefy.

So while I cannot speak directly to how well this works for gaming, I can say it is a great keyboard for general usage. It is also great for data visualization, which I suppose in some ways has similarities to gaming needs.
------------------------

WHAT I DO NOT LIKE
At this price, I have zero dislikes with this keyboard.
------------------------

CONCLUSION
Overall, this is a whole lot of keyboard for 20-25 bucks. It’s well made, it has fantastic visibility, it gives a very consistent typing experience, and its LEDs are perfectly balanced in intensity so that they contribute to better performance (rather than detracting from.)

-The red logo at the top. I mean, kind of a silly complaint but they could have just as easily made it backlit as well. They did on their mouse and it look amazing!

Conclusion:
If you just want a cheap RGB/backlit key board on a budget of less than $30, go ahead and get this. I do not think you will regret it.
If your budget is higher, then obviously you should just get a better overall keyboard. I don't think I will miss this one when I eventually do.

title: Almost perfect - 9/10
text:
The controller feels fantastic in your hands. This is especially apparent after trying to use the tiny joycons with their even tinier buttons and joysticks. If your an adult with moderate to large hands you need this controller. Playing games like Resident Evil 5 or Doom feel worlds better with a controller that is designed for hands larger than a 10 year old's. Using the controller mount for the joycons is not a substitute for a pro controller. After using the pro controller, you realize that the joycon's tiny buttons, joysticks, and shoulder buttons are things you tolerate. Even if you decide against buying this controller (most likely due to the price), buy a cheaper third party traditional controller. Comfort - 10/10

The buttons are large, which I love, reminding more of the larger buttons seen on the original SNES controller. The buttons along with the D-pad have a matte finish that feel great. A special mention of the D-pad must be made. This D-pad feels fantastic. Compared to the 8bitdo SN30 pro, it is NO CONTEST. The D-pad for Nintendo's pro controller is top of the line and blows the third party D-pads out of the water. The Joysticks feel good, maybe even great. They have raised edges with ridges for increased grip which feel good on your thumbs. I still prefer the concave shape of the Xbox One joysticks but the switch pro controller joysticks are comfortable, responsive, and accurate. Compared to the Wii U pro controller, the joysticks feel less sturdy though. The Wii U pro controller feel sturdy and require more effort to move them, which I like. This is not a big deal but I feel some may not like joysticks that have less resistance. Buttons and Joysticks - 9/10

When it come to the value, the switch pro controller is a sea of grey. It really depends on the value you place on each individual feature found in the pro controller. The third party enhanced switch controllers are around 20$ cheaper and feel close to the same but lack many of the features the pro controller has (it doesn't even have basic rumble). You can also find even cheaper controllers that don't have even the most basic features of a pro controller but are still fine controllers if all your looking for is a comfortable gaming experience for your hands. I like the HD rumble and motion controls and would like to have the convenience of amiibo support (even though I don't really see it lasting much longer) so I don't mind paying the 70$. Nintendo's controllers are also known for lasting forever, so you most likely won't need to buy another one for the rest of your life (I still use the gamecube and Wii U pro controllers I got at the launches). Overall Value - 8/10

title: OK , but disapoints as follow up to ME2
text:
As games go, Mass Effect is just OK. Unfortunately as great as Mass Effect 2 this a huge disappointment. Really all EA had to do was take the mechanics they had created in the previous game, carry them over without screwing them up and put all of their effort into writing an amazing and emotionally satisfying story that makes everyone happy with their three game ride. Unfortunately they failed on all accounts. The game play mechanics for combat in ME3 verges on broken since the cover system that everything hinges on is so frustrating. The roll option they added to the X button along with it being storm and crouch behind cover was horrible. It NEVER does the option you want out of the three. Real fun watching as Shepard does a little shoulder role and stands up to be blasted when you desperately need to hide.
The story also poor. Very forced and disjointed. Vignettes thrown together to give previous characters cameos with no depth to it. The end is just pathetic- why spend three games getting people emotionally invested in characters just to have none of it matter and all be unresolved. Treating a game like it is an student art film shows a real lack of understanding of story telling. OK, you don't have to give the players everything they want and tie up a nice happy ending in bow for us but at least you have to give a reason to feel that the hours invested meant something and come to resolution. I can't believe that no one at EA as they writing this didn't stand up and say "Hey guys isn't this crappy ending kind of like giving our customers the finger for buying three of our games"?

title: What if...?
text:
Many of us do not have the opportunity to see the fruits of our "What if questions..." Those are the types of questions that arise during those contemplative times where we wonder about the decisions we've made and the trajectory those same decisions have set us on. Wes Moore, by the strange coincidence of learning about a wanted man who shared his name shares his answers to many of those what if questions in his book, The Other Wes Moore.

Wes Moore sheds light on those things that defined the type of place he and the other Wes Moore grew up in. Things such as family, community, respect and manhood. There are decisions that are made which are out of both of the lives of these men who share a name that also help them to define the norms of their world. Those decisions, their environments, their own decisions and the people around them ultimately help them to lead lives that are at ultimate odds with one becoming a Rhodes Scholar and what many might deem a model citizen while the other is a high school dropout living the rest of his life in jail. This, as you'll find, is no spoiler.

The Other Wes Moore should cause the reader to step back and question his or her own assumptions about socioeconomic conditions and the role of community and family in the development of young people. Both of these young men came from families who wanted them to succeed - to be more than what the world expected them to be. The Other Wes Moore is a wonderfully written story, communicated clearly, which portrays lives that are borne out of similar contexts whose subtleties are more than footnotes in the mental and emotional formations of both Wes's. Was it what some would identify as "luck," that got one Wes Moore into Johns Hopkins and the other in Jessup? What part do resources (financial and familial) play? Are there any clear advantages that one had over the other?

This is a book that was hard for me to put down. I'm guessing that it's a book that will be hard for me to forget. It will leave you asking what sort of legacy you yourself will leave as opposed to asking, "What if...?"

title: A system seller for those that like action games
text:
For fans of action games, and those looking for a game that makes you feel like a legitimate BAMF and that you deserved being that BAMF, then this is it. Being that this is my first experience with a FROMSOFT title, I would recommend that anyone that thinks that they wont like the souls games to try this one out. Bloodborne is a completely different universe than the Souls games, and the gameplay is very different. Bloodborne emphasizes aggression and dodging, where Souls games are much more methodical and defensive. I tried DS3 after playing through most of Bloodborne since I loved Bloodborne so much, but I just cannot seem to enjoy or play DS3 well at all.

To those that are willing to join the hunt and it is your first time with a FROMSOFT game, then my advice is, there is a certain mindset you need to play effectively as a hunter, you wont have it at first, but over time, you will gain it. Dying is a natural thing in this game, and if you havent died at least 20 times in your first playthrough, then you must be a god of some sort. Look at your deaths as learning experiences, what did you do wrong that caused you to die? Often, its just that you completely underestimated an enemy, or you drew way too much aggro from multiple enemies, effectively "biting off more than you can chew.

There will be times where you hit a wall, just explore elsewhere, grind some more levels and items, or just take a break and come back to it later. Just remember, the more angry or annoyed you are, the worse you tend to play.

My personal opinion is that Bloodborne is one of the best games Ive played, and is a definite system seller. The game tends to guide you in the beginning, The first boss that most people meet is challenging for a newbie, but can be beaten within a few tries... the problem is the first required boss, Father Gascoigne, he is a brick wall that most people hit. He can only really be truly beat by just getting better at the game and understanding the kind of gameplay that the game promotes, being aggressive, getting in the face of most enemies, balancing dodging with attacks while keeping a close eye on the enemy and their movements.

PS+ isnt really necessary to get the full experience of the game, it adds an extra level, but the full story and the lore have no connection to the multiplayer aspect of the game.

title: K580 vs K556
text:
I like Redragon products. I bought 2 K556, an S101 M101 keyboard/mouse combo, and the H301 headset. I chose the K580 keyboard because its not something I needed but felt I could offer valuable feedback on it in a comparison with the other keyboard I have and have been using.

I will start by saying that between the two, you can't really go wrong. It just depends on what you need and how you need the keyboard to function. There are a few things about each keyboard that are quirky and I would change but really, its not that big of a deal.

Essentially, these keyboards do the same things but do them differently. For instance, the K556 controls volume by pressing FN and F2 or F3, similarly the K580 presses FN and scrolls the wheel up or down. still a 2 handed process... not much difference between the two. the K580 does have stand alone media play features next to the wheel, no secondary button needed.

The K556 and K580 both have the ability to program and store macros. the K580 makes them a bit easier to access with the G buttons at the top of the keyboard. If you use Macros, this is a nice feature to have. The K556 also has macro capabilities, but I believe that they are 2 button dependent.

As said there isn't much difference in these keyboards function. I like them both a great deal. There are a few things I should mention. "quirks" unique to each one.

They are both very solid feeling. The K580 is a *bit* lighter than the K556. The K556 feels more planted on my desk. It takes a slight bit more effort to move. I like that a bit more than the K580. Not a big deal though.

The software between the two keyboards is different. The K556 has a lot more function than the K580. The K556 has individually programmable key colors which, if you game... is really nice. I have my K556 keys color sorted for the games I play and it helps find them faster. if you need to hit V hitting C isn't helpful. Marking V as its own color, improves accuracy. The K580 and all gaming keyboards, need this function.

The K580 has a better font and for whatever reason "key feel" than the K556. The font is a little larger and printed a bit more clearly which is REALLY nice. A small detail, but its very pleasing. Also the blue switches in the K580 are very nice. Switches can be changed pretty easily. I would rather the K556 have blue switches. After using the K580, I may buy new switches for the K556 to bring it up to K580 typing feel. Of course this is subjective, between the two my personal preference is clearly blue. Once I got used to the mechanical style keys and the shape/size/layout of the keyboard creative writing/typing is very nice.

They share a similar size. I chose the K556 originally because I wanted a small footprint on my desk. The K580 stays in that same minimalist theme.

Both of these have their strong points and both of them have their own quirks and features. If it were up to me they would only share more of the software features and leave each keyboard to its own "personality". If the K580 had the individual key color assignment, it would be pretty well perfect.

I hope this helps someone make a choice in a decision between the two. I know I struggled with finding the right keyboard and nearly all reviews were not telling me what I wanted to know. Possibly because most people do not have both available to compare against each other.

title: Pure Bliss For An Intimidated Noob
text:
My 10 year old son and 39 year old self are having a blast with this game. Neither of us has ever played a "real" guitar before. We have played guitar hero, but there is just one strum bar and five buttons for frets on those guitars. For Rocksmith we have a 6 string guitar with 22 frets. That was (and still is) extremely intimidating to us.

First thing I had to do was tune my guitar. Rocksmith walked me through it and checked the tones for me (good thing for a tone deaf guy). The cool thing (for me at least) was that the software knew the problem before I did. If I hit the wrong string, it knew and told me to check which string I hit.

So I went through about 5 tutorials and tried to 100% them. The tutorials are excellent. It starts easy...if you can't get it, then it slows it down to get you used to moving across the frets and strings in time. For a noob like me, this was great. The game amazed me when it told me exactly what I was doing wrong in the tutorials (ie: wrong string, wrong fret...it knew). After you get through the first test, it does the same riff with more notes and complexities. It allowed me to practice and have a sense of success before it upped the level.

You can choose to play lead guitar, rhythm, or bass. You can use your electric guitar for bass, but I have not tried yet. I have only tried lead guitar so far but plan on trying the others.

There are 20 or so more lessons to do, but I was interested in trying a song (knowing I would fail). Low and behold, they actually up the level of play on each song as you improve. So the first time through the easier songs was not impossible even for me to achieve some success. I felt like "I can actually do this with some practice".

The part I recently tried was the guitarcade which is awesome. Retro style arcade games that work on your guitar technique. The first game is similar to jet pack joyride, but based solely on how loud you strum the strings and control the volume. The next game is like the old Root Beer Tapper game but you have to hit the right string to "shoot" down the right area. title: Pure bliss for an intimidated noob
text:
My 10 year old son and 39 year old self are having a blast with this game. Neither of us has ever played a "real" guitar before. We have played guitar hero, but there is just one strum bar and five buttons for frets on those guitars. For Rocksmith we have a 6 string guitar with 22 frets. That was (and still is) extremely intimidating to us.

First thing I had to do was tune my guitar. Rocksmith walked me through it and checked the tones for me (good thing for a tone deaf guy). The cool thing (for me at least) was that the software knew the problem before I did. If I hit the wrong string, it knew and told me to check which string I hit.

So I went through about 5 tutorials and tried to 100% them. The tutorials are excellent. It starts easy...if you can't get it, then it slows it down to get you used to moving across the frets and strings in time. For a noob like me, this was great. The game amazed me when it told me exactly what I was doing wrong in the tutorials (ie: wrong string, wrong fret...it knew). After you get through the first test, it does the same riff with more notes and complexities. It allowed me to practice and have a sense of success before it upped the level.

You can choose to play lead guitar, rhythm, or bass. You can use your electric guitar for bass, but I have not tried yet. I have only tried lead guitar so far but plan on trying the others.

There are 20 or so more lessons to do, but I was interested in trying a song (knowing I would fail). Low and behold, they actually up the level of play on each song as you improve. So the first time through the easier songs was not impossible even for me to achieve some success. I felt like "I can actually do this with some practice".

The part I recently tried was the guitarcade which is awesome. Retro style arcade games that work on your guitar technique. The first game is similar to jet pack joyride, but based solely on how loud you strum the strings and control the volume. The next game is like the old Root Beer Tapper game but you have to hit the right string to "shoot" down the right area. I had trouble with volume and finding strings and these were fantastic ways to practice. It includes high scores, mini achievements, and online rankings. I also tried the slide arcade and a duck shooting game that helps practice slides, frets and strings. There are many more arcade games that I have not tried because I don't know the concept (ie: bending) yet. Some games are more fun than others, but the fun and rewarding way to practice is top notch.

The main thing this does not do is teach you to play guitar by reading sheet music. That was not important to me, but worth noting.

We try and limit video game play for our kids, but this game is so educational that we bend the rules and let our kids play Rocksmith at times when they normally are not allowed to play games.

I highly recommend this game for anyone who wants to learn to play a real guitar for fun. It provides learning, fun, and a sense of accomplishment. It will provide our family many hours of fun time together.

title: One headset for all your gaming needs
text:
I own PS3 wireless headset (very nice but PS3 only), a cheap wireless headset (RCA connection with no mic) (adequate), Sony headphones (nice but simple headphones), Pioneer headphones (Junk), Logitech headset (Nice but heavier and PC only).

As you can see, I have a number of headsets but none of them can be used for all my gaming needs.

This is the most comfortable headset I own.

Nice packaging.

The cord is nice and long for normal playing sessions...not long enough for me to play in bed, which is when I play the most...atleast until I get an extension.

The instructions are short and easy to follow.

Chat with sound setup
PX22 headset --> wired amplifier (3.5 mm) --> converter wires if needed --> your console/PC

Sound without chat setup
PX22 headset (3.5 mm) --> converter wires if needed --> device

NOTE: The USB plug is used to power the amp and chat. It does not send game audio (music/sound fx) to the headset. You have to plug the amp into your gaming console with the headphone jack. This can be tricky (ie: if you use HDMI for PS3, then you have to set it up for multiple sound outputs and connect the old scart cable with RCA outputs), but the instructions are easy to follow and work. The main problem with this is that you have to change your setup every time you switch consoles. Depending on your television and/or reciever, you may be able to set this up with so that you don't have to change it every time you switch.

The RCA splitter cable should allow you to connect this to your TV output or your Wii/PS2/original XBOX/DVD/ etc. They included wires for just about every standard audio input you might need.

You can unplug the headset from the amplifier and plug them into your phone/tablet/etc for audio only (no chat).

The sound quality is excellent for my needs. These are stereo headphones, so do not expect surround sound.

There is a nifty spot to plug your phone into the PX22 remote box so that you don't have to take the headphones off when you get a call. Just plug the phone in...play your game, when you get a call accept it and move the remote switch to phone and boom. It's a pretty nice feature.

The biggest negative for me is that it's wired...I much prefer wireless (although batteries can be an issue if you have an extended gaming session). If this headset were wireless, it would replace all of my gaming headsets.

In conclusion, I think this headset is perfect for anyone who likes multi-player gaming on multiple systems. The price is excellent for the quality.

If you have any questions, please post in the comments.

title: 4.5 stars for the keyboard plus great support experience makes for 5 stars
text:
This is a great gaming keyboard. I use it with a G700 gaming mouse and love the combination.

I love the button lighting options. There are 5 brightness levels for two different sets of keys. You can dim or brighten the w,a,s,d, up arrow, left arrow, right arrow, down arrow keys separately from all the rest of the keys. I usually keep the w,a,s,d, up arrow, left arrow, right arrow, down arrow buttons on the brightest setting and all the rest of the keys on the 2nd lowest setting. It makes it easy to find the movement keys in the dark.

NOTE: When playing games and focusing on the screen, I do sometimes notice a subtle flickering in my peripheral vision coming from the keyboard. The best way I can describe it is like an interlaced image or viewing the LCD on a camcorder that is watching a monitor/television. It's seldom and maybe my eyes failing me :) It is annoying for a split second and seldom enough that it does not bother me.

There is a volume wheel (instead of two separate keys) which is nice.

NOTE: I have a problem where the volume wheel will lag (2-10 seconds) the first time you roll it up or down. After you "warm it up", the volume control is very responsive. It is annoying, BUT I am giving the benefit of the doubt to Logitech (since no other reviews mention this) and I believe it is due to some Windows setting that I need to figure out.

G1-G5 Keys are awesome. You have 6 programmable G-keys and 3 profile M-keys that allow you to create up to 18 custom keystrokes for those 6 keys for each game or application you use. I have yet to find a function/macro that I couldn't program into these keys. And you

My only complaint about the G-keys is their placement. These 6 keys are placed in a column at the far left of the keyboard. I use the Escape and Control key a lot and my hands automatically search for them at the bottom left and top left corners of the keyboard. I can't tell you how many times I hit the G1 key instead of escape and the G6 key instead of control. I resolved this problem by programming the G1 key as a second Esc key and the G6 key ass a second (really 3rd) Ctrl key. This works, but takes away two of my programmable key slots...this has not been a problem yet as I have not created a profile to use all 18 programmable key slots, but the potential is there. If I had a choice, I would prefer the M-Profile keys (above the F-keys) be offset to the right allowing the G-keys to be placed above the F1-F5/6 keys.

The pass-through USB is nice if you use a USB memory stick or USB headset. The only problem I have is the placement. It is placed on the behind the keyboard. My keyboard is on a wide keyboard drawer, so placing the USB port on the side would have been more ideal for me. It's not a big deal since I rarely use memory sticks and have a wireless headset, but worth mentioning.

Using the pass-through USB is optional, so if you have all of your USB ports filled (as I did) then you can leave the pass-through cable unplugged.

Received my first keyboard and the row of lights on the F,G,H,J,K,L,;,' keys went out after the first week. I contacted support and went through their friendly tech support. They offered to replace the keyboard. They paid for a shipping label back and I sent it off. I was surprised when I received the replacement keyboard before they received the defective one. I expected to be without a keyboard for 1-2 weeks and am very appreciative of companies with support like this. Logitech gets extra points for their friendly and quick support. After several months, I am happy to say that I have had no problems with the lights on the 2nd keyboard.

In conclusion, this is a fantastic keyboard. I use it for gaming and software development. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys gaming and wants a high quality keyboard.

title: A Ton of Wasted Potential
text:
First of all, most comparisons will be to Prof Layton games. While that is a fair comparison, this game is really a hodge podge of genres...all of which I like, but doesn't work in the simplified format they provide in this game.

Prof. Layton-ish - Yes, this game has puzzles like Layton but it really has 5-10 different types of puzzles (Sequence, tangem, fill in the word, push blocks, find the difference, etc) that get re-used over and over. If you are looking for a Professor Layton clone for the 3DS, I think you will be disappointed.

JRPG-ish - You collect spirits to battle the boss spirit at the end of each dungeon. The spirits level up with each successful usage. These battles are okay, but far from good. Portrait conversations and people spread across town to talk to.

Zelda Adventure-ish - Go into a dungeon, sneak past some guards, push boxes to complete a path to get further in, with only a single boss battle.

The story and characters are done fairly well. They even have plenty of side quests which add more depth to the main characters and sub-plots. The voice acting and art style work well.

I like the detail they gave to the city. They filled it with plenty of locations and people, but in the end it's really empty. The people say mostly useless things like "I love Paris" and the locations are simply used to go underground.

There are supposed to be 250 puzzles, but they are really just the same puzzles re-hashed. You have to roam around the city to random points marked on the map to see if you have found the next dungeon or not. There is usually a sheepish riddle that can help you figure where you might go next. Then in the dungeons you wander around sneaking past guards and pushing boxes to get further into the dungeon. There are a couple of doors where you have to solve a puzzle to get past. And finally you battle the dungeon boss with leveled up spirits (basically one time attack cards).

In the end, I was very disappointed. I was mostly interested in this for the puzzles and this is definitely no competition to Professor Layton. The concept they put together is interesting but feels like you are doing busy work just to get to the next puzzle/story.

I would not recommend this game.

title: Fun and disappointing at the same time
text:
I'm a 37 year old male who grew up with and enjoy Super Mario games.

I finished Super Mario 3D Land, including the regular levels and all of the Special levels and got all the medallions in each level in around 17 hours. I also got all the post cards. 17 hours isn't bad value in my opinion. My biggest disappointment was that there were only a handful of levels that were truly challenging and it was only because I wanted to get the 3 medallions in them. The difficulty is way off of the normal mario games. Don't get me wrong, I like that it's accessible enough for all ages to complete...it's just that I think that completing all the side goals should be more challenging.

One nice thing that adds replay-ability is that every level keeps track of the fastest time it was finished. Even if you have beaten everything like I did, you can always go back and try to beat the level in record time. I might do this some, but I'm more of the type of player that likes to explore and find everything (like the medallions). If you are getting this game for a 7-12 year old, it is more than worth the price and will keep them occupied for awhile. If you are a Mario fan like me, you will have fun and hold onto the game to make another run through it maybe a year later. I did enjoyed this game, but New Super Mario Bros on the DS was better overall in my opinion. I still haven't completed everything in that game after 2 years.

Now that the designers have experience designing levels for the new game, I think they'll make a much superior Super Mario 3D Land 2 that won't disappoint at all.

title: I Waited Too Long To Get These!
text:
I bought the DSi XL Hand Grip by the same company who makes this one. I was extremely disappointed with those grips (see my review there) and was afraid to purchase another grip from the same company. After reading the reviews and seeing the marketing manager comment in the reviews I decided to give them another chance and I am glad I did.

I have slightly large hands which feel cramped while playing the 3DS without grips. This grip feels nearly perfect. It is perfectly balanced in my hands while sitting in a chair AND comfortable while when playing in bed on my side. I can easily reach and use all buttons (ie: R & L) without any interference from the grips.

It holds the 3DS very secure. I have no fear of it falling out.

The stand is useful and will likely become more useful. I use the stand while playing (non-3D) games with my wife (like Professor Layton). Netflix is supposed to be available on the 3DS eventually and the stand will be great for that (ie: when the adults are using the television and the kids want to watch something on Netflix). The stand also has a slot for an additional SD card.

You can easily switch games, access the stylus, input/remove charging cord (not docked), change volume, turn wireless on/off, and connect your headphones (huge one for me) while the 3DS is secured in the grips.

The only item these grips block is access to the SD card. You will have to remove the 3DS from the grips if you switch out SD cards. I don't think this will be an issue for me, but if you take tons of pictures or have your music library on a card then it could be a pain.

The only thing that would put this grip even more over the top would be incorporating a rechargeable battery into the grips. I have Nyko PSP grips that do this and it is wonderful to have that extra juice. This would add weight to the grips and the price would probably double or triple though.

For under 10 bucks, these grips are perfect and I highly recommend them.

title: Best Wireless Mouse I Have Used
text:
I have been using this mouse for 5-6 months at home.

The battery life is great. I can go about 5 days without needing to charge it. NOTE: I don't play fps so I don't need the higher end resolution/sensitivity so that may allow me to get more wireless time out of my mouse. I use the mouse about 3 hours per day on average.

Speaking of batteries, the G700 was designed to use one AA. It came with an Sanyo Eneloop 2,000 mAh battery. I have yet to replace it and still get excellent charges from it. The fact that I can easily replace the battery without having to go through the hassle and increased expense of buying an uncommon rechargeable battery is wonderful.

When the battery does run out or if I just want to keep the charge topped off, I simply plug in the wired connection that plugs into my USB port in the back of my computer. The mouse is able to be used while charging, so I can minimize downtime and don't have to go searching for another battery in the middle of something important...like checking my email :)

This mouse has 13 programmable buttons (including macros), which is wonderful for playing games and for regular applications. There are 5 profiles, so you can program the buttons differently for different games/applications.

I have a several devices that connect to my network nearby and have yet to notice any lag or disconnect. wireless N card in my computer, a Roku XD|S box, and wireless networking in my television. I also have a wireless receiver/controller for my old Xbox and another for my PS2. I almost always have my iPhone with me while I am working on the computer. I have the G930 wireless headset that I use while playing PS2/Xbox/PC games in this room. Plenty of possibilities for interference, but none has occurred. I simply use the micro USB receiver in the back of my computer which is close to floor.

If you like a mouse with some weight to it, this one is perfect. I have had far too many mice that feel cheap and have no weight/resistance. This mouse feels solid and provides a comfortable amount of resistance for my liking.

I strongly recommend using a mouse pad. I have a white desk and have gotten some black coloring from the mouse on the desk from constant the rubbing. Luckily, the black markings come off with a bit of pressure and the desk if fine.

I wish the mouse utilized the common USB connection that most of my USB accessories use, but I do appreciate that uses the same charging connection as my G930 headset!

I would recommend this mouse to anyone (gamer or not).

title: Worthy Addition to Dragon Quest
text:
I have played all the Dragon Warrior / Quests except II, III, and VI. IV and VIII were my favorites of the ones I did play.

This is an excellent rpg for the DS. The music is wonderful. The graphics are excellent for a DS (played mine on the DS XL). The story concept is original and good. The story implementation is decent for a jrpg but I expect better from square enix/level 5. It contains excellent leveling and character customizations that one would expect from a good jrpg from Square Enix / Level 5. It does not compare to DQ VIII due to the DS limitations but it does add some nice changes (side quests, multiplayer, custom character look, paper doll, and treasure maps).

My favorite new addition were the treasure maps. You had to use clues from the map to find a dungeon and then traverse the dungeon and defeat a boss. You don't have to do these dungeons unless you want to, although they help for grinding.

It takes about 40-50 hours to complete the main quest. You can take longer to do the additional side quests, treasure maps, alchemy completion, and monster completions.

Issues that keep this from being 5 stars for me.

No wi-fi (for multiplayer nor tag mode). This game was created for multiplayer, but only with friends that are in the same room. Since this game has turn-based battles, it just makes sense that wi-fi is easily possible and would do wonders for multiplayer needs.

Tag mode is also a semi-multiplayer option, but is rendered useless since it depends on passing by a random person, who happens to own DQ IX and happens to have their DS in their pocket which happens to be setup for DQ IX tag mode...yeah...it's not happening.

Party members have zero personality. They add nothing to the story and you have no attachment to them. They never speak...have no back-story...etc. This is not mandatory in a rpg, but it makes a big difference to me (ie: FF VI, DQ VIII, Dragon Age Origins being among my favorites).

I didn't care for the side quest system. Side quests are placed around the world and can be difficult to find. You have to talk to a certain NPC and they'll give you a quest. There are plenty of side quests that I didn't see because I didn't talk to the right people at the right time. You can only accept 10 side-quests at a time. If you have 10 active side quests and are offered another one, then you have to cancel an open side quest in order to accept the new one. If you complete a side quest, then it does not count toward your 10. I forgot where to go back upon completion of a few so I never accomplished them. This can be alleviated if you want to exit the DQ universe and look for hints or a walkthrough online (just not the way I like to play games).

Don't get me wrong. Overall, I had a good time with this game and would recommend it to any jrpg fan. I just don't think it's the best in the series and it had the potential to be the best handheld rpg ever.

title: Fun for Father and Son
text:
I am 36 years old. My son is 6 years old. We both play this and have a blast. I have played all the NES, SNES, N64, Gamecube, and Wii Mario games. This game utilizes everything from the earlier SMB games and adds some new things. It has levels that pay tribute to old levels (ie: 8-7 is different but reminiscent of 8-7 in the original SMB). There is even a level that has floors similar to the original Mario Bros arcade game. In my opinion, this is the best 2D Mario game out. The level design and fun factor in this game is off the charts. In fact, it inspired me to get some old classic handheld mario games...Super Mario Land 1,2, and 3 and the Wario Land games for the GB/GBC. I've heard great things about those and I'm looking forward to playing them.

In case anyone is wondering...this is a different game than New Super Mario Bros. for the Wii...they both contain completely different levels. The Wii version allows up to 4 players to play on the same Wii at the same time...it's a fun game, but I like this DS game better.

There are 3 save slots, so my son has his own save and I have my own. He loves the game but has trouble after world 3, so I have to help him through some of the more difficult parts. He loves the minigames and begs me to play them with him. If you have 2 DS systems and 1 cartridge, then you can play the minigames against each other which is fun. I can't say I love the minigames as much as he does, but they are fun, quick, and it makes him happy. I just finished the main game a few minutes ago and it was a blast from beginning to end.

Each world is easy enough for casual gamers to get through and there are 3 coins in each level to collect...collecting all these coins gives more challenge for the more advanced gamer. The game got more difficult around world 6, so I went back through the earlier worlds again to collect those coins and to build up my extra lives. Then I came back to finish the game. To complete the game, you only have to go through 6 of the 8 worlds...the other 2 worlds have to be unlocked somehow.

Now that I completed the game, I need to go back and collect all those coins and unlock the two worlds I haven't gotten to yet.

text:
Outstanding graphics. The characters are as detailed as I have seen. The settings are very well done. There were several times where the screen tearing was distracting.

I don't mind foul language if it adds to the story/setting and is not frequent, but this game goes overboard with the language and it takes away from the immersion that has been setup.

text:
My wife and I played this with our 5 year old son. It's easy enough for him to get through most levels to move the story along which is why it's fun for the casual gamer. I was ready to be finished with it by the halfway point, but we continued through the end for my son's sake. Luckily it wasn't too long to complete since we weren't trying to finish all the goals...it's great that the designers created it for casual and hard core gamers.

text:

My favorite part of the game was the skill system where you customize your characters abilities. There is a lot you can do to customize your party.

All in all, it was the perfect into for me into the series as I know Star Ocean 2 is a longer game. I will play through this one again.
